en: Oṃ, salutations to Sarasvatī.
The *Tīrthacintāmaṇi*. Oṃ, salutations to Rāmacandra.
The bee of his eyes is fixed upon the tips of Rādhā’s breasts, which rival the beauty of golden lotuses; he possesses the splendor of a smiling lotus-face,
and his body is dark like the tamāla tree of the new sky.
May Akrūra-mitra destroy my cruel karma.
Having carefully examined the *Śrī-Kṛtyakalpadruma*, the *Pārijāta*, the *Ratnākara*, and other such works,
and having bowed my head to Madhusūdana;
Vācaspati expounds the ritual for visiting sacred fords.
In that regard, the Mahābhārata states:
"The sages have proclaimed the sacrifices in the Vedas here in due order,
as well as their fruits in every respect, both after death and in this world, according to the truth."
O lord of the earth, sacrifices cannot be accomplished by a poor man;
for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
These are attained only by kings or by men who are prosperous; never by those deficient in wealth, by the lowly, by those who are solitary, or by those who are ununited.
O Yudhāṃvara, O lord of men, learn that which even those in poverty can attain,
which is equal to the meritorious fruits of sacrifices.
This supreme secret of the sages has been told by me to you:
the meritorious visiting of sacred fords excels even sacrifices.
Without fasting for three nights, without visiting sacred fords,
and without giving gold and cows, a man is born poor.
One does not obtain that fruit by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees which one obtains by visiting sacred fords.
Even he who performs such acts as pilgrimages here out of ignorance becomes enriched with all his desires and is glorified in the heavenly world.
He always obtains a dwelling place abounding in wealth and grain;
endowed with sovereignty and knowledge, he is forever possessed of enjoyment.
By him, his fathers and great-grandfathers have been delivered from hell.

"By those who are destitute" means by those lacking companions; "by those who are solitary" means by those lacking wives; "by those who are ununited" means by those lacking officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "without fasting"—the meaning is that the fruit of each [of these acts], namely the three-night fast, visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the gift of gold, and the gift of a cow, is the absence of poverty.
Likewise: "He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained..."
Through knowledge, austerity, and fame, one enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.

Restraint of the hand is the desisting from seizing the property of others. Restraint of the feet is the desisting from going to improper places. [3] Restraint of the mind is the desisting from base desires. Knowledge is the understanding of sacred sites (*tīrtha*), virtues, and so forth. Austerity (*tapas*) is characterized by dwelling at sacred sites, fasting, and the like. Fame is renown for one's virtuous conduct. Likewise: "One who has turned away from accepting gifts, who is content with whatever comes," and so on.
And being liberated from egoism, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
Free from deceit, without worldly undertakings, moderate in diet, with senses conquered,
and liberated from all attachments— he indeed enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.

Turning away from accepting gifts, however, occurs immediately after the journey, since it is mentioned only after the journey has already begun. "Free from guile" means devoid of deceit. "Without undertakings" means devoid of activities such as the acquisition of wealth. Regarding the phrase "from all attachments"—here, "attachment" refers to unenjoined attachment.
Likewise:
"And one who is free from anger, O Indra among kings, truthful, and firm in his vows."
And he who treats all beings as himself attains the fruit of the sacred ford.
"Like unto oneself" means one who is devoted to the welfare of all beings; thus says Śaṅkha:
"He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained..."
Through knowledge, austerity, and fame, one enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords.
However, this practice of restraining the hands and so forth is prescribed as the very commencement of the pilgrimage prior to bathing at the sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The wise man, full of faith and concentrated, while visiting the sacred fords..."
One who has committed evil would be purified; how much more so one who performs pure deeds?
He shall not go to the womb of an animal, nor is he born in an evil land;
indeed, the Brahmin becomes a dweller in heaven and finds the means to liberation.
One who lacks faith, one who is evil-minded, an atheist, one whose doubts are not severed, and one who relies solely on worldly reasoning— these five do not partake in the fruits of the sacred fords.
For one who is evil-minded and seized by many sins, there is only the pacification of sin at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), but not the aforementioned fruit. As it has been said:
"For men possessed of sin, there may be the pacification of sin at a sacred ford;
for men of pure soul, the sacred ford bestows the aforementioned fruit."

One whose doubts are unsevered is devoid of certainty regarding the goal, the means, and the procedure; being intent on fallacious reasoning, he subverts the scriptures. As stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"If one should enter a sacred ford after having conquered desire, anger, and greed, there would be nothing that could not be attained by him through that pilgrimage."
Those wise men who wander among the sacred fords according to the prescribed rule, enduring all pairs of opposites, go to heaven.
They endure all dualities and are patient with hardships such as cold and heat. In the *Brahma Purāṇa* it is said:
"Fish dwell at the bathing-places of the Gaṅgā, and flocks of birds reside in the temples."
Devoid of devotion, they do not obtain fruit from those holy fords or from the temples of the gods.
Then, having placed one's devotion within the lotus of the heart,
one should serve the sacred fords with a concentrated mind.

The pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā) which has been described by the lords of sages— whether performed, undertaken, or even merely approved— a celibate student (brahmacārī) performs that according to the prescribed rule.
Well-restrained and duly appointed by his teacher.
Whether upon the loss of all one's possessions, or even when one's own side has been defeated,
or even when one's entitlement to perform sacrifices has ceased— placing virtuous Brahmins at the very forefront.
A Brahmin, however, may wander among the sacred fords.
For it has been declared by the lords of sages of pure nature that the fruit of a sacred ford is indeed the fruit of a sacrifice for one who possesses the qualification for the *iṣṭi* sacrifices.
Better is the home and all the duties of a householder.
[6] Thus, for one established in the householder stage of life (*gṛhasthāśrama*),
going on pilgrimage has been prohibited by those of old; or rather, all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are [equivalent to] fire—
We say that they are certainly not equal to the office of the Hotṛ priest.

Regarding the passage beginning with "brahmacārī" (the religious student): the summary meaning is that both the religious student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) have the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to go on pilgrimage, whereas the one who maintains the sacred fire (*sāgni*) does not. Likewise, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Whoever should go on a pilgrimage, being well-restrained, must first [stay] in his own home."
Having observed a fast, pure and vigilant,
one should worship Gaṇeśa, bowing with devotion.
The wise man, having diligently gratified the gods, the ancestors, and virtuous brahmins according to his financial capacity,
returns once again in the very same manner.
And one should worship the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins.

For one who acts in this manner, the fruit described for visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth shall indeed be attained; there is no doubt in this matter. "Well-restrained" (*susaṃyata*) means having observed the rule of eating only one meal on the previous day and so forth. On the following day, having observed a fast, and on the day after that, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the planets, and one's chosen deity, and having performed the *pārvaṇa* rite, he should feed the Brahmins. This *pārvaṇa* rite should have clarified butter as its primary substance. Furthermore, when traveling to another country, whatever *śrāddha* he performs, he should do so with clarified butter.
It is declared that this applies for the purpose of departure, and there is no doubt that it also applies for entry.

[7] Thus, from the statement in the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa*. Now, some say it is an *ābhyudayika* (prosperity-rite); that is not so, because of the parsimony of application when it is presented as the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because no specific distinction is stated regarding the *pārvaṇa* rite which is already established. Gaṇeśvaramiśra and others also hold this view. Shaving of the head also occurs on the day of fasting, as well as at Prayāga, during a pilgrimage, or upon the death of one's father or mother.
One should perform the shaving of the hair; one should not remain shorn of hair without purpose.

This is according to the statement of Viṣṇu recorded in the *Smṛtisamuccaya*: "When one intends to go on a pilgrimage in the guise of a pilgrim (*kārpaṭī*), the shaving of the head (*vapanam*) comes first. This meaning is consistent with the fact that the departure occurs after the performance of the *śrāddha*.
Following that, one assumes the [pilgrim’s] attire. As it is said in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"If one is prepared to go to Gayā, having performed the *śrāddha* according to the prescribed rule..."
Having assumed the guise of a pilgrim and having performed a circumambulation of the village,
he then went to another village and partook of the remnants of a śrāddha feast.
Thereafter, one should go every day, avoiding the acceptance of gifts;
for one traveling to Gayā, there shall be the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step.

Although this practice of wearing the dress of a *kārpaṭika*—after worshipping Gaṇeśa, the planets, and one’s chosen deity—is heard of specifically in relation to Gayā as the fruit of the journey, it should nevertheless be observed for journeys to other sacred sites (*tīrtha*) as well, according to the maxim: "What is determined in one instance applies elsewhere. Furthermore, when a specific result is sought, since this [practice] is the very fruit of the journey, it is appropriate that it constitutes the fruit of the journey elsewhere too, because it is more intimately connected (*antaraṅga*). One should not, however, assume a different result elsewhere based on the *Viśvajit* maxim, because that is more remote (*bahiraṅga*) and thus involves a greater conceptual burden in its application. [8] A "different village" refers to a distance of no more than one *krośa*, because of the prohibition against traveling more than a *krośa* after performing a *śrāddha*, as stated in the rule: "And on a road, when a *krośa* has been completed," etc.
In the Matsya Purāṇa, there is a statement by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"O child, I shall describe to you the sequence of the procedure for pilgrimage,
according to the rite of the sages, exactly as it was seen and heard."
Listen also to the fruit of one who has mounted a bull:
he dwells in a terrible hell, for the wrath of cows is indeed dreadful;
moreover, the ancestors of that embodied being do not accept his water offerings.
If a man should go by vehicle due to the pride of having acquired power and wealth, that sacred site (tīrtha) is fruitless for him; therefore, he should avoid using a vehicle.
The *Kalpataru* states that this prohibition of vehicles refers only to the act of traveling [by them], because it is heard in the *Matsyapurāṇa* within that very context. And they recite:
"In a bullock-cart, it is declared to be the killing of a cow; in a horse-drawn vehicle, however, it is fruitless; in a human-drawn vehicle, it would be half of that; but by foot, it is fourfold."

Regarding the phrase "with the feet," there arises a superior fruit of pilgrimage (tīrtha-phala) distinct from [the mere wearing of] sandals and the like; however, there is no fault in wearing them, as no prohibition is heard. This is also the natural sense of the *Mitākṣarā* and other works.

As for the reading, "The sandal (pādukā) carries one upward," that is determined to be without authority because it is disregarded by all authors of legal digests (*nibandha*). And thus, when the prohibition of sandals is set aside—
In rain, heat, and similar conditions, one should go with an umbrella and a staff; and at night or in forests, desiring protection for the body, one should always go wearing sandals.

Thus, by the statement from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and the natural force of the word "always" (*sadā*) which admits no opposition, the wearing of shoes is mandatory even during a pilgrimage to sacred sites (*tīrthayātrā*). Likewise regarding the rainy season: as for the prohibition of that [wearing shoes] during the rains, it is optional (*kāmya*), like the prohibition of beds and such at all times.
Therefore, this is the sequence for performing the pilgrimage:

on a certain day, having performed a single meal (*ekabhakta*) and so forth, and on the following day, having performed the tonsure (*muṇḍana*) and fasting (*upavāsa*) which are required as qualifications for the rite, and on the day after that, having performed the daily obligatory duties (*nityakriyā*), one should worship Gaṇeśa, the planets, and one's chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*).

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, on this pilgrimage to a sacred site (*tīrthayātrā*), I shall perform the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*," and having completed the *śrāddha* with clarified butter, having honored three Brahmins, and having satisfied them with gold and other gifts—one should say:
"Oṃ, today, on the first lunar day (*pratipad*), desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by the Aśvamedha sacrifice, I shall perform this pilgrimage to [the sacred site named] Amuka."

Having thus resolved, he should assume there itself the attire of a *kārpaṭika*—consisting of wearing a ring and a saffron robe, as well as carrying an umbrella, sandals, and a staff—and having circumambulated the village to which he has settled, he should go to another village within the distance of one *krośa* and perform his breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) with the clarified butter remaining from the *śrāddha*.

Then, on the following day at dawn, having put on a pair of clean garments, performed his bath and ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and assumed the attire of a *kārpaṭika*, he should set out toward the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) during the forenoon.

And the wearing of the [pilgrim’s] dress is an auxiliary to the journey; therefore, it is only at the time of traveling, and not even during daily activities such as eating, for there is no authoritative evidence [to that effect].

In this very manner, one should travel every day until reaching the sacred site (*tīrtha*), and likewise at the sacred site, one should wear the dress of a *kārpaṭika* while recollecting the holy field (*kṣetra*) and so forth.

However, it is not [required] even at the time of bathing or performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) there, for there is no authoritative evidence [for it]. In the same way, having returned from the sacred site, near one’s own village or in another village, on the day following the day he first arrived, he should observe a fast and, on the subsequent day, worship the planets and his chosen deity.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "Today, on this pilgrimage, I shall perform the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha*," and having performed the *Pārvaṇa* rite there itself with clarified butter, he should worship three Brahmins as before. Then, having reached his own village and circumambulated it as before, he should enter his home, discard his disguise at the place where he had assumed it, and perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) with the clarified butter remaining from the *śrāddha*. Śaṅkha says:
"Having reached a sacred site (*tīrtha*), one should perform the bath at that site as a matter of course."
One obtains the fruit born of bathing, but not the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred fords.

If one sets out for the purpose of paying respects to a father or other relative residing in a foreign land, but happens to reach and bathe at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) along the way, he obtains only the fruit arising from that bath.
Paiṭhīnasi states: "He who goes for the sake of another obtains a sixteenth part [of the merit]."
Half the fruit of the sacred ford belongs to him who goes there by chance.

For the sake of another, such as for wages and so forth; or by way of incidental connection—that is, when one has set out for another sacred site (tīrtha)—Gaṇeśvara Miśra and others have also stated this. In the Devīpurāṇa:
"One should never examine a Brāhmaṇa at sacred sites;
Manu declared that one who arrives seeking food should simply be fed."
The offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) with roasted flour (śaktu), or with groats (saṃyāva), or with milk-rice (pāyasa),
or with oil-cake (piṇyāka), or with jaggery (guḍa), is prescribed by the sages.
[11] *Piṇyāka* is sesame paste. Likewise, it is stated in that very same source:
"And the *śrāddha* should be performed there, excluding the offering of water (*arghya*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*)."
A śrāddha performed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), which is not even looked upon by dogs, crows, vultures, or ravens, is said to bring satisfaction to the ancestors.

Whether out of season or at the proper time, when men have reached a sacred site (tīrtha), they must always perform the śrāddha rite; likewise, the libation to the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) must be performed.
The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) there is praised and is exceedingly difficult for the ancestors to obtain;
one must not delay at all, nor should one create any obstacle.

Regarding the word *tatra*: this is a locative case used in the sense of location (*adhikaraṇa-saptamī*), and not a locative in the sense of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), according to the maxim that "among case-endings associated with a subordinate word (*upapada*), those expressing a grammatical relation (*kāraka*) are stronger. Therefore, some maintain that every *śrāddha* performed at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) is devoid of the water-offering (*arghya*) and the invocation (*āvāhana*), and not merely that which is occasioned by the arrival at a sacred site.

That is not correct; for, seeing the concluding summary stating "it must be performed by those who have [already] arrived," and because the opening and conclusion form a single syntactical unit, we understand from this that the prohibition of the *arghya* and *āvāhana* applies specifically to the *śrāddha* occasioned by the arrival at a sacred site.

If it is argued that the invocation (*āvāhana*) has as its fruit the presence of the ancestors and others, and since they are eternally present at a sacred site (*tīrtha*), it would be appropriate to omit the invocation in a *śrāddha* performed solely at such a site due to its futility—this is not so. For the presence of either a physical body or a mental construct has already been refuted by the arguments in the *Devatādhikaraṇa*. Then for what purpose is the invocation performed elsewhere? Know that it is for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*); for this very reason, even the mantra for invocation is not recited [in the case of a *tīrtha-śrāddha*].

[Objection: But if, in this way, the mantra "namo vaḥ" has an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), how can there be a modification (*ūha*) of the mantra, given that this [mantra] has a meaning inherent in the rite (*samavetārtha*)? [Response: If that is so, then why is the plural form used for each individual person?

It is said: [12] Although this [mantra] has an inherent nature because it reveals those respective deities, the plural is used for each person; for one says separately, "O ancestors, this is your garment."

This is due to the force of the scriptural statement itself. Now, one might object: "If, in this way, the case-ending has a meaning not inherent in the archetype (*prakṛti*), then the same would apply in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well—for instance, in the mantra *aditiḥ pāśān pramumoktu* (may Aditi release the bonds). If you say 'yes' to that, then in the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for a father too, the mantra *etad vaḥ pitaro vāsaḥ* (this is your garment, O fathers) would have to be used, because the case-ending there also has a meaning not inherent in the archetype. If you argue thus, you are mistaken. For the non-inherent nature of case-endings is twofold: either by the force of the mantra's own expression or by the force of the syntactical context (*vākya*).

Among these, the first [point] concerns the section on the *pāśa* (rope): for this very reason, even in a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) where there are many ropes, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the word *pāśa* must be used in the plural form.

The second point, however, applies specifically to the scope of the scriptural statement (*vākya*), based on the principle that "as far as the plural number is concerned, it is indeed based on explicit injunction" (*vācanika*). Furthermore, it refers to an "inappropriate time" (*akāla*), meaning a time other than the new moon day (*amāvasyā*) and so forth, but not including the night and such times, because that would contradict prohibitions.

As for the statement that "at an improper time" refers to the night and so forth—since there is no day of the week (*vāra*) or lunar date (*tithi*) that is not a time for *śrāddha*, because *śrāddha* is prescribed everywhere—some maintain that it is precisely the night and such that is restated as being an improper time.
That is not correct; for while all days and dates are times for *śrāddha*, they do not constitute the time for the obligatory (*āvaśyaka*) *śrāddha*.

This *tīrtha-śrāddha*, however, is mandatory. Therefore, the meaning is this: even on an occasion such as the first lunar day (*pratipad*) when a *śrāddha* is not otherwise obligatory, a *śrāddha* must nevertheless be performed if one has reached a sacred site (*tīrtha*).

Regarding this, some say: "But for one who, by the turn of fate, obtains a sacred site in the evening or at another improper time, there is indeed a suspension of the *śrāddha* occasioned by that attainment; for on that day the prescribed auspicious hour (*muhūrta*) is absent, and on the following day it is no longer the 'day of attainment'."

In reality, however, even in that case, performing the *śrāddha* on the following day immediately after the two *muhūrtas* of sunrise is indeed appropriate. This is because the injunction for the *śrāddha* specifies precisely those *muhūrtas* ordained for the occasion of its occurrence; nor does delay constitute a fault, as the fault lies in one's own failure to perform it. Furthermore, it does not follow that the *śrāddha* must be performed at the very end of the period of injury (the *kṣata*) immediately upon its occurrence. For the *muhūrtas* ordained immediately after the occurrence—specifically those prescribed as the locus for that *śrāddha* by the rule "it must be performed by those who have attained [the time]"—are what are being transgressed.

Regarding "the offering of *piṇḍas*": since the offering of *piṇḍas* is already established as an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*, the explicit mention of the *piṇḍadāna* again is intended to show that where a *śrāddha* cannot be performed due to a lack of materials or other such reasons, the offering of *piṇḍas* must nevertheless be performed.

A single *śrāddha* is performed for a single pilgrimage or at a single sacred site (*tīrtha*); however, it is repeated when there is a difference in pilgrimages or a difference in sacred sites, because its performance is contingent upon those specific occasions.
For this very reason, when one reaches various sacred sites on Gayā on a single day, there are multiple *śrāddhas* occasioned by each of those sites.
Paiṭhīnasi: One should immerse an image made of kuśa grass in the waters of a sacred ford.
Whoever one intends for that immersion, he shall obtain an eighth part of the merit.
A *pratikṛti* is an image. As for the verse:
"You are Kuśa, the son of Kuśa, fashioned by Brahmā in ancient times;
when you have bathed, he too has bathed, for whom this knot-binding is intended."

Regarding the immersion of *kuśa* grass tied with a knot by means of this mantra, the authors of its commentary state that it is not a mandatory requirement (*anupagraha*) because it lacks a specific scriptural basis. Fasting at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) is for the sake of a special merit and is not obligatory, according to the statement of Devala: "Having reached a sacred ford, one who is engaged in vows, fasting, and observances, bathing there for three days and staying for three nights, is liberated from all sins and becomes prosperous."

Thus, in this context, the fruit of the three-night fast and the ritual baths is liberation from all sins and the attainment of well-being. This is because they form a single syntactical unit through a qualified connection (*viśiṣṭānvaya*), just as in the case of the statement, "The consecrated [fire] becomes the *āhavanīya* when purified. It is not a separate connection for each individual element, as that would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). However, some maintain that in every sacred ford (*tīrtha*), one must undergo tonsure and fasting on the day of arrival, asserting that "tonsure and fasting—this is the rule for all sacred fords."
Excepting Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Viśālā, and likewise Virajā.
This is because, according to the statement in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, the natural force (*svarasa*) of the word "all" (*sarva*) and the specific prohibition of places such as Gayā indicate this.
That is not correct, because if the word "all" were not restricted, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To explain:
Listen to the reason why even terrestrial sacred sites possess merit:
just as certain parts of the body are considered most preeminent.
The sanctity of sacred fords (tīrthas) is traditionally held to arise from their marvelous power, from the earth, from water, from fire, and from the acceptance [of them] by sages.

Thus, because the *Mahābhārata*, in the section on sacred fords (*tīrtha-uddeśa*), through the words of Bhīṣma, designates both land and water that yield extraordinary fruits as "sacred fords" (*tīrtha*), it would follow that the acts of shaving (*vapana*) and fasting (*upavāsa*) should apply to springs and such located within one's own country. This is not an acceptable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), as it would contradict the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) throughout all regions.

Nor can the word "all" (*sarva*) be taken as referring only to sacred fords outside one's own country; for if it were so, it would entail the abolition of the shaving at Prayāga, which is approved by all the learned people of Madhyadeśa.

Nor should it be said that the term "all" refers exclusively to those great pilgrimage sites where shaving the head is specifically prescribed, for no such injunction is heard regarding locations other than Prayāga. Thus:
"The wise man who, having reached the Gaṅgā, does not have his head shaved..."
All his ritual acts are in vain; such a man becomes a traitor to the sacred fords.
Whoever should not have their head shaved at the Gaṅgā in the field of Bhāskara shall dwell in the Raurava hell for an eon, together with ten million members of his lineage.
Having reached the Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, the accumulations of sins remain for kalpas clinging to the hair; therefore, one should have them shaved off.
For as many hairs on the nails and body as fall into the waters of the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.

If it is argued that, based on such statements, tonsure (*muṇḍana*) may be performed in the Gaṅgā even outside of Prayāga, let it be so for the moment; nevertheless, the use of the plural number remains unaccounted for, since the injunction for tonsure applies specifically to Prayāga and the Gaṅgā alone. Nor can it be claimed that tonsure in those other places is established by force of this specific prohibition, because sublation (*bādha*) has already been stated.
In reality, however, since none of the authors of the *Kalpataru* and others have recorded any injunctions for tonsure in the Gaṅgā [outside of these two], such injunctions are entirely baseless.

Now, shaving is prescribed in seven cases: at the Gaṅgā, in the field of Bhāskara, upon the death of one's mother, father, or guru, at the time of conception, and during the drinking of the Soma juice.
If it is argued that shaving of the head is required even at the Gaṅgā because of the statement written in the *Smṛtisamuccaya*—"Prayāga is the field of Bhāskara; there [is] shaving"—[we reply:
"Shaving and fasting: this is the rule for all sacred sites, with the exception of Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Viśālā, and likewise Virajā."

Thus, since the statement from the *Skanda Purāṇa* enjoining shaving at a sacred site other than Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Viśālā, and Virajā effectively prohibits shaving at the Gaṅgā, one might argue that there should be an option between them, like the choice of taking up or not taking up the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. This would indeed be the case if there were no contradiction due to a difference in scope. But is it not so? For instance:
As many as are the particles of nail and hair driven by the wind that fall into the waters of the Jāhnavī for men of meritorious deeds, [so many years do they dwell in heaven].

"Then one is glorified in all the worlds for thousands of years"—from such statements which enjoin the complete shaving of the head at the Gaṅgā, it is determined that, by virtue of the support of the undisputed conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), they refer to the Gaṅgā as delimited by Prayāga, whereas the prohibitive statement refers to the Gaṅgā as not so delimited. If this is so, how then is the plural number in the phrase "in all holy places" (*sarvatīrtheṣu*) to be explained? Since it has been established that the term *sarvatīrtha* denotes Prayāga through a *bahuvrīhi* compound, its plurality is not intended to be significant, just as in the case of the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*). If this is so, how then is there a specific prohibition regarding Gayā and other such places?

Thus, when the prohibition of *māṣa* beans and the like is already established by the specific injunction "when there is a sacrificial pap (*caru*) of *maudga* [beans]," the further statement "indeed, *māṣa* beans are unfit for sacrifice" is intended to show that even as substitutes, *māṣa* beans are not to be accepted because they are absolutely unfit for sacrifice. Likewise, even in the prohibition against sowing [seeds] at Gayā and other such places, it is intended to express absolute lack of merit (*aprāśastya*).
If it is asked what is the authority for the term "all holy places" (*sarvatīrtha*) referring specifically to Prayāga, [the answer is]:
"O son of Kuntī, perform in this manner the bathing at all holy places."
Even the evil committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
Know that this is a statement from the *Matsyapurāṇa* situated within the description of Prayāga.
Thus ends the general rule [18].
Now, the procedure for Prayāga;
herein, in the Padma Purāṇa:
"The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever one bathes in her."
Therefore, it is said that ten times that [distance] is where she meets with the Vindhya.
Therefore, the northward-flowing [current] at Kāśī is said to be a hundred times more meritorious than that;
and the Gaṅgā at the confluence with the Yamunā is said to be a hundred times more meritorious than [the current] at Kāśī.
That river which flows westward becomes a thousandfold more meritorious;
O King, by its mere sight, it removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
The Gaṅgā, flowing westward where she meets the Kālindī, destroys the sins committed during a kalpa; she is difficult to attain, O King, during the month of Māgha.
O King, that confluence is celebrated on earth as nectar;
indeed, even for the gods, a single moment there during the month of Māgha is difficult to obtain.
Likewise: "O King, whatever holy places exist on earth and whatever cities are here, they all come to the Veṇī to bathe during the month of Māgha."
The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; the Rudras, Ādityas, and hosts of Maruts; the Gandharvas, world-protectors, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas.
Those endowed with the powers of *aṇimā* and the rest, as well as other seers of reality;
Brahmāṇī, Pārvatī, Lakṣmī, Śacī, Medhā, Aditi, and Rati.
O King, all those wives of the gods, as well as the daughters of the nāgas—
Ghṛtācī, Menakā, Rambhā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā— [were there].
[19] All the hosts of Apsarases as well as the hosts of Pitṛs,
O lord of men, all come to bathe in the Veṇī during the month of Māgha.
In the Kṛta Yuga they appear in their own form; in the Kali Yuga, they exist in concealed forms.
All holy places become black due to the fault of association with sinners;
however, at Prayāga, they become white through bathing during the month of Māgha.
Likewise:
"O Govinda, Acyuta, Mādhava! O Lord, while the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, may you grant me the fruits as described through this bath."
Having recited this mantra, one should bathe while observing silence;
thereafter, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Śrīdhara.
The merit that men obtain by bathing with heated water at home is indeed attained when the sun is situated in Capricorn during the sixth year.
O King, it is traditionally taught that the fruit of bathing outside [the village] at the beginning of the twelve-year cycle is twofold for a pond and fourfold for a river and so forth.
O King, at a natural pool in the wilderness the merit is tenfold, at a great river it is a hundredfold,
and at the confluence of a great river it is four hundredfold.
O King, by merely bathing in the Gaṅgā when the sun is in Capricorn, a human being obtains all that fruit multiplied a thousandfold.
Likewise: "O lord of men, those who bathe here in the Ganges during the month of Māgha do not fall from the abode of the gods for a thousand cycles of the four yugas."
[20] O best of kings, the sages have declared that a bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā in the month of Māgha is multiplied a hundredfold, becoming a thousandfold.
O King, Prajāpati, who is devoted to the welfare of his subjects, established Prayāga as a place of purification for the heavy burden of the flood of sins.
This place is truly a slaughterhouse with its white and black waters;
for it was ordained of old by Brahmā as a site for the sacrificial animals that are sins.
The stream that is white and black, intermingled with the Sarasvatī—
that path to the world of Brahmā, the Creator indeed brought forth.
Likewise:
The month of Māgha produces knowledge when practiced mentally; it bestows the fruit of ultimate reality and liberation;
and at the sacred fords on the slopes of the Himalayas, it destroys all sins.
The month of Māgha has been declared by the exponents of the Vedas to bestow the world of Indra;
in the Badarī forest, Māgha bestows all desires and grants liberation.
The month of Māgha at the Narmadā destroys sin, removes suffering, bestows the fruits of all desires, grants the world of Rudra, and annihilates evil.
O best of the twice-born, the month of Sārasvata destroys sins and yields the fruit of the world of Brahmā; likewise, the month of Māgha at Viśālā bestows the fruit of Viśākhā.
The Ganges is proclaimed to be a forest fire for the fuel of sin, bringing about the destruction of the cause of rebirth, and leading to the world of Viṣṇu and liberation.
[21] The Sarayū, Gaṇḍakī, Sindhu, Candrabhāgā, Kauśikī, Tāpī, Godāvarī, Bhīmā, Payoṣṇī, and Kṛṣṇakauśikī.
A man who bathes in the Kāverī, the Tuṅgabhadrā, and whatever other rivers flow to the ocean, goes to the heavenly world, cleansed of all sin.
In Naimiṣa one attains identity with Viṣṇu; at Puṣkara, proximity to Brahmā;
and indeed, the world of Ākhaṇḍala (Indra) belongs to one who bathes at Kurukṣetra during the month of Māgha.
O Brahmin, the month of Māgha at Devahrada bestows the fruit of yogic perfection;
at Prabhāsa, one becomes a member of Rudra’s retinue during Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn.
O Brahmin, by means of the Māgha bath in the Gomatī, a man becomes a deity-bodied being born of Devakī and attains freedom from rebirth.
On Hemakūṭa, Mahākāla, Oṃkāra,
and likewise on Nīlakaṇṭha and Arbuda, one is glorified in the world of Rudra starting from the month of Māgha.
O Brahmin, O King, when the sun is in Capricorn during the confluence of all rivers,
the attainment of all desires occurs through bathing there.
O best of the twice-born, the month of Māgha is attained at Prayāga by the fortunate,
for there the white and black waters grant freedom from rebirth.
The gods dwelling in heaven constantly sing: "Alas, our month of Māgha will take place at Prayāga,
where men who have bathed shall never again experience the pains of the womb."
They behold [him] and abide in the presence of Viṣṇu.
[22] Likewise: In ancient times, he was weighed on a scale together with sacred fords, vows, gifts, austerities, and sacrifices by the Creator.
Between those two, Māgha and Prayāga,
Māgha was the more venerable, and he was superior even to both of them.

The destination that men reach through strenuous austerities— such as subsisting on air, water, or leaves, and emaciating the body— as well as through yogic practices accumulated over a long period of time; [that same destination is reached by others].
Indeed, by bathing at Prayāga, they go to that same destination.
For those who have bathed at the holy site of Prayāga, where the celestial river meets [the Yamunā], at the rising of the sun upon the Makara sign,
the door of their home is adorned.
A swarm of bees stirred by the ears of an elephant.
He who effortlessly destroys all sins and bestows the entire fruit of the Rājasūya and Gomedha sacrifices as well as that of ritual ablution;
Surely, how is it that Prayāga is not described?
Likewise, at the mere moment [of arrival], he obtains that merit which exists in the four Vedas and indeed in truthful speech,
simply by bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
[23] Likewise: One who is firm in his vows should perform the consecration there at the confluence;
he obtains a fruit equal to that of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
The sacred precinct of Prayāga extends five yojanas;
by entering it, one performs an Aśvamedha sacrifice at every step upon the earth.
Likewise: "O King of kings, there are three pools, and in their midst flows the Jāhnavī;
by entering Prayāga, one's sin is destroyed at that very moment."
"Three" refers to one at the city of Prayāga, a second at the city of Pratiṣṭhāna, and a third at Alarka-nagara to the south of the Yamunā; "kuṇḍas" means wells. Likewise:
"One should bathe for one month at Prayāga, firm in one's vows."
One is liberated from all sins, just as it was instructed by the Self-Existent One.
But one who is pure, self-restrained, non-violent, and endowed with faith is liberated from all sins and shall go to the supreme state.
Prayāga, however, is the region characterized by the Brahma-yūpa pillar. And so it is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Listen again, O King, to the majesty of Prayāga:
Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Gotīrtha, and the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean."
And Gayā, Dhenuka, and likewise Gaṅgāsāgara;
These and many others, those meritorious mountain peaks,
ten thousand holy fords (*tīrtha*), and thirty crores more besides.
The wise have said that she is eternally established at Prayāga;
there are three fire-pits, and in their midst flows the Jāhnavī.
Departing from Prayāga, preceded by all sacred fords,
the goddess who is the daughter of the Sun is renowned throughout the three worlds.
The Yamunā, the purifier of the world, has joined with the Gaṅgā;
that which lies between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is considered the most supreme on earth.
O tiger among kings, Vāyu has declared that three and a half crores of sacred fords do not equal even a sixteenth part of Prayāga.
In heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, all that is known as the Jāhnavī;
having presided over Prayāga, both Kambala and Aśvatara [are present].
Furthermore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, this sacrificial altar which is Bhogavatī belongs to Prajāpati;
there, the Vedas and the sacrifices exist in embodied form.
The sages whose wealth is asceticism worship Prajāpati, O King;
likewise, the gods and the wielders of the discus perform sacrifices with ritual offerings.
Therefore, O Bhārata, there is nothing more meritorious in the three worlds;
by its power, O Lord, it surpasses all other sacred fords.
Having thus beheld that supreme station, the holy ford of Prayāga,
one is liberated from all sins, like the moon released from Rāhu.
[25] Likewise: Having gone from there to Prayāga, which is protected by all the gods,
one should dwell for a month as a celibate student and offer libations to the ancestors and the gods.
Wherever he is born, he obtains his desired objects;
likewise, even one who is shrouded by hundreds of sins would attain [purity] if he were to immerse himself in the Sitāsita (the confluence of the white and black rivers).
If the sun is situated in Capricorn during the month of Māgha, he does not sink into the wombs [of rebirth].
The Māyā of Viṣṇu is indeed difficult to conquer and is very hard to abandon even for the gods;
yet, O lord of men, it is consumed at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
Having enjoyed manifold pleasures in those various worlds,
they subsequently merge into the Discus-bearer at Prayāga, like fish entering the ocean.
Even Citragupta is not at all able to know the measure of the merit of one who performs ablutions at the confluence of the white and dark waters in the month of Māgha when the sun is in Capricorn.
O King, for those who bathe at the confluence of the white and black [waters] during the month of Māgha, the complete fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices is certainly attained.
Likewise:
"O King, whatever sin has been accumulated by men over births lasting until the end of the kalpa,
that shall be reduced to ashes for those who bathe at the confluence of the white and dark rivers during the month of Māgha."
In the future, there shall be the world-renowned confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
that indeed is the *kāmika* (wish-fulfilling) tīrtha, and by bathing there with devotion, [one’s desires are fulfilled].
[26] Whatever desire one may have, that indeed shall be theirs:
for one desiring enjoyments, there shall be enjoyments; for one desiring a kingdom, there shall be a kingdom;
for one desiring heaven, there shall be heaven; and for one desiring liberation, there shall be liberation.
Whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) there may be in the three worlds that bestow desired objects,
they all resort to the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, one shall indeed go to the city of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for those who bathe at the confluence of the white and dark rivers (the Gaṅgā and Yamunā) during the month of Māgha in Bhārata,
there is no return to this world even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
In the *Mātsya*: "One who speaks the truth, has conquered anger, is established in supreme non-violence,
follows the Dharma, knows reality, and is devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins."
One who bathes between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā is liberated from sin;
there one obtains in abundance all the desires conceived by the mind.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "The fruit that one obtains at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse by means of a thousand bhāras of gold,
that same fruit one obtains day after day at the Veṇī during the month of Māgha."
Now, regarding the fruit of bathing for three days, the *Matsya Purāṇa* states:
"Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a hundred thousand cows..."
That same merit shall belong to one who bathes for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
Likewise: "Whatever fruit is obtained by one who remains without food for more than a hundred years,
that same fruit is obtained by bathing at Prayāga for three days during the month of Māgha."
Likewise: "Whatever merit is gained through the practice of yoga over three hundred years,
that shall be attained by bathing for just three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha."
Likewise:
"The man who bathes for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha casts off his sin and goes to heaven, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin."
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "The fruit that one obtains on earth by bathing for three days at Prayāga during the month of Māgha cannot be attained even by a thousand horse-sacrifices."
Likewise, O King, in ancient times Kāñcanamālinī gave the fruit of three days of bathing in the month of Māgha to a Rākṣasa; by that act, that evildoer was liberated.
The destruction of my evil occurred after three days; with twenty-seven days remaining, whatever merit was left to me, by that I attained the state of a deity.
Delighting on Kailāsa as a dear friend of the Daughter of the Mountain,
she likewise became one who remembers her past lives through the grace of Prayāga.
Likewise: Even those men who have committed many sins, if they bathe here at this sacred ford of Prayāga for three days, [are purified].
By the very nature of things, they do not sink into the hells;
rather, they dwell even in heaven like gods.
Likewise: In ancient times, there was a king named Vīrasena in the region of Avanti;
resorting to the bank of the Narmadā, he performed the Rājasūya sacrifice.
He also performed sixteen horse-sacrifices according to the prescribed rites, in which the sacrificial fees consisted of gold, silver, and other riches, and were adorned with golden ornaments.
Full of faith, devoted to the deities, a giver of cows and a giver of gold, he bestowed upon the twice-born a mountain-like heap of grain.
There was a Brahmin named Bhadraka, who was foolish, of low birth, a farmer,
of wicked conduct, and excluded from all religious duties.
Distressed by his labor in the fields and deceived by his kinsmen,
he wandered here and there and departed, oppressed by the rain.
Having taken refuge on the ridge of the mountain of the gods, he settled at Prayāga;
honoring the great Māghī festival, he bathed there for three days.
Having become sinless merely by bathing, that best of the twice-born departed from Prayāga and returned once more to that very place.
[29] That king and that brahmin both perished at one time;
their identical destiny was seen by me in the presence of Śakra.
Luster, beauty, strength, womanly charm, the celestial vehicle, ornaments,
a garland of *pārijāta* flowers, and dancing and singing on both sides.
Having thus seen the majesty of this sacred field, O sinless brahmin, how can it be said that the Māgha [bath] at the White and Black [confluence] is equal to a Rājasūya sacrifice?

Regarding the fact that these [three days] yield the fruit of bathing, there is an option (*vikalpa*) based on the principle of the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi*). However, the specific undertaking (*parigraha*) is purely optional (*aicchika*), as there is no determining factor (*vinigamaka*) [to the contrary].

As for the claim that—even when the three-day period has been embraced by a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—one performs the morning bath again at that very time with a unique resolve (*asādhāraṇa-saṃkalpa*) regarding the morning bath on the day before the seventh (*māgasaptamī*): that is incorrect, because at that time only a single bath is prescribed; otherwise, if one were to desire the fruit of those three days, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anantya*) of baths. How then is the repetition of the bath justified when multiple holy sites (*tīrtha*) are encountered during the day? It is due to a specific scriptural statement (*viśeṣavacana*).
The learned authorities maintain that the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) for three days pertains exclusively to the morning bath. Likewise, in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:

"At the confluence of white and blue waters, twenty *dhanus* in extent, one who bathes from the month of Māgha shall not return [to this world] again; he becomes as one who has performed the Rājasūya sacrifice."
Even the wind of the month of Māgha, as it touches the white and black waters,
surely does not touch the unfortunate, for it is the destroyer of great sins.
The two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, dwell on the vast bank of the Yamunā;
having bathed and drunk there, one is liberated from all sins.
And having gone there to the abode of the wise Mahādeva,
a man delivers ten ancestors and ten descendants.
And at the well known as Sāmudra in Pratiṣṭhāna,
if one who is a celibate student and has conquered anger stays for three nights, [he obtains great merit].
With his soul purified of all sins, he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice,
[at the place] to the north of Pratiṣṭhāna and to the east of the Bhāgīrathī.
Known in the three worlds by the name Haṃsaprapatana,
O Bhārata, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice merely by bathing there;
for as long as the moon and the sun endure, so long is one honored in heaven.
Likewise:
"Then, having gone to Bhogavatī, to the north of Vāsuki,
there is that supreme sacred ford named Daśāśvamedhika."
Having performed the consecration, that man shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
he becomes wealthy, handsome, skillful, a donor, and righteous.
Whatever merit is found in the four Vedas, whatever fruit is found in truthful speech,
and whatever dharma resides in non-violence— that fruit is obtained by going there.
There, to the north of Vāsuki, is the place named Bhogavatī;
whoever performs an ablution there shall obtain the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Likewise: On the northern bank of the Yamunā and to the south of Prayāga,
there is a sacred ford (tīrtha) known as Ṛṇamocana, which is remembered as supreme.
Having stayed for one night and bathed, one is liberated from all debts;
one attains the heavenly world and shall forever become immortal.
Likewise:
Hear now what the fruit is for those who have killed a Brahmin or a cow at Prayāga;
they should bathe at the three times of day and consume moderate food.
One shall be liberated in three months at Prayāga; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having bathed and drunk there at the Yamunā,
one obtains merit through its glorification and beholds auspicious things upon seeing it.
Having bathed in it and drunk from it, one purifies one's lineage up to the seventh generation.

And here, the morning bath (*prātaḥsnāna*) is to be performed at the time of dawn (*aruṇodayavelā*), because of the statement of Viṣṇu: “One who is to bathe in the morning should bathe after observing the eastern quarter seized by the spreading rays of the dawn. As for the claim that the morning bath at Prayāga may also be performed at the time of sunrise based on hearing such statements as “at the rising of the sun in the month of Makara,” that is not correct; for that [statement] prescribes only the fruit and does not prescribe the time. Moreover, since it is possible to maintain syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) through the indication of proximity (*sāmīpyalakṣaṇā*), a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) is improper. [As the saying goes: “If one does not bathe in the month of Māgha while the sun is in Capricorn and before the sun has risen, [one suffers].”
How may one be liberated from evils, or how may one go to the third heaven?
This is because in many such passages, the performance of the bath before sunrise is heard of;
furthermore, the midday bath is optional (*kāmya*) and must be performed within two *prahara*s (six hours), as stated in the injunction: "One should perform it only in the forenoon.
Now, regarding tonsure (*muṇḍana*):

although the author of the *Kalpataru* has neither mentioned tonsure at Prayāga nor cited its authoritative source, nevertheless, the various scriptural statements accepted by many authors of digests (*nibandha*) are here collected. For instance:
"One should perform the shaving of the head at Prayāga, and the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍapātana*) at Gayā."
One should give gifts at Kurukṣetra, or cast off the body at Vārāṇasī.
What is the use of offering funeral cakes at Gayā, or of dying at Kāśī,
or of making gifts at Kurukṣetra, if one has performed the tonsure at Prayāga?

Now, there is the injunction: "One should perform the shaving of the head at Prayāga. Since a desire for a fruit arises in that context, a fruit mentioned in an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is connected [to the injunction] according to the principle of the *rātrisatra* sacrifice. And as for that fruit—since it is heard [in scripture] that "What [is the use] of offering the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) at Gayā? and so forth—the fruit produced by the offering of the funeral cake at Gayā is [the result]. Therefore, one who desires the fruit produced by the offering of the funeral cake at Gayā, the fruit produced by dying in Kāśī, or the fruit produced by giving at Kurukṣetra, is the qualified person (*adhikārī*) for this [act].

This, however, is considered: although, because shaving consists of the act of clipping, there is no appearance of a connection with a result for the prescribed cutting—since the result is indicated there by way of reference (anuvāda) and because there is a difference between "cutting" (*vapana*) and "clipping" (*vāpana*)—nevertheless, since the action already prescribed is being referred to, and because the reference merely serves to provide the result therein while the injunction (*vidhi*) remains primary, the connection with the result here belongs to that which is indeed prescribed.

If it be objected that, in this case, the fruit would belong to the one who causes the shaving, and not to the one who shaves, we say no; for since the injunction itself is directed toward the act of shaving, the word *kuryāt* (he should do) is used with the elision of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the sense of "he should cause it to be done.

If it be further objected that, having thus clarified the meaning as being inherently causative, the practitioner desiring the aforementioned fruit should express his intention as, "I shall cause the shaving to be performed at Prayāga," we reply:
True, but according to the maxim that "the modification follows the model," the verbal expression *kariṣye* ("I shall do") is appropriate here, following the form of the original model (*prakṛti*).

For this very reason, some maintain that even in cases where the sacrifice is performed through the agency of officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the sacrificer, in accordance with the injunction "he shall sacrifice" (*yajeta*), declares only "I shall sacrifice" (*yakṣye*) and not "I shall cause [others] to sacrifice" (*yājayiṣye*).

To this, it is replied: according to the principle "the modified sacrifice is like the archetype" (*prakṛtivad vikṛtiḥ*), there is indeed an extension (*atideśa*) of the ritual properties of the archetypal sacrifice to the modified sacrifices; however, there is no rule prescribing the specific wording of Vedic sentences for ordinary (secular) speech, as such a rule would be subject to many exceptions.

Nor should it be argued that because of the scriptural hearing, "one should dwell according to what is heard," whatever word is heard must not be abandoned; for that rule applies to words referring to a deity and to words such as *japa* (muttering) which serve an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭa*). This word, however, refers to the meaning, since it is the very act of sowing that is taught here.

If it is argued: "Let it be so; nevertheless, let the state of having the *ṇic* suffix elided (*luptaṇickatva*) be indicated [by the root itself], so that the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvayadhī*) would occur with 'kuryāt' (he should do) alone," then—alas!—if the act of shaving (*parivāpana*) is thus enjoined, since the employment of words is within our own control, we follow the maxim: "What non-expressive word shall we employ? Thus, let it simply be "kārayiṣye" (I shall cause to be done); and the usage "yakṣye" (I shall sacrifice) is not a valid example, because of the disparity between the two cases.

For in that context, *yāga* is the relinquishment (*tyāga*) of an oblation (*havis*) intended for a deity, and it has the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) alone as its agent. *Homa*, on the other hand, is the restatement (*anuvāda*) of that relinquishment preceded by a distribution (*saṃvibhāga*), resulting in the casting into the fire (*prakṣepa*) of the substance thus relinquished; it has the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) as its agent. Therefore, the priests are "sacrificers" (*yājaka*) in the sense of performing the sacrifice, but not the "performers" (*yaṣṭṛ*) of the primary act. For this very reason, the commentary states: "Viśvāmitra caused Triśaṅku to sacrifice. This is the general direction.
Likewise, tonsure (*muṇḍana*) is performed even at the Gaṅgā delimited by Prayāga.
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on one's head cut off in the waters of the Jāhnavī, for that long one is honored in the heavenly world.
As many nails and hairs as are carried by the wind and fall into the waters of the Jāhnavī for men of meritorious deeds,
for that many thousands of years they are honored in the heavenly world.

Because the injunction for tonsure is established even in that [Ganges] by such statements accepted by the learned; indeed, in this way, this tonsure at Prayāga—which has heaven as its fruit and liberation as its fruit—is not accomplished simultaneously through either *tantra* (simultaneous performance) or *prasaṅga* (incidental performance), because the two have distinct qualifications based on different desires, and because those two desires cannot coexist at once. Consequently, when there is a requirement for sequence, the tonsure at the Ganges comes first, because of the scriptural statement "having reached the Ganges" (*gaṅgāṃ prāpya*) and so forth, which indicates it is qualified by the mere arrival [at the river]; whereas for the tonsure at Prayāga, no such time is prescribed.

If it is argued that even at Prayāga, by such scriptural injunctions as "shaving and fasting," the simultaneity of shaving and fasting is established, and since fasting there is to be performed on the day it is prescribed, shaving should likewise be performed then—this is true; however, because both fasting and shaving there are occasioned by the same underlying cause, and because that shaving is accomplished through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) by means of the optional (*kāmya*) shaving at the Gaṅgā itself.

As for that which was said: "In that regard, the shaving (*muṇḍana*) performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*) has no fixed time; therefore, its performance may take place on another day at any spot within the precincts of Prayāga. Now, if this shaving were merely optional (*kevalakāmya*), it would follow that it should occur every day, just like the ritual bath (*snāna*).

If one argues that it is triggered by a specific occasion (*prāptinimittaka*), then it must be performed on the very first day, because the occasion (*nimitta*) and the desire (*kāmanā*) coincide on that same day, making it impossible to delay the timing.
On this point, some say:
If he should go to a sacred ford again after a year less two months,
he must then diligently perform a tonsure and a fast.
Based on this statement, one should not undergo a second tonsure at that same sacred site within ten months of a tonsure performed for the sake of a single specific qualification (*upādhi*).

Nor should it be argued that, by this logic, even the very first tonsure at Prayāga would be invalid, since it too would be "second" in relation to a tonsure at the Ganges defined by that same [temporal] limit;

for they say that since the tonsure prescribed for Prayāga has a different purpose (*adhikāra*) than the tonsure at the Ganges, it cannot be accomplished either through incidental application (*prasaṅga*) or through a single performance (*tantra*), and thus its separate performance there is logically required.

That is not so, because this statement lacks a foundation; even if it were well-founded, it would concern shaving the head as a consequence of reaching [the river], due to its association with fasting caused by that same reason, and because of the expression "one should go.
To this, it is replied:
"He who does not have the shaving of the head performed at the Gaṅgā or in the field of the Sun..."
Together with ten million of his kin, he shall be boiled in the Raurava hell for the duration of an eon.
Because of such passages, one hears of censure for its non-performance and the hearing of rewards for its performance.
Thus, shaving at Prayāga is established as both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*).

And since the purpose of the scripture is accomplished by performing it even once, it is determined that during a single pilgrimage, there is only one instance, and it is restricted to a specific time. The same applies to shaving on the Gaṅgā as delimited by those [specific times].

Others, however, say: "There is one shaving for each occasion, namely the arrival at Prayāga and the Gaṅgā; likewise, there is one fruit for each, namely heaven. Therefore, since the two occasional rites coincide with the two optional ones, they are performed by way of *tantra* (simultaneous performance). Thus, on the very day of arrival, there is a single shaving in the Gaṅgā within the precincts of Prayāga; in this manner, all four [rites] are accomplished. In this regard, when shaving would apply to women who have arrived at Prayāga, it is said:
"Having gathered up all the hair, she should cut off two finger-breadths."
In this very way, one should prescribe that shaving the head is better for women.

They say that because these [rules], though heard in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta-prakaraṇa*), can be connected elsewhere as well due to the equality of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), at Prayāga too, "shaving" (*vapana*) consists merely in the cutting of two finger-breadths from the tips of the hair.

Others, however, maintain that the shaving of the head is indeed occasioned by the arrival at Prayāga; although it is optional (*kāmya*) because a fruit is heard in the texts, there is no evidence for a separate act. Likewise, the shaving occasioned by the arrival at the Gaṅgā is also optional because a fruit is heard. Furthermore, in both cases, the fruit is heaven alone. They say that because the conditions for both arrivals exist on the day of arrival, and because the desire for both exists, the accomplishment of both occurs simultaneously (*tantra*) on that very day.
This is the formal argument (*prayoga*) here:

Alternatively, for one who has not performed the *Vaidhātrī* sacrifice, having stayed the previous day east of the *Gotama-āśrama*, one should perform the morning bath and other rites on the day of entry and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) regarding the entry into Prayāga.

For example: "Oṃ! Today, desiring to obtain the fruit of as many horse-sacrifices as there are steps to be traversed while traveling upon the ground within the precincts of Prayāga, I shall perform the journey upon that ground within the precincts of Prayāga, preceded by entering the precincts of Prayāga"—having thus made this formal resolve (saṃkalpa), and having reached Prayāga, first bathed with water drawn up [from a well], and then, being pure and a student (varṇī), having entered during the month of Māgha—

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to go to the city of Viṣṇu, I shall perform a bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā," one should bathe according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*); if that is unknown, one should bathe according to the general procedure common to all.

But in the month of Māgha, one should bathe after making the resolve: "Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from the gift of a thousand *bhāras* of gold to Brāhmaṇas during the Kali age at Kurukṣetra, I shall perform a bath in the Veṇī during the month of Māgha."

At the confluence of the white and black currents, delimited by twenty *dhanus* on the western outer flow of the Gaṅgā, at the bathing place marked by the Yamunā’s current—*Oṃ*, desiring non-return [to this world], I shall perform the bath in the *Sītāsita* (White-Black) confluence during the month of Māgha. At that very spot, for one characterized by truthfulness, freedom from anger, devotion to non-violence, adherence to dharma, knowledge of reality, and dedication to the welfare of cows and Brahmins, the fruit of the bath is liberation from sin and the attainment of abundant desires as conceived in the mind. The ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows: *Oṃ adyāpunarāvṛttikāmo māghe sitāsite snānam ahaṃ kariṣye |* *In that very place, for one distinguished by truthfulness, freedom from anger, devotion to non-violence, adherence to dharma, knowledge of reality, and dedication to the welfare of cows and Brahmins, the fruit of the bath is liberation from sin and the attainment of abundant desires as conceived in the mind.
Thus is the ritual procedure:* (Note: The text provided contains an ellipsis regarding the specific ritual formula; the translation reflects the structure and intent of the available portion.)
Oṃ. Desiring today the liberation from sins and the attainment of emancipation, I shall perform a bath between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.

In the case of other optional rites (*kāmya*), one should omit the word "emancipation" (*mukti*) and employ the specific name of that particular goal. Then, having bathed in this manner and performed the daily duties up to the worship of the deities, [one should say]:
Oṃ. Desiring today the majesty of the heavenly realm for as many years as there are hairs on my head and body to be cut off, I shall have my hair shaved in the Gaṅgā.

Having thus resolved, while seated on the ground, he should cause his hair and so forth to fall into the Gaṅgā in such a way that they fall by themselves. Then he should observe the fast with the mantra: "Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of heaven, I shall perform the fast for the holy ford (tīrthopavāsa).
Some maintain that the fruit of this is the attainment of the world of Brahmā.

Thereupon—the person entitled to perform the *śrāddha* must perform the *pārvaṇa* rite occasioned by reaching the sacred ford (*tīrtha*). In the event that this is not possible, he should at least offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for six ancestors. In reality, however, although fasting is possible as an occasional duty (*naimittika*), because it would involve the cumbersome assumption of a reward according to the logic of the *Viśvajit* sacrifice, this fasting is indeed fruitless by virtue of the scriptural injunction itself. Consequently, having fulfilled his entitlement through this very fasting, he should bathe on the following day at the *Ṛṇamocana* ford.

For instance: at Kambalāśvatara, extending as far as the wall of the village of Prayāga, on the Yamunā river delimited by its northern bank, lies the Ṛṇamocana Tīrtha. There, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Om! Today, desiring liberation from all debts, the attainment of the heavenly world, and immortality, I shall perform a bath in the Ṛṇamocana Tīrtha," one should perform the bath and the libations (*tarpaṇa*).

But for the morning bath, [one should say]: "Om! Today, desiring the state of being a great king of elephant-riders, I shall perform a bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the rising of the sun during the month of Makara."

Oṃ! Desiring to attain merit equal to that produced by the practice of yoga for a period of one hundred years, I shall perform the morning bath at Prayāga for three days beginning today during the month of Māgha.
Likewise—desiring to go to heaven preceded by liberation from sin, I shall perform the bath at Prayāga for three days beginning today during the month of Māgha.
Oṃ! Desiring to attain fruit equal to the fruit produced by a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), I shall perform the bath at Prayāga during the month of Māgha beginning today.
Oṃ, desiring the attainment of liberation, from today onwards, I shall perform the bath at Prayāga for three days during the month of Māgha.
Likewise: Oṃ, desiring to dwell in heaven like a god through immersion in all the hells, from today onwards, I shall perform the bath at Prayāga during the month of Māgha.
Likewise, regarding the bath for three days in proximity to the full moon of Māgha:

Oṃ! Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by the gift of mountains of grain, the devotion of deities, and the giving of cows and gold—equivalent to the fruit arising from the performance of many preparations for the sixteenth *sattīrtha* Aśvamedha sacrifices according to rule and the distribution of gifts to Brāhmaṇas—I shall perform a bath at Prayāga for three days beginning today.
However, those of the Middle Country recite:
"If [the full moon] in the months of Pauṣa or Māgha is joined with an Amāvāsyā, a Sunday, a lunar eclipse, or the Śravaṇa asterism..."
That is to be known as Ardhodaya, which is superior to hundreds of solar festivals.
The *vyatīpāta* occurring at dawn is listed among the daily conjunctions (*yoga*).
However, the Gauḍas say:
"The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha at the time of sunrise..."
If it could be obtained at Prayāga, it would be equal to a thousand solar eclipses.

In the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), however, it is stated generally: "At the solstices (ayana), there shall be ten million merits; at the equinoxes (viṣuva), the fruit is one hundred thousand;
at the Ṣaḍaśītis, a thousand; and likewise at the Viṣṇupadīs."

Others, however, maintain that those specific fruits associated with particular times which are recorded in relation to the Gaṅgā have been elaborated upon in that very context; and those superior results should be understood as applying there. Regarding the bath in the Yamunā on its northern bank near Kambalāśvatara, to the west of Prayāga:
*Oṃ, today, desiring liberation from all sins, I shall perform a bath in the Yamunā near Kambalāśvatara.*
Having thus resolved, one should perform the ritual bathing and libations (*tarpaṇa*) there. In this regard, even drinking this water yields the same fruit.

This bathing, however, takes place in the presence of Mahādeva. As for going to that place: one should go to that site after making the following resolve: "Oṃ, today, desiring the liberation of ten ancestors and ten descendants, I shall undertake the journey to the abode of Mahādeva in the form of the banks of the Yamunā, characterized by [the presence of] Kambala and Aśvatara. Having thus resolved, one should proceed to that place.
Now, near Vāsuki there is a place named Daśāśvamedhika; regarding the journey there—one should go there after making this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*):

"Oṃ, today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruits arising from the study of the four Vedas, from truthful speech, and from non-violence, I shall perform the journey to Daśāśvamedhika. Thus having resolved, one should go there.

Regarding the bath there: having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "Oṃ, desiring wealth, beauty, dexterity, generosity, and righteousness, and wishing to obtain a result equal to the fruit born of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), I shall perform a bath at the Daśāśvamedhika Tīrtha," one should perform the bath and the libations (*tarpaṇa*).

Regarding the bath in the Bhogavatī river at that very place: having made the formal resolve, "Oṃ, desiring to obtain a result equal to the fruit born of the horse-sacrifice, I shall perform a bath in the Bhogavatī," one should perform the bath and the libations.
On the eastern bank of the Gaṅgā is the city named Pratiṣṭhāna; right there is a well named Sāmudra. For one who observes celibacy and has conquered anger, that is the fruit [of the rite].

Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice through the purity of one's self, one should make this formal resolve: "From today for three nights, I shall stay near the Sāmudra well.
Having thus resolved, one should remain there for three nights. Then, to the north of Pratiṣṭhāna and to the east of the Gaṅgā, there is a pool named Haṃsaprapatana; bathing there—

"Oṃ! Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), and desiring to be honored in heaven for as long as the moon and sun endure, I shall perform the ritual bath at Haṃsaprapatana. Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the bath and the libations (*tarpaṇa*).

But regarding the bath in the Yamunā within the precincts of Prayāga, one should perform the bath and libations after making the resolve: "Oṃ! Desiring to purify my seven lineages, I shall perform the ritual bath in the Yamunā within the precincts of Prayāga."

This is the fruit even in merely drinking this water. Whenever one stays at Prayāga for a month, observing celibacy and habitually performing libations to the ancestors and deities, the fruit of performing immersion there is the attainment of many desired objects.
Whenever one performs the monthly bath—[reciting]:

"Oṃ, desiring today liberation from all sins and the attainment of the supreme state, I shall perform the bath at Prayāga for a month starting from today"—the fruit of that bath performed throughout the month of Māgha is absorption into the Discus (Viṣṇu) preceded by the enjoyment of manifold pleasures in those respective worlds.

And likewise: having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus—"Oṃ, desiring to be absorbed into the discus (*cakrin*) preceded by the enjoyment of manifold pleasures based upon those respective worlds, I shall perform the ritual bath at Prayāga from today until the month of Māgha"—one should bathe twice every day during the month of Māgha. However, for a bath in the Gaṅgā alone as delimited by Prayāga, one should bathe there after making the resolve: "Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by bathing in the three and a half million sacred sites (*tīrtha*) located in the earth and the intermediate space, I shall perform the ritual bath in the Gaṅgā as delimited by Prayāga."

Then, on a certain day in any month, that shaving at Prayāga must be performed in some pure place within the city of Prayāga, such as in the vicinity of the Brahma-yūpa pillar; for even one who has already had his hair shaved by the Gaṅgā has the right to perform it there, depending on the difference in his desires and because of its necessity.

"Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā, a fruit equal to the fruit produced by dying at Kāśī, and a fruit equal to the fruit produced by giving gifts at Kurukṣetra, I shall have the shaving of my head performed at Prayāga. Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), it should be performed right there on the spot. Some, however, practice it [elsewhere].
And so it is said in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*: "There, a gift should be given according to the extent of one's wealth."
By that, the fruit of the sacred ford indeed increases; there is no doubt in this matter.
O Indra among kings, he dwells in heaven until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa.
Likewise, in the *Mātsya*: "He who indeed bestows a cow, or gold, gems, pearls, or even some other gift, between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā..."
Likewise, in that very same place: "He who there gives a Kapilā cow— of pale-red color,
with horns of gold, hooves of silver, a cloth around her neck, and full of milk."
At Prayāga, having duly instructed a virtuous Śrotriya who is clad in white garments, tranquil, knower of dharma, and a master of the Vedas;
And that cow should be given by him at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
along with costly garments and various kinds of jewels.
For as many thousands of years as there are pores on the bodies of that cow and her calf, for so long is he honored in the heavenly world.
In whatever place that [animal] takes birth, the cow is born there;
and by that deed, the donors do not see hell.
Having reached the Northern Kurus, he rejoices in imperishable bliss;
one who gives a single milch cow is worth more than giving hundreds of thousands of cows.
A single cow may ransom one's sons, wives, and likewise servants;
therefore, among all gifts, the gift of a cow is preeminent.

In a place that is difficult to traverse, treacherous, and terrible—a gateway to great sins—it is Gaurī alone who provides protection; therefore, she should be given to the most excellent of the twice-born.
Thus, the application here is as follows:
Oṃ, salutation to the cow Vilagavī together with her implements and her calf. Oṃ, salutation to the Brāhmaṇa.

Oṃ. Today, for this specific purpose, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, I, desiring protection from the transference of various terrible and great sins, and desiring the attainment of the world of heaven for as many thousands of years as there are hair-pores on the cow to be given, followed by the non-seeing of hell, the reaching of Uttarakuru, and the subsequent attainment of inexhaustible joy for a long time, along with many sons, wives, and servants, hereby bestow upon you, O Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such lineage and such-and-such name, this tawny cow—having golden horns, silver hooves, a cloth around her neck, yielding milk, accompanied by her calf, and endowed with costly garments and various many jewels—dedicated to the deity Rudra. I give her to you.
Thus he should give. Then the response is "Svasti" (May it be well).

Then—*Oṃ*. Today, for the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of this gift of a tawny cow (*kapilā-gavī*) together with her implements and her calf, I bestow this gold, whose deity is Agni, as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) upon you, the Brāhmaṇa named Amukadevaśarman of the Amuka lineage.
Then, having said "Svasti," the recipient should take hold of the tail and perform the hymn of desire (*kāmastuti*) according to his own *śākhā*. It is as follows:

In the *Ṛgveda*: "Who gave this? To whom did he give? Desire gave to Desire. Desire is the giver; Desire is the receiver. Desire entered the ocean. With Desire I receive you. O Desire, this is yours. You are a first-calf cow (*gṛṣṭi*); may Heaven give you; may Earth receive you. In the *Yajurveda*, having received [the gift] with the words: "May Heaven give you; may Earth receive you," [one says]: "Who gave? To whom did he give? Desire gave to Desire. Desire is the giver; Desire is the receiver. O Desire, this is yours."
