Sāmaveda: "Who has given this? To whom has he given it? Desire has given it to Desire. Desire is the giver; Desire is the receiver. Desire entered the ocean. With Desire I receive you; O Desire, this is yours. [45] Atharvaveda: "Who has given this? To whom has he given it? Desire has given it to Desire. Desire is the giver; Desire is the receiver. Desire entered the ocean. With Desire I receive you; O Desire, this is yours. May the Earth receive you; may this great intermediate space protect you from before."

In other instances of giving, the fruit is an increase in the merit of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), up to the attainment of residence in heaven until the dissolution of all things (*āhūtasaṃplava*).
Likewise, in the *Mātsya*: "He who enters the earth between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā..."
Whether it be gold, jewels, pearls, or whatever other gift may be received.
Whether in his own rites, in rites for the ancestors, or even in the worship of deities,
that sacred ford (tīrtha) becomes fruitless for him as long as he consumes that wealth.
A man should not accept gifts at sacred fords or in holy shrines, nor at any such auspicious occasions; he should never be heedless in these matters.
And regarding the *nimittas*, such as the transition [of the sun] and so forth, he is "not negligent," meaning free from negligence, that is to say, composed (*samāhita*).

Thus, in the case of accepting gifts at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), as long as the wealth accepted at that ford remains, the act of bathing and so forth at that ford does not produce the fruit of heaven for the recipient; this is the general fault in accepting gifts at any sacred ford. However, the specific fault in the case of the Gaṅgā and similar sites will be explained in the section on the Gaṅgā.
A "sacred ford" (*tīrtha*) refers to the Gaṅgā and so forth, while a "sanctuary" (*āyatana*) refers to Puruṣottama and so forth. Likewise, it is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
He who gives his daughter in marriage between these two [rivers], the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā,
does not see the terrible hell on account of that deed.
Having gone to the Northern Kurus, he rejoices in imperishable bliss;
he obtains righteous sons and wives endowed with beauty.

And thus the formula for the giving away of the daughter (*kanyādāna*) is as follows: having recited up to the words "this girl, whose deity is Prajāpati," one should employ the following: "Desiring the attainment of many sons and wives endowed with inexhaustible time, joy, righteousness, and beauty, and [desiring] the non-seeing of terrible hells and the subsequent going to Uttarakuru, I give her away as a wife.
Regarding the inhalation of smoke at Prayāga, in that very same place:
"That man who, with his head downward and arms raised upward, should drink smoke..."
He is honored in the heavenly world for a hundred thousand years.
But a man who has fallen away from the Agnihotra, O Indra among kings,
having enjoyed various pleasures, attains that sacred ford once again.
[47] Now, the fruit of death according to the Matsya Purāṇa:
From Prayāga to Pratiṣṭhāna, and from the pool of Vāsuki to the north,
there are the two Nāgas Kambala and Aśvatara, and the Nāga Bahumūlaka.
This is the field of Prajāpati, renowned throughout the three worlds;
having bathed there, they go to heaven, and those who die there are not born again.
The *Ṛgveda* also says:
"Those who bathe at the confluence of the white and dark rivers fly up to heaven."
Those wise ones who indeed cast off the body,
those people partake in immortality.

The meaning here is that whoever meets their death in this field of Prajāpati becomes a partaker of liberation. It means it possesses ten sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*). Death here is desirable, and all social classes (*varṇa*) have the right to die there. As it is said in the *Pādma*:
"O dear one, your mind should not be turned away from dying at Prayāga, neither by the words of the Vedas nor even by the words of the world."
Ten thousand holy fords (tīrthas), as well as sixty crores of others—
their presence is proclaimed to be in that very place, O joy of the Kurus.
Whatever destination belongs to a wise man who is devoted to yoga yet stands on a wrong path,
that same destination belongs to one who gives up their life at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Whether a man be afflicted by disease, or dejected, or even advanced in age,
he who reaches the Gaṅgā and Yamunā and there gives up his life—
With celestial palaces possessing the hue of glowing gold and the brilliance of the sun,
that man rejoices in heaven amidst the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
The preeminent sages declare that one obtains all desired objects;
[the chariot] is divine, composed of every kind of gem, and crowded with various banners.
Surrounded by excellent women in a celestial palace marked by auspicious signs,
he awakens from sleep to the sounds of singing and musical instruments.
As long as one does not remember their [former] birth, so long are they honored in heaven;
thereafter, having fallen from that heaven, their karma exhausted, they descend from the celestial realm.
He is born into a prosperous family, fully endowed with gold and jewels;
he remembers that very same sacred ford (tīrtha), and by remembering it, he goes there.
Likewise: "Whoever, having reached the foot of a banyan tree, should give up their life,
transcends all worlds and goes to the world of Rudra."
There indeed the twelve Ādityas have taken refuge in that Rudra;
they burn the entire world, yet the one who dwells at the root of the banyan tree is not burned.
The *vaṭa* is the Akṣayavaṭa;
and there the Lord Hari is present, preceded by Prajāpati—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Thus it is stated in the *Mātsya*.
Listen now to the fruit that belongs even to him who gives up his life on the delightful, vast, and swan-white sandy bank of the Urvashī.
[49] O lord of men, he shall dwell together with his ancestors in the heavenly world for sixty thousand and sixty hundred years.
That best of men shall always behold Urvaśī in the world of the gods,
and he is constantly honored by the gods, sages, gandharvas, and kinnaras.
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended from the celestial realm with his merit exhausted,
he obtains a hundred maidens who resemble Urvaśī.
He shall become the husband of many thousands of women in their midst;
he becomes a lord of the earth, the enjoyer of ten thousand villages.
Awakened by the sound of girdles and anklets,
he enjoys vast pleasures and then attains that sacred ford once again.
Likewise: "Always wearing white garments, self-restrained and with senses controlled,
eating but once a day for a month, one shall become a lord of enjoyments."
He obtains a hundred women adorned with golden ornaments and becomes a lord of great enjoyments over the earth as far as the oceans.
Endowed with wealth and grain, he becomes a constant giver;
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he remembers that sacred ford once again.
Likewise: "He who, having reached Koṭitīrtha, should give up his life,
is honored in the heavenly world for ten million thousand years."
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended from the celestial realm with his karma exhausted,
he shall be born handsome and endowed with gold, jewels, and pearls into a noble family.
Likewise:
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, whoever perishes in the Ganges,
having died, attains heaven and does not behold hell.
Awakened from sleep by the musical performances of hosts of apsarases,
he travels in a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes.
Then, having fallen from heaven and descended from the celestial realm with his karma exhausted,
he shall be born into a great family enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls.
Likewise:
One should maintain a fire of dried cow dung between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā;
[thereby] one becomes possessed of unimpaired limbs, free from disease, and endowed with all five senses.
As many as are the pores on the body of that wise one,
for so many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he shall become the lord of Jambudvīpa;
after enjoying vast pleasures, he remembers that sacred ford once again.
Likewise: "But as for one who, having cut his own body, gives it to birds— listen to what the fruit is even for him when he is devoured by the winged creatures."
He is honored in the world of Soma for a hundred thousand years;
even when he falls from there, he becomes a righteous king.
Virtuous, endowed with beauty, learned, and pleasant of speech,
having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he attains that sacred ford once again.
Likewise, in that very same *Padma Purāṇa*: "Listen, O King, O Lord! A wise man who is faithful and has conquered his senses obtains at Prayāga the fruit of fasting until death."
For him who goes [on this path], O King, there is the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice at every step;
he shall deliver ten generations of ancestors and ten generations of descendants.
One is liberated from all evils and goes to the supreme state.
Likewise: "In the sacred precinct of Prayāga, extending five yojanas,
[one sees] seven generations of ancestors who have passed away and fourteen who are yet to come."
But that man who would sacrifice his life saves all beings.
Likewise,
having begun with: "By the very same path by which the Gaṅgā has issued forth, the Yamunā has gone," [it continues:]
He who gives up his life there attains the supreme goal;
it is known as Agnitīrtha, situated on the southern bank of the Yamunā.
The western sacred ford of the King of Dharma is known as Naraka;
having gone there, those who die proceed to heaven and are no longer subject to rebirth.
Likewise, proceeding to the northern bank of the Yamunā: "And many other sacred fords (tīrthas) are remembered as removing all sins;
those who bathe in them go to heaven, and those who die there are not subject to rebirth."
Both the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā are remembered as yielding equal fruits;
yet, solely by virtue of her seniority, the Gaṅgā is honored everywhere.
Likewise: through thousands of other births, yoga may or may not be attained;
likewise, through thousands of yogas, yoga may or may not be attained.
But for one who bestows all kinds of jewels upon the brahmins,
yoga may or may not be attained through that gift given.
For one who dies at Prayāga, all this comes to pass; it is not otherwise.
Even for one who remembers Prayāga while dying elsewhere, the fruit is attained right there.
Whether one is in one's own country, in the forest, in a foreign land, or at home—[the result is the same].
But he who, even while merely remembering Prayāga, should give up his life;
The preeminent sages declare that one attains the world of Brahmā,
where the earth is made of gold and the trees bear fruit according to every desire.
There he goes to that world where ṛṣis, munis, and siddhas dwell,
on the beautiful and auspicious bank of the Mandākinī, crowded with thousands of women.
He rejoices here together with the ṛṣis through his own performed deeds;
in heaven, he is honored by the Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Gandharvas, and the deities.
Then, having fallen from heaven, he becomes a lord of Jambudvīpa;
thereafter, reflecting again and again upon auspicious deeds, he remains so.
There is no doubt that he becomes virtuous and endowed with wealth;
through his actions, mind, and speech, his righteousness is firmly established.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Exposition on Prayāga, in the Tīrthacintāmaṇi composed by the venerable Vācaspatimiśra.
[53] Now follows the procedure for Puruṣottama and others.
In that regard, in the *Brahma-purāṇa*, within the dialogue between Brahmā and the Brahmanical sages, there is this speech of Brahmā:
On earth, Bhāratavarṣa is declared to be the land of action;
indeed, nowhere else on the earth is karma ordained for mortals.
There, in the land of Bhārata, situated by the southern ocean,
lies the region renowned as Oḍra, which bestows both heaven and liberation.
Extending as far as the ocean to the region of the stainless mandala,
that land is adorned with every virtue by those of meritorious conduct.
O best of sages, there are indeed sacred fords and holy shrines that are to be known as existing in Utkala.
O best of the twice-born, on that shore of the ocean, in that region,
there lies a supreme secret place that grants liberation and destroys all sins.
Everywhere strewn with sand, pure, and granting all desires,
this field extends for ten yojanas and is exceedingly difficult to attain.
There is a most meritorious river there, flowing from the foothills of the Vindhya;
renowned as Citrotpalā, it is auspicious and the remover of all sins.
Likewise:
"Just as Soma is among the stars, and as the ocean is among bodies of water,
so Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas)."
Just as Pāvaka is among the Vasus and Śaṅkara is among the Rudras,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Meru is among peaked mountains and the Himalaya is among mountains, so Puruṣottama is the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Skanda is among generals and Kapila is among the Siddhas,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Airāvata is among the lords of elephants and Bhṛgu among the great sages,
so Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Uccaiḥśravas is among horses and Uśanas among poets,
so Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Vyāsa is among the sages and Kubera among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as the mind is among the senses, and as the earth is among the elements,
so is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as the Aśvattha is among all trees and the wind is among those that blow, so is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Arundhatī is among women and the thunderbolt is among weapons,
so is Puruṣottama the most excellent of all sacred fords.
Just as the syllable *a* is among all letters and the *gāyatrī* is among meters,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is among the social classes and Vainateya among birds,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Lakṣmī is among women and the Jāhnavī is among rivers,
so Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O best of the twice-born, just as the head is the most excellent among all limbs,
so too is Puruṣottama the most preeminent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as the science of liberation is remembered as the highest among all sciences,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords.
Just as a king is among men and the wish-fulfilling cow among milch cows, so is Puruṣottama the most excellent of all sacred fords.
Just as the crest-jewel is the best among all ornaments,
so is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as gold is the foremost among all jewels and Vāsuki among serpents,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Prahlāda is among all the Daityas and Rāma is among those who bear weapons,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as the Makara is among fish and the King of Beasts among animals,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent of all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Varuṇa is among aquatic beings and Yama is among those who exercise restraint,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as Kṣīroda, the lord of rivers, is the best among the oceans,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
O best of the twice-born, just as Nārada is the most excellent among the celestial sages,
so too is Puruṣottama the most distinguished among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as life is the foremost among priests, and time is the foremost among those who reckon, so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as gold is the best among riches and the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is the best among purifiers,
so too is Puruṣottama the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as the horse sacrifice is proclaimed to be the most excellent among sacrifices,
so too is Puruṣottama the best among all sacred fords.
Just as grain is among herbs and the king of grasses is among blades of grass,
so Puruṣottama is the most excellent among all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Just as among all dharmas, Dharma is the savior from saṃsāra,
so too among all sacred fords (tīrthas), Puruṣottama is the most excellent.
Truly, truly, again truly, that field is the supreme and great one;
having seen once that which is called Puruṣa, or having died once in the waters of the ocean,
or having known once the Brahma-vidyā, there is no dwelling in a womb again.

The meaning is this: for each of these—beholding the sacred field (*kṣetra*), dying in the waters of the ocean, and awakening to the knowledge of Brahman—the fruit is the absence of dwelling in a womb.
Thus, that most difficult-to-attain field, endowed with all virtues, exists there, O best of sages, as the renowned Puruṣottama.
In whatever place that Universal Soul, the Supreme Person,
the Lord of the World who pervades the universe, resides, there everything is established.
[57] "O best of sages, Rudra, Śakra, and we gods led by Agni always dwell in that region;
so too do the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Pitṛs, and gods and humans."
All the yakṣas, vidyādharas, and sages of celebrated vows;
the ṛṣis such as the Vālakhilyas and others; and the lords of progeny such as Kaśyapa and others.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Nāgas, and likewise other inhabitants of heaven;
the four Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, and various Śāstras as well.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, sacrifices accompanied by sacrificial fees,
various holy rivers, sacred fords, and shrines;
The oceans and likewise the mountains are situated in that region;
thus it is a most meritorious land, frequented by gods, sages, and ancestors.
To whom would dwelling in a place endowed with every enjoyment not be pleasing?
What other excellence could that land possess superior to this?
There dwells in person the Lord Puruṣottama, the bestower of liberation;
blessed are those men, renowned as wise, who dwell in Utkala.

Having bathed in the waters of the king of holy fords (tīrtharāja), those mortals who behold Puruṣottama dwell in heaven and not in the abode of Yama— those who reside in the meritorious field of Utkala at Śrī Puruṣottama.
Fruitful is the life of those wise men of Utkala who behold him with his beautifully copper-red lips, his clear and wide eyes,
his lovely brows, hair, and crown, and his charming, vine-like ears.
The lotus-face of Kṛṣṇa, with its beautiful nose, lovely cheeks, fine forehead, and auspicious marks, generates joy for the three worlds.
O brahmins, formerly in the Kṛta age, there was a glorious king known as Indradyumna, whose prowess was equal to that of Śakra.
He was truthful, pure, and skillful, the best among all wielders of weapons;
he was handsome, fortunate, heroic, a giver, an enjoyer, and sweet-spoken.
He was the performer of all sacrifices, devoted to Brahmanas, and true to his promise;
he was skilled and accomplished in the science of archery, the Vedas, and the Shastras.
He was beloved by men and women like the moon on a full-moon night;
he was difficult to gaze upon like the sun, yet as sweet as the moon.
A Vaiṣṇava who is endowed with truthfulness, who has conquered anger and subdued the senses,
who is devoted to the knowledge of the supreme self, who seeks liberation, and is intent upon dharma.
Thus that king, a mine of all virtues, protected the earth;
then, a thought arose in him regarding the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
How shall I propitiate Janārdana, the God of gods?
In which field, sacred ford, riverbank, or hermitage [shall I do so]?
Thus absorbed in thought, he then surveyed the earth with his mind,
beholding all the sacred fords, holy fields, and shrines.
Having reflected upon all those things, he went again in his mind to the famous and supreme sacred field, Puruṣottama, which bestows liberation.
Having gone there with his abundant army and vehicles,
that king performed the horse sacrifice according to the rules, bestowing profuse sacrificial fees.
Having caused a magnificent palace of great height to be built, renowned throughout the earth,
the valiant one installed there Saṅkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā.
Having duly performed the rite of the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha) there, the lord of the earth likewise performed bathing,
giving gifts, recitation of mantras, burnt offerings, and the sprinkling of water upon the deities.
Having worshipped Puruṣottama daily according to the rules with devotion,
he then attained liberation through the grace of the God of gods.
The sages said:
"O Lord, why was there no Vaiṣṇava image previously situated in that most excellent, beautiful, and Vaiṣṇava sacred field of Puruṣottama?"
Having gone there with his army and vehicles,
that king established Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and the auspicious Bhadrā.
O Lord of the World, we have a great doubt and wonder in this matter;
we all wish to hear it—please tell us the reason for that.
Brahmā said:
Listen to this ancient tale that destroys all sins;
I shall relate it in brief, as Hari was questioned by Śrī in the past.
On the golden peak of Mount Meru, which is endowed with every wonder,
he beheld the Lord of the World, the imperishable creator of the universe, residing there.
Having bowed her head to the Goddess out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
she asked this great question concerning the unsurpassed place on earth.
Śrī said:
"Speak, O Lord of all worlds, regarding the doubt residing in my heart,
concerning this mortal world— a land of great wonders and a field of karma so exceedingly difficult to attain."
O Lord of Gods, by what means are men liberated from the great ocean of worldly existence, which is a vast sea of greed, delusion, grasping, the grasper, desire, and anger?
Speak, O Lord of all gods, for you consider us who are bowed before you as ascetics;
apart from you, there is no one in this world capable of resolving our doubts.
Brahmā said:
Having heard these words of hers, Janārdana, the God of gods,
spoke with supreme affection words that were exceedingly essential and like nectar.
O Goddess, that best of sacred fords, renowned as Puruṣottama, exists there— a place of easy means, easily accomplished, effortless, and of great fruit.
There is no one equal to him to be found in the three worlds;
by chanting his name, O Goddess of gods, one is liberated from all sins.
It was not known by all the immortals, nor by the Daityas, nor by the Dānavas.
O fair-faced one, Marīci and other eminent sages [worship] my Lord Gopati on the shore of the southern ocean, where the Nyagrodha tree stands.
But he who, when a kalpa has arisen with its great downpour of meteors,
does not meet destruction because he remains established right there in that very state;
Merely by seeing him, or even by once stepping upon his shadow, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin; what need is there to mention other sins?
Those living beings who have performed circumambulation and offered salutations—
all of them, their sins shaken off, shall go to the abode of Keśava.
On the northern bank of the Nyagrodha and to the south of Keśava, there stands a palace; for that is indeed the abode consisting of Dharma.
Having seen that image there, fashioned by the Lord himself,
men go from there to my world without any effort.
O beloved, once, seeing them as they were departing, the King of Dharma approached me,
bowed his head, and spoke.
Yama said:
"Salutations to you, O Blessed One, O God, Lord of the worlds, Master of the universe!
[I bow] to the God who dwells in the Ocean of Milk and reclines upon the coils of Śeṣa."
To Viṣṇu— the bestower of boons, the most excellent, the giver of boons, the agent, the imperishable,
the all-pervading Lord of the universe, the unborn, the omniscient, and the unconquered.
Dark as the petal of a blue lotus, with eyes like white lotuses, the omniscient, devoid of qualities, peaceful, the sustainer of the world, and imperishable.
The creator of all worlds, the bringer of happiness to all worlds,
the ancient Person, the one to be known, both manifest and unmanifest, eternal.
The creator of the high and the low, the lord of the world, the teacher of the universe,
endowed with the Śrīvatsa upon his chest and adorned with a garland of forest flowers.
He is clad in yellow garments, possesses four arms, and holds a conch, a discus, and a mace;
he is adorned with necklaces and armlets, and wears a crown and bracelets.
Endowed with all characteristics yet devoid of all sense organs,
it is immutable, immovable, subtle, of the nature of light, and eternal.
I bow to that Lord of the World, the Sovereign and the Bestower of Bliss, who is free from existence and non-existence, all-pervading, and beyond primordial nature.
Thus, in former times, the King of Dharma, having praised [the Lord] with various kinds of hymns in the vicinity of the banyan tree, then prostrated himself.
O highly fortunate lady, seeing him standing bowed with palms joined in reverence,
I asked Antaka, O Goddess, the reason for his hymn of praise.
The Blessed One said:
"O mighty-armed Vaivasvata, you are indeed composed of all the gods;
for what purpose have you praised me in this way? Tell me that briefly."
Yama said: In this meritorious sanctuary, renowned as Puruṣottama,
an image made of sapphire was fashioned, which fulfills all desires.
Having seen her with single-minded devotion and faith, O lotus-eyed one,
men who are free from desire go to the world called Śveta.
Therefore, O destroyer of enemies, I am unable to perform this task;
be gracious, O Great God, and withdraw this manifestation, O Lord.
Having heard these words of Vaivasvata, she spoke thus:
"O Yama, I shall conceal her on all sides with sand."
Then, O Goddess, that image was hidden by me with creepers;
thus, men desiring heaven do not see it there.
Having covered him with creepers and cloths of gold, O Goddess,
she dispatched Yama toward his own city in the southern direction.
Brahmā said: When the image of sapphire had indeed vanished, at that time,
in that most excellent and meritorious field renowned as Puruṣottama.
The Blessed Lord Janārdana, the God of gods, related to her in the past all that had occurred there.
O twice-born ones, [this is the account of] Indradyumna’s journey, his sight of the sacred field,
the description of that field, and its spiritual rewards.
The sight of Baladeva and especially of Kṛṣṇa,
as well as that of Subhadrā, and their greatness in every respect, [is described] right there.
The vision of Narasiṃha, as well as the proclamation of his glorious manifestations;
the installation of Ananta-Vāsudeva within the Prasāda, that most excellent of all worlds; and the praise of his qualities upon seeing him.
The majesty of Śvetamādhava, a description of Svargadvāra,
the sight of the ocean, as well as the ritual bathing and the libations.
O twice-born ones, [I shall describe] the majesty of bathing in the ocean,
as well as the fruit of the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha) and likewise that of Mahājyaiṣṭhī, pertaining to Indradyumna.
The bathing of Kṛṣṇa and the Plough-wielder (Balarāma), as well as the fruit of all pilgrimages;
furthermore, the description of the realm of Viṣṇu and of the sacred field itself.
That Supreme Person spoke the truth to her as previously told.
The sages said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, tell us that ancient matter which I ask concerning the past."
Just as those images were formerly fashioned by Indradyumna.
And by what manner was Mādhava pleased with him?
Tell us all that, for our curiosity is indeed great.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O tigers among sages, to the Prāṇa which is equal to the Vedas;
I shall relate the ancient account and the origin of the images.
When the great sacrifice had commenced and the palace was completed, he wondered: "O Lord of Gods, by what means can the welfare of all the worlds be secured?"
O Lord of Gods, I do not know by what means I behold Puruṣottama, the creator of all worlds, the author of heaven, its maintenance, and its end.
[65] But the king became possessed by anxiety; he did not sleep by day or night, nor did he enjoy various pleasures, nor did he bathe or adorn himself.
Whether made of stone, clay, or wood, those images of Viṣṇu that are praised upon the earth are those that are endowed with all the auspicious marks.
"Of these three, that which is praised and worshipped by the gods brings joy when it is installed"— thus he became intent on reflection.
Having worshipped Puruṣottama according to the Pañcarātra ritual,
the king, overcome with anxiety, began to offer praise.
Indradyumna said:
O Vāsudeva, salutations be unto you; salutations to you, the cause of liberation!
Protect me, O Lord of all worlds, from the ocean of birth and saṃsāra.
O You who resemble the stainless sky, salutations to You, O Supreme Person!
O Saṅkarṣaṇa, salutations be to You; protect me, O Supporter of the Earth!
Homage to you, who shine like the interior of gold; homage to you, whose banner is the sea-monster! Homage be to you, O beloved of Rati; protect me, O destroyer of Sambara!
Homage to you, who resemble collyrium; homage to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees!
O Aniruddha, homage be to you; protect me and become a granter of boons.
Salutations to you, abode of the wise; salutations to you, beloved of the wise.
O Nārāyaṇa, let there be salutations to you; protect me, who have come to you for refuge.
Homage to you, best among the strong; homage to you, whose weapon is the plow!
Homage to you, foremost of the wise; homage to you, born from the lotus!
O four-faced one, abode of the world, protect me, O Great-Grandfather!
Salutations to you who resemble a dark blue cloud; salutations to you, worshipped by the thirty gods.
Save me, O Viṣṇu, Lord of the World, who am submerged in the ocean of existence!
Salutations to you, O destroyer of the sons of Diti, who resemble the fire of universal dissolution!
O Narasiṃha of great heroism, O flaming-eyed one, protect me!
Just as in the past the earth was lifted from the netherworld by you with your fangs.
Likewise, O Great Boar, protect me from the ocean of suffering;
these forms of yours, O Kṛṣṇa, which grant boons, have been praised by me.
You alone exist in separate forms as Baladeva and the others;
O Lord of Gods, O Master, Garuḍa and the rest are likewise Your limbs.
O Acyuta, the guardians of the quarters along with their weapons, Vāsava and the others, as well as whatever other manifestations of yours have been described by the wise, O Lord of Gods—
O Lord of the World, with your gracious and wide eyes,
all of them have been worshipped and praised by me, and likewise you all have been saluted.
"Grant me a boon that bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa;
for those manifestations of yours, such as Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others, have been proclaimed, O Hari."
Those [deities] are connected with your worship and are dependent upon you;
O Lord of Gods, in the ultimate sense, no distinction exists between them and you.
The various forms of yours that have been described are merely figurative;
how can a human being speak of You, who are non-dual, in terms of duality?
For you alone, O Hari, are all-pervading, of the nature of consciousness, and stainless;
your supreme form is devoid of both existence and non-existence.
Untainted, stainless, subtle, immutable, immovable, and eternal;
liberated from all limiting adjuncts, it is established as pure existence alone.
Indeed, even the gods do not know you; how then could I know you, O Lord?
Furthermore, as for that other form of yours, clad in yellow garments and possessing four arms—
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, wearing a crown and armlets,
endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, and adorned with a forest garland.
Therefore, O God, best among all the gods and granter of fearlessness to your devotees, the wise and others who rely upon you worship you.
Save me, O Lord with the beautiful lotus-face, for I am submerged in the ocean of sense-objects;
I see no other refuge in the world to whom I might go for protection.
O Beloved of Kamalā, O Madhusūdana, be gracious toward me;
for I am joined with hundreds of old age and diseases and oppressed by manifold sufferings.
Overcome by joy and sorrow, deluded, and tightly bound by the fetters of karma,
I have fallen into this most fierce and terrible ocean of saṃsāra.
In this ocean difficult to cross due to the waters of sense objects, agitated by the fish of passion and hatred,
deep with the whirlpools of the senses, and crowded with the waves of craving and grief.
O Lord, deluded by illusion, I have wandered for a very long time in that which is devoid of wonder, without support, essence-less, and utterly fickle.
Being born again and again among thousands of different species,
I have undergone many thousands and tens of thousands of births.
O Janārdana, various things have been experienced by me in this saṃsāra;
the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs and various treatises have been studied by me.
The Itihāsas and Purāṇas, as well as numerous arts and crafts;
discontent and contentment; accumulation, depletion, and expenditure.
O Lord of the World, I have experienced the decline, increase, and rise of fortune,
as well as the separations and reunions with wives, enemies, friends, and kinsmen.
Various fathers and likewise mothers have been seen by me;
I have experienced many sorrows as well as manifold pleasures.
Relatives, sons, brothers, and kinsmen have been obtained;
likewise, I have dwelt within the womb of women, slippery with feces and urine.

O Lord, great suffering was experienced by me while dwelling in the womb; likewise, O Hṛṣīkeśa, those many sufferings pertaining to childhood and youth, as well as those in old age, have indeed been undergone by me.
Those sufferings which exist at death, on the path of Yama, and in the abode of Yama— I have experienced them all in the hells, crowded with agonies.
And [the destruction] of worms, insects, and trees; of elephants, horses, deer, and birds;
of buffaloes and cows; and likewise of other forest-dwellers.
Among all the twice-born and among the wombs of Śūdras alike— among the wealthy and the learned Vedic scholars, as well as the poor and the ascetics.
O Lord, I have been born again and again in the houses of kings, royal servants, and other embodied beings.
O Lord, I have repeatedly entered into the state of servitude to many men;
likewise, I have experienced poverty, sovereignty, and lordship.
"I have killed, and others have killed; I have caused to be killed, and likewise others have been caused to be killed.
I have given many times to others, and by others has been given to me."
And for the sake of my father, mother, friends, kinsmen, and wife,
I have repeatedly succumbed to wretchedness, my face washed with tears.
O Lord, among gods, animals, humans, moving beings, and stationary things,
there is no place where I have not gone.
When shall I dwell in hell, O Lord of the World? When in heaven? When among the worlds of men, and when among the animal realms?
Just as on a water-wheel, a jar bound by a rope moves upward and downward,
and at what time does it remain in the middle?
And so I say, O best of gods: supported by the rope of karma, I move up, down, and across by means of the cycle of wandering.
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, so terrifying and hair-raising,
I have wandered for a very long time and never see its end.
O Hari, my senses are agitated; I do not know what I should do today.
Overwhelmed by grief and craving, I am senseless—toward which direction shall I go?
[70] Now, O Lord, I have come to you for refuge, overwhelmed with distress.
Save me, O Kṛṣṇa, for I am suffering and submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra.
Have mercy, O Lord of the World, if you consider me a devotee;
apart from you, I have no kinsman who will take care of me.
O Lord, having obtained you as my protector, may I have no fear anywhere—
whether regarding life or death, or likewise concerning security and well-being, O Master.
But as for those lowest of men, O God, who do not worship you according to the prescribed rule—
how can there be a good rebirth for them from the bondage of saṃsāra?
O Lord, what atonement can there be for those wicked men, the lowest of humanity, who defile you, a god? Is there any escape for them from that ocean of hell?
In whatever birth I may be born, O Father Hari, due to the bondage of my karma, may there always be firm devotion unto you.
Having propitiated you, O Supreme One, even the Daityas and other men who were self-restrained attained the highest perfection; who, O God, would not worship you?
Even Brahmā and the other gods are unable to praise you, who transcend primordial nature;
likewise, O Lord, though you have been praised by me through a state of ignorance.
Therefore, forgive this offense of mine if you have compassion for me;
for the virtuous, O Hari, grant forgiveness even to one who has committed an offense.
Therefore, be gracious, O Lord of Gods; I am your devotee who has taken refuge in you.
Since you have been praised by me, O God, with a mind imbued with devotion, may all that [praise], along with its constituent parts, be complete. O Vāsudeva, salutations be unto you!
[71] Brahmā said: Thus praised by him at that time, the one whose banner is Garuḍa was pleased and granted him, O best of sages, the fulfillment of his heart's desire.
The wise person who, having fully worshipped the Lord of the World, praises Him every day with this hymn, certainly attains liberation.
The wise person who, being pure, recites this supreme hymn at the three junctions of the day,
that man attains virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
Whoever should read it, or listen to it, or cause it to be heard with a concentrated mind,
that person, cleansed of all impurities, goes to the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
This auspicious [work] is blessed, a destroyer of sins, and a bestower of devotion and liberation;
it is secret, very difficult to obtain, and meritorious, and should not be given to just anyone.
One should never give this to an atheist, a fool, an ungrateful person, one who is arrogant, one of wicked intellect, or one who lacks devotion.
It should be given to one endowed with devotion, possessed of virtuous qualities and good character,
a devotee of Viṣṇu, peaceful, and distinguished by faith and the performance of religious observances.
This is the supreme cause for the destruction of all sins, known as compassion, which bestows both happiness and liberation,
and grants the fruit of every desire without exception.
This hymn of praise to Puruṣottama has been spoken by me.
[72] Those who constantly meditate upon that ancient Puruṣa, who is exceedingly subtle and resembles the clear sky, become partakers of liberation and enter Viṣṇu.
Just as clarified butter is offered with mantras into the sacrificial fire.
He alone is the God who destroys the suffering of existence; there is no other superior to him, nor any other besides him.
He is the creator, the protector, and indeed the bringer of the end.
Viṣṇu is the essence of all things without exception.
Of what use is their learning, of what use are their excellent virtues, their sacrifices, their gifts, or their fierce austerities,
if they possess no devotion here to Kṛṣṇa?
In the Teacher of the World, who bestows the bliss of liberation.
In this world, he is the fortunate one, he is pure, he is the wise one; he is most excellent through sacrifices, austerities, and virtues;
he is the performer of sacrifice, the giver, and the speaker of truth.
He who possesses devotion for the one called Puruṣottama.
Having thus praised and bowed down to the eternal Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, who bestows the fruits of all desires, those tigers among sages—
Overcome with anxiety, the protector of the earth spread kusha grass upon the ground;
with his mind fixed on that alone, he lay down to sleep upon the surface of the earth.
"How can the god of gods, Janārdana, come before my very eyes? At that time, may he be the god who removes my suffering"—thus he thought.
While that king was asleep, Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world,
[appeared] as the god bearing the conch and discus, with the mace and lotus in his hands.
It was equipped with the Śārṅga bow, arrows, and sword, a blazing circle of supreme splendor,
possessing the hue of the sun at the end of an eon, resembling blue lapis lazuli.
Seated upon the back of a Garuda, auspicious and possessing eight arms, he addressed that wise one: "Excellent, O King, O high-minded one!"
O protector of the earth, I am pleased with this divine sacrifice, as well as with your devotion and faith; why do you grieve in vain?
O King, regarding this eternal image which is worthy of royal worship:
I shall tell you the means by which you, O ruler of the earth, will obtain it.
When this night has passed and the stainless sun has risen,
at the edge of the ocean's waters, adorned with various trees.
Likewise,
O King, the great water of the salt ocean is seen at the shore, completely overwhelmed by its waves.
A great tree clinging to the bank stands firm both on land and in the waters;
though struck by the tides, it does not waver, being steadfast.
[74] Taking an axe in your hand, go then from the edge of the ocean;
wandering alone, O King, whatever tree you see—
Having observed this sign, cut down that tall tree of wondrous appearance without hesitation as it is being felled.
"O King, having seen her and reflected upon that very sight, fashion a likeness of her; abandon this delusive anxiety."
Having spoken thus, the illustrious Hari vanished from sight;
and he too, having observed the dream, was filled with supreme wonder.
Watching for that night, he remained with his mind fixed upon her;
the self-possessed one recited mantras and hymns dedicated to her.
When the night had turned to dawn, he, with his mind fixed on nothing else,
bathed properly in the ocean according to the prescribed ritual.
Having given gifts to the Brahmins, including villages and cities,
and having performed his morning rites, that best of kings departed.
Neither with chariot, nor on foot, nor with elephant, nor with a charioteer—
that lord of the earth entered the great ocean shore all alone.
He beheld that great tree, radiant and of vast proportions, with a massive trunk and lofty branches— sacred, extensive, and truly magnificent.
[75] Of great height and massive body, sleeping near the water’s edge,
with the dense luster of the color of madder, devoid of name and caste.
Likewise, the lord of men, seeing the tree of Viṣṇu, was filled with joy;
he then cut it down with a sharp and sturdy axe.
Thus the mind of Indra’s friend became divided;
yet, as he gazed at the piece of wood, a wondrous sight appeared.
Then both the high-souled Viśvakarman and Viṣṇu, assuming universal forms and equal in their noble birth, arrived there.
Blazing with their own splendors and adorned with divine garlands, perfumes, and ointments,
they then approached that king, the friend of Indra.
They both said, "O Great King, what will you do here?
For what purpose, O mighty-armed one, has this lord of the forest been cut down by you?"
How indeed was that tree felled, while you were alone in a great wilderness, in a desolate and dense forest, and on the bank of a mighty river?
O brahmins, having heard their words, that king was filled with joy and spoke to them words that were both gentle and sweet.
Seeing those two brahmins arrived there like the moon and the sun,
he paid homage to the Lords of the World and stood with his face cast downwards.
The king said:
"It is my intention to fashion an image for the worship of the God of gods, who is without beginning or end, infinite, and the Lord of the world."
I was pointed out by the supreme Great-Souled God of Gods at the end of a dream, and what was indicated has been related by me to you both.
Brahmā said: Having heard the words of the king, who was like the lord of the gods,
the Lord of the Universe, being pleased, spoke these words to him with great favor.
The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, O protector of the earth, that this mind is so supreme,
[given] to this terrible ocean of saṃsāra which resembles the leaf of a plantain tree."
In this world which is devoid of essence, abounding in suffering, agitated by desire and anger,
turbid with the whirlpools of the senses, difficult to cross, and hair-raising;
In this world which whirls with hundreds of various diseases and resembles a bubble upon water,
it is for this reason that your mind has been directed toward the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Blessed are you, O tiger among kings, adorned with all virtues;
blessed is the earth, together with its subjects, mountains, forests, and groves.
Together with its villages and cities, adorned by the four castes—
therein you, O tiger among kings, were the sovereign lord who protected the subjects.
"Come, come, O highly fortunate one! Stay with us two upon this pleasant and cool tree, engaged in discourses based on the Dharma."
"But this companion of mine has arrived, the best among artisans;
he is like Viśvakarman himself, visibly skilled in all crafts.
He shall fashion the images as I have directed; leave the bank."
Brahmā said: Having heard those words of the twice-born one, the king then left the shore of the ocean and went into his presence.
That best of kings stood in the very cool shade of a tree;
then, the Soul of the Universe assumed for him a form identical to his own.
"O best of Brahmins, have an image made for the chief of artisans—
a supreme form of Kṛṣṇa, profoundly peaceful, with eyes as broad as lotus petals."

[One should meditate upon] the second [deity], the immensely powerful god named Ananta, who bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, who holds the conch, discus, and mace, who is fair-complexioned with the luster of the ocean of milk, who is marked with the Svastika, and who wields the plow-weapon.
Indeed, his end was not known by the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, vidyādharas, or uragas; therefore, he is remembered as Ananta (the Infinite).
The sister of Vāsudeva,
the third [of his sisters], Subhadrā, who was gold-colored, most beautiful, and endowed with all auspicious marks.
Having heard these words of his, Viśvakarman, the performer of noble deeds,
had auspicious images fashioned at that very moment.
They were beautifully adorned with ears graced by two variegated earrings.
With hands placed upon a wheel and a plow, they are esteemed by the virtuous;
first, it has the appearance of a white color, with a radiance equal to the autumnal moon.
With blood-red eyes, a massive body, and a head formidable with matted locks,
he was divine, clad in blue garments, and wielding a great mace.
The second has lotus-eyes, resembles a dark blue cloud,
is like the color of an *atasī* flower, and has eyes as broad as lotus petals.
I salute Hari, who is clothed in yellow garments, exceedingly fierce yet auspicious, marked with the Śrīvatsa,
holding the divine discus in his hand, and the remover of all sins.
The third [form] has the luster of gold, with eyes as broad as lotus petals,
covered in variegated garments, and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
Viśvakarman fashioned her, endowed with various ornaments, draped with strings of jewels, possessing full and elevated breasts, and truly beautiful.
Then that king, seeing them created in a single moment,
covered with pairs of divine garments and adorned with various jewels, [was amazed].
The statues, endowed with all the auspicious marks and exceedingly beautiful,
having reached a state of supreme wonder, spoke these words:
Indradyumna said:
"O two gods, why have you both arrived here assuming the forms of brahmins?
You are both performers of wondrous deeds, divine in nature yet appearing as humans."
Are you two gods or even humans, or perhaps yakṣas or vidyādharas? Are you Brahmā and Viṣṇu, or the Vasus, or the Aśvins?
I do not know whether you two are real beings or exist in the form of an illusion;
I have come to you for refuge—reveal yourselves to me.
The twice-born said: "I am neither a god, nor a yakṣa, nor a daitya, nor the king of the gods;
I am neither Brahmā nor Rudra—know me to be Puruṣottama."
The remover of suffering for all worlds, possessing infinite strength and prowess,
he is indeed to be worshipped by all beings, for his end is not known.
It is found in all scriptures and proclaimed in the Vedāntas;
it is that which is called Vāsudeva by yogis as being attainable through meditation.
I alone am Brahmā himself; I am Viṣṇu, and indeed I am Śiva.
I am Indra, the king of the gods, and Yama, the restrainer who has gone beyond all bounds.
O King, the elements beginning with earth, the three sacrificial fires, the consumer of oblations,
Varuṇa the lord of waters, I myself, the earth, and the mountains [are all under my control].
Whatever consists of speech in the world, the universe of moving and unmoving beings, the entire world of the mobile and immobile—there is nothing whatsoever other than Me.
I am pleased with you, O best of kings; choose a boon, O you of excellent vows.
I shall grant whatever is desired and established in your heart;
for those devoid of merit, a vision of me does not occur even in a dream,
yet you, because of your firm devotion, have seen me face to face.
[80] Brahmā said:
O twice-born ones, having heard these words of Vāsudeva,
the king’s body became covered in horripilation, and he sang this hymn of praise.
The King said:
O Beloved of Śrī, obeisance be unto You; O Lord of Śrī, clad in yellow garments;
O Giver of Śrī, Lord of Śrī, Abode of Śrī; obeisance to You, O Sanctuary of Śrī.
I bow down to the primordial Puruṣa, the Lord, the Master of all, whose face is turned in every direction— the partless, supreme, eternal God.
Beyond sound, beyond qualities, devoid of existence and non-existence,
untainted, devoid of attributes, subtle, all-knowing, and the source of all beings.
Resembling a monsoon cloud, devoted to the welfare of cows and Brahmins,
the protector of all, all-pervading, and the source of all existence.
I bow to the God who bears the conch and the discus, who holds the mace and the club,
the boon-granting Lord whose complexion is like the petal of a blue lotus.
I bow to Hari, Hṛṣīkeśa, who reclines upon the serpent-couch, who dwells in the Ocean of Milk, and who removes all sins.
Once again, O Lord of the gods of gods, I bow to you, the all-pervading bestower of boons,
Viṣṇu, the Lord of all worlds, the imperishable cause of liberation.
Brahmā said:
Having thus praised that god, having prostrated with palms joined in reverence,
and having fallen upon the surface of the earth, he spoke while bowing low.
[81] The king said:
"If you are pleased with me, O Lord, I choose this supreme boon:
may the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and mahoragas [be under my power]."
The Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Sādhyas, Kinnaras, and Guhyakas,
as well as the highly fortunate Ṛṣis who are experts in various treatises;
Wandering mendicants engaged in yoga, those who contemplate the true meaning of the Vedas,
and others who know the path to liberation— all meditate upon the supreme state.
Through your grace, I desire to attain that most difficult-to-reach state which the wise behold as devoid of qualities, stainless, and peaceful.
The Blessed One said:
"May all be well with you; may you obtain everything according to your desire.
By my grace, it shall be exactly as you wish; of this there is no doubt."
"O best of kings, rule over a great kingdom for ten thousand and nine hundred years without interruption."
You shall attain that supreme, divine state, difficult even for gods and asuras to reach—
a state that fulfills all desires, is peaceful, secret, unmanifest, and imperishable.
Higher than the highest, subtle, untainted, immovable, and eternal;
free from anxiety and sorrow, and devoid of action and its cause.
Therefore, I shall show you that supreme state called the Knowable,
having attained which you will reach supreme bliss and the highest goal.
And may your fame, O Indra among kings, endure upon this earth as long as the world, the sky, the moon, the sun, and the stars exist.
As long as the seven oceans exist, and as long as Mount Meru and the other mountains remain,
and as long as the gods abide in heaven, so long shall they remain everywhere immutable.
There is a sacred ford named Indradyumna-saras, born from the components of a sacrifice;
having bathed there even once, a person shall attain the world of Śakra.
O dear one, he who shall cause alms to be given at that auspicious lake will uplift twenty-one generations of his family and go to the world of Śakra.
Honored by apsarases and by the melodic songs of gandharvas,
he shall dwell there in a celestial chariot for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
To the south of the lake, situated toward the southwest, stands a banyan tree; near it is a pavilion.
Covered with groves of *ketakī* flowers and crowded with various trees,
[this place was visited] on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, under the constellation presided over by the ancestors (*pitṛ-daivata*).
Under the constellation Ṛkṣa, they will lead us there, and having led us, they will indeed keep us for seven days in a pavilion,
adorned with beautiful courtesans and splendid ornaments.
With various kinds of sports, enchanting dances and songs,
and with yak-tail whisks on golden handles, as well as fans adorned with jewels.
Then supreme women will stand fanning us;
likewise, celibate students, ascetics, and those who have completed their studies—the best of the twice-born—will be there.
Forest-dwellers, householders, perfected ones, and other brahmins offered praise with hymns consisting of various syllables and words, and with the sounds of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
O King, they will again offer praise to Rāma and Keśava;
then, having praised them, beheld them, and bowed down with devotion, [they shall depart].
That person shall dwell for ten thousand divine years in the glorious city of Hari,
being honored by apsarases and by the sounds of the songs of gandharvas.
There, a follower of Hari indeed sports with Keśava in a sun-colored celestial chariot, resplendent with necklaces of jewels.

He dwells in a supreme palace with all desired objects and great enjoyments; then, upon the exhaustion of his merit from asceticism, having returned here, he becomes a human being— a glorious Brāhmaṇa,
a lord of ten million in wealth, and certainly a master of the four Vedas.
Brahmā said:
O Brahmins, having thus granted him the boon and established an agreement, Hari vanished from sight along with Viśvakarman.
Then that king, thrilled and with the hair on his body standing on end,
considered himself to have accomplished his purpose through the sight of Hari.
Then [he took] Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā, the bestower of boons,
in chariots resembling celestial palaces (vimānas), variegated with jewels and gold.
Then, having greeted them with sounds of victory and auspiciousness,
the wise king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, brought them in.
Having established it in an auspicious, pure, and very beautiful location, amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and the auspicious chanting of the various Vedas, [84]
Then, on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, at a time marked by auspicious signs,
he performed the consecration ceremony together with the twice-born at a most propitious moment.
Having performed everything according to the prescribed method and the ritual seen in the injunctions, with the approval of his preceptor, the lord of the earth—
Then the lord, having given the sacrificial fee to the preceptor according to the rules,
likewise gave wealth to the officiating priests and others in accordance with the prescribed rites.
Having performed the consecration according to the rules in that most excellent palace,
he installed them all through rites prescribed by the sacred ordinances.
Then, having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with various fragrant flowers,
and with very beautiful garments enriched with gold, gems, and pearls;
And with various divine jewels, edicts, villages,
and towns, he gave horses, his own territories, cities, and royal capitals.
Having thus bestowed many kinds of gifts and ruled the kingdom as was fitting,
he performed various sacrifices and gave gifts on numerous occasions.
Then the king, having accomplished his purpose and renounced all possessions,
went to that supreme abode, the highest station of Viṣṇu.
Thus, O best of sages, I have related to you this most excellent king and the majesty of the sacred field; what else do you wish to hear?
[85] Having heard these words of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest,
the Brahmins regarded them as a marvel and then questioned him once again.
The sages said:
O best of gods, at what time should one go to Puruṣottama?
And by what rite, O Lord, should the Pañcatīrtha be performed?
And tell me, one by one, the specific fruit that comes from bathing and giving gifts at each individual sacred ford, as well as the fruit of beholding the deity.
Brahmā said: He who, having conquered his senses and subdued his anger, performs penance for ten thousand times seven years at Kurukṣetra on a single foot while abstaining from food;
Having observed a fast and beheld Puruṣottama even once on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one obtains a fruit far greater than that.
Therefore, O best of sages, in the month of Jyeṣṭha, mortals who desire the heavenly world should, with great effort and well-restrained senses, behold Puruṣottama.
Having duly performed the Pañcatīrtha rite in the month of Jyeṣṭha,
the best of men should behold that Puruṣottama on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight.
Those who behold the imperishable God, Puruṣottama, on the twelfth lunar day,
reach the world of Viṣṇu and never again fall away.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should go with great effort during the month of Jyeṣṭha;
having duly performed the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha), Puruṣottama is to be beheld.
Even one who stands at a great distance, if with devotion he glorifies Puruṣottama day after day, being purified in soul, shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
A man who, full of faith and concentrated in mind, undertakes a pilgrimage to Kṛṣṇa,
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having seen the wheel situated atop the palace from afar,
a man who bows down to it with devotion is suddenly liberated from sin.
[87] Now follows the procedure for the five sacred bathing places (*pañcatīrtha*).
According to the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Brahmā said:
O twice-born ones, hereafter I shall proclaim the procedure for the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha),
as well as the fruit obtained through bathing, giving gifts, and beholding the deity there.
Having gone to the Mārkaṇḍeya lake and bathed, being pure and facing the north,
one should indeed immerse oneself three times while reciting this mantra:
Save me, who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, seized by sin, and devoid of consciousness; O Lord of the Bhaga-eyes, enemy of Tripura, homage be to you!
Salutation to Śiva, the peaceful one, and the remover of all sins;
O Lord of Gods, I perform this bath; may my evil be destroyed.
Standing in water reaching up to his navel, the wise man should, according to the prescribed rule, gratify the deities, the sages, the ancestors, and others with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Having bathed in this manner and likewise sipped water for purification, one should then proceed to the abode of Śiva;
having entered the temple of the deity and performed three circumambulations.
O brahmins, having worshipped the Lord of Mārkaṇḍeya with the root mantra and having prostrated with the Aghora mantra, one should propitiate him.
[88] Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva— this is the root mantra. Oṃ, obeisance be to you who are the non-terrible, the terrible, the most terrible, to all, to every one of them, in your forms as Rudras.
Thus is this Aghora mantra:
"O Three-eyed One, salutations be to you; salutations to you, O Moon-adorned One!
Protect me, O Sightless One, O Mahādeva; salutations be to you!"
Having thus bathed in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake and beheld Śaṅkara,
a person obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Completely liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all that is summoned (the end of the kalpa).
Having reached this world, a Brahmin may become deeply learned;
then, having attained the yoga of Śaṅkara, he shall obtain liberation.
Then, having gone to the Kalpavṛkṣa and performed three circumambulations of it,
one should worship that banyan tree with supreme devotion using this mantra.
Oṃ, homage to you of unmanifest form, the cause of the great dissolution;
homage be to you, Nyagrodha, who is seated upon the great essence.
O immortal one, you are always present in this kalpa; O banyan tree, the abode of Hari!
O Nyagrodha, remove my sin; O Kalpavṛkṣa, salutations be unto you.
Having performed a circumambulation with devotion and having bowed to the Kalpavaṭa tree,
a person is suddenly liberated from sin, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
[89] O twice-born ones, by stepping into the shadow of that Kalpa tree, a man may abandon even the sin of killing a Brahmin; what need is there to mention other sins?
O twice-born ones, having seen Viṣṇu in the form of a banyan tree, born from the body of Kṛṣṇa, supreme and consisting of Brahmanic splendor, they prostrated before him.
He obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and even more;
likewise, having uplifted his own lineage, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having paid homage to Vainateya, who stands before Kṛṣṇa,
one is liberated from all sins and shall thereafter proceed to the city of Viṣṇu.
Having seen Vaṭa and Vainateya, whoever beholds Puruṣottama,
Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Subhadrā, attains the supreme goal.
Having entered the temple of Viṣṇu and performed three circumambulations of it,
one should worship Saṅkarṣaṇa and Subhadrā with devotion and propitiate them.
Homage to you, O Rāma, wielder of the plow; homage to you, whose weapon is the mace!
Homage to you, beloved of Revatī; homage to you, who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Homage to you, O best of the strong; homage to you, O upholder of the earth! Homage be to you, O enemy of Pralamba; protect me, O elder brother of Kṛṣṇa!
Thus he propitiated Ananta, the unconquerable one worshipped by the thirty gods,
who resembles the peak of Mount Kailāsa and whose face is more beautiful than the moon.
The god wears blue garments, his head is formidable with hoods,
he possesses great strength, holds a plow, and is adorned with a single earring.
A person who worships Rauhiṇeya with devotion shall obtain their desired fruit;
liberated from all sins, they go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed happiness there until the dissolution of the world,
the wise one returns here upon the exhaustion of his merit to a preeminent family of yogins.
Having become the most eminent of Brahmins and having mastered the meaning of all the scriptures,
one attains knowledge therein and achieves liberation, which is difficult to obtain.
Having thus worshipped the wielder of the plow, the wise man, being well-composed, should then worship Kṛṣṇa with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having worshipped Kṛṣṇa, the teacher of the world, with devotion using the twelve-syllable mantra and offerings such as perfumes and flowers, one should prostrate and seek his grace.
Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the Universe! Victory to you, destroyer of all sins!
Victory to you, slayer of Cāṇūra and Keśin! Victory to you, annihilator of Kaṃsa!
Victory to you, whose eyes are like lotus petals; victory to you, the wielder of the discus and the mace!
Victory to you, dark as a blue rain-cloud; victory to you, the bestower of all happiness!
Victory to you, O God, worshiped by the world; victory to you, the destroyer of saṃsāra!
Victory, O Lord of the World, O Protector! Victory, O Bestower of the fruits of one's desires!
In this terrible, essence-less ocean of worldly existence, which is frothing with suffering.
In this world, turbulent with the seizing demons of anger, fierce, flooded by the waters of the sense-objects,
filled with the spray of waves of various diseases, and difficult to cross due to the whirlpool of delusion;
"I am submerged, O best of gods; save me, O Puruṣottama!
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, the giver of boons who is affectionate toward his devotees, [he spoke].
The god who removes all sins and bestows the fruits of all desires—
dark-complexioned, with a beautiful nose, two arms, and eyes as broad as lotus petals.
Broad-chested and long-armed, clad in yellow garments with a beautiful countenance,
holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, and adorned with a crown and armlets.
Having seen [the Lord] endowed with all the marks and adorned with a forest garland, a person, having joined his palms in reverence, should prostrate himself like a staff.
O twice-born ones, one obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices—
that fruit which is proclaimed to result from bathing and giving gifts at all sacred fords.
A person obtains that fruit by seeing Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him—
the fruit which is found among all the gods and the fruit which is found in all sacrifices.
A man obtains that fruit by bowing to Kṛṣṇa,
which is the fruit gained through all forms of giving, religious observances, and self-restraint.
A person obtains that fruit by seeing Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him—
the fruit which is proclaimed to result from various kinds of fierce austerities.
A person obtains that fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him,
which fruit is proclaimed as resulting from celibacy properly practiced.
A person attains that fruit by seeing Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him—
the very fruit which has been declared to result from renunciation as it has been described.
A person attains that fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa and bowing down to him.
Moreover, O twice-born ones, what is the use of speaking much regarding his majesty?
Having seen Kṛṣṇa with devotion, a person attains liberation, which is difficult to obtain;
freed from sins arising over ten million kalpas, his soul becomes purified.
Endowed with supreme ritual action and possessed of all virtues,
he shall travel in a resplendent celestial chariot that fulfills every desire.
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, a man shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
there, for a hundred kalpas, he shall enjoy all desired pleasures.
Together with Gandharvas and Apsarases, like the four-armed Viṣṇu,
he descended from there and came here into a family of preeminent Brahmins.
He becomes all-knowing and a lord of all goddesses, free from envy;
devoted to his own duty, peaceful, generous, and intent on the welfare of living beings.

Having attained Vaiṣṇava knowledge, one shall then obtain liberation. Although here, because of the hearing of the words "having seen" and "having bowed," the connection with the fruit would seem to apply only to the combination [of acts], lest there be a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), nevertheless, since the fruit is concluded in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) with regard to seeing alone, the connection with the fruit applies to each [act] individually.
Then, having worshipped Subhadrā, who is affectionate toward her devotees, with her own mantra:
And one should propitiate them, O brahmins, by prostrating with palms joined in reverence.
Homage to you, O all-pervading Goddess; homage to you, the bestower of auspiciousness and happiness!
Protect me, O lotus-petal-eyed one; O Kātyāyanī, let there be homage to you!
Having thus propitiated that goddess, the sustainer of the world and benefactress of the world—
Subhadrā, the auspicious sister of Baladeva and bestower of boons— [93]
By means of a celestial chariot that moves at will, a person shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
having sported there like a god until the dissolution of all things, he shall remain.
Having attained human birth here, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas;
having obtained the yoga of Hari there, one certainly attains liberation.
Brahmā said:
Having thus seen Kṛṣṇa and having prostrated before Subhadrā,
a man certainly attains virtue, wealth, desire, and liberation.
Having emerged from the temple of the deity, a man would have accomplished his purpose;
having paid homage in the sanctuary, he should then depart from there with a concentrated mind.
Where Viṣṇu, resembling a sapphire, dwells covered by sand,
one should bow to him even though he is invisible, and from there proceed to the city of Viṣṇu.
O brahmins, he who is composed of all the gods and who slew the foremost of the asuras sits there, his body formed in the shape of half a lion.
Having beheld that god Narakesarin with devotion and having prostrated before him, a mortal is liberated from all sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
Those men on earth who are devotees of Narasiṃha—no evil deed of theirs shall bear fruit; rather, their desired goal shall be attained.
Therefore, with every effort one should take refuge in Narasiṃha,
for he bestows the fruits of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
Therefore, O tiger among sages, one should always worship him with devotion—
the king of beasts, possessed of great heroism, who bestows the fruit of all desires.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, Śūdras, and those of the lowest castes—
having worshipped that best of gods who had assumed the form of a lion with devotion— [attained their goal].
They are liberated from inauspicious sufferings arising from ten million births;
and having fully worshipped that best of gods, they obtain their heart's desire.
O twice-born ones, it bestows the state of a deity, the lordship of the immortals, and the status of the Lord of Wealth;
it likewise grants the state of a yakṣa or vidyādhara, as well as other [attainments].
In this context, he states the fruit of the practice of the Narasimha mantra—
Brahmā said:
"Listen as I speak of the power of Narasimha."
Of the unconquered, the immeasurable, and the bestower of both enjoyment and liberation.
O twice-born ones, who is able to describe all of his qualities? I shall speak of him, whose body was formed from half a lion, only in brief.
Whatever accomplishments are heard of here, achieved by gods and humans, they all come to fruition through his grace; of this there is no doubt.
By the grace of that God, one's movement becomes unimpeded in heaven, on earth, and in the underworld, in the cardinal directions, in water, in the sky, and upon mountains.
O Brahmins, for that Lord Narasiṃha, who is ever compassionate toward his devotees, there is nothing in this world of moving and unmoving beings that is impossible for him to accomplish.
[95] I shall describe the ritual procedure that benefits devotees,
by which this one whose form is half-lion becomes propitiated.
Listen, O tigers among men, to this eternal king of manuals,
which concerns the reality of Narasiṃha and which has not been understood even by the gods and asuras.
The lord of sages, the master of practitioners, subsists on vegetables, barley-gruel, roots, fruits, oil-cakes, and parched grain flour, or else lives on milk alone.
Clad in a loincloth made of kāśa grass, intent on meditation, and having conquered his senses,
he should dwell in a forest, a region of victory, on a mountain, or at the confluence of rivers.
Having installed [the image] in a saline soil, in a sacred field of accomplishment (siddhakṣetra), or likewise in a sanctuary of Narasiṃha,
one should personally perform worship according to the prescribed rite.
Having fasted on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, O best of sages,
one who has restrained the senses should mentally recite the mantra twenty lakhs of times.
O Brahmins, the practitioner who is joined with minor offenses (upapātaka) and even those joined with great sins (mahāpātaka) shall be liberated from them; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed a circumambulation there, one should worship Narasiṃha with perfumes,
flowers, and incense, bowing one's head to the Lord.
One should place jasmine flowers anointed with camphor and sandalwood upon the head of Narasiṃha; from that, perfection arises.
The Blessed One is never obstructed in any of his activities;
all the gods, including Brahmā, Rudra, and others, are unable to withstand him.
[96] Furthermore, what need is there to mention the Dānavas in this world, the Siddhas, Gandharvas, and humans,
the Vidyādharas, the hosts of Yakṣas, along with the Kinnaras and Mahoragas?
They all go to destruction, consumed by the divine and fierce splendor;
by reciting [the mantra] once with the "Flame of Fire" (agniśikhā), one gains protection from every calamity.
The armor, when recited twice, protects even gods and dānavas from bhūtas,
piśācas, rākṣasas, and whatever other adversaries may exist.
O best of the twice-born, this divine armor, which grants fearlessness even from gods and asuras, becomes effective within a radius of twelve yojanas when recited three times.
The Lord, the divine Narasiṃha of great strength, protects [it];
therefore, having fasted for three nights, one should go and enter the gate.
Having kindled the Lord Jātavedas with palāśa wood,
one should offer oblations there of palāśa fuel-sticks soaked in the three sweets.
O tiger among the twice-born, when two ayutas have passed, the one who accomplishes the fire of the *kaṭaka* [mantra] will then,
in an instant, cause the door of the subterranean opening to become manifest.
Then the wise man, clad in armor, should enter the opening without hesitation;
as he proceeds while situated in that narrow passage, darkness and delusion perish.
O twice-born ones, the royal road is seen to have been crossed by the Blessed One;
there, O twice-born ones, remembering Narasiṃha, he enters Pātāla.
Having gone there, one should recite the reality of that imperishable Narasiṃha;
thereafter, thousands of women will appear, engaged in playing lutes and waving whisks.
The Brahmins come forth from the city and say, "Welcome!
They lead the lord of practitioners by the hand and cause him to enter;
then the best of the twice-born make him drink the divine elixir.
Upon merely drinking it, one becomes possessed of a divine body and great strength;
one sports with celestial maidens until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa.
With his body dissolved, he merges into Vāsudeva; of this there is no doubt.
Just as one who has no appetite for fodder turns away, so too does he depart once more.
A silk cloth, a spear, a sword, yellow pigment, and likewise a jewel; elixir, an alchemical potion, sandals, and even a person.
O best of sages, [he gave] a black antelope skin, realgar, red arsenic,
a water-pot, a rosary, as well as the sixth [siddhi], Sañjīvanī.
Having acquired the perfected vidyā and the scriptures, the supreme practitioner [visualizes] the three-pronged [vajra] within his heart, enveloped by waves of blazing sparks of fire.
Cast down but once, it would burn away all the sins born of ten million lifetimes;
poison cast upon poison would destroy it, and it would destroy leprosy residing in the body.
Having committed such acts as foeticide within one's own body, one is purified by means of the divine rite;
for those possessed by great malevolent spirits, one should meditate upon [the deity] as blazing.
[98] Then, by means of the heart-mantra, even terrible planetary influences will quickly perish;
when tied around the necks of children, it becomes a constant protection.
It certainly effects the destruction of swellings, tumors, and goiters;
for the eradication of disease, one should perform a fire-oblation with sacrificial fuel-sticks and clarified butter mixed with milk.
By practicing this for one month at the three junctions of the day, it shall destroy all diseases;
I see nothing within the realm of the moving and the unmoving that is incurable by this reality.
Whatever success he desires,
that he certainly attains after having worshipped the Lord of Beasts one hundred and eight times.
One should smear with cow’s milk seven types of earth taken from an anthill, a cremation ground, and a crossroads, mixed with red sandalwood.
Having fashioned an image of a lion measuring six finger-breadths,
one should especially draw it upon birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā).
Having bound it around the neck of a man-lion (narasiṃha) and having performed worship at a body of water, the knower of mantras should recite [the mantra] without regard for a fixed number.
If one recites the mantra for seven days with the senses fully restrained,
the entire earth becomes covered with water in an instant.
Alternatively, one should worship Narasiṃha at the top of a dry tree;
having recited the essential mantra eight hundred times, one may ward off falling rain.
The supreme practitioner, having thus bound it to a cloth, should whirl it around;
in a mere moment, a great wind will arrive—of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, one should sprinkle it with water over which the mantra has been recited seven times;
then, the practitioner should bury that image at the door of the person [against whom it is directed].
If it is extracted, his lineage will perish; but when it is removed, it bestows peace.
Therefore, O tigers among sages, one should always worship it with devotion.
Having seen, praised, bowed to, and worshipped Narakeśarī— the king of beasts, possessed of great heroism, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires—
men obtain kingdoms, heaven, and even liberation, which is difficult to attain.
Having beheld Narasiṃha, a person obtains his desired fruit;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
But by seeing that god, who bears the form of a lion, even once with devotion,
one is liberated from all impurities arising from ten million births.
In battle, in distress, in a difficult pass, when afflicted by thieves, tigers, and the like; in the wilderness, when life is in danger, and amidst poison, fire, and water.
And when afflicted by kings and others, or by the distress of planetary influences and diseases in battle,
a person who remembers Him is liberated from all calamities.
Just as darkness meets its destruction upon the rising of the sun,
even so do all calamities come to an end at the sight of him.
When Narasiṃha is propitiated, one attains the supreme abode at Guṇḍikāñjanapātālapāda, as well as other desired objects.
Whatever desires a man contemplates while worshipping Narakeśarī, he attains those very desires; there is no doubt in this matter.
He speaks of the subject at hand:
Having seen that Lord of the gods of gods, having worshipped him with devotion, and having prostrated before him,
one obtains ten times the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Completely liberated from all evils, adorned with all virtues,
his self enriched by the fulfillment of all desires, and free from old age and death.
