By means of a golden celestial chariot, garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
which fulfills all desires, moves at will, and is exceedingly radiant.
With the color of the rising sun, adorned with hanging strings of pearls,
accompanied by hundreds of celestial women, and resounding with the music of divine gandharvas.
Having extracted the twenty-one lineages, a man— joyful and happy like a god,
and being praised by apsarases— shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there in the world of Viṣṇu, O best of the twice-born,
that man assumes a four-armed form and is joined by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having enjoyed a bliss that brings complete delight until the dissolution of the world at the end of the kalpa,
he has now returned here upon the exhaustion of his merit to a preeminent family of yogins.
A Brahmin may become a master of the four Vedas, one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
then, by resorting to Vaiṣṇava yoga, he shall attain liberation.
And likewise, in that very same place,
Brahmā said:
"Having beheld Vāsudeva, who is named Ananta, and having bowed down with devotion..."
[101] A man who is completely liberated from all evil goes to the supreme state.
Endowed with all the primary marks, with eyes as long as lotus petals,
marked on his chest with the Śrīvatsa, he is exceedingly serene and possesses four arms.
His chest was covered by a forest garland; he wore a crown and armlets, was clad in yellow garments, possessed broad and well-filled shoulders, and was adorned with two earrings.
Having bathed in the Śvetagaṅgā, he who beholds Śvetamādhava and also Mādhava known as Matsya goes to Śvetadvīpa.
The sages said:
O Lord of the World, you ought to describe in its entirety and in detail the greatness of Śvetamādhava and indeed the image of that Hari.
Likewise, in that very same place,
Brahmā said: "O Brahmins, in the Kṛta Yuga there was one named Śveta, who possessed great strength."
Having gone to that supreme field, the ocean situated in the southern direction.
Then Śveta caused a palace of auspicious characteristics to be built,
measuring one hundred dhanus, to the south of the God of gods.
Then, O best of Brahmins, by Śveta, with a mountain made of white stone,
that Blessed One was fashioned as Śvetamādhava, resembling the moon.
Regarding King Śveta by name— the Lord’s words to him:
"O Indra among kings, my devotees who are composed in mind shall go to heaven even by touching with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass the water of the white Gaṅgā."
But whoever should go to this image named Mādhavī, which possesses the luster of the moon,
resembles a conch shell or cow’s milk, and destroys all sins without exception—
Having bowed once with devotion to her whose eyes resemble lotuses,
one indeed leaves all worlds and is glorified in my own realm.
There, surrounded by celestial maidens for many Manvantaras,
he was served by Siddhas and Gandharvas while sweet songs were sung to him.
He enjoys vast pleasures at his will together with my [deities];
having fallen from there and come here, he becomes a human being, a Brāhmaṇa.
He will be a knower of the Vedas and Vedānta, illustrious, possessing enjoyments, and long-lived;
he will be enriched with stables for elephants, horses, and chariots, surrounded by wealth and grain, pure, handsome, highly fortunate, and endowed with sons and grandsons.
Then, having reached Puruṣottama at the foot of the banyan tree by the ocean, he once again—
Having abandoned the body while remembering Hari, one shall then go to the peaceful state;
having beheld Śvetamādhava nearby, as well as Matsyamādhava.
In the past, when the world was a single ocean of water, he assumed the form of Rohita and remained at the bottom of the netherworld (rasātala) for the purpose of recovering the Vedas.
Having reflected upon where the white fish was situated,
[he beheld] the primordial descent, the form of Mādhava in the shape of a fish.
Having bowed down and become self-restrained, one is liberated from all sufferings and goes to the supreme abode where Lord Hari himself resides.
Furthermore, when he returns here to the surface of the earth at the proper time,
that man shall become unassailable by having approached Matsya-Mādhava.
He shall become a donor, an enjoyer, a performer of sacrifices, a devotee of Viṣṇu, and one true to his promise;
having subsequently attained union with Hari, he will then obtain liberation.
The majesty of Matsyamādhava has been fully proclaimed by me;
having seen it, O tigers among sages, one shall attain all desires.
In that very same *Brahma Purāṇa*,
the sages said:
"O Blessed One, we wish to hear about the ritual purification (*mārjana*) performed at the abode of Varuṇa."
Bathing, giving gifts, and other such acts are performed [there]; tell me their entire fruit.
Brahmā said: Listen, O tigers among sages, to the ritual purification according to the rules,
with devotion and a focused mind, for this Purāṇa is meritorious and bestows liberation.
Bathing in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake is praised at all times;
it is especially on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight] that it destroys all sins.
In the same way, bathing in the ocean is praised at all times;
especially on the full moon day, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Mārkaṇḍeya, the banyan tree, Kṛṣṇa, the son of Rohiṇī, and the great ocean, as well as the lake of Indradyumna— this is remembered as the procedure for the five sacred sites (pañcatīrthī).
This is the single ritual procedure for this occasion:

*Oṃ amday. On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, desiring first to attain the world of Viṣṇu and subsequently not to fall away from it, I shall perform the vision of Puruṣottama.* Or else:

[104] On the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyaiṣṭha, having observed a fast, on the twelfth day when the sun has risen—*Oṃ*, today, on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Jyaiṣṭha, desiring to obtain a fruit even greater than the fruit produced by the performance of penance standing on one leg for seventy thousand years, while fasting, with senses subdued and anger conquered, performed at Kurukṣetra as the locus, I, observing a fast, shall perform the vision of Puruṣottama.
Or rather, he may behold Him according to the rite of the five sacred sites (*pañcatīrthi*). As follows:

As before, having fasted and gone to the Mārkaṇḍeya lake, having performed his bath and other rites, and taking *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and water, he should say: "Oṃ! Today, desiring the attainment of liberation preceded by the acquisition of Śaṅkara-yoga, and preceded by becoming a learned Brāhmaṇa in this world—characterized by the enjoyment of many excellent pleasures lasting until the dissolution of all things (*saṃplava*)—and characterized by going to the world of Śiva, being liberated from all sins, and attaining fruits equal to those of ten horse-sacrifices; for that purpose, I shall perform the vision of Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara preceded by bathing in the Mārkaṇḍeya pool."

Thus is the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). Therein, one should bathe according to the procedure prescribed in one’s own Vedic branch (*śākhā*); if that is unknown, one should bathe according to the common Puranic procedure. Then, with uninterrupted continuity:
*Oṃ, O Blessed One, O Enemy of Tripura, protect me here—I who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, seized by sin, and devoid of consciousness; salutations be unto you.*
Salutations to Śiva, the peaceful one, and the remover of all sins;
O Lord of Gods, I perform this bath, may my transgression be destroyed.
With this mantra, one should immerse oneself there three times, facing north.

Then, in water reaching up to the navel, having offered libations to the gods and others with water mixed with sesame seeds, and likewise to the ancestors and others, one should emerge from the water, put on two washed garments, wash both thighs and shanks with earth and water, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), enter the temple of Śiva, circumambulate Śiva, and worship him three times with the root mantra "Oṃ Naṃ Śivāya," performing the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra) and prostrating:
"Oṃ, O Three-eyed One, salutations be unto you; salutations to you, O Moon-adorned One!"
Protect me, O Virūpākṣa; O Mahādeva, homage be to you!

Having recited this and propitiated [the deity], one should dismiss [him] with: "O Blessed One, Mārkaṇḍeyeśvara, forgive me. Then, having gone to Akṣayavaṭa, one should say: "Om, today, desiring the destruction of my sins, I shall perform three circumambulations of Akṣayavaṭa preceded by prostrations."
Having made this resolve, one should circumambulate him three times and prostrate. Then, having made the resolve as before, one should worship the Akṣayavaṭa with devotion.
The mantra for that worship is:
*Oṃ, salutations to the one of unmanifest form, the cause of the great dissolution.*
Salutations to you, Nyagrodha, who are seated upon the great essence.
O Vaṭa tree, you are immortal throughout the aeon and the abode of Hari;
O Nyagrodha, O Kalpavṛkṣa, remove my sin—salutations be unto you!
Then:
*Oṃ, today, desiring the destruction of sins such as the killing of a Brahmin, I shall perform the rite of stepping upon the shade of the Akṣaya-vaṭa.*
Having thus resolved, one should stand for a moment in its shade. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*):

"Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of a fruit superior to the fruits produced by the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and desiring to be honored in the world of Viṣṇu preceded by the upliftment of my own lineage, I shall perform the viewing of the Akṣaya-vata," one should gaze upon the Akṣaya-vata. Even by prostrating, this very same fruit is obtained. Then, having gone near Vainateya (Garuḍa) who stands before Kṛṣṇa:
"Oṃ, today, desiring to go to my own city of Viṣṇu due to being liberated from all sins, I shall perform a salutation to Vainateya.
Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should pay homage to him. Then, having sat down at the gateway of Viṣṇu’s abode facing either east or north, [one should say]:
"Oṃ, today, desiring to attain the supreme goal, I shall behold Puruṣottama."

Having thus resolved, one should gaze upon the face of Puruṣottama. Then, having likewise resolved upon the vision of Saṅkarṣaṇa, one should perform it. In the same manner, having resolved upon the vision of Subhadrā, one should perform it. Then, having entered the abode of Viṣṇu, one should circumambulate Viṣṇu three times. Thereafter—

"Oṃ! Today, desiring the attainment of my desired fruit, liberation from all sins, the departure to my own world of Viṣṇu, the enjoyment of pervasive happiness during the dissolution of the world (saṃplava) summoned therein, thereafter birth in an eminent family of yogic Brahmins, thereafter becoming an eminent Brahmin who has mastered the meaning of all scriptures, and thereafter the attainment of liberation preceded by the acquisition of knowledge—I shall perform the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Having thus made this formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should worship Saṅkarṣaṇa. The mantra for that is:
"Oṃ, salutations to you, O wielder of the plow (Haladhṛk), O Rāma; salutations to you, O you whose weapon is the mace (Muṣalāyudha)."
Homage to you, beloved of Revatī; homage to you, who are kind to your devotees.
Homage to you, best among the strong; homage to you, upholder of the earth! Homage be to you, O enemy of Pralamba; protect me, O elder brother of Kṛṣṇa!
[107] Then, having performed the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) and recited this very mantra, one should prostrate and seek grace. Thereafter—having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*):

"Oṃ, desiring today to attain liberation, I shall worship Puruṣottama with the twelve-syllable mantra"—one should worship Puruṣottama with the twelve-syllable mantra, "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya," using perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*). Then—
Oṃ! Victory to you, Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Victory to you, destroyer of all sins!
Victory to you, slayer of Cāṇūra and Keśin! Victory to you, annihilator of Kaṃsa!
Victory to you, whose eyes are like lotus petals; victory to you, the wielder of the discus and mace!
Victory to you, dark as a blue rain cloud; victory to you, the bestower of all happiness!
Victory to you, O God, worshipful by the world! Victory to you, destroyer of saṃsāra!
Victory to you, Lord of the worlds, O Protector! Victory to you, bestower of the fruits of desire!
In the terrible ocean of saṃsāra— devoid of essence, with suffering for its foam,
turbulent with the crocodiles of anger, fierce, and flooded by the waters of the sense-objects—

O best of gods, I am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, which is agitated by the waves of various diseases and is exceedingly difficult to cross due to its whirlpools of delusion; save me, O Puruṣottama!
Having recited this mantra and prostrated, one should seek his favor. Then, immediately after seeking his favor—
[one should meditate on him as] Kṛṣṇa, with broad shoulders, two arms, eyes as wide as lotus petals, a broad chest, mighty arms, yellow garments, and a beautiful face.
[108] Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, adorned with a crown and armlets,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and decorated with a forest garland.
One should behold Kṛṣṇa. There, one should form the resolve:
"Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), I shall perform the beholding of Kṛṣṇa;
[I shall perform] bathing and giving gifts based upon all sacred fords (*tīrtha*)."

Or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the study of all the Vedas and the practice of all forms of knowledge; or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the study of all the Vedas and the practice of all forms of omniscience.
Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by all the vows, observances, and restraints of giving;
or the fruit produced by the practice of various severe austerities.
Or one who desires to attain the fruit of equanimity.
Or, one who desires to attain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the perfectly practiced holy life (*brahmacarya*); or,
[one who desires] that which is produced by the perfect maintenance of the householder stage of life (*gṛhāśrama*).
Or one who desires to attain the fruit equal to the fruit [of the path].
Or alternatively—

Oṃ. Today, desiring—preceded by the deliverance from twenty-one lineages—the liberation from the many sins accumulated over ten million previous births; endowed with supreme glory and all virtues; acting as the agent for the creation of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) of excellent splendor filled with the fulfillment of all desires; proceeding to the city of Viṣṇu and remaining there for a hundred kalpas accompanied by Gandharvas and Apsarases; enjoying manifold delights like those of Viṣṇu himself with four arms; thereafter, being born into an eminent Brahmin family in this world; becoming omniscient, free from pride regarding all Vedas, devoted to one's own dharma, peaceful, charitable, and intent on the welfare of living beings; and finally, attaining the Vaiṣṇava yoga and liberation—I shall perform the vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Even in the case of prostration, one of the previously mentioned fruits is obtained. Now follows the worship of Subhadrā.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of liberation preceded by the acquisition of Hari-yoga, and the subsequent state of being a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas, and thereafter sporting like a god until the final dissolution (*saṃplava*)—invited to that very abode of Viṣṇu’s city which is produced by the celestial cow (*kāmadhenu*)—I shall perform the worship of Subhadrā," one should worship her with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*). The mantra for worship is as follows:
Oṃ, homage to you, O all-pervading Goddess; homage to you, the bestower of auspiciousness and happiness!
Protect me, O lotus-petal-eyed one; O Kātyāyanī, let there be homage to you!

This mantra is for prostration and propitiation. Thus, having seen Saṅkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā, and having worshipped, bowed to, and praised them, one should exit the temple; then, having bowed again to Puruṣottama, one becomes one who has accomplished his purpose. Then, from Puruṣottama, one should go to the image of Viṣṇu made of sapphire (*indranīla*), first established by Brahmā, which is situated to the south of Puruṣottama and hidden beneath sand to the northwest of the Akṣayavaṭa tree; there, one should say: "Oṃ! Desiring today to go to the city of Viṣṇu, I shall perform prostration before the Viṣṇu made of sapphire."
Having thus formed this resolution, one should prostrate.

Oṃ. Today, desiring the attainment of a fruit equal to the fruit born of a hundred horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) performed for the sake of liberation from great sins (*mahāpātaka*), preceded by the deliverance of twenty-one generations of my lineage; desiring to be adorned with all virtues, enriched by the fulfillment of all desires, and freed from old age and death; desiring to be praised by Apsarases like the gods, filled with joy and happiness; desiring to possess a golden vimāna resounding with the tinkling of a network of golden bells, enriched by every object of desire, possessing the splendor of the rising sun, accompanied by hundreds of celestial women draped in pearl necklaces, and resonating with the songs of divine Gandharvas; desiring to travel to the city of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇupura*) by means of that vimāna, and to experience therein a bliss that gladdens the mind; desiring to assume a four-armed form; and desiring, preceded by the enjoyment of many excellent pleasures belonging to myself and accompanied by Gandharvas and Apsarases pervading the entire dissolution (*saṃplava*); desiring the state of being a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the four Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the various branches of knowledge, established in this world within an eminent family of Yogins; and desiring the attainment of liberation caused by the Vaiṣṇava yoga of the abode—[for these reasons] I shall perform the vision of Narasiṃha.
Having thus resolved, he should gaze upon Him. It is the same in worship; it is likewise in prostration. Then, having gone to Vāsudeva known as Ananta, [he should say]:
"Oṃ, today, desiring liberation from all sins and the attainment of my own supreme state, I shall perform the beholding of Vāsudeva known as Ananta.
It is the same in prostration as well. Then, having gone to the Śvetagaṅgā,
"Oṃ, today, desiring to go to Śvetadvīpa, I shall perform the vision of Śvetamādhava preceded by bathing in the Śvetagaṅgā.
Having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), and having performed the ritual bath and libations (tarpaṇa) at the Śvetagaṅgā according to the Vedic rite, one should behold Śvetamādhava. Then:

Oṃ. Today, desiring to attain the state of a Brāhmaṇa—endowed with pure form, great fortune, sons, and grandsons; surrounded by wealth, grain, elephants, horses, chariots, and garlands; possessing abundant enjoyments as one pleases; honored by many divine maidens together with many divine beings in the world of Brahmā; attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas while being praised by them; preceded by the knowledge of the Vedas and Vedāṅgas in this life; and thereafter attaining the status of Puruṣottama at the foot of the banyan tree on the shore of the ocean, casting off the body while remembering Hari and proceeding to the peaceful abode—I shall perform prostrations to Śvetamādhava.
Having thus resolved, he should go forward one step toward that very place and prostrate himself. Then, having gone again to the Śvetagaṅgā and made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa):

"Oṃ, today, desiring to go to Śvetadvīpa, I shall perform the vision of Matsyamādhava preceded by bathing in the Śvetagaṅgā," he should perform the ritual bath and libations (tarpaṇa) at the Śvetagaṅgā according to the Vedic rite and behold Matsyamādhava.

"Oṃ! Today, desiring to attain liberation preceded by the attainment of union with Hari, which is subsequent to becoming a king who is truly devoted to Viṣṇu, a giver and enjoyer whose basis is the surface of the earth following the journey to the supreme abode presided over by Nārāyaṇa, I shall perform the viewing and salutation of Matsyamādhava.
Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the viewing and salutation of Matsyamādhava.
This is the ritual for the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyaiṣṭha.
In the Brahmapurāṇa: "Bathing in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake is praised at all times;
it especially destroys all sins on the fourteenth lunar day."
In the same way, bathing in the ocean is praised at all times;
especially on the full moon day, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
[112] Likewise: When the full moon of the month of Jyaiṣṭha coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra,
one should especially go to that supreme and most auspicious king of holy places.
Because of the expression "especially," bathing in the ocean is not prohibited elsewhere as well.
Purified in body, speech, and mind, with his being fixed on that [the deity] and no other thought;
free from all pairs of opposites, devoid of passion, and without envy.
One should perform three circumambulations with a concentrated mind around the beautiful Vaṭa tree, the wish-fulfilling tree, where Janārdana himself is present.
O twice-born ones, by seeing which one is liberated from the sins accumulated over seven births,
and attains abundant merit as well as a desirable state of existence.
O Brahmins, I shall declare his names and his measure in each age, according to their respective numbers and in due order, beginning with the Kṛta Yuga.
O twice-born ones, Vaṭa, Vaṭeśvara, and Purāṇapuruṣa—
these are proclaimed as the names of the Vaṭa tree throughout the ages beginning with Kṛta.
One yojana, three-quarters of a yojana, half a yojana,
and a quarter of a yojana are proclaimed as the dimensions of the Kalpavṛkṣa in the Kṛta and subsequent ages.
Having paid homage to that banyan tree with the previously mentioned mantra,
one should proceed facing south for three hundred *dhanvantaras*.
Where that sign is seen— the beautiful gateway to heaven—
is the wood drawn from the waters of the ocean, endowed with every excellence.
Having prostrated and then performed worship once more,
one is liberated from all diseases and the like, as well as from sins, malevolent planets, and so forth.
Having previously seen Ugrasena at the gateway to heaven, he went to the ocean,
performed his ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and, being pure, meditated there upon the supreme Nārāyaṇa.
One should then assign the eight-syllable mantra to both the hands and the body;
the wise declare it to be "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya."
What is the use of many mantras that cause confusion of the mind?
The mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" alone accomplishes all aims.
Because they are the offspring of Nara, the waters are indeed called "Nārāḥ.
Since they were formerly the abode (ayana) of Viṣṇu, he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
The gods have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; the twice-born have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal;
knowledge has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; and ritual actions have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal.
Dharma has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; austerity has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal;
charity has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; and the vow has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal.
The worlds have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; the imperishable syllable has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal;
the eternal has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; the ultimate state has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal.
The earth is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the water is devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
the fire is devoted to Nārāyaṇa; the sky is devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
both the ego and the intellect are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
Whatever exists— past, present, and future— that which is designated as a living being,
whether gross, subtle, or supreme, all has Nārāyaṇa as its essence;
so too do all objects such as sound, and the sense organs such as hearing.
Both primordial nature and the individual soul are entirely of the essence of Nārāyaṇa;
whether in water, on land, in the underworld, in the cardinal directions, among the serpents, in the sky, or upon the mountains.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa remains supporting all this;
what more need be said here? This entire world, both moving and unmoving, [is supported by him].
"O twice-born ones, everything from Brahmā down to a blade of grass consists of Nārāyaṇa;
I do not perceive anything here that is superior to Nārāyaṇa."
All this world, both moving and unmoving, that is perceived is pervaded by him;
for water is the abode of Viṣṇu, and he indeed is the lord of the waters.
Therefore, one should always remember Nārāyaṇa, the destroyer of sins, within the waters;
especially at the time of bathing, being supremely pure, one should perform the ritual attendance (upasthāna).
One should remember Nārāyaṇa, meditate upon him, and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the hands and the body;
one should place the syllable *oṃ* and the syllable *na* upon whatever is designated as the individual soul (*jīva*).
One should place [the mantras] on the thumb, the hand, and the foot, as well as on the tuft and the head;
with the remaining palms, one should place them on the fingers beginning with the index finger.
One should place the syllable *oṃ* on the left foot and the syllable *na* on the right;
likewise, one should place the syllable *mo* on the left hip and the syllable *nā* on the right.
One should place the syllable *rā* at the region of the navel, the syllable *ya* on the left arm,
the syllable *ṇā* on the right, and place the syllable *ya* upon the head.
Having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa below, above, in the heart, on the sides, behind, and in front, the wise man should thereafter begin the armor-rite (kavaca).
May Govinda protect me in the east, Madhusūdana in the south,
the divine Śrīdhara in the west, and Keśava likewise in the north.
May Viṣṇu protect [the deity] in the southeast; may the imperishable Mādhava protect in the southwest;
may Hṛṣīkeśa protect in the northwest, and likewise Mādhava in the northeast.
May Varāha protect [me] on the surface of the earth, and likewise may Trivikrama protect me above;
having thus performed this armor-rite, the wise man should thereafter meditate upon himself.
"I am the god Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace. Having thus meditated upon oneself as that [deity], one should recite this mantra.
You are Agni, the lord of bipeds, the depositor of seed, the kindler of desire;
you are the foremost of all beings, the imperishable master of living souls.
O Lord of Waters, you are indeed the source of nectar and the womb of the gods;
O King of Tīrthas, remove all my sin; homage be to you!
Having recited thus according to the prescribed rule, one should then perform the bath;
otherwise, O best of the twice-born, bathing there is not recommended.
Having performed the consecration and purification with mantras dedicated to the water-deities,
one should then recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times while submerged within the water.
[116] Just as the horse-sacrifice (*hayamedha*), O Brahmins, is a ritual that removes all sins,
so too is the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn here the destroyer of all evil.
Having crossed over, having put on two clean, washed, and purified garments,
and having restrained the breaths, sipped water, and worshipped the Sun at the twilight junction;
Then, having cast a handful of flowers into the water,
he should perform the ritual service (upasthāna) to the Sun with his arms raised, using those [prescribed] hymns.
One should recite the purifying goddess Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times,
and having recited other solar mantras as well, remaining composed in mind.
Having circumambulated the sun, paid homage, and sat down,
and having performed his private recitation while facing the east, he should offer libations to the deities and the sages.
One who knows the mantras, being well-composed, should satisfy humans, the ancestors, and others with water mixed with sesame seeds, pronouncing their names and lineages.
O twice-born ones, having first performed the libation for the deities with a concentrated mind,
one subsequently becomes entitled to the libation for the ancestors.
At the time of a Śrāddha ceremony and at the time of the fire-oblation (havana), one should offer with a single hand;
for the libation (tarpaṇa), one should employ all three hands—this indeed is the rule that always applies.
With the left hand holding [the vessel] and the right hand [offering],
those who are restrained in speech should say, "May [they] be satisfied," while pronouncing the name and lineage.
If one, out of delusion, performs the libation for the ancestors with sesame seeds grown on the body [of a corpse],
his ancestors are satisfied by means of skin, flesh, blood, and bone.
[117] One should not perform the libation for the deities and ancestors with sesame seeds that remain on one's limbs;
that water would become blood, and the giver would become a sinner.
O tigers among sages, if water is given on the ground while the giver stands in the water, that gift is in vain; it does not reach anyone.
If a man, standing on dry land, offers water into the water, that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless.
One should never offer water for libation to the ancestors while still standing in water;
rather, having emerged and gone to a clean place, one should perform the water-libation.
Water that is not poured upon the ground is not accepted [as an offering], whether it be in water-vessels, in bowls, when one is angry, or when offered with only one hand.
"O twice-born ones, the earth has been given by me as an imperishable abode for the ancestors;
therefore, one who desires the gratification of the ancestors should give there itself."
Born upon the surface of the earth, established indeed within the earth,
and returning to dissolution within the earth— therefore, one should offer water upon the earth.
Having spread out those kusha grasses with their tips intact and having invoked them with mantras,
one should seat the gods on those with tips pointing eastward, and likewise the ancestors on those with tips pointing southward.
Having gratified the gods, the ancestors, and others, and having sipped water while restraining his speech,
[he should prepare] a very beautiful square space measuring one cubit, provided with four doors.
O Brahmins, having first drawn the city on the shore of that great ocean,
one should draw there in the center an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
[118] Having thus drawn the mandala, O twice-born ones,
one should worship there the unborn, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa according to the rite of the eight-syllable mantra.
Hereafter, I shall explain the supreme purification of the body:
one should contemplate the form of the letter *ā* in the heart, red in color and joined with the letter *ra*.
One should place upon the head the blazing three-pointed fire, the burner that destroys evil, which has the form of an *ārā* situated in the center of the lunar disc.
Raining down white-colored nectar and flooding the earth,
one whose sins have thus been shaken off shall thereafter possess a divine body.
Then the wise one should assign the eight-syllable mantra to himself,
beginning with the left foot and placing it in successive order.
The practitioner should perform the purification of the hands (karaśuddhi) with the root mantra, including the five-limbed Vaiṣṇava rite as well as the fourfold emanation (caturvyūha).
One should place each individual letter separately upon the fingers;
one should then place the syllable *oṃ*, the world of *bhūr*, and the color white upon the left foot.
The syllable *na*, red in color, is situated on the right side of the earth;
the syllable *mo*, dark blue in color, is situated on the left hip, established by all.
The syllable *nā* is the seed of all, situated in the south;
the syllable *rā*, with the luster of saffron, is Janaloka, resting upon the navel.

The letter *ya* is yellow in color and rests upon the left shoulder; the letter *ṇa* has the luster of collyrium and is situated on the right side. This letter *ya* is located at the head, wherein all worlds are established.

Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu—[this is] the head. Oṃ, obeisance to Jvalana—[this is] the crest-lock (śikhā). Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu—[this is] the armor (kavaca). Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu; [may there be] the binding of the directions with the flashing, flashing [light]. Oṃ huṃ phaṭ—[this is] the weapon (astra). Oṃ: Vāsudeva, white, is at the head. Oṃ Āṃ: Saṅkarṣaṇa, red, Garuḍa, fire, splendor, and the sun, is on the forehead. Oṃ Āṃ: Pradyumna, yellow, wind, and cloud, is at the neck. Oṃ Āṃ (Śrīṃ): Kṛṣṇa Aniruddha, endowed with all powers, is at the heart.
Having thus manifested himself in four forms, he should then perform the ritual action:
Viṣṇu stands before me, and Keśava behind;
Govinda is on my right side, while Madhusūdana is on the left.
Above is Vaikuṇṭha, and on the surface of the earth is Vārāha;
as for those intermediate directions, Mādhava is present in all of them.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
I am indeed composed of Vāsudeva, protected by Narasiṃha.
Having thus become one with Viṣṇu, one should then commence the ritual action;
as it is in oneself, so it is in the deity—one should unite all the principles (tattvas).
[120] And then one should perform the sprinkling with the *praṇava*, ending with the syllable *phaṭ*; this is declared to be auspicious and the remover of all obstacles.
Therein, one should visualize the mandalas of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
one should place Viṣṇu in the center of the lotus, as well as those of Wind and Space.
Then, having meditated in his heart upon the syllable Oṃ in the form of light—
eternal and luminous, seated within the pericarp—
he should then install the eight-syllabled mantra in its proper sequence.
Worship performed with these [mantras] both individually and collectively is considered supreme;
one should worship the eternal God with the twelve-syllable mantra.
Then, having fixed it in his heart, he should place [the deity] outside the pericarp—
the Great Being with four arms, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Having meditated upon the Great Yoga, which is eternal and has the form of light,
the mantra-practitioner should then invoke it in due order within the inconceivable mind.
The invocation mantra:
May the boon-granting Lord Nārāyaṇa— manifest as the Fish, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf—
come before me.
Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa, homage!
This is the mantra for installation. [121] In the pericarp.
Oṃ! Here, upon the footstool of Mount Sumeru, is a seat prepared with lotuses;
for the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, remain here, O Madhusūdana!
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, salutation!
The mantra for the water offering (arghya):
Oṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, the Lord of the lords of the three worlds.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations! The mantra for the water for the feet:
Oṃ, O eternal God Padmanābha, here is water for the feet for Your two feet.
O Viṣṇu, lotus-petal-eyed Madhusūdana, please accept this.
Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance.
This is the mantra for the madhuparka offering.
O Mahādeva, this madhuparka prepared by Brahmā and the other gods has been offered to you with devotion by me; accept it, O Puruṣottama.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
In that very same Brahmapurāṇa, the mantra for the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is as follows:
"The white water of the Mandākinī is auspicious and removes all sins."
Please accept this water for sipping, which has been offered by me with devotion.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations! [122] The mantra for bathing:
You are the waters and you are the earth; you are indeed light and you are the wind.
I bathe [thee] with water that serves merely to sustain the world.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations!
The mantra for the garment:
Oṃ, O God, you are endowed with a garment and possessed of the color of sacrifice.
O Lord Keśava, accept this garment of golden-hued luster.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations! The mantra for anointing:
Oṃ, O Keśava, I do not know your body nor even your movements.
Having accepted the perfumes offered by me, let them be anointed.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa; salutations.
The mantra for the sacred thread (upavīta):
Oṃ, [this] threefold [thread] was [woven] by the Lotus-born [Brahmā] with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
O Acyuta, this sacred thread of yours is joined with the Sāvitrī knots.
Oṃ, homage to Nārāyaṇa, homage! [123] This is the mantra for ornaments:
Oṃ, you who are endowed with divine jewels, possessing a radiance equal to fire and the sun!
O Mādhava, let these ornaments beautify your limbs.
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance!
Oṃ oṃ—obeisance! Oṃ na—obeisance! Oṃ mo—obeisance! Oṃ nā—obeisance! Oṃ rā—obeisance! Oṃ ya—obeisance! Oṃ ṇā—obeisance! Oṃ ya—obeisance! Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance!
In this manner, one should worship with the root mantra, both individually and collectively.
The incense mantra:
O divine essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and sweet-smelling,
this incense offered by me with devotion— please accept it.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations! The mantra for the lamp:
Oṃ, [I offer] the light of the sun and the moon, and likewise that of lightning and fire.
O God, you alone are the lamp among all lights; please accept this.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa; salutations! The mantra for the food offering:
Oṃ, may this fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, [be accepted].
O Keśava, this food offering has been presented by me with devotion unto you.
Oṃ, salutation to Nārāyaṇa, salutation!
And likewise, in that very same Brahmapurāṇa:
"One should place Vāsudeva on the eastern petal and Saṅkarṣaṇa on the southern [petal]."
One should place Pradyumna in the west and likewise Aniruddha in the north.
Likewise, one should place Vārāha in the southeast, Narasiṃha in the southwest,
Mādhava in the northwest, and Trivikrama in the northeast.
Likewise, one should place Garuḍa in front of the eight-syllable mantra;
similarly, one should place the great mace (mahāgadā) to the right of the deity.
Then, the learned one should place the Śārṅga bow to the left of the deity;
he should place two divine quivers on the right and a conch shell on the left.
Having established Śrī on the right, one should place Puṣṭi on the left;
then, in front, the Vanamālā, followed by the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha.
One should place the heart-mantra and the others in the four directions starting from the east;
then one should place the weapon-mantra of the God of gods in the corner.
Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa,
as well as Vāyu, Dhanada, Īśāna, Ananta, together with Brahmā.
One should worship them with their respective mantras, likewise below and above;
thus having worshipped Janārdana, the Lord of Gods, situated within the mandala.
A person shall obtain their desired objects; there is no doubt in this matter.
By this very procedure, one [worships] Janārdana situated within the mandala.
Whoever should behold it worshipped shall enter the imperishable Viṣṇu;
by whomsoever Keśava has been worshipped even once according to this rite.
Having crossed over birth, death, and old age, he shall attain the abode of Viṣṇu—
whosoever, unwearied, constantly remembers Nārāyaṇa with devotion.
Every day, Śvetadvīpa was prepared as his dwelling;
it was illuminated by [mantras] beginning with Oṃkāra and ending with a salutation.
One's own name is designated as the "mantra" for all sentient beings;
by this very procedure, one should offer fragrances and flowers.
One should perform [the rites] for each one individually in the sequence as prescribed;
thereafter, one should bind the mudrās as impelled by the stated order.
The knower of mantras should perform the recitation with the root mantra twenty-eight times,
eight times, or likewise one hundred and eight times.
And likewise, at the proper times, he should remain thus composed according to his ability.
The lotus, the conch, the śrīvatsa, the mace, Garuḍa,
the sword, the discus, and the Śārṅga bow— these are proclaimed as the eight mudrās.
The mantra for dismissal:
Go, go to the supreme abode, O Ancient Puruṣottama,
where the gods, beginning with Brahmā, attain the highest state.
Those who do not know the ritual of worship should perform it with mantras as prescribed;
they should always worship Acyuta there using the root mantra (mūlamantra).
[126] Brahmā said: Having thus worshipped that Puruṣottama according to the rules with devotion,
and having bowed his head, he should afterwards propitiate the Ocean.
You are the vital breath of all beings and the source of all rivers, O Lord of Streams;
O King of Tīrthas, beloved of Acyuta, homage be to you—protect me!
Having thus bathed properly in that ocean within that most excellent sacred field, O twice-born ones,
and having duly worshipped the healthy Nārāyaṇa on the shore;
Having prostrated before Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Subhadrā, and the ocean,
a human being obtains the fruit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Completely liberated from all evil and freed from all suffering,
he was as glorious as a celestial being, proud of his beauty and youth.
Having uplifted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and resounding with divine gandharvas.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there and sported with the Apsarases for more than a hundred Manvantaras, he remains free from old age and death.
Having arrived here due to the exhaustion of his merit, he was born into a family endowed with every virtue;
he was handsome, fortunate, illustrious, truthful, and a master of his senses.
A Brahmin who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras should be a performer of sacrifices and a devotee of Vishnu;
having attained Vaishnava Yoga, he shall thereafter obtain liberation.

During an eclipse of the planets, at the transit of the sun, at the solstices, as well as at the equinoxes, on the anniversaries of the beginning of the Yugas, at the *ṣaḍaśīti* moment, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, and at the end of a day; [127]
On the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Māgha, or on other auspicious lunar days,
those of great wisdom who bestow gifts there upon the Brahmins—
Those who offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) to their ancestors there according to the prescribed rite obtain a fruit a thousand times greater than that obtained from other sacred sites.
Their ancestors indeed attain inexhaustible satisfaction;
thus has the fruit of bathing in the ocean been correctly described by me.
O Brahmins, the fruit of giving and indeed of the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) bestows the fruits of dharma,
artha, and kāma, and it increases longevity, renown, and fame.
It bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men; it is auspicious, the destroyer of suffering, the remover of all sins, meritorious, and the granter of the fruits of all desires.
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, and lakes exist upon the surface of the earth—all those holy sites enter it; therefore, it has attained preeminence.
O best of the twice-born, this should not be spoken to an atheist;
they wander from one sacred site to another, each proclaiming its own particular greatness.
O twice-born ones, as long as the majesty of the king of holy places is not described—
[he who is] the king of all sacred sites, the ocean, the lord of rivers.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, this place is superior to all holy fords and bestows all desires;
just as darkness comes to an end when the sun has risen.
[128] By bathing in the King of Tīrthas, there is likewise the destruction of all sins;
for indeed, ninety-nine crores of tīrthas are present therein.
O twice-born ones, who is able to describe the virtues of the King of Tīrthas?
Therefore, O twice-born ones, whatever is performed here— whether bathing, giving gifts, fire-offerings, recitation, or worship of the gods— all that becomes inexhaustible.
In that very place,
Brahmā said:
"Then, O best of the twice-born, one should go to the holy ford (tīrtha) born from the constituent parts of a sacrifice."
There lies the auspicious and purifying lake named Indradyumna-saras.
Having gone there, pure and glorious, having sipped water (ācamana) and meditated upon Hari in his mind, and having performed the ritual worship of the water, he should utter this mantra:
O Tīrtha born from the constituent parts of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, destroyer of all sins!
I perform my bath in you today; remove my evil, salutations be unto you.

Having recited thus and bathed according to the rules, O Brahmins, one should satiate the gods, sages, and ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds, and then, having sipped water, remain restrained in speech.
Having offered rice-balls to the ancestors and having worshipped Puruṣottama,
a person fully obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices.
Having rescued seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will, like a god.
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures there for as long as the moon and stars endure,
he falls from that state and, having come here, certainly attains liberation.
[129] Now, the formal application (prayoga):
therein—

On the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha conjoined with or presided over by the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, or on another lunar day, [I, so-and-so], desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by a hundred horse-sacrifices; for the upliftment of twenty-one generations; for liberation from all sins; for being freed from all miseries; for possessing a divine form, youth, and pride like that of the gods; for ascending to the world of Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot of sun-like color, adorned with divine perfumes and the music of Gandharvas; for enjoying there, within a period of more than a hundred Manvantaras, manifold excellent pleasures and enjoyments along with many Apsarases; and subsequently, for attaining birth as a Vaiṣṇava Brāhmaṇa endowed with all worldly virtues, handsome, fortunate, glorious, truthful, self-controlled, and a knower of the meaning of the Vedas and Śāstras—a master of the Vaiṣṇava path—followed by the attainment of Vaiṣṇava Yoga and finally Liberation (Mokṣa); I shall perform the worship of Nārāyaṇa preceded by a bath in the ocean according to the procedure prescribed in the Brahmapurāṇa.

Having thus resolved and circumambulated the Akṣaya-vaṭa tree three times, one should then, being pure, sit upon a pure spot on the shore of the ocean three hundred *dhanus* to the south. Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the three-syllable mantra "Oṃ Namaḥ" on the two thumbs, then on the two feet, then on the tuft of hair (*śikhā*), and then on the head; thereafter, one should place the syllable *nā* on the two index fingers, *rā* on the two middle fingers, *ya* on the two ring fingers, *ṇā* on the two little fingers, and *ya* on the palms.

Then, one should place the syllable *oṃ* on the left foot, *na* on the right foot, *mo* on the left hip, *nā* on the right hip, *rā* at the navel, *ya* on the left arm, *ṇā* on the right arm, and *ya* on the head.
Then, having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa below, above, in the heart, on both sides, behind, and in front—[one recites]: "Oṃ! May Govinda protect me in the east; Madhusūdana in the south."
In the west is the god Śrīdhara, and likewise Keśava in the north.
May Viṣṇu protect [the deity] in the southeast; may the imperishable Mādhava protect in the southwest;
may Hṛṣīkeśa protect in the northwest; and likewise may Vāmana protect in the northeast. May Varāha protect upon the surface of the earth, and may Trivikrama protect above.
Having recited this mantra,
which constitutes the formation of the armor, and having meditated thus: "I am the god Nārāyaṇa, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace," [one should address] the ocean.
Oṃ! You are Agni, the lord of bipeds, the depositor of semen, the kindler of desire;
you are the primary essence of all beings, the imperishable master of living souls.
O Lord of the Waters, you are indeed the churning-stick for nectar and the source of the gods;
O King of Tīrthas, take away all my sin; homage be to you!

Then, having entered the ocean and completed the prescribed rite of bathing, one should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and purification (*mārjana*) with the three mantras dedicated to the Waters, beginning with *oṃ āpo hi ṣṭhā mayobhuvaḥ*, *oṃ yo vaḥ śivatamo rasaḥ*, and *tasmā araṅgamāma*; and having done so, submerged in the water, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times.

Having emerged from the water, put on two washed garments, and performed the *saṃdhyāvandana* ending with the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times—having muttered another solar mantra such as "vibhrāḍ" or a similar triad of solar mantras, circumambulated the sun, and sat facing east upon a seat provided with three *darbha* blades—he should perform the *brahmayajña*. Then, having offered libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods and others with water mixed with barley upon *kuśa* grass with tips pointing east on the ground, and having offered libations to the ancestors and others with handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds upon three *kuśa* blades with tips pointing south, he should—if following the Kāṭhaka tradition for the ritual bath—perform the rites subsequent to the libations. Then, having offered a handful of water (*añjali*) to the Sun, worshipped the Sun, and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), he should remain silent and draw a square altar (*vedi*) measuring one cubit with four doors. In its center, he should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, and visualize within his heart the syllable *A* (Ā), red in color, three-pointed, and in the form of a blazing fire. Next, he should visualize the syllable *Ā* (Ā) situated in the middle of the lunar disc, white in color, bathing him in nectar at the crown of his head. By this means, his sins are shaken off and he becomes possessed of a divine body.

Then, having performed the purification of the two hands from the elbows to the tips of the fingers with the mantra *namo nārāyaṇāya*, one should place the three syllables of *namaḥ* on the thumbs of the hands, then on the hands themselves, then on the feet, then on the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and then on the head. Thereafter, one should place the letter *nā* on the two thumbs, the letter *rā* on the two index fingers, the letter *ya* on the two middle fingers, the letter *ṇā* on the two ring fingers, and the letter *ya* on the two little fingers.

Then, one should place the syllable *oṃ*, white in color and representing the *bhūrloka*, on the left foot; the syllable *na*, red in color and representing the *bhuvarloka*, on the right foot; the syllable *ma*, dark-colored and representing the *svarloka*, on the left hip; the syllable *nā*, red in color and representing the *maharloka*, on the right hip; the syllable *rā*, saffron-colored and representing the *janaloka*, at the navel; the syllable *ya*, yellow in color and representing the *tapoloka*, at the base of the left arm; the syllable *nā*, with the luster of collyrium and representing the *satyaloka*, at the base of the right arm; and the syllable *ya*, red in color and the very nature of Brahman, on the crown of the head.

Then: *Oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ* for the head; *Oṃ jvalanāya namaḥ* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*); *Oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ* for the armor (*kavaca*); *Oṃ viṣṇo sphura* for the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*); and *Oṃ huṃ phaṭ astram* for the weapon (*astra*). One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) thus: *Oṃ vāsudevam śuklam* on the head; on the forehead, one should place *saṅkarṣaṇa* who is red, as well as Garuḍa, Fire, Splendor, and Āditya, with the syllable *ām*.

One should place the yellow Pradyumna, who is like a rain-cloud, with the syllable *ām* upon the neck. One should place Kṛṣṇa Aniruddha, endowed with all powers, with the syllable *ām* upon the heart. Then: "Viṣṇu stands before me, and Keśava behind;
Govinda is on the right side, and Madhusūdana on the left."
Above is Vaikuṇṭha, and on the surface of the earth is Vārāha;
as for all those intermediate directions, Mādhava is present in them all.
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping,
I am protected by Narasiṃha, for I am indeed composed of Vāsudeva.
Having reflected thus, one should contemplate—beginning from "the syllable *oṃ* of white color" and ending with "I am indeed composed of Vāsudeva"—upon the deity situated facing oneself.

Then, with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ*, one should perform a sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for the destruction of obstacles, both for oneself and for the deity. Thereafter, having visualized a solar disc upon the pericarp, a lunar disc above that, and a fire-disc above that, one should place the wind in the center of space, an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the wind, and Viṣṇu in the center of that.

Then, having meditated upon the syllable Oṃ in the form of light within the heart and having stabilized it in the pericarp, one should contemplate the Great Being with four arms, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns—
the eternal Great Yoga in the form of light.
Having reflected thus upon the Supreme Lord: "Oṃ! May the boon-granting Lord Nārāyaṇa—manifest as the Fish, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf—come before me."
One should invoke with this mantra.
Then, upon the pericarp: "Oṃ, here on the footstool of Mount Sumeru is a seat prepared of lotus."
For the sake of the welfare of all sentient beings, remain here, O Madhusūdana!
Thus one should establish [the deity].
With the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Viṣṇu, Hṛṣīkeśa, the God of gods, the Lord of the lords of the three worlds; this is the arghya. Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance," one should offer the arghya.
Oṃ, O Lord of Gods, Padmanābha, Sanātana! O Viṣṇu, lotus-petal-eyed Madhusūdana, accept this water for washing the feet.

One should offer the water for washing the feet with the mantra: "This is the *pādya*; Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations. Then: "Oṃ, O Great God, this *madhuparka* prepared by Brahmā and the others for you, which I have offered with devotion—accept it, O Supreme Lord."
One should offer the *madhuparka* with the mantra: "This is the *madhuparka*; Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance.
Oṃ, may you accept this auspicious water of the Mandākinī, which removes all sins;
please accept this water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) offered by me with devotion.
One should offer water for sipping with the mantra: "This is for sipping; *oṃ* salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations.
Then: "*Oṃ*, you are the waters and the earth, you are light and indeed the wind;
by means of this water, which serves merely to sustain the worlds, I bathe [you]."
[134] One should offer the bathing materials with the mantra: "This is for the bath; *oṃ* salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations.
*Oṃ*, O Lord, you are endowed with garments and possessed of the color of sacrifice;
O Lord Keśava, your two garments possess the luster of gold.

One should give the garment with the mantra: "Oṃ, this garment; Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance. Then: "O Keśava, I do not know your body nor even your movements; please accept these fragrances offered by me and anoint yourself."

One should offer the unguent with the mantra: "This is the unguent; Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations. [Then one should offer] the sacred thread with the mantra: "O Acyuta, this sacred thread is produced by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma mantras by the Lotus-born One (Brahmā), and is joined with the knot of Sāvitrī; it is for you."
One should give the sacred thread with the mantra: "This is the sacred thread; *oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya namaḥ*.
Then: "*Oṃ*, O Keśava, may these ornaments, endowed with divine jewels and possessing a luster like that of fire and the sun, adorn your limbs."
One should give the ornament with the mantra: "This ornament, Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations. [135] Then follows the worship.

In that regard—one should worship each [syllable] individually with the separate [mantras]: *Oṃ oṃ namaḥ*, *Oṃ na namaḥ*, *Oṃ mo namaḥ*, *Oṃ nā namaḥ*, *Oṃ rā namaḥ*, *Oṃ ya namaḥ*, *Oṃ ṇā namaḥ*, *Oṃ ya namaḥ*. Then, one should worship with the entire mantra: *Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya namaḥ*.

Then, one should worship with the twelve-syllable mantra: "Oṃ namo bhagavate vāsudevāya namaḥ. [And offer incense with: "Oṃ! Divine essence of the forest tree, rich in fragrance and sweet-smelling; this incense offered by me with devotion—may it be accepted."

One should offer incense with the mantra: "This is the incense; Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance. Then: "Oṃ, just as there is light in the sun and moon, and likewise in lightning and fire, so may this lamp, O Lord, the light among lights, be accepted by You alone."

One should offer the lamp with the mantra: "This is the lamp; Oṃ, obeisance to Nārāyaṇa, obeisance. Oṃ! This fourfold food, endowed with the six flavors, is offered by me with devotion as a naivedya for you, O Keśava.
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) with the mantra: "Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa, salutations.

Having worshipped in this manner, one should place Vāsudeva on the eastern petal, Saṅkarṣaṇa on the south, Pradyumna on the western petal, Aniruddha on the northern petal, Vārāha on the southeast petal, Narasiṃha on the southwest petal, Mādhava on the northwest petal, and Trivikrama on the northeast petal.

Then, in front of the eight-syllabled Lord who faces the practitioner, one should place Garuḍa; on the right, a great mace; on the left, the Śārṅga bow; on the right, two quivers; on the left, a conch; on the right side, Śrī; and on the left side, Puṣṭi.
Then one should place the forest garland, the Śrīvatsa mark, and the Kaustubha gem; the placement of the discus and other emblems is in the eight directions.

Then one should install Indra in the east, Agni in the southeast, Yama in the south, Nirṛti in the southwest, Varuṇa in the west, Vāyu in the northwest, Dhanada in the north, Īśāna in the northeast, Ananta below, and Brahmā above.
Then, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others, ending with Brahmā, in those locations where the installation was performed. For instance:

Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva; Oṃ, obeisance to Saṅkarṣaṇa; Oṃ, obeisance to Pradyumna; Oṃ, obeisance to Aniruddha; Oṃ, obeisance to Varāha; Oṃ, obeisance to Narasiṃha; Oṃ, obeisance to Mādhava; Oṃ, obeisance to Trivikrama; Oṃ, obeisance to Garuḍa; Oṃ, obeisance to the Great Mace (Mahāgadā); Oṃ, obeisance to the Bow Śārṅga; Oṃ, obeisance to the two Quivers (iṣudhi); Oṃ, obeisance to the Conch (śaṅkha); Oṃ, obeisance to Śrī; Oṃ, obeisance to Puṣṭi; Oṃ, obeisance to the Forest Garland (vanamālā); Oṃ, obeisance to Śrīvatsa; Oṃ, obeisance to Kaustubha; Oṃ, obeisance to Indra; Oṃ, obeisance to Agni; Oṃ, obeisance to Yama; Oṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti; Oṃ, obeisance to Varuṇa; Oṃ, obeisance to Vāyu; Oṃ, obeisance to Dhanada (Kubera); Oṃ, obeisance to Īśāna; Oṃ, obeisance to Ananta; Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā.

Thus, having worshipped with meditation (*dhyāna*) as prescribed, one should then perform that which results in the entry of the imperishable Viṣṇu upon seeing Nārāyaṇa, who is endowed with his natural retinue.

Then, having displayed the mudrās of the lotus, conch, śrīvatsa, mace, Garuḍa, kaustubha, discus, and Śārṅga bow, and having recited the eight-syllabled mantra one hundred and eight times, or twenty-eight, or more—[one should say]:
*oṃ gaccha gaccha paraṃ sthānaṃ purāṇa puruṣottama*.
Wherein the gods, beginning with Brahmā, attain the supreme state.
Having thus bowed his head to Viṣṇu who had been worshipped, he said:
"O Lord of Rivers, you are the life-breath of all beings and the source of all streams;
O King of Tīrthas, beloved of Acyuta, salutations to you—protect me!"
Having recited this, one should propitiate the ocean. Then, one should prostrate before Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Subhadrā.
Thus concludes the ritual for the worship of Nārāyaṇa preceded by bathing in the ocean at the sacred field of Puruṣottama.
Thereafter, having gone to Indradyumna-saras—

Oṃ. Today, desiring the attainment of liberation preceded by returning to this world, followed by the enjoyment of many excellent pleasures lasting as long as the moon and stars, based upon going to the world of Viṣṇu like a god by means of a wish-fulfilling cow and celestial chariot, which effects the upliftment of seven preceding and seven succeeding generations of my lineage and is equal in fruit to the merit arising from ten horse-sacrifices, I shall perform the offering of rice-balls to the ancestors at the Indradyumna lake and the worship of Puruṣottama according to the procedure prescribed in the Brahmapurāṇa.

Having thus resolved, having sipped water (ācamana) at the Indradyumna lake, and having meditated upon Hari, he should worship Hari with the recitation of the mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya. Then, entering the water and bathing according to the prescribed rules, he should recite at the conclusion:
Oṃ! O Tīrtha born from a limb of the Aśvamedha sacrifice, destroyer of all sins!
Today I perform my bath in you; remove my evil. Salutations be unto you!

Having recited this and bathed, one should perform the libation for the celestial sages with water mixed with barley and the libation for the ancestors with water mixed with sesame seeds; then, having sipped water and observed silence, one should offer the six funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) for the six generations according to the procedure prescribed in one’s own *Gṛhya-sūtra* and worship Puruṣottama.

Furthermore, whatever acts such as bathing, giving gifts, fire-offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and worship of the gods are performed on the shore of the ocean, all that becomes inexhaustible.

During an eclipse, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), at the beginning of a yuga, on the waning of a lunar day (tithi-kṣaya), during the Vyatīpāta yoga, on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Māgha, or on any other festival day—or at any other time whatsoever—whatever other holy site (tīrtha) there may be for bathing and so forth, that becomes a thousandfold more efficacious when performed at the ocean.
Whenever one offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa-dāna) on the shore of the ocean, it yields the fruit of inexhaustible satisfaction for one’s ancestors.
Having performed this, one who has fasted on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) should visit the five holy sites (pañcatīrthī).
Whoever should behold Puruṣottama on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Having attained the previously mentioned fruit and having sported in the abode of Acyuta,
he goes to the supreme station from which he does not return again.

The *pañcatīrthī* consists of Mārkaṇḍeyasara, Akṣayavaṭa, Sāgara, Indradyumnasara, and Rauhiṇeya. Therefore, for one who has commenced the fast on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), there are five rites: first, a ritual bath in the Mārkaṇḍeya lake; then, circumambulation of Akṣayavaṭa; then, a ritual bath in the ocean; then, a ritual bath in the Indradyumna lake; and finally, the sight of Rauhiṇeya. Then, on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), having performed the daily obligatory rites up to the worship of the deity, there is the sight of Puruṣottama.

[139] Regarding the phrase "as previously stated"—the meaning is that this refers to the fruit which was previously described for one who has visited Puruṣottama without having performed the *pañcatīrthī*. The phrase beginning with "having sported" (*krīḍitvā*) and so forth means that even greater than that, a fruit arises here. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows:

"Oṃ! Desiring to attain the fruit born from the sight of Puruṣottama based on the full moon day of the bright fortnight of Jyaiṣṭha, preceded by a journey to the abode of Acyuta, and to go to the supreme abode from which there is no return, I, having commenced the fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) and performed the rite of the five holy fords (pañcatīrthī), shall perform the sight of Puruṣottama on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Jyaiṣṭha.

Having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should observe the fast on the eleventh day after performing the pañcatīrthī, and on the twelfth day, one should behold Puruṣottama; thereafter comes the breaking of the fast (pāraṇā). Thus it is stated in the Brahmapurāṇa.
Brahmā said:
Likewise:
"Listen, O tigers among sages; I shall speak to you in brief.
I praise the month of Jyeṣṭha again and again."
Whatever sacred fords, rivers, lakes, lotus ponds, tanks, oblong ponds, wells, and pools there are upon the earth—
Various rivers and oceans always visibly enter Puruṣottama for seven days, beginning from the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, whatever is performed there at that time— such as bathing, giving gifts, and beholding the deity— that becomes inexhaustible.
O best of the twice-born, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, she removes ten sins; therefore, she is remembered as Daśaharā.
The man who, being well-restrained, beholds Kṛṣṇa the wielder of the plow and Bhadrā at that [shrine],
shall be liberated from all sins and go to the world of Viṣṇu.
O brahmins, by beholding Puruṣottama, Rāma, and Subhadrā during either the northern or southern solstice, a man shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having seen Govinda, the Supreme Person, being swung on the swing, a man,
having become self-restrained on the full moon day of Phālguna, should proceed to the city of Govinda.
O twice-born ones, when the day of the equinox has arrived, having performed the ritual of the five holy fords (pañcatīrthī) according to the rules, one should behold Saṅkarṣaṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and Bhadrā.
A person obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, which is difficult to attain;
liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
He who beholds Kṛṣṇa adorned with sandalwood paste on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha goes to the abode of Acyuta.
He who beholds Puruṣottama on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha when it is conjoined with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Likewise, in that very same place:
"When Mahājyaiṣṭhī occurs through the conjunction of a lunar mansion and a zodiacal sign,
then mortals should go to Puruṣottama with great effort."
O twice-born ones, having beheld Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Bhadrā on the Mahājyaiṣṭhī day,
a man obtains the fruit of twelve pilgrimages and even more.
At Prayāga and Kurukṣetra, at Puṣkara, Naimiṣa, and Gayā;
at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuñjāgra, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
At Kokāmukha, at Śūkara, at Mathurā,
in Marusthala, at Śālagrāma, at Vāyutīrtha, at Mandāra, and at the ocean of the Sindhu.
At Piṇḍāraka, Citrakūṭa, Prabhāsa, and likewise at Kanakhala;
at Gaṅgādvāra, Dvārakā, and likewise at Badarikāśrama.
At Lohadaṇḍa and Aśvatīrtha, which liberate one from all sins;
at Kardamāla, Koṭitīrtha, and likewise at Amarakuṇḍaka.
At Lohākula, at Ikṣumārga, at Somatīrtha, at Pṛthūdaka,
at Utpalāvartaka, and at Pṛthūttuṅga together with Kuñjaka;
O twice-born ones, [he dwelt] at Ekāmra, Kedāra, Kāśī, Virajā, Kālañjara,
Gokarṇa, Śrīśaila, and Gandhamādana.
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Pāripātra, and Himālaya;
on Sahya, Śuktimat, Gomanta, and likewise Arbuda.
O twice-born ones, [the merit is equal to that] at all the tirthas of the Gaṅgā, those of the Yamunā,
those of the Sarasvatī, at the Gomatī, and at the seven sons of Brahmā.
O twice-born ones, the Godāvarī, Sīmarathī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Narmadā, Tāpī, Payoṣṇī, Kāverī, Śiprā, and Carmaṇvatī;
The Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Śatadrū, the Bāhudā,
as well as the Ṛṣikulyā, the Kumārī, the Vipāśā, and the Dṛṣadvatī.
The Śarayū, the excellent Gaṅgā, and the great river Gaṇḍakī;
the Kauśikī, the Karatoyā, the Trisrotā, and the Madhuvartinī.
There is the great river Vaitaraṇī and those others which have not been mentioned;
now, O best of the twice-born, what is the use of speaking at length?
On the earth, at all sacred fords, at the various shrines of Hari,
in the oceans, on the mountains, and in other rivers as well.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, that same fruit a man shall obtain by beholding Kṛṣṇa on the Mahājyaiṣṭhī day.
Therefore, O best of sages, those who desire the fruit of all their wishes should go with every effort to Puruṣottama on the occasion of Mahājyaiṣṭhī.
Having beheld Rāma on the full moon of Jyeṣṭha, and Kṛṣṇa together with Subhadrā,
a man goes to the world of Viṣṇu, having uplifted a hundred generations of his lineage.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all things at the call [of Brahmā],
he returns here upon the exhaustion of his merit and becomes a twice-born master of the four Vedas.
Devoted to his own duty, peaceful, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and having conquered his senses,
one who resorts to Vaiṣṇava yoga shall thereafter attain liberation.
Thus concludes the Mahājyaiṣṭhī. Now follows its ritual application (*prayoga*):

*Oṃ, today, on the full moon day of Jyaiṣṭha joined with the Jyeṣṭhā asterism, while the Sun is situated in the sign of Taurus, I, desiring to obtain a fruit greater than that of the twelve pilgrimages, shall perform the viewing of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā.*
Having thus resolved, he should look upon them.

Alternatively, one who desires—preceded by the deliverance of a hundred ancestors and the attainment of the world of Viṣṇu—the enjoyment of abundant pleasures lasting until the dissolution of all things occurring in that realm; thereafter, the birth as a Brahmin devoted to his own dharma as a knower of the four Vedas, peaceful, a devotee of Kṛṣṇa, and with senses subdued; and finally, the attainment of Vaiṣṇava yoga leading to liberation—should resolve: "I shall perform the viewing of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā."

Oṃ. Today, on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, conjoined with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, while the sun is situated in the sign of Taurus (Vṛṣa), I, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by bathing and giving gifts at all the sacred fords, temples of Nārāyaṇa, oceans, mountains, rivers, lakes, and reservoirs on earth during the solar eclipse, shall perform the vision of Kṛṣṇa.
Likewise, it is said in the Brahma Purāṇa:
"O Lotus-born One, at what time should the bath for Kṛṣṇa take place?"
Tell me the procedure for that bath which one performs here in such a manner.
Brahmā said:
Listen, O sages, as I describe the meritorious bath of Kṛṣṇa,
Rāma, and Subhadrā, which destroys all sins.
O twice-born ones, when the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived and the moon-ruled asterism [Mṛgaśīrṣa] coincides with the full moon,
that is the time for bathing at all times for Hari.
O twice-born ones, there stands a pure and stainless well containing all sacred fords; at that time, Bhogavatī becomes manifest there.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, having drawn water on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha with golden jars enriched with gems, for the sake of the consecration of Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā.
Having prepared a most beautiful couch, adorned with banners,
very firm, easy to traverse, and decorated with cloths and flowers.
It was spacious, perfumed with incense for the bathing of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa,
draped with white cloths, and hung with strings of pearl necklaces.
There, O twice-born ones, having placed Kṛṣṇa, who was dressed in blue garments, amidst various kinds of musical instruments,
and having seated Subhadrā in the middle, they proceeded with the sounds of victory and auspiciousness.
O twice-born ones, he was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of men and women belonging to various castes— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others.
Then householders, bath-graduates (snātakas), ascetics, and celibate students bathe Kṛṣṇa, who is on the bier along with Halāyudha.
[145] Likewise, O best of the twice-born, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) previously mentioned bathe him individually with their own waters mixed with flowers.
Afterwards, with the sounds of clashing drums, the resonance of kettledrums and clay drums, the blare of trumpets, the sound of cymbals, and likewise various kinds of mṛdaṅga drums;
And with various other musical instruments adorned with the ringing of bells,
and with the auspicious sounds of women and enchanting words of praise.
With the sounds of various hymns and purifying chants augmented by the recitation of the Sāman,
[he was honored] by ascetics, those who have completed their studies, householders, and celibate students.
At the time of bathing, they praise the best of gods with supreme joy,
accompanied by dark-complexioned and fair-skinned courtesans who are bent low by the weight of their breasts.
And with women wearing yellow and red garments, adorned with garlands of flowers,
divine earrings set with jewels, and golden clusters of blossoms.
Rāma and Keśava were fanned with yak-tail whisks having golden handles by yakṣas,
vidyādharas, siddhas, kinnaras, and hosts of apsaras.
Surrounded by gods, gandharvas, and cāraṇas moving through the sky—
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts,
as well as the world-protectors and others— praise Puruṣottama.
[146] Homage to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person! O God who brings about the creation, maintenance, and end of heaven; O Lord of the worlds, O Master of the universe!
With devotion, we pay homage to that god Brahmā, the sustainer of the three worlds, the cause of liberation, and the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Having thus praised Kṛṣṇa, the exceedingly powerful Rāma,
and Subhadrā, O best of sages, the gods then took their positions in the sky.
The gods and gandharvas sing, and likewise the apsarases dance;
divine musical instruments are sounded, and very cool breezes blow.
Then, moving through the sky, the clouds rained down flowers mixed with incense,
while the sages, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas raised shouts of victory.
All the gods beginning with Śakra, the sages, the imperishable ancestors,
the lords of creatures, the nāgas, and whoever else dwells in heaven.
Then, having taken the substances for the consecration accompanied by auspicious materials and preceded by ritual mantras, the hosts of deities [approached].
Indra, Viṣṇu of great heroism, as well as the sun and moon,
Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, and likewise wind and fire.
The wise Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aryaman, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Aṃśu, together with Vivasvat,
and accompanied by his two wives, as well as Mitra and Varuṇa.
The Lord was surrounded by the Rudras, Vasus, Ādityas, and the two Aśvins,
together with all the Viśvedevas, Maruts, Sādhyas, and Pitṛs.
[147] By Gandharvas and Apsarases, by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas,
by innumerable celestial sages (devarṣi) as well as by the most excellent Brahman-sages (brahmarṣi).
[He was attended] by the Vaikhānasas, the Vālakhilyas, those who subsist on air, those who drink the rays [of the sun],
and the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases, all of whom were thoroughly established in every branch of knowledge.
Surrounded by all the meritorious vidyādharas and those perfected in yoga,
there were the Grandfather [Brahmā], Pulastya, and Pulaha of great asceticism.
Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Atri, Marīci, and Bhṛgu;
Kratu, Hara, Pracetas, Manu, and likewise Dakṣa.
O best of the twice-born, the seasons, the planets, the celestial luminaries,
the personified rivers, and the eternal Vedas were all present there.
The oceans and lakes, various sacred fords,
the earth, the sky, the quarters of space, and the trees, O best of the twice-born;
Aditi, the mother of the gods, Śrī, Svāhā, Sarasvatī,
Umā, Gaurī, Sinīvālī, as well as Anumati and Kuhū.
Rākā and Dhiṣaṇā were the wives, as were the other wives of the dwellers of heaven;
and Himavat, Vindhya, and Meru of manifold prowess [were there].
Airāvata with his followers, as well as the divisions of time known as kalās and kāṣṭhās; the half-months, months, seasons, nights, days, and years.
Uccaiḥśravas, the best of horses; Vāmana, the king of elephants;
Aruṇa and Garuḍa; and the trees together with the medicinal herbs.
And the Lord Dharma, the god, arrived there together with them;
then all those gods, the inhabitants of heaven, having gathered as brahmins, took hold of him.
O twice-born ones, there were all kinds of materials for the consecration and auspicious items, along with golden jars filled with divine requisites.
With the auspicious waters of the Sarasvatī, with those of divine essence,
and with the water of the celestial Gaṅgā, Kṛṣṇa was united with Rāma.
Standing in the sky, they bathe [him] with golden jars filled with flowers;
likewise, the celestial chariots of the gods move through the sky.
High and low, divine, moving at will, and stable;
variegated with celestial jewels, they were frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
Adorned on all sides with songs, musical instruments, and banners,
the best of sages then, filled with joy, offered praises to Kṛṣṇa who was united with Rāma, as well as to Subhadrā, after they had been bathed.
Victory, victory to you, O Guardian of the World, protector of devotees!
Victory to Padmanābha, victory to the Upholder of the Earth!
Victory, victory to you, O Primordial God; victory, O You of many manifestations! Victory to Vāsudeva; victory, O Primordial Cause!
Victory, victory to you, O divine Fish; victory, O best of the thirty gods!
Victory, victory to you, O one who reclines upon the ocean; victory, O supreme among yogis!
Victory, victory to you, O younger brother of the Sun! Victory, O King of the Gods!
Victory, victory to you, O enemy of Kaiṭabha! Victory, O best of gods!
Victory, victory to you in the form of the tortoise! Victory, O best of sacrificers!
Victory, victory to you whose navel is a lotus! Victory, O upholder of the mountain!
Victory, victory to You who recline in Yoga! Victory, O bearer of speed!
Victory, victory to You whose form is the universe! Victory, O wielder of the discus!
Victory, victory to you, O Lord of Beings! Victory, O Supporter of the Earth!
Victory, victory to you who recline upon Śeṣa! Victory to you, clad in yellow robes!
Victory, victory to you, O beloved of the moon! Victory, O abode of yoga!
Victory, victory to you, O burner of the Daityas! Victory, O abode of dharma!
Victory, victory to you, O treasury of virtues! Victory, O abode of Śrī!
Victory, victory to you who ride upon Garuḍa! Victory, O abode of bliss! Victory, O banner of Dharma! Victory, O abode of ascetics! Victory, victory to you, O dweller in the deep forest!
Victory, victory to you, who are accessible to yogis; victory, victory to you, who dwell in the sacrifice!
Victory, victory to you, who are to be known by the Vedas; victory, O Bringer of Peace!
Victory, victory to you, O one inconceivable to yogis! Victory, O bestower of nourishment!
Victory, victory to you, O embodiment of knowledge! Victory, O source of the lotus!
Victory, victory to You, who are to be known through devotion; victory, O bestower of liberation!
