Victory, victory to You of pure body; victory, O abode of all beings!
Victory, victory to you, O bringer of joy; victory, O multitude of virtues!
Victory, victory to you, O performer of sacrifices; victory, O one devoid of qualities!
Victory, victory to you, the granter of liberation! Victory, O refuge of the earth!
Victory, victory to you, endowed with splendor! Victory, O refuge of the world!
Victory, victory to Lakṣmī’s consort! Victory to the lotus-eyed one! Victory, victory to the possessor of enjoyments! Victory to the one clad in blue garments!
Victory, victory to You, O One endowed with Yoga! Victory to You, whose body is dark like the atasi flower!
Victory, victory to You, whose abode is situated within the ocean!
Victory, victory to You, the beloved of the world! Victory to You, the supremely peaceful One!
Victory, O Essence of Wisdom! Victory, O Wielder of the Discus! Victory, O Bringer of Peace!
Victory, victory, O Bringer of Liberation! Victory, O Dispeller of Impurity!
Victory to you, O Kṛṣṇa, Lord of the World! Victory to you, younger brother of Śaṅkarṣaṇa!
Victory to you, whose eyes are like lotus petals! Victory to you, the bestower of the fruits of all desires!
Victory to you whose chest is adorned with a garland; victory to you who wield the discus and the mace!
Victory to you, the beloved of Padmālayā; victory, O Viṣṇu, homage be to you!
Brahmā said:
Having thus offered praise, the gods led by Śakra, with delighted minds,
as well as the hosts of Siddhas and Cāraṇas and all others who dwell there, [remained].
The sages and the Vālakhilyas, those best of seers, having prostrated before Kṛṣṇa who was united with Rāma, and before Subhadrā, remained stationed in the sky.
Having seen, touched, and paid homage to Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā, those dwellers of the third heaven then departed for their respective abodes.
Then the celestial palaces of the gods moved through the sky—
divine, of various heights, moving at will, and stable.
Variegated with divine jewels and frequented by hosts of apsarases,
they were adorned on all sides with songs, musical instruments, and banners.
And at that time, those mortals who behold Puruṣottama,
Balabhadra, and Subhadrā, go to the imperishable state.
Having seen the Imperishable Supreme Person seated upon a couch together with Subhadrā and Rāma, a man goes to that eternal station; of this there is no doubt.
Whatever fruit is recorded for the gift of a hundred tawny cows at Puṣkara,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa upon his bed.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the ritual release of a bull according to the rules,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon the platform.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to result from the gift of a cow yielding ghee,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa upon his bed.
Whatever fruit is declared to be obtained by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance according to the rules,
that same fruit a man attains simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa seated upon his bed.
Now, O best of the twice-born, what is the use of speaking at length or repeating this again and again? Such is the majesty of that deity when seated upon the couch.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for all sacred fords through vows and gifts,
that same fruit is obtained by beholding Kṛṣṇa on the platform together with Halāyudha.
O best of sages, a man who performs auspicious deeds attains Subhadrā as well;
therefore, both men and women should behold that Puruṣottama.
Then, one obtains the fruit arising from bathing and other rites at all sacred fords;
by the water remaining from Kṛṣṇa’s own bath, one’s self is consecrated.
A woman who is barren, or whose children have died, one who is unfortunate, afflicted by planetary influences,
seized by Rākṣasas and the like, or likewise overwhelmed by diseases;
Immediately consecrated with the water remaining from their bath,
they obtain all desired objects, whatever wishes they may long for.
One desiring sons shall obtain sons; one desiring good fortune and happiness shall attain them;
one afflicted by disease is freed from disease; and one longing for wealth shall receive wealth.
Whatever meritorious waters exist upon the surface of the earth,
they do not equal even a sixteenth part of the water remaining after his bath.
Therefore, O twice-born ones, one should sprinkle with that water which remains after Kṛṣṇa’s bath; for it indeed bestows all desires upon all limbs.
Those who, having bathed, behold Kṛṣṇa as he proceeds facing southward, are liberated from sins such as the killing of a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
A man who beholds Kṛṣṇa walking toward the south obtains that fruit which is proclaimed in the scriptures as resulting from three circumambulations of the earth.
Whatever fruit of pilgrimage on earth is proclaimed,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is said to be obtained by seeing Nārāyaṇa and Nara at Vadaryā,
a man obtains that same fruit by seeing Kṛṣṇa facing southward.
Whatever fruit is obtained through bathing and giving gifts at Gaṅgādvāra and Kubjāmra,
a man obtains that same fruit by seeing Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing and giving gifts at Kurukṣetra when the sun is eclipsed,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by seeing Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed to be obtained at Prayāga on the great Māghī day,
a man obtains that same fruit by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is obtained by bathing and giving gifts at Śālagrāma during the great Caitra festival,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit is traditionally said to be obtained at Puṣkara during the Kārttikī festival of great significance,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing and giving gifts at the confluence of the Gaṅgādvāra,
he obtains that same fruit simply by seeing Kṛṣṇa facing southward.
O twice-born ones, [one obtains this merit] at the Gaṅgā, at all sacred fords (tīrthas), as well as others;
likewise at the Sarasvatī fords and at other lakes.
Whatever fruit is declared for bathing and giving gifts according to the prescribed rites,
a man obtains that same fruit simply by beholding Kṛṣṇa facing the south.
At Puṣkara and other holy fords, at Gayā and Amarakaṇṭaka,
and at sacred sites such as Naimiṣa, as well as in sacred fields and shrines.
O Kṛṣṇa, whatever fruit a man obtains by bathing and giving gifts when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, that same fruit he obtains simply by seeing you facing the south.
Now, what is the use of speaking again and again with redundant words? Whatever has been said here regarding the fruit of meritorious action—
O best of the twice-born, [this has been stated] by the wise in the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata,
in all the Dharmaśāstras, and likewise elsewhere.
Having seen Kṛṣṇa together with Sahalāyudha, Bhadra, and his entire retinue proceeding toward the south, a man obtains that same fruit.

Now, the procedure for this is as follows: Having made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), saying, "Oṃ, today, on the full moon day of Jyeṣṭha conjoined with the asterism Anurādhā, desiring to attain the imperishable state, I shall perform the vision of Puruṣottama situated upon the platform," one should behold Puruṣottama standing on the platform.
[155] Thus, at that time, for each of the visions of Balabhadra seated on the couch and Subhadrā seated on the couch, this very same fruit [is obtained].
Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the gift of a hundred tawny cows (kapilā-gavī) based on the Puṣkara rites;
or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the ritual gift of land—should perform [this rite].

Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by duly performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by duly observing a month-long fast;
or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the vow and giving of the Sarvajña.
"I shall behold Kṛṣṇa together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā seated upon the couch.
Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should look [upon Him].
Then, immediately after this vision, for one who desires liberation from all sins such as the killing of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*) upon seeing Kṛṣṇa proceeding toward the southern direction—

Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by three circumambulations of the earth; or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by a pilgrimage to all the sacred fords (tīrthas) on earth as their locus;
or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by beholding Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarī as their locus.
Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing and giving gifts at the time of a solar eclipse at Gaṅgādvāra, which took place at the site of Kubjāmraka;

or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing and giving gifts at the time of a solar eclipse at the site of Kurukṣetra; or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing during the Great Māgha at the site of Prayāga.
Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing and giving gifts at the site of Śālagrāma during the month of Caitra;
or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing at Puṣkara during the great Kārttikī festival;
or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, or at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, at Gaṅgādvāra.
Or, one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing and giving gifts performed according to the rules at all sacred fords (*tīrtha*);

or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing during an eclipse of the sun at sacred fords such as Puṣkara, forests such as Naimiṣa, holy sites (*kṣetra*) such as Prayāga, or shrines (*āyatana*) such as Puruṣottama;
or one who desires to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit of all meritorious deeds prescribed in the Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, Dharmaśāstras, and so forth.
"I shall behold Kṛṣṇa as he proceeds toward the south accompanied by Balabhadra and Subhadrā.
Having thus made this resolve, one should look upon them as they travel toward the southern quarter.
Likewise, in that very place:
There is a sacred ford named Indradyumna-saras, born from the components of a sacrifice;
by bathing there even once, people attain the world of Śakra.
Whoever shall cause alms to be given on the very bank of that lake,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, will go to the world of Śakra.
Being honored by apsarases and by the melodic songs of gandharvas,
he shall dwell there in a celestial chariot for as long as the reigns of fourteen Indras endure.
To the south of the lake, situated in the southwest direction, stands a banyan tree; near it is a pavilion.
On the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, under the constellation presided over by the ancestors (Maghā), they will lead me there;
indeed, having taken me there, they will remain for seven days.
Then, having bathed, seen [the deity], and bowed down with devotion,
a person shall dwell for ten thousand divine years in the glorious city of Hari.
Honored by apsarases and by the melodic songs of gandharvas,
the attendant of Hari indeed sports there with Keśava.
In a celestial palace with the brilliance of the sun, shining with necklaces of jewels,
he dwells in that supreme abode amidst the great enjoyments of all his desires.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, a man shall become a Brāhmaṇa;
he will certainly become a glorious lord of ten million, a master of the four Vedas.
And those who behold Rāma and Keśava as they proceed to the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa, seated thus upon the chariot and offering salutations upon seeing it; |||
Kṛṣṇa, Balarāma, and Subhadrā go to the abode of Hari;
those who behold Kṛṣṇa stationed in the pavilion for seven days [attain that same state].
O King, those Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women, and Śūdras who [worship] Saṅkarṣaṇa and Subhadrā go to the world of Viṣṇu.
[158] With flowers, perfumes, as well as incenses, lamps, excellent food offerings,
various kinds of presents, fasts, and circumambulations;
Through shouts of victory, as well as hymns, songs, and enchanting instrumental music,
nothing whatsoever that they desire remains difficult for them to attain.
"O best of kings, by my grace this shall undoubtedly come to pass.
Having spoken thus to him, the god vanished right there.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, with every effort one should behold that Lord Puruṣottama at Guṇḍikā, who grants all desires.
One without a son obtains sons; one without wealth obtains wealth;
the sick man is freed from disease; and a maiden finds a virtuous husband.
A man obtains income, fame, renown, intelligence, strength, knowledge, fortitude, cattle, progeny, and the perfection of beauty and youth.
Whatever enjoyments a man or a woman desires upon seeing that Supreme Person, they obtain them all without a doubt.
Having performed the pilgrimage known as Guṇḍikā according to the rules and with a well-composed mind,
whether it be a man or a woman, during the bright fortnight of the month of Āṣāḍha.
O best of the twice-born, having seen Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā,
one obtains the fruit of fifteen horse-sacrifices and even more.
Having uplifted seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors from himself,
he shall travel by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will and is adorned with every kind of jewel.
He was attended by Gandharvas and Apsarases like an immortal god.
A man who is handsome, fortunate, and heroic shall go to the city of Viṣṇu;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa.
With his every desire fulfilled and free from old age and death,
he shall return here upon the exhaustion of his merit and become a twice-born man learned in the four Vedas.

Having resorted to Vaiṣṇava yoga, one shall thereafter attain liberation. Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, today, desiring to go to the abode of Hari, I shall behold Kṛṣṇa together with Balabhadra and Subhadrā, who are seated upon the chariot proceeding toward Guṇḍikā," one should then behold Kṛṣṇa at Guṇḍikā, seated upon the chariot along with Balabhadra and Subhadrā.
This is the formal argument (prayoga) in this case:

Oṃ. Today, on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, under the constellation presided over by the Pitṛs, desiring to obtain fruits exceeding those born of fifteen horse-sacrifices; desiring the prior upliftment of my own lineage—seven descendants and seven ancestors; desiring to go to the city of Viṣṇu like a god, accompanied by a beautiful, fortunate, and heroic self acting like a deity, seated in a wish-fulfilling celestial chariot (kāmagavi-vimāna) adorned with all jewels and served by Gandharvas and Apsarases; desiring the attainment of liberation preceded by the attainment of Vaiṣṇava yoga and the state of being a twice-born knower of the four Vedas in this world for as long as the dissolution of the universe lasts, endowed with the full enjoyment of excellent personal pleasures free from old age and death—I shall perform the viewing of Kṛṣṇa together with Ratha, Rāma, and Subhadrā at the Guṇḍikā-maṇḍapa, preceded by the Guṇḍikā-yātrā.
Having thus resolved, one should go there and behold them. In that very place, for the worship of Kṛṣṇa and others:
*Oṃ, today, desiring to obtain my own desired fruit, I shall perform the worship of Kṛṣṇa together with Saṅkarṣaṇa and Subhadrā according to the procedure prescribed in the Brahmapurāṇa.*

Having thus resolved, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, excellent food offerings, various kinds of presents, circumambulations, the utterance of "yajña," hymns, charming musical instruments, and by fasting on that day. Regarding this very point, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, Brahmā said:

Having performed the pilgrimage according to the prescribed rite at Guṇḍikāvāyā, during the festival of rising, on the full moon of Phālguna, and likewise at the equinox, and having beheld Kṛṣṇa and bowed down before him;
One shall obtain Saṅkarṣaṇa and Subhadrā, and indeed receive the fruit everywhere;
such a person shall go to the world of Viṣṇu for as long as fourteen Indras endure.

Therefore, at Guṇḍikā—whether on the *utthāna-dvādaśī*, or on the full moon of Phālguna, or at the water-solstice (*jalaviṣuva*), or at the grain-solstice (*dānyaviṣuva*), or during the appearance and prostration for Kṛṣṇa, or during the appearance and prostration for Saṅkarṣaṇa, or during the appearance and prostration for Subhadrā—the meaning is that for each of these, staying in the world of Viṣṇu for as long as fourteen Indras [is the fruit].
Likewise, in that very same place:
"To whatever extent a man performs the festival procession (*yātrā*) in the month of Jyeṣṭha according to the prescribed rite..."
For that many kalpas he enjoys happiness in the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
The meaning is that on any lunar day (tithi) in the month of Jyeṣṭha, the fruit of the pilgrimage is the enjoyment of happiness based in the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of a kalpa.
Likewise, in that same place,
Brahmā said:
O Brahmins, listen as I describe the fruit of the return-journey,
which a man who is well-restrained obtains by performing it in that sacred field.
In that most excellent, meritorious, and beautiful field, Śrī Puruṣottama,
which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men and brings happiness to all living beings.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, a man or a woman who has restrained her senses,
being composed, should undertake the pilgrimage on the tenth day according to the prescribed injunctions.
"He who performs the consecration, free from deceit and pride,
shall enjoy various pleasures and will certainly attain liberation.
The sages said:
O Lord, we wish to hear from you as you speak of the installation ceremony,
the ritual procedure, the worship, the offerings, and the fruit thereof for the Master of the World.
Brahmā said: Listen, O tigers among sages, to the installation rite as enjoined by the sacred law,
which a man or a woman, having performed it with devotion, certainly attains.
O best of the twice-born, when the twelve-year pilgrimage is fully completed,
one should then perform, according to the rules, the sin-destroying consecration ceremony.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the eleventh day, being composed,
having gone to a holy body of water, and having sipped water while restrained and pure;
[162] Then, being well-composed, one should perform the ritual bath according to the prescribed rules.
Whatever procedure has been prescribed by the sages for the act of bathing,
by that very rule his bathing is ordained.
Having bathed according to the proper ritual procedure, he who knows the rules for names and lineages should then satisfy the gods, the sages, the ancestors, and others with libations.
Having crossed over and put on two clean, pure, washed garments,
and having sipped water according to the prescribed rule, he should then face the sun.
Having mentally recited one hundred and eight times the purifying goddess Gāyatrī— the mother of the Vedas, meritorious, and the remover of all sins—
With faith and well-composed mind, one should recite the meritorious solar mantras;
then, having circumambulated three times, one should bow down to the Sun.
For the three [upper] castes, bathing and the recitation of mantras as prescribed in the Vedas have been declared;
for women and Śūdras, only bathing according to the Vedic injunctions is ordained, excluding the recitation.
Then, remaining silent, he should go home and worship Puruṣottama,
having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water according to the rules.
One should bathe the deity with ghee, and immediately thereafter with milk,
as well as with honey, fragrant water, and water from sacred fords mixed with sandalwood.
Then, with devotion, one should clothe him in an excellent pair of garments;
one should worship Puruṣottama with supreme devotion using lotuses and other Vaiṣṇava flowers, such as jasmine and the like.
[163] Having thus worshipped Hari, the Lord of the World, who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
one should burn incense mixed with aguru in front of the deity.
O best of sages, one should burn guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter;
and one should devoutly light a lamp with clarified butter according to one's capacity.
Furthermore, O best of sages, being composed, one should offer twelve other lamps,
either with ghee or again with sesame oil.

One should offer as the food offering (naivedya) milk-rice (pāyasa), fried cakes (apūpa), wafer-bread (śaṣkulī), and balls of dough (vaṭaka); likewise, one should present sweetmeats (modaka), molasses (phāṇita), and other fruits.
Having thus worshipped Puruṣottama with the fivefold offerings,
one should recite "Oṃ namaḥ puruṣottamāya" one hundred and eight times.
Then, with devotion, one should propitiate that God, the Supreme Person:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds, bestower of fearlessness upon your devotees!"
O Supreme Person, save me who am submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra;
O Lord of the World, those twelve pilgrimages which were performed by me for you—[may they bear fruit].
"O Govinda, by your grace, may those [desires] of mine be fulfilled.
Having thus propitiated that god and prostrated himself like a staff, he bowed down.
Then one should worship the Guru with devotion using flowers, garments, and unguents;
for, O best of sages, no difference exists between these two.
O best of sages, with faith and well-composed mind, one should create a variegated mandala of flowers above the deity using various kinds of blossoms.
Having made this firm resolve, one should thereafter keep watch during the night;
one should also cause the story of Vāsudeva and his songs to be recited.
Meditating upon, reciting, and praising the God, the wise man should pass the night.
Then, at the clear dawn of the twelfth day (dvādaśī),
he should invite twelve Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and have performed their ablutions.

Having bathed according to the proper rite and wearing clean garments, one who has conquered his senses should [approach] those learned in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, who are versed in the Vedas and have their senses restrained.
One should bathe Puruṣottama, who resides there, with devotion as before,
using perfumes, flowers, offerings, food oblations, and likewise lamps.
With various kinds of offerings, prostrations, and circumambulations;
with recitations, hymns of praise, and salutations; and with enchanting songs and instrumental music.
Having thus worshipped the Lord of the World, one should then worship the Brāhmaṇas;
having given them twelve cows as well as gold.
O twice-born ones, preceded by faith and devotion, one should with devotion give them an umbrella, a pair of sandals, wealth, and clothing and other such items.
Since Govinda is truly pleased when he is honored with sincere devotion,
one should therefore give a cow, clothing, and likewise gold to the teacher.
With devotion, he should also offer an umbrella, a pair of sandals, and a bronze vessel;
thereafter, he should feed those Brahmins with food beginning with milk-rice (pāyasa).
[165] Then, having provided cooked food, both hard and soft, along with molasses and sugar,
he [saw] those Brāhmaṇas satiated by the meal and composed in mind.
One should devotedly give twelve water-pots filled with water, and,
free from envy, one should give them a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
One should present the water-pot and the sacrificial fee to the preceptor;
having thus worshipped those brahmins and the guru who has bestowed knowledge.
O best of the twice-born, a wise man should worship with supreme devotion one who is equal to Viṣṇu,
offering gold, garments, cows, grain, wealth, and other excellent gifts.
Having worshipped him and paid homage, one should utter this mantra:
"The Lord of the World, all-pervading, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace."
"May the beginningless and endless God, the Supreme Lord, be pleased.
Having uttered this, and having circumambulated the Brahmins three times,
one should then respectfully bow with the head and bid farewell to the preceptor.
Then, one should follow those brahmins with devotion as far as the boundary;
and having followed them all and paid homage, one should inform them [of one's intention].
Then, accompanied by his kinsmen and relatives, he should eat while remaining silent,
along with others who have acquired wealth through hardship, the destitute, beggars, and those desiring material goods.
By acting thus correctly, a man or a woman obtains the fruit of thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of royal consecrations.
Taking with him a hundred ancestors and a hundred descendants of his own lineage, O brahmins, that best of men, possessing divine form,
endowed with all auspicious marks, and adorned with every ornament, departed.
With all his desires fulfilled, free from affliction like a god,
he was endowed with beauty and youth, and adorned with every virtue.
Being praised by apsarases and adorned by gandharvas,
he travels in a celestial chariot that has the brilliance of the sun, moves at will, and is steadfast.
Adorned with banners and flags and embellished with all kinds of jewels,
it illuminated all directions in the sky, free from any fatigue.
Young, possessed of great strength and wisdom, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
there, for the duration of a hundred kalpas, he enjoys pleasures as he desires.
Being praised by Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, gods, Vidyādharas, and Uragas,
as well as by the best of sages, he remains free from all affliction.
O Brahmins, just as the Lord of the World, the God who bears the conch and the discus, so did he appear joyful, assuming a four-armed form.
Having enjoyed excellent pleasures there and sported with the Apsarases,
at the end of that he goes to the abode of Brahmā, which grants all desires.
Adorned by accomplished Vidyādharas, gods, and Kinnaras,
a person who has enjoyed happiness there for ninety kalpas of time—
Therefore, O best of Brahmins, he comes from that world of Rudra— which grants the fruits of all desires, is served by hosts of gods, and bestows both happiness and liberation.
[167] Adorned with hundreds of thousands of celestial palaces,
it was graced by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Daityas, and Dānavas.
Having enjoyed happiness there for a period of eighty kalpas, at the end of that time, the man goes to Goloka, which is endowed with every enjoyment.
Adorned by gods, siddhas, and apsarases, it is exceedingly beautiful;
having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures there for seventy kalpas.
One who is self-composed and has conquered the senses is rare to find in the three worlds;
therefore, he comes from this world to the unsurpassed realm of Prajāpati.
Surrounded by Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Munis, and Vidyādharas,
he joyfully enjoyed various kinds of happiness there for sixty kalpas.
At its end is the abode of Śakra, endowed with various wonders,
frequented by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, gods, Vidyādharas, and Uragas.
Surrounded by Guhyakas, Apsarases, Sādhyas, and other celestial dwellers,
that man arrives there and enjoys happiness for fifty kalpas.
Then, having gone to the celestial realm, adorned with celestial chariots and accompanied by all the gods, the wise one attained that which is difficult to obtain and purifying.
At the end of that, having gone to the auspicious world of the Yogins which bestows liberation,
he shall enjoy there for forty kalpas pleasures that are very difficult to attain.
From there, he goes to the world known as Nakṣatra, which is very difficult to attain;
thence, for thirty kalpas, he enjoys excellent pleasures according to his desire.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, he comes to the world of the Moon,
where that Soma dwells, adorned by all the gods.
There, for twenty kalpas, he enjoys exceedingly rare pleasures;
thereafter, he goes to the world of Āditya, which is honored by the gods.
O best of the twice-born, having enjoyed auspicious pleasures there for ten kalpas in that merit-filled realm, which is full of various wonders and frequented by Gandharvas and Apsarases;
Therefore, you shall come to the world of the Gandharvas, which is very difficult to attain;
enjoy all its pleasures for one entire kalpa according to your desire.
Having eaten it, he returns to the earth and becomes a righteous king—
a universal monarch of great heroism, adorned with all virtues.
Having ruled the kingdom according to his own dharma and performed sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees,
he finally went to the auspicious world of the yogis, which bestows liberation.
Having enjoyed supreme pleasures there until the dissolution of all things at the call [of Brahmā],
he returns from there and is born here into a family of yogins.
O Brahmins, when a Vaiṣṇava of excellent lineage— rare to find and esteemed by the virtuous—
is available, that best of Brahmins, a master of the four Vedas, should perform sacrifices accompanied by the distribution of sacrificial fees.
"By resorting to Vaiṣṇava yoga, one shall thereafter attain liberation.
At the point of defining the world of Viṣṇu, Prajāpati, wishing to know who goes there, says:
"Near the King of Banyan trees, on the shore of the southern ocean..."
Those by whom the Blessed Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed Lord of the World, has been seen,
sport together with Apsarases as long as the heavens endure with the moon and stars.
Resembling molten gold, they are free from old age and death;
they are devoid of all suffering and are rid of thirst and exhaustion.
[169] Having four arms and great heroism, adorned with forest garlands,
marked with the Śrīvatsa on their chests, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace.
Some were dark like blue lotuses, some resembled gold;
others were dark-complexioned and adorned with earrings, while yet others were like diamonds.
Proud of their beauty and youth, they wander in that divine city;
there, in Puruṣottama, they behold Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā.
"O twice-born ones, I do not see any world superior to the world of Viṣṇu;
for those worlds which are heard of in the heavenly realm belong to those of meritorious deeds."
Those worlds do not equal even a sixteenth part of the world of Viṣṇu;
atheists and men devoted to sense-objects do not go there.
Neither ungrateful, nor treacherous, nor thieves, nor those with uncontrolled senses are they,
who always worship Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, with devotion.
Those Vaiṣṇavas go there to the world of Viṣṇu, without a doubt,
at that most difficult-to-attain sacred field on the shore of the southern ocean.
Those men who cast off their bodies near the Kalpa tree,
as well as those who die at Puruṣottama, go there.
Now, the procedure for this: having performed twelve processions in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should perform the installation after making the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).

Oṃ. Today, on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, desiring to attain a fruit equal to that of performing one thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices and one hundred Rājasūya sacrifices; desiring for myself and fifty ancestors and descendants of my lineage to assume divine forms, endowed with all auspicious marks, adorned with every ornament, possessing all desires fulfilled like gods, free from fever, decorated with all virtues, praised by many Apsarases and Gandharvas, with bodies adorned with all jewels, free from fatigue, youthful, possessed of great strength and heroism, illuminating all directions, having a complexion like the sun at its zenith, possessing a stable palace equipped with wish-fulfilling banners and flags, and thereby going to the world of Viṣṇu; desiring to be praised there by many Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, Suras, Vidyādharas, and the best of Uragas and Munis, assuming a four-armed form bearing the conch, discus, and mace, joyful and free from fever, enjoying various desired pleasures for a hundred Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the abode of Brahmā, which is graced by many Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Suras, Kinnaras, and Uragas, and to enjoy happiness there for nine Kalpas; thereafter, desiring a continuous flow of the fruits of all desires and the attainment of bliss and liberation served by hosts of gods, with a white body adorned by hundreds of thousands of palaces, graced by Siddhas, Vidyādharas, Yakṣas, Daityas, Dānavas, and Rudras, and to go to the world of Rudra where one enjoys happiness for eighty Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the most beautiful Goloka, served by many Suras, Siddhas, Apsarases, and Guhyakas, and to enjoy unmentioned manifold pleasures difficult to find even in the three worlds for seventy Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of Prajāpati surrounded by joyful Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Suras, Vidyādharas, Uragas, and Guhyakas, and to enjoy various wonders for sixty Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the palace of Śakra surrounded by Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Suras, Vidyādharas, Uragas, and Guhyakas, and to enjoy happiness for fifty Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of the gods, adorned with all deities and difficult to reach, where one enjoys rare pleasures for forty Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of the Moon (Śaśāṅka), which is very difficult to reach, and to enjoy desired excellent pleasures for thirty Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of the Moon, and to enjoy many auspicious pleasures for twenty Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of the Sun (Āditya), served by Puṇya-Gandharvas and Apsarases full of various wonders, and to enjoy many auspicious pleasures for ten Kalpas; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of the Gandharvas, which is very difficult to reach, and to enjoy all pleasures for one Kalpa; thereafter, desiring to attain the status of a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) on earth—endowed with supreme righteousness, great heroism, and all virtues—and to perform many sacrifices with proper fees; thereafter, desiring to go to the world of Yogins which grants liberation, and to enjoy excellent pleasures until the dissolution of the universe; thereafter, desiring to obtain birth as a preeminent Brāhmaṇa learned in the four Vedas within a Vaiṣṇava family of Yogins approved by the virtuous, and after performing many sacrifices with fees, to attain the Yoga of Viṣṇu and subsequently achieve liberation—I shall perform the twelve-fold consecration following this pilgrimage.

Having thus resolved, he should go to a body of water and enter it; having invoked the sacred fords (*tīrthas*) with the words "May they come," and having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa, he should bathe according to the procedure prescribed in his own *sūtra*, perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*), and emerge. Having put on two washed garments, sipped water (*ācamana*), and facing the sun, he should mutter the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Then, having muttered the solar mantras as well according to his knowledge, he should circumambulate the sun three times, bow to him, and proceeding silently to the sanctuary, worship Puruṣottama.

It is as follows: first, one should bathe Puruṣottama silently with cow’s ghee measured at one hundred and eight fruits, then with honey, then with scented water, then with water from sacred fords (tīrtha), and then with sandalwood water.

Thereafter, one should devoutly clothe him in an excellent pair of garments. Then one should worship him with fragrances and flowers such as jasmine. Then one should offer incense of aguru or guggulu, and offer a lamp of ghee.
After that, one should also offer twelve other lamps with either ghee or oil.

And as for the food offering (*naivedya*), one should present milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), fried pastries (*śaṣkulī*), dumplings (*vaṭaka*), sweetmeats (*modaka*), molasses (*phāṇita*), and fruits. *Phāṇita* is a product of jaggery (*guḍa*), or it may be a piece of sugar-candy shaped like a lotus-root (*śālūka*). Then, one should recite the mantra "Oṃ namaḥ puruṣottamāya" one hundred and eight times. Thereafter:
Oṃ, salutations to you, O Lord of all worlds, bestower of fearlessness upon devotees!
Save me, O Puruṣottama, who am submerged in the ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
O Lord of the World, O Govinda, by your grace, may those twelve expeditions which have been undertaken by me against you come to fulfillment.

Having recited this, one should seek his favor. Then one should prostrate oneself like a staff. Then one should worship the Guru as if he were Viṣṇu. Then one should construct a flower-pavilion over Puruṣottama.
Then, during the night, one should keep a vigil with discourses and songs concerning Vāsudeva. Meditating upon, praising, and bowing to Viṣṇu, one should pass the night.

Then, at dawn, one should invite twelve Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, whose senses are restrained, and who are well-versed in the Purāṇas. Then, having performed the ritual bathing and other rites as before, and having bathed Puruṣottama, one should perform worship ending with prostrations like a staff as previously described, and with faith, one should give to the Brahmins twelve pairs of garments, pieces of gold, umbrellas, and a pair of sandals.

Then one should give to the preceptor a cow, clothing, gold, an umbrella, sandals, and a bronze vessel. Then, having fed the invited Brahmins with milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cooked food, solid foods, and molasses, one should give them twelve jars accompanied by sweetmeats (*modaka*). One should also give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's means.

Then, to the preceptor, one should give one water-jar together with sweetmeats, as well as gold and a sacrificial fee. Thereafter, having honored the preceptor with gold, clothing, cattle, grain, and other excellent articles, and having paid homage to him—
Oṃ! May the Supreme Lord, the all-pervading Master of the World, who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who is the deity without beginning or end, be pleased.

Having uttered this, and having circumambulated the Brahmins three times in each of the three directions, one should dismiss them with the preceptor as the primary guest. Following them as far as the boundary, and having again paid obeisance to all of them, one should return home and eat in silence together with one's kinsmen.
Likewise, in this manner, on whichever lunar day (tithi) it may be—

"Oṃ! From this day forth, until as long as the sky, moon, and stars endure, desiring to sport with many apsarases, and being free from old age, death, all suffering, and the exhaustion of craving; possessing four arms, adorned with a great heroic vanamālā garland, endowed with the śrīvatsa and uraḥka marks, and bearing the conch, discus, and mace; proud of my own youth and beauty; and wishing to wander through the city of Viṣṇu until the final dissolution—I shall behold Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā.
Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should look upon them:
"Those who always worship Vāsudeva, the teacher of the world, with devotion..."
Those Vaiṣṇavas go there to the world of Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
[174] On the shore of the southern ocean, in that most rare field,
having beheld Kṛṣṇa, Rāma, and Subhadrā as well, they go there.
Regarding the daily worship of Viṣṇu: likewise, the meaning is that the fruit of occasionally beholding Puruṣottama and other [manifestations] is the attainment of the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus, in that very same [text]:
"Having worshipped for a year, or even for just a month..."
By him has been performed sacrifice, by him has been offered oblation, and by him has been practiced great austerity.
Having enjoyed various delights together with celestial nymphs, he goes to the supreme abode where Hari, the Lord of Yoga, resides.
O Brahmins, at the end of the kalpa, that best of men returns once more to the world of mortals and is born in the home of yogis, intent upon knowledge and the object of knowledge.
Having attained the Yoga of Viṣṇu, one attains autonomy from Hari;
likewise, having proceeded to the world of Viṣṇu—
those who cast off their bodies near the Kalpa-tree [attain that state].
Those men who have died in Puruṣottama go there.
Any man who dies while remembering Puruṣottama between the Vaṭa and the Sāgara also goes there; of this there is no doubt.
"Furthermore, in the center of the city shines a temple adorned with jewels.
Having begun thus—it continues:
"There go those men who have died in Puruṣottama."
[175] And that field, proclaimed as the Supreme Person, is difficult to find in the world;
having abandoned their bodies there, men go to the same realm as Hari.
Even worms, insects, moths, and those belonging to the animal realm,
having cast off their bodies there, attain the supreme goal.
Whether on a path, in a cremation ground, in a house pavilion, or even in the areas of streets— wherever it may be—
one who desires or does not desire [death] shall cast off the body there.
By renouncing [these], a human being attains liberation.
Those men who cast off their bodies there at Puruṣottama, having reached the Kalpa tree, are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Those who cast off their bodies between the Vaṭa and the Sāgara attain the supreme liberation, which is difficult to obtain; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the procedure for Puruṣottama.
Now, the procedure for Kṛttivāsas.
For it is said in the Brahmapurāṇa:
"Likewise, in the land of Utkala, Maheśvara dwells as Kṛttivāsas;
his sacred field removes all sins and is most difficult to attain."
Equal in auspiciousness to Vārāṇasī, it is endowed with ten million liṅgas;
it is renowned as Ekāmra and is possessed of eight sacred fords (tīrthas).
O best of the twice-born, at that sacred site named Vindusaras,
one should diligently offer libations to the gods, the seers, human beings, and the ancestors.
One who knows the rules for names and lineages, having bathed there according to the prescribed rite with water mixed with sesame seeds, shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
During an eclipse of a planet, at the transit of the sun, at the solstices,
as well as at the equinoxes, at the beginning of a yuga, at the *ṣaḍaśīti* [solar transits], and on other auspicious lunar days.
Those who bestow gifts such as wealth and other goods upon Brahmins there indeed obtain a hundredfold more fruit than at any other sacred site.
Those who offer a ball of rice (piṇḍa) to the ancestors on the bank of the Sarasvatī provide inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
Then, with speech restrained and senses controlled, one should go to the abode of Śambhu;
having entered and performed a circumambulation there, one should first pay homage.
Having caused Bhava to bathe with ghee, milk, and other substances, being pure oneself,
one should anoint him with fragrant sandalwood and saffron.
[177] There, one should worship the God who bears the moon upon his crest, the Lord of Umā,
with various kinds of pure flowers such as the bilva, arka, lotus, and others.
One should worship with the mantra taught in the Āgamas and with the root mantra;
having thus worshipped that deity with perfumes, flowers, garments, and so forth.
With incense, lamps, food offerings, and likewise with gifts and hymns;
with prostrations like a staff and with captivating songs and instrumental music.
Having thus worshipped the God of gods, the Lord of Umā, according to the prescribed rite with dances, recitations, prostrations, shouts of victory, and circumambulations;
Completely liberated from all sins, proud of his beauty and youth,
having delivered twenty-one generations of his lineage, he was adorned with divine ornaments.
Adorned with a golden celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells,
he was being sung to by Gandharvas and graced by Apsarases.
Illuminating all directions, he goes to the world of Śiva,
where he enjoys divine happiness that grants delight to the mind.
He remained there together with the inhabitants of that world until the dissolution at the end of the kalpa;
then, upon the exhaustion of his merit, he returned from there to this earth.
In the home of yogins, an excellent twice-born who is learned in the four Vedas is born;
having attained the Pāśupata yoga, he then attains liberation.
[178] On the occasion of the rising from sleep, as well as at the passage of the sun, likewise at the solstice,
on the eighth day known as Aśoka, and likewise at the consecration of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa).
And those who behold the Lord of Gods, the imperishable one clad in an animal skin,
they go to the world of Śiva by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
Those of great wisdom who behold that deity at any time whatsoever are indeed liberated from evil and go to the world of Śiva.
To the west, east, south, and north of the deity,
that sacred field extending for two and a half yojanas bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In that beautiful, excellent field, those who bathe in the pool and behold that Lord Maheśvara known as Bhāskareśvara, [attain liberation].
Having previously worshipped the three-eyed God of gods, who was himself honored by Āditya,
they were liberated from all sins and ascended an excellent celestial chariot.
Being sung of by Gandharvas, they go to the world of Śiva;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa.
Upon the exhaustion of their merit, they indeed come here and become righteous;
likewise, they become performers of sacrifices, donors by nature, and lords of the earth.
Those who, having bathed in the waters of Lake Bindusaras, worship and behold Mukteśvara, Siddheśa, Svarṇajāleśvara, as well as the renowned Parameśvara, Śuṣmāṇa, and Atikeśvara.
[179] Completely liberated from all evil, seated upon the finest celestial chariots and being sung of by Gandharvas, they indeed go to the world of Śiva.
There, those best of the twice-born remain for one kalpa,
having enjoyed vast and delightful pleasures in the world of Śiva.
Upon the exhaustion of their merit, they come here and are born into a preeminent family;
or else, they are born in the homes of yogis as masters of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
The best of the twice-born are born devoted to the welfare of all beings,
skilled in the meaning of the scriptures on liberation, and possessing an even-mindedness toward all things.
Having obtained the excellent yoga of Śambhu, they then proceed to liberation;
for in that supreme and meritorious field, O twice-born ones, there is a liṅga which is seen.
Whether in a forest or within a chariot, at a crossroads or in a cremation ground, wherever he may stay, he regards all beings as equally worthy or unworthy of worship.
Having seen that linga, undisturbed and well-composed through faith,
he bathed it with devotion using fragrances and beautiful flowers.
With incense, lamps, and offerings of food, as well as with prostrations, hymns of praise,
full-length salutations like a staff, and likewise with dance, song, and other such arts.

Having worshipped in this manner according to the prescribed rite, a man—or a woman, O tigers among the twice-born—endowed with faith, shall go to the world of Śiva; she attains the fruit previously mentioned. There is no need for deliberation on this point.
O best of sages, who is able to describe all the qualities of that most excellent field, except for the great lords among the gods?
[180] Having gone to that most excellent field, a man or a woman who is constantly endowed with faith during the months beginning with Mādhava—
He who, with his senses restrained, duly performs the rites at that sacred ford (tīrtha) there, attains his desired enjoyments and goes to the world of Śiva.
Having extracted twenty-one generations of his lineage, he goes to the world of Śiva;
O Brahmins, having bathed on whichever lunar day it may be in the waters of Lake Bindu.
One should behold the god Virūpākṣa and the goddess Śivā, the bestower of boons,
as well as Gaṇa Caṇḍa, Kārttikeya, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the Bull.
He goes to the Kalpavṛkṣa tree, to Sāvitrī, and to the world of Śiva,
in the auspicious Śivakṣetra of Ekāmra, which is equal to Vārāṇasī.
He who performs a bath there obtains auspicious liberation. Thus concludes the procedure for Kṛttivāsas. Now follows Koṇārka.
For it is thus:
"O best of sages, this field which I have proclaimed is very difficult to attain;
it is the shore of the ocean at Koṇārka, which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
Having bathed in the ocean, offered the arghya water to the Sun, and prostrated,
whether a man or a woman, one shall obtain the fruit of all desires.
[181] Then, taking a flower and restraining his speech, he should go to the abode of the Sun;
having entered, he should worship Bhānu and perform three circumambulations of him.
One should worship Koṇārka with devotion using both Tantric and Vedic mantras,
as well as with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Having thus worshipped Koṇārka, the thousand-rayed lord of the world, with prostrations like a staff, shouts of victory, and other such honors;
A man obtains the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices;
freed from all sins, he becomes a youth with a divine body.
O twice-born ones, having uplifted seven generations of descendants and seven generations of ancestors,
he shall travel by means of a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and moving at will.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, he goes to the world of the Sun;
having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
Having arrived here through the exhaustion of his merit, he shall be born into an eminent family of yogis as a Brahmin learned in the four Vedas, pure and devoted to his own duty.
Having attained the yoga of the Lord of Heaven, one shall thereafter obtain liberation.
The man who performs the Madanabhañjikā procession during the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra shall obtain there the aforementioned fruit.
At the rising and setting of the sun, at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), at the equinoxes, and at the solstices.
O twice-born ones, whether on a Sunday, on the lunar day, or at any time whatsoever,
those men who undertake a pilgrimage there with their senses restrained—
By means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, they go to the world of the Sun;
that man who gives up his life there in the domain of Savitṛ [attains that realm].
Having ascended to the world of the Sun, he rejoices in heaven like a god;
returning again to the human state, he becomes a righteous king.
Having attained union with the Sun, one shall thereafter obtain liberation.
Concerning the sacred field of Koṇārka:
there Mahādeva resides on the bank of the lord of rivers and streams.
It is renowned as Rāmeśvara, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
There, having bathed properly in the great ocean, they worship the Enemy of Kāma with perfumes,
flowers, incense, lamps, and excellent food offerings.
Through prostrations, as well as hymns, songs, and enchanting instrumental music,
one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and likewise the fruit of the Aśvamedha.
Likewise, those great-souled ones attain supreme perfection,
traveling by means of a celestial chariot that moves at will and is adorned with garlands of networks of tiny bells.
Being sung to by Gandharvas, they go to the world of Śiva,
enjoying unsurpassed pleasures until the dissolution of all things at the end of the kalpa.
Having returned here due to the exhaustion of their merit, they become masters of the four Vedas;
then, having attained the yoga of Śaṅkara, they proceed to liberation.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for Koṇārka. [183] Now, the Viraja-kṣetra.
Likewise—
Brahmā said:
"In Virajā, the mother Virajā, who is Brahmāṇī, is firmly established."
Upon seeing her, a mortal purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation.
Having bathed, beheld that goddess, worshipped her with devotion, and prostrated before her,
a man uplifts his own lineage and goes to my world.
And other Mothers of the World,
who remove all sins, grant boons, and are affectionate toward their devotees, also abide there in Viraja.
There flows the river Vaitaraṇī, which removes all sins;
by bathing in it, O best of men, one is liberated from all evils.
There, Hari himself dwells in the form of a boar;
having seen him and bowed with devotion, a person shall go to the city of Viṣṇu.
At Kapilāgograha, at Somatīrtha known as Ālāvusa,
at Mṛtyuñjaya, at Kroḍatīrtha, and likewise at Vasusiddheśvara.
Whatever fruit a wise man obtains at these sacred fords,
that same fruit he attains by bathing and offering libations at Virajā.
Whoever indeed offers a funeral ball (piṇḍa) in my field, Viraja, brings about inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; there is no doubt in this matter.
O best of sages, those men who cast off their bodies in my field, Viraja, indeed attain liberation.
Thus ends the section on Viraja-kṣetra. Now follows the fruit of beholding Kapila near the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
according to the Brahma Purāṇa.
That mortal who, having bathed in the ocean, beholds the pure Kapila Hari and the goddess Vārāhī, goes to the abode of the gods.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the sacred field of Kṛttivāsa:
"Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit of a horse-sacrifice, I shall perform a bath in the Vindusaras lake.
Having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should bathe there according to the prescribed rules. And regarding the giving of gifts—
The fruit here is a hundred times greater than that of giving gifts at other tīrthas. Now follows the worship of Kṛttivāsas.

Oṃ. Desiring, by means of the worship of Kṛttivāsa according to the procedure prescribed in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, first to deliver twenty-one lineages, then to be liberated from all sins, then to be honored with songs by many Gandharvas and Apsarases who are proud of their beauty and youth and adorned with divine ornaments, then to ascend a golden celestial chariot (*vimāna*) garlanded with a network of tinkling bells that illuminates all directions at once, then to go to the world of Śiva, then to dwell there for as long as the world endures accompanied by many men, then to enjoy divine pleasures, then to be born subsequently as an eminent twice-born master of the four Vedas in the house of a yogin, and finally to attain liberation preceded by the acquisition of *Pāśupata-yoga*—I [perform this worship].
I shall do.

Having thus resolved, he should circumambulate the Lord and offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). Then, having bathed Him with cow's ghee weighing one hundred and eight *palas*, followed by honey, then scented water, then water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), and then sandalwood water; and having offered the *madhuparka* and again water for sipping, he should apply anointment of sandalwood and anointment of saffron. Then, with flowers such as the *arka* and lotus, using the mantra prescribed in the Āgamas—or if that is unknown, with "Oṃ, obeisance to Kṛttivāsas" and "Oṃ, obeisance to Śiva"—he should worship Him three times. Having offered incense, a lamp, food offerings (*naivedya*), gifts, and clothing, he should worship Him with hymns, prostrations like a staff, songs, instrumental music, dance, recitation (*japa*), salutations, shouts of victory, and circumambulations.

On the occasion of Śiva’s lying down (śayana), his rising (utthāna), a solar transit (saṃkrānti), or on the Aśokāṣṭamī, one should behold Kṛttivāsas after making this formal resolve (saṃkalpa): "Om! Today, on the occasion of Śiva’s lying down, desiring to go to the world of Śiva by means of a celestial chariot (vimāna) with the color of the sun, I shall perform the beholding of Kṛttivāsas. Having thus resolved, one should behold him. The same applies to the occasion of Śiva’s rising and so forth. However, at other times:
"Oṃ, desiring today to go to the world of Śiva, I shall perform the vision of Kṛttivāsa.
Having thus made this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should behold him.
This [is the procedure] for the vision of Bhāskareśvara situated in this sacred field (*kṣetra*).

"Oṃ! Today, desiring—being seated upon an excellent celestial chariot (vimāna) freed from all sins and being praised by many Gandharvas—to go to the world of Śiva; to enjoy manifold excellent pleasures therein until the end of the dissolution (saṃplava); and thereafter, worldly sovereignty, the performance of righteous sacrifices, charity, and virtuous conduct, and the attainment of a divine abode—I shall perform the vision of Bhāskareśvara preceded by bathing in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having thus made the formal resolve (saṃkalpa), one should bathe in the pit and behold Him. Upon beholding any one of Mukheśvara, Siddheśa, Svarṇajāleśvara, or Parameśvara:

Oṃ! Today, desiring—after bathing in the waters of Vindusaras and worshipping Mukteśvara—to attain liberation preceded by the attainment of excellent Śumbhu-yoga; to become a preeminent twice-born one of equal intellect, skilled in the meaning of the scriptures on liberation and devoted to the welfare of all beings, having mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, residing in either the home of a yogin of the foremost Yoga-lineage of this world or elsewhere; enjoying vast and delightful manifold pleasures for the duration of one kalpa while seated in a supreme celestial chariot freed from all sins and being praised by many gandharvas; and thereafter [attaining that state]—I shall perform the vision of Him.

Having thus resolved, one should bathe in the Vindusaras lake, worship Mukteśvara, and behold him. The same applies to Siddheśvara and other such shrines. However, for the worship of a *liṅga* situated on a public road, [the formula is]:
"Oṃ! Desiring to go to the world of Śiva today, I shall perform the worship of the Śiva-liṅga located in the Kṛttivāsa field according to the procedure prescribed in the Brahmapurāṇa."

Having thus resolved, and having beheld the *liṅga* with faith, one-pointed mind, and perfect composure, one should worship it with bathing, perfumes, flowers, delightful incense, lamps, food offerings (*naivedya*), prostrations, hymns of praise, full-length bows (*daṇḍapraṇāma*), dance, song, and instrumental music. Then, regarding the journey to the sacred field (*kṣetra*), one should go there after making this resolution:
"Oṃ! Desiring to attain many cherished desires today and desiring to go to the world of Śiva, I shall undertake the journey to the Kṛttivāsa-kṣetra.
Having thus resolved, one should proceed.
Now follows the ritual for Koṇārka:
"Oṃ, desiring the attainment of my desired fruit, I shall perform the bath in the ocean, the offering of arghya to the Sun, and prostration to him.

Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and having performed the bath in the ocean including the prescribed libations (*tarpaṇa*), one should prostrate before the Sun. Then, taking a flower and remaining silent, one should enter the monastery of Koṇārka.

Oṃ! Desiring to obtain a divine body free from all sins, preceded by the upliftment of seven generations of my maternal and paternal lineages and the attainment of a fruit equal to the fruit born of ten horse-sacrifices; desiring to travel to the world of the Sun by means of a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) possessing the color of the sun and radiant with various fragrances, while being sung to by many Gandharvas; desiring to enjoy excellent and manifold pleasures until the end of the cosmic dissolution (*saṃplava*) as invited to that very place; desiring thereafter to be born into a preeminent family of yogis belonging to this world, as a Brahmin well-versed in the four Vedas who performs his own duty and is free from impurity; and desiring thereafter to attain the state of a Lord of the Day (*divaspati*) followed by the attainment of liberation—according to the procedure declared in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, I shall perform the worship of Koṇārka.

Having thus resolved, one should circumambulate the sun three times and worship it with the traditional Vedic mantras, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, prostrations with joined palms, and shouts of victory. [188] Now, herein follows the ritual for Rāmeśvara:

Oṃ. Desiring to obtain the supreme perfection equal to the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices; desiring to go to the world of Śiva, being sung of by Gandharvas while seated in a celestial chariot adorned with garlands of networks of tinkling bells, and remaining there until the dissolution of all beings; desiring thereafter to enjoy the highest manifold pleasures, and subsequently to attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Yajurveda in this life, followed by the attainment of Yoga through the Śaṅkara path and finally liberation—I shall perform the worship of Rāmeśvara according to the procedure prescribed in the Brahmapurāṇa.

Having thus resolved and bathed in the ocean according to the prescribed rites, one should worship Rāmeśvara just as one does Koṇārka. Now follows the ritual procedure for the field of Virajā: *Oṃ, today, desiring the purification of my lineage up to the seventh generation, I shall perform the beholding of Virajā.*
Having thus resolved, he should behold [the image].
The fruit of beholding, worshipping, and prostrating before this [image], preceded by bathing, is the attainment of the world of Brahmā after first effecting the liberation of one's own lineage.
The fruit of bathing in the Vaitaraṇī is complete liberation from all sins.
The fruit of beholding Viṣṇu in the form of a boar is the attainment of the world of Viṣṇu;
the same applies to the vision of Vārāhī.
Thus [ends the section] composed by the Great Professor Śrī Vācaspatimiśra.
In the *Tīrthacintāmaṇi*, the second section is the *Puruṣottamaprakāśa*.
189] Om, salutation to Gaṅgā.
With the heavy burden of the broad hips and full breasts of the city’s young celestial nymphs, who were eager for water-sports,
and with the sweet warbling of golden kalahamsas fluttering amidst the breaking waves;
I worship the celestial river, who possesses a Brahma-like splendor as if she had been summoned by him.
The waves of the Gaṅgā, crushed by contact with the slopes of the breasts of the young wives of the gods intoxicated with wine,
are kissed by rows of bees and by the corners of the eyes of restless young female cakravāka birds.
May the yellow direction of the worlds constantly grant unimpeded auspiciousness.
First, regarding its majesty— here in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"From there, O Brahmin, flows forth that river which removes all sins."
The Gaṅgā was tawny with the unguents from the limbs of celestial nymphs.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Those countries, those provinces, those forests, and those mountains,
through the midst of which flows the holy Bhāgīrathī, that best of rivers."
Neither by austerity, nor by celibacy, nor again by sacrifices or by renunciation,
do people attain that goal which one attains by serving the Gaṅgā.
Those men who, having committed sinful deeds in the earlier part of their lives,
resort to the Gaṅgā in their remaining years, they too attain the supreme goal.
If a man were to stand on one foot for a thousand yugas,
and another were to stay by the Gaṅgā for a single month, they would be equal— or perhaps not even equal.
Even a man who performs austerities with his head downward for ten thousand ages,
or one who remains as he pleases on the banks of the Gaṅgā— he alone attains liberation.
For all beings here whose minds are afflicted by suffering and who are seeking a refuge, there is no destination equal to the Gaṅgā.
The Gaṅgā delivers after death those lowest of men who, seized by many powerful evil deeds, were falling into hell, provided they have taken refuge in her.

The connection is that they fall after passing away. Those who constantly approach the Gaṅgā, whose garments are desired [by all], are appointed by the sages for men and by the gods together with Indra.
For that man who, in this world, worships the Gaṅgā until the fall of his body, there is no fear from dangers, nor from sins, nor from kings.
The illustrious Gaṅgā, vast and universal in form, [delivers] the blind, the dull-witted, and those destitute of wealth,
[honored] by the gods including Indra, by sages, and by the Dānavas.
When cultivated, it unites one with all objects of desire.
The meaning is that even those such as the dull-witted and the blind, who are ineligible for ritual action (*karma*), become partakers of their desired fruits through service to the Gaṅgā.
[191] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
During the dark fortnight, beginning from the sixth day, she remains present upon the earth;
the merit [of this] is equal to that of the new moon for ten days continuously.
Starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, for ten days,
he indeed manifests his presence in Pātāla himself.
Starting from the eleventh day of the bright fortnight for ten days,
ending with the fifth, she is always present in heaven.
The word "puṇyam" (merit) is used here in the genitive sense; the meaning is that from the full moon until the new moon, there is extraordinary merit in the Gaṅgā.
As stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"In the Kṛta age all holy places [are supreme], but in the Tretā age, Puṣkara is the highest."
In the Dvāpara age Kurukṣetra is preeminent, but in the Kali age the Gaṅgā is distinguished above all.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"But in the Kali age, all sacred fords naturally release their respective powers into the Gaṅgā; yet that goddess [the Gaṅgā] herself does not go anywhere."
In the Vārāha Purāṇa: "Even men of sinful character shall attain an auspicious state by the mere touch of the wind that has been moistened by droplets of the Gaṅgā's water."
Now, the majesty of the waters of the Gaṅgā. In that regard, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"That very Viṣṇu, who is omnipresent, whose nature is consciousness, is Janārdana."
That very [essence] exists in the form of liquid as the water of the Gaṅgā; there is no doubt in this matter.
In the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:

"The killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a guru, the killer of a cow, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed—all these are purified by the waters of the Gaṅgā; no doubt should be entertained in this matter."
Yama says: Whether it be situated in a field or drawn up from a well, whether cold or even warm,
the water of the Gaṅgā removes sin until the end of life.
Stale water is to be avoided; stale leaves are to be avoided.
The water of the Ganges is not to be avoided; the leaf of the Tulasī is not to be avoided.
In the Mahābhārata:
"The number of stones or even of the waters of the ocean may be calculated through all possible efforts, but [not so the merit of one who honors a guest]."
But the waters of the Gaṅgā do not have the power to describe the extent of its qualities here.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Even that man who does not perform the entire procedure for pilgrimage to sacred sites shall partake in the fruit here, through the majesty of the waters of the Gaṅgā."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Even compared to a multitude of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), the drops of water from the Gaṅgā are superior,
in that they bestow upon devotees results beyond their imagination."
By merely rinsing his mouth once with devotion using the water of the Gaṅgā,
a person enjoys divine flavors produced from the udders of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) in heaven.
Having destroyed all evil here, he shone, sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā;
like the sun at its rising, having dispelled the intense darkness, it blazes forth.
Even one seized by manifold sins born of mind, speech, and body becomes purified upon beholding the Gaṅgā; there is no doubt in this matter.
Likewise:
"The knower of yoga who eats food consecrated by the waters of the Ganges becomes free from sin, like a snake that has cast off its slough; he is the best among men."
One attains the accomplishment leading to heaven and liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, when the wind, anointed with the waters of the Gaṅgā, touches a person,
it too completely casts off all evil.
In the *Nāradīya*: "Heaps of sinful deeds as vast as the Himālaya and Vindhya mountains perish through the waters of the Gaṅgā for those whose calamities have been destroyed by devotion to Viṣṇu."
In the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*: "Merely upon entering the Gaṅgā for the purpose of bathing with devotion, the sins of men, such as the killing of a Brahmin, depart completely, crying out 'Alas! Alas!'"
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
One should dwell constantly on the banks of the Gaṅgā and always drink the water of the Gaṅgā.
Now, the fruit of serving the Gaṅgā. In that regard, the Skanda Purāṇa states:
"He alone is to be worshipped by the gods, mortals, and great sages."
He who, having taken refuge in the Gaṅgā, dwells happily and without fear.
Likewise:
"A man who might stand with his head downward for ten thousand years—
he who serves the Gaṅgā for a single month is superior to him."
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "What is the use of the eightfold yoga, what use are austerities, and what use are sacrifices?
Dwelling indeed upon the Gaṅgā is the cause of the knowledge of Brahman."
Whether one stands on a single foot for a thousand yugas,
or stays for one month at the Ganges— these two may be equal, or they may not be equal.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "What is the use of sacrifices rich in great wealth, or what is the use of austerities that cause torment?
Since the Gaṅgā, who bestows liberation from everything, remains here available for easy service."
One does not obtain that fruit through sacrifices, restraints, observances, gifts, or even renunciation which one may obtain upon reaching the Gaṅgā.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains at Prabhāsa by means of a thousand cows when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, that same fruit he obtains day after day at the Gaṅgā.
But he who, having abandoned all other means and being firmly resolved, desires liberation and dwells happily on the bank of the Gaṅgā— he indeed is a vessel for liberation.
In Vārāṇasī especially, the Gaṅgā grants liberation immediately.
Always on the fourteenth and the eighth day of every month,
and indeed on both fortnights, as well as on all festival days at all times.
And he dwelt on the banks of the Gaṅgā for as long as he lived, according to his vow.
The righteous soul for whom this succeeds is a god; there is no doubt about this.
As stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Whatever fruit a man enjoys after performing the kṛcchra and other restrictive observances," [he attains that same fruit].
And by always performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance on the bank of the Jāhnavī, one obtains that very merit.
The fruit that is obtained here by one devoted to the service of the Gaṅgā in half a day cannot be attained even through hundreds of sacrifices, despite their equality.
Whatever fruit is obtained through all sacrifices, austerities, gifts, yoga, Vedic study, and ritual acts, that one may obtain simply by dwelling on the bank of the Gaṅgā with devotion.
Whatever merit belongs to those who speak the truth, whatever merit belongs to lifelong celibates,
and whatever merit belongs to those who maintain the sacred fire— that indeed is obtained by residing on the Gaṅgā.
Now, the fruit of devotion to Gaṅgā. Regarding this, the *Brāhma* [Purāṇa] states:
"Immediately thereafter, [one delivers] ten million generations of one's own mother’s, father’s, and wife’s lineages."
Devotion to the Gaṅgā certainly delivers one from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Contentment, supreme sovereignty, knowledge of reality, happiness of the self,
and perfection in modesty and conduct arise for the devotee of the Gaṅgā.
A mortal becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done simply by reaching the Gaṅgā;
if he is devoted to her and intent upon her, he is liberated indeed—of this there is no doubt.
He who, out of devotion, eats food cooked with that water and partakes of that water,
indeed finds the means to liberation without effort.
Initiated in all sacrifices, he partakes of the Soma drink day after day.
Those embodied beings for whom all rites are performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
having cast off their bodies, abide forever in the state of Śiva.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "He who might stand perpetually on one foot for a thousand yugas is surpassed by him who resorts to the waters of the Gaṅgā as he pleases."
In the Mahābhārata: "Just as the gods consume the nectars situated in the moon and the sun through their mouths consisting of mantras and so forth, so do men [consume] the water of the Gaṅgā."
[197] Now, the fruit of drinking the water of the Gaṅgā.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
Likewise, by the giving away of daughters in marriage elsewhere, through gifts of land with devotion,
and by gifts of food, gifts of cows, as well as gifts of gold and so forth;
Whatever merit is proclaimed to come from the giving of chariots, horses, and elephants,
a hundred times that merit arises from a single mouthful of water from the Gaṅgā.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for thousands of Cāndrāyaṇa fasts,
a fruit even greater than that is obtained from drinking the water of the Gaṅgā.
In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "By drinking even a mere mouthful, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
For him who drinks the water at will, power resides in his hand."
Likewise:
"The water of the Sarasvatī is digested in three months, that of the Yamunā in seven,
that of the Narmadā in ten months, and that of the Gaṅgā in a year."
For embodied beings who have died anywhere within the waters [of these sacred sites], there is the attainment of the fruit of those respective holy places; no deliberation is required in this matter.
Likewise:
"He who performs a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa penances for the purification of the body is surpassed by one who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā according to his desire."
In the future, he who beholds the Gaṅgā, praises her, bathes in her with devotion, and drinks her water,
attains heaven, stainless knowledge, yoga, and liberation.
In the Mahābhārata: But he who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā heated by the rays of the sun—
that is superior to barley-gruel (yāvaka) prepared from grains released after being offered to cows.
The accomplishment is friendliness (*maitra*). *Yāvaka* refers to boiled barley.
This is the ritual procedure (*prayoga*) here:

"Oṃ! Today, desiring to obtain a merit a hundred times greater than the merit arising from the gift of many maidens, lands, food, cows, gold, chariots, horses, and elephants, I shall perform the drinking of Ganges water in a mouthful (*gaṇḍūṣa*)."

Oṃ! Today, desiring liberation, I shall freely drink the water of the Gaṅgā. Oṃ! Today, desiring to attain a purity superior to that resulting from the consumption of barley and barley-gruel (yāvaka) obtained by means of the release of a cow, I shall drink the water of the Gaṅgā heated by the sun. Now follows the ritual of beholding [the deity].
In that regard, the Mahābhārata states:
"Just as serpents become devoid of poison at the sight of Tārkṣya,
so too, by the sight of the Gaṅgā, one is liberated from all sins."
Even a man seized by sins born of the actions of speech, mind, and body becomes purified upon seeing the Gaṅgā; of this I have no doubt.
By beholding, touching, and bathing in the Gaṅgā, a man delivers seven generations of ancestors below him, seven generations above him, and those others who follow them.
Through seeing, touching, drinking, and likewise by chanting the name "Gaṅgā," merit purifies men by the hundreds and thousands.
[199] In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "Knowledge, sovereignty, long life, stability, universal respect,
and being the locus of auspicious things— this is the fruit born from the sight of the Gaṅgā."
The fickleness of all the senses, addiction to vices,
and indeed the cruelty of men quickly perish simply from the sight of the Gaṅgā.
Violence toward others, deceit, and the observation of the faults of others—
all these perish for hypocritical men simply by the sight of the Gaṅgā.
In the *Pādmapurāṇa*: "A man should look [upon it] again and again, or likewise touch it again and again with devotion, whatever eternal and immortal state he desires."
In the future,
whatever merit may arise from constructing ponds, wells, tanks, water-stations, shelters, and the like, that merit shall be obtained simply by the sight of the Gaṅgā.
Likewise: "Whatever fruit arises for men from the vision of the Supreme Self, that very same fruit shall indeed arise from the vision of the Gaṅgā through the spirit of devotion."
Likewise: "The fruit that a man obtains by bathing and by visiting Naimiṣa, Kurukṣetra, the Narmadā, and Puṣkara— "
The great seers have declared that in the Kali age, [merit] comes from the mere sight of the Gaṅgā.
[200] Herein is the formal application (*prayoga*):

*Oṃ, today, desiring the destruction of all sins, I shall perform the beholding of the Gaṅgā.* Or: *Oṃ, today, desiring the destruction of many sins born of speech, mind, and action, or desiring the deliverance of twenty-one generations of persons; and this is the fruit upon touching [the water].*

Or, desiring knowledge, sovereignty, long life, stability, universal respect, and a virtuous refuge; or desiring to obtain the fruits arising from the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, water-stations, and almshouses; or desiring to obtain the fruits of bathing and serving at Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, Kurukṣetra, and the Narmadā;
or desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by the vision of the Supreme Self—*Oṃ*, with devotion I shall perform the vision of the Gaṅgā today.
Now, the remembrance of the Gaṅgā.

In that regard, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states: "The Gaṅgā always rescues those joined with inauspicious deeds who are sinking in the ocean of existence and falling into hell, as soon as she is remembered."
In the *Mātsya*: "Even a man who has committed evil deeds attains the supreme goal if he remembers the Gaṅgā from thousands of yojanas away."
In the future,
by the mere remembrance of the Gaṅgā, the cage of the multitude of sins will shatter into a thousand pieces, just as a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Likewise:
"Whether walking, standing, meditating, waking, eating,
breathing, or speaking, he who constantly remembers the Gaṅgā shall be liberated from bondage."
And those who, even while staying a thousand yojanas away, remember the Gaṅgā with devotion—they too are liberated from all great sins; there is no doubt in this matter.
Varied palaces, women adorned with diverse ornaments,
health, and the perfection of the mind— these are the fruits born of remembering the Gaṅgā,
for those by whom the merit-bearing Gaṅgā has been entered even once with devotion.
The auspicious Goddess delivers a hundred thousand of those families from worldly existence.
