In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "That man who, though standing at a distance, should call the Gaṅgā to mind with his thoughts, obtains the merit of a thousand Cāndrāyaṇa fasts; of this there is no doubt."

The application here is as follows: *Oṃ, today I shall perform the recollection of Gaṅgā, desiring the absence of falling into hell— or desiring the attainment of the supreme state, or desiring the destruction of the mass of sins—

or desiring liberation from all great sins without exception, or desiring various divine abodes, diverse ornaments, many women, health, and the abundance of wealth, or desiring the attainment of the fruit produced by a thousand *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts.*

Oṃ. Desiring liberation from sins today, or out of devotion, I shall perform the remembrance of Gaṅgā. Even by the mere utterance "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" with devotion, this very fruit is obtained; and through the remembrance of Gaṅgā in various ways during a vigil, liberation is the fruit.
Now, regarding glorification (*kīrtana*):
in that regard, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
"The name 'Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā,' even if uttered from across hundreds of *yojanas*..."
When recited while standing, it destroys the evil accumulated over three lifetimes.
Regarding the Gaṅgā, the Mātsya Purāṇa states: "By chanting her name one is released from sin; by seeing her one beholds auspicious things;
and by bathing in and drinking from her, one purifies one's lineage unto the seventh generation."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "The Gaṅgā delivers seven generations of descendants, seven generations of ancestors, and seven more beyond them— even when she is merely mentioned incidentally by men."
Even one who, though without desire, performs the recitation of the name of the Ganges,
that river which carries merit, is also a recipient of heaven.
In the Nāradīya [Purāṇa]: "Even one who has reached every state of existence or is devoid of all merit may attain an auspicious destination merely by the glorification of the Gaṅgā."
The formal ritual procedure (*prayoga*) here is as follows:
"Oṃ! Desiring the destruction of the sins accumulated over three lifetimes, I shall perform the recitation of 'Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā.
Or, desiring the salvation of twenty-one generations of my lineage, or desiring a share in heaven, or desiring the attainment of an auspicious rebirth."
[203] Touching.
Regarding that, in the Vārāha-purāṇa, in the section concerning the Gaṅgā:
Whether one is a killer of a Brahmin, a killer of a teacher, a killer of a cow, or touched by all manner of sins—
a man who is touched by the waters of that [river] is liberated from all evils.
Oṃ. Today, desiring the destruction of all sins, beginning with the great transgressions (mahāpātaka), I shall perform the touching of the Gaṅgā. Now follows the specific aspiration;
regarding this, it is said in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
"When shall I speak of that Gaṅgā? When shall we obtain a bath there?"—thus desired by men, she delivers a hundred generations of one's lineage.
Oṃ. Desiring to deliver a hundred lineages, I shall today perform the aspiration for the Gaṅgā.
Now, the ritual bath.
Regarding this, in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
O Maitreya, for one who has bathed in her waters, sin is instantly destroyed and the attainment of unprecedented merit arises immediately.
In Bhārata,
the reward that accrues to men of restrained soul who have bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices.
[204] *Prayataḥ* means restrained in the eleven sense-faculties. *Vyuṣṭiḥ* is the accumulation of merit.
Likewise: "Having dispelled the intense darkness, he shines like the sun at its rising."
Having thus destroyed his evil, he shines, sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "By a single bath alone, performed according to the prescribed rite, a devoted man will certainly and immediately obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at the Gaṅgā."
Likewise: "The sin of men accumulated over many births perishes merely by bathing in the Gaṅgā; instantly one becomes a vessel for merit."
Likewise: "Sin committed in another place perishes on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
sin committed on the banks of the Gaṅgā perishes by bathing in the Gaṅgā."
Likewise: By bathing with effort in the Ganges at night, by day, or during the twilight, one obtains the merit born of an Ashvamedha sacrifice; even at home, by using water drawn from it.
Whatever merit is found in all sacred fords and in all shrines, one obtains all that fruit from bathing in the Gaṅgā; of this there is no doubt.

In this context, it should be understood that, according to the principle of the accomplishment of yoga (*yogasiddhi*), the desire for any one of the fruits [of the rite] constitutes a qualification of the eligible person (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*).
"Whether joined with a great sin (*mahāpātaka*) or joined with all sins,
one is liberated from all sins by bathing in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rule."

There has never been, nor will there ever be, a bath superior to bathing in the Gaṅgā. It removes great sins (mahāpātaka) accumulated over previous births, but not those of this life; otherwise, it would result in a lack of qualification for the rite.
Specifically, in the Kali Yuga, the daughter of Jahnu (Jāhnavī) removes all sin.
Likewise:
"Having destroyed the faults born of desire arising from body, speech, and mind,
one rejoices in heaven like a god through bathing and devotion."
For a year,
or for six months, the man who bathes continuously in the Gaṅgā is liberated from all sins and, together with his entire lineage, attains equality [with the divine].
Endowed with all enjoyments, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu for the duration of two parārdhas; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
Likewise: "That mortal who bathes in the Gaṅgā constantly throughout his entire life is liberated while still alive; upon the end of the body, he is truly liberated."
Likewise: "The merit from bathing at dawn is tenfold; likewise at midday;
at evening it is a hundredfold; and in the presence of Śiva, it is infinite."
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "Bathing in the Gaṅgā is superior to the gift of ten million tawny cows.
In the Mātsya Purāṇa:
The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever she is plunged into; [206] in the Āgneya-purāṇa, there is this statement of the Sun:
"Those who perform rites such as bathing in the water heated by my rays..."
Those who shall act here will go forth, having pierced through my mandala.
Likewise, Varuṇa said to her: "Even one who remains at home, if he shall glorify you during his bath, he will go eternally to heaven."
Now, the procedure for this is as follows:
*Oṃ, today, desiring the immediate destruction of sins and the immediate attainment of unprecedented merit, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā;

or, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by bathing at Kurukṣetra; or, desiring the splendor arising from a hundred sacrifices for one who is self-restrained; or, desiring a radiant appearance preceded by the removal of sin.*
Oṃ. Desiring to obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha), I shall perform the ritual bath in the Ganges with devotion according to the prescribed rule.
Even at night, during the twilight, or likewise when bathing at home using water drawn from the Ganges, there is indeed the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Or, desiring to obtain any one of the merits produced by all holy fords (tīrtha) and all sacred shrines (āyatana), I shall perform the bath in the Ganges.
Oṃ. Today, desiring liberation from all sins, I shall perform the ritual bath in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rules;
or, desiring the destruction of sins committed on the banks of the Gaṅgā; or, desiring to obtain a fruit greater than that produced by the gift of ten million tawny cows.
Oṃ! Desiring to go forth preceded by the piercing of the solar orb, I shall perform today the bath in the waters of the Gaṅgā heated by the rays of the sun.

Oṃ! Desiring to be honored in the world of Viṣṇu—liberated from all sins, joined with my entire lineage, and endowed with all enjoyments—for a period of one parārdha plus a second [parārdha] beginning from today, I shall perform the bath in the Gaṅgā for six months starting from today.

Oṃ! Desiring to rejoice like the gods in the heavenly realm, preceded by the destruction of the defects born of desire arising from body, speech, and mind, I shall perform with devotion the bath in the Gaṅgā for one year starting from today.
Oṃ, desiring to obtain ten times the fruit produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā this morning, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā at midday.
Oṃ, desiring to obtain a hundred times the fruit produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā this morning, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā this evening.
Oṃ, desiring the infinite fruit produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā today, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā in the presence of Śiva.

Oṃ, desiring liberation while living in this life (*aihika-jīvanmukti*) and liberation at the time of the body's end (*dehāntakālika-mukti*), I shall perform my bath in the Gaṅgā from today until the end of my life.
[208] Now, the bath at specific times.
In that regard, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"The man who bathes continuously in the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha,
having remained for a long time in the worlds of Śakra, [returns] together with his kinsmen."
Then one shall dwell in the city of Brahmā for ten million times a hundred billion kalpas.
And here, the adoption of the solar month is based on the practice of the learned; as stated in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*:
"The man who bathes in the Gaṅgā continuously according to the prescribed rule..."
One [attains it] in six months, while another attains it once only during the northern course of the sun.
The merit of these two shall be equal, as it is likewise during the equinoxes;
and at all the transits of the sun, one obtains the fruit of the Cāturmāsya sacrifice.
This very merit would be obtained during the months of Māgha and Kārttika;
likewise, the fruit of an entire year would be attained on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika.
And this [observance] is white (śukla) because it is the first;
at the beginning of the Manu-period and at the beginning of the Yuga, one obtains the fruit of three months.
On the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa, and on the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) through conjunction with Puṣya.
A bath in the Gaṅgā on the fourteenth day under the constellation Ārdrā is very difficult to obtain;
likewise so is one on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, Māgha, or Kārttika.
Likewise, the new moon day of Māgha is extremely difficult to encounter at the Gaṅgā;
on the eighth day of the dark fortnight, the merit is a thousandfold, and on all other festival days (parvan), it is a hundredfold;
and this eighth day of Māgha is [so called] because of its inclusion within that conjunction.
In that regard as well, the dark fortnight is superior because it is embraced by the virtuous.
In that very context:
"On the new moon day, [the merit is] a hundredfold; on the day of the sun's disappearance (the solstice), it is a thousandfold."
During an eclipse of the moon or sun, [the merit is] one hundred thousandfold; during a Vyatīpāta conjunction, it is infinite.
The *Kalpataru* states that the conjunction (*saṃkrānti*) of the sun and moon at the same degree is called *vyatīpāta*.
However, the fruit [of bathing] during the three months of Phālguna and Āṣāḍha would be [great];
for if one performs a bath in the Gaṅgā with a spirit of devotion on one's birth-star (*janmarkṣa*), [the merit is immense].
The flood of sins accumulated since birth is destroyed in an instant.
Likewise,
it is said in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "When on the fourteenth day there is a conjunction with the Vyatīpāta yoga and the Ārdrā nakṣatra,
that is the most meritorious time, difficult to obtain even for the gods."
Then, whoever bathes in the Gaṅgā with devotion shall obtain that fruit;
even if one dies anywhere else, that merit arises from dying in the Gaṅgā.
When the eighth day of the dark fortnight coincides with the Ārdrā asterism and the Vyatīpāta yoga, a bath in the Gaṅgā is difficult to obtain; indeed, that conjunction is exceedingly rare.
He who, being knowledgeable in the ritual injunctions, regularly performs the bath in the month of Māgha through a stroke of fate,
by that same stroke of fate remembers his former birth.
At that very moment, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices, austerities, and gifts;
indeed, one becomes a knower of the meaning of all scriptures and free from disease.
Likewise:
"At the time of the sun's passage into a new sign, at the end of the fortnights, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
a man who bathes in the Gaṅgā shall go to the abode of Brahmā according to his desire."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "He who bathes in the Jāhnavī during an eclipse of the moon or sun has bathed at all sacred fords; why should he wander the earth?"
The Smṛti states: "The merit is said to be a hundred-thousandfold under the moon, and tenfold under the sun;
but when one has reached the bank of the Gaṅgā, it is ten millionfold under the moon and ten times that under the sun."
Likewise, it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa: "The fruit that results from properly giving away ten million cows is obtained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu."
Likewise, it is declared that on the day of the Sun (Sunday),
the thirteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight in the month of Magha, conjoined with the asterism Māgha and the Varuṇa yoga, possesses a hundredfold merit.
If it could be obtained on the Gaṅgā even for hundreds of solar years, Śaṅkha says:
"And likewise on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha."
Having bathed in the waters of the Gaṅgā, a person is liberated from all sins.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight, on a Tuesday under the asterism Hasta, this daughter of the mountains descended from the mountain to the world of mortals;
and the noble ones say that she removes sins on this very lunar day called Daśamī.
One would bestow a merit even a hundredfold greater than that of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
"During the transits of the sun, at the *vyatīpāta* yoga, during eclipses of the moon and sun,
and on the full-moon day, one who bathes in the Gaṅgā shall deliver ten million members of their lineage."

[211] Vyatīpāta is the equality of the declinations (krānti) of the sun and the moon; so says the Kalpataru. However, some maintain that it is a new moon day on a Sunday conjoined with any one of the asterisms Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, or Mṛgaśiras. Regarding this, Bṛhanmanu says:
"In Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, and the head of Mṛgaśiras..."
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) falls on a Sunday, that is called Vyatīpāta.
Yama said: Especially on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
a person who bathes in the waters of the Gaṅgā is liberated from all sins.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "O Jāhnavī, whatever sins I have that are designated as great transgressions (mahāpātaka), take them away from me upon the arrival of Govinda-dvādaśī."
Govindadvādaśī is the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna. In the Brāhmaṇḍa Purāṇa it is said: "Always on the fourteenth and the eighth days of every month..."
And on both fortnights, indeed, on all festival days, [one should bathe] in the Jāhnavī.
The Bhāgīrathī, and especially the sacred fords and shrines that remove all sins, come together in great abundance.
Having bathed with devotion in the waters of the Gaṅgā on the birth-star of one's own self, a man shall uplift his entire lineage.

Likewise: "When the moon, its orb fully complete, enters into conjunction with the constellation known as Māsa (Mṛgaśīrṣā) while Jupiter is present, that is remembered as the greatness of the lunar day."
O best of gods, the Mahājyaiṣṭhī is remembered as yielding infinite fruit;
on that day, a bath in the Jāhnavī is superior to [the merit of] a hundred solar eclipses.
The Smṛti states: "If the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, occurring at the time of dawn,
can be obtained on the Gaṅgā, it is equal to a hundred solar eclipses."

In these two statements, the fruit resulting from bathing during a solar eclipse is indeed that which arises from bathing in the Gaṅgā; for even regarding bathing, the principle applies that "when something proximate is available, the cognition [of it] is internal. Therefore, the meaning is that the fruit here, consisting of a hundredfold increase and so forth, belongs specifically to the bath in the Gaṅgā taken at the time of a solar eclipse.
Now, the formal ritual procedure (*prayoga*) here is as follows:

*Oṃ, desiring to dwell in the city of Brahmā for a period measured by ten million times ten thousand kalpas, preceded by a very long stay together with those born of my own lineage in the realm of Śakra, I shall perform the bath in the Gaṅgā beginning today during the month of Māgha.*

Oṃ. Today, at the sun’s transit during the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), desiring to obtain merit equal to that produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā for six continuous months during the *vaidhṛta* yoga, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
The same applies to the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*).
Regarding the nine occasions—the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the *viṣṇupadī*, and the eight *ṣaḍaśītis*:

Oṃ. Today, on the occasion of such-and-such saṃkrānti, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā for the uninterrupted four months [of Māgha], I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
This same formula applies to the entire Māgha-bath and the entire Kārtika-bath as well.
On Akṣaya-navamī:

Oṃ. Today, on the ninth day of the month of Kārttika, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā for an uninterrupted year according to the prescribed rule, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ. Today, at the beginning of a Manvantara, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā for an uninterrupted three-month period according to the prescribed rule, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
The same applies to the beginnings of the Yugas.

A bath in the Gaṅgā on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, on the eighth lunar day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism, on the full moon of Vaiśākha, on the full moon of Māgha, on the full moon of Kārttika, and on the new moon of Māgha, is exceedingly rare (*atidurlabha*). This "exceedingly rare" status means being a thousandfold superior. For it is understood from the very statement that what is normally a thousandfold [meritorious] at other times becomes "exceedingly rare" on these specific occasions. Accordingly: *Oṃ, today, on the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, desiring to obtain a fruit exceeding a thousandfold the fruit produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.*
In the same way, this should be understood for all six [days], beginning with the eighth.
Oṃ, today, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha, desiring to obtain a thousandfold the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā, I shall perform my bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, today, on this auspicious festival day, desiring to obtain a hundredfold the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā, I shall perform my bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, today at the end of the day, desiring to obtain a fruit a thousand times greater than the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, today during a solar eclipse, desiring to obtain a fruit a hundred-thousand times greater than the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
The same applies during a lunar eclipse.
Oṃ. Today, on this *vyatīpāta* [astrological conjunction], desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from bathing in infinite Gaṅgās, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ. Desiring to obtain the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā for a continuous period of three months, beginning today until the month of Phālguna, I shall perform the Gaṅgā-bath.
The same applies in the month of Āṣāḍha.
Oṃ. Desiring the destruction of the multitude of sins accumulated from birth until today, or desiring the upliftment of my entire lineage, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ. Today, on the fourteenth day joined with the Vyatīpāta yoga and the Ārdrā nakṣatra, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by dying in the Gaṅgā, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ. Today, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Māgha, joined with the Vyatīpāta yoga and the Ārdrā nakṣatra, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruits produced by remembering past births, performing all sacrifices, practicing austerities, and giving gifts, and desiring mastery of all scriptures and freedom from disease, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ. Today, on the occasion of the *saṃkrānti*, desiring to go to the abode of Brahmā, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā. The same [formula applies] for the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), a lunar eclipse, and a solar eclipse. Today, during a solar eclipse, desiring to obtain the fruit resulting from bathing in all sacred fords (*tīrtha*), I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā. During a lunar eclipse, it is the same. Oṃ. Today, while the sun is seized by Rāhu, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit resulting from bathing in the Gaṅgā multiplied ten million times, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ, on this night, when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the gift of ten million cows given in full measure, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, today, when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, desiring to obtain a hundredfold the fruit produced by the gift of ten million cows given in full measure, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ, today, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra, conjoined with the Vāruṇa nakṣatra, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by bathing in the Gaṅgā at the time of a hundred solar eclipses, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, today, on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, desiring liberation from all sins, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ, today, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of Jyaiṣṭha, conjoined with the Hasta nakṣatra, the son of the Earth (Mars), desiring the destruction of the ten kinds of sin and the attainment of merit a hundred times greater than that produced by ten thousand horse-sacrifices, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, today, on the day of the Saṃkrānti, desiring the deliverance of many millions of my ancestors, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
In the same way, during a *vyatīpāta*, a *puṣya* asterism, a lunar eclipse, or a solar eclipse, one should say:

"Oṃ, today, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, at the time of a solar eclipse, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from bathing in the hundred Ganges, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā.
Now, regarding bathing at specific locations:
on this matter, the *Padma Purāṇa* states:
"The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever she is immersed."
Where she meets with the Vindhya mountain, it is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra.
The Jāhnavī at the city of Kāśī is said to be a hundred times more [efficacious] than at the Vindhya;
and likewise, the confluence with the Vindhya at Karṇatīrtha and other such sites. Thus:
The Gaṅgā is easily accessible everywhere, yet she is difficult to attain at three specific places:
at Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Those who bathe in these places go to heaven; those who die there are not subject to rebirth.
In the *Mātsya*: "The Gaṅgā is equal to Kurukṣetra wherever she is plunged into;
where she meets the Vindhya, she is ten times more meritorious than Kurukṣetra."
Beyond that, it is said to be a hundredfold more powerful where it flows westward;
from that, it is a thousandfold more powerful where it flows northward;
and from that, it is a thousandfold more powerful where it flows in both directions.
In the future,
at Gaṅgādvāra and Kuśāvarta, hear the meritorious fruit of bathing:
it shall be equal to the fruit of seven Rājasūya sacrifices and two Aśvamedhas.
Having dwelt there for six months and a half, a person obtains the fruit of six Viśvajit sacrifices as well as the merit of the gift of ten thousand cows.
Having bathed in the Gaṅgā and at the step-well, one obtains imperishable merit by visiting Govinda, the best of gods, and Rudra, who resides at Kaṇakhala.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O Sage, hear now of the highly meritorious sacred site named Śaukara,
wherein Acyuta formerly manifested in the form of a boar."
A man shall obtain here the merit of a hundred performers of the Agnicayana sacrifice and of two Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices,
as well as the fruit of a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices.
Right there is the sacred ford of Brahmā, as well as that of ten thousand Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices and even three Aśvamedha sacrifices; one who bathes there obtains the fruit thereof.
Likewise,
there is the sinless holy site named Kubjā, where all diseases perish and the sins of men arising from all their births are destroyed.
Then they say: "The sacred ford of Kapila is where Kapilā cows were given daily by him;
having bathed there, one obtains a fruit equal to that of giving eighty thousand [cows]."
Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Vilvaka, Nīlaparvata,
and the Kaṇakhala tīrtha, one whose sins are shaken off shall go to heaven.
Having mentioned Kāśī in the same manner,
he then described the holy site named Pavitra, which is more purifying than all other holy sites;
by bathing there, a person obtains the merit of two Viśvajit sacrifices.
[218] Beyond that is the sacred ford called Veṇīvāhya, where the Sarayū, most meritorious, has united with the highly auspicious Gaṅgā, like a sister meeting her own sister.
Know that from the washing of Hari’s right lotus-foot comes the celestial river (Ganges),
and the water from his left foot is the Sarayū, which originates from Lake Mānasa.
Worshipping Rudra and Viṣṇu at that sacred ford (tīrtha), he attained the state of Viṣṇu;
bathing there bestows the fruit of fifty horse-sacrifices and destroys all sins.
The place known as Dardarī is situated at the confluence of the Veṇī; beyond that is the Gaṇḍaka Tīrtha where the Gaṇḍakī river joins [the Ganges].
A bath there is equal in merit to the gift of a thousand cows.
Beyond that is the meritorious Rāmatīrtha, where Vaikuṇṭha is present.
Then, at the meritorious Somatīrtha, that sage Mudgala,
having worshipped Śiva and meditated upon him, attained the status of a Gaṇa.
There is a meritorious tirtha named Campaka, where the Gaṅgā flows northward;
it should be understood as being like Maṇikarṇikā, destroying even the greatest of sins.
Then there is the sacred ford named Kalaśa, where the sage Agastya arose from a water-pot; it is there that the eminent sage, while worshipping Rudra, became a supreme ascetic.
Somadvīpa is a place of great merit, a sacred ford equal to Vārāṇasī,
where Soma worshipped the Lord while being held upon Rudra’s head.
Having bathed there where the sister of Viśvāmitra meets with the Gaṅgā, that beloved guest, highly esteemed by the enemy of Vṛtra, [proceeded].
[219] What could be greater than this: that at the great holy ford (tīrtha) of Jahnuhrada, bathing for embodied beings effects liberation from twenty-one generations?
In the city of Ekaśākhā, on the Gaṅgā at Jahnuhrada;
from there is Adititīrtha, where Aditi, having performed penance, obtained Hari as her son from Kaśyapa— bathing there brings great prosperity.
Having performed austerities there at that great sacred ford, Śiloccaya,
living beings go to heaven along with their grass and other possessions, by virtue of resorting to the qualities of that holy site.
There is a sacred site named Indrāṇī where Indrāṇī, having performed austerities, obtained Vāsava as her husband; by bathing here, one gains the same merit as at Prayāga.
The holy Āmrātaka is a sacred ford where Viśvāmitra, while practicing austerities,
attained the status of a Brahman-sage by resorting to that sacred site, though he was originally a Kṣatriya.
At that place of great prosperity, by means of his own ascetic penance, Smara became the son of Hari named Pradyumna; thus it is known as Pradyumna-tīrtha.
To the south of that [confluence] is Prayāga, where the Yamunā flows from the Gaṅgā;
by bathing there, one obtains inexhaustible merit, just as at Prayāga itself.
Dakṣiṇaprayāga is well known as Muktaveṇī or Saptagrāma.
Having bathed at Gaṅgādvāra, Prayāga, and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, one should proceed to the cities of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
In the Mahābhārata:
"O King of kings, at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean,
the wise declare that [the merit] is ten times that of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."
[220] Now, the formal application (*prayoga*) here is as follows:
*Oṃ, desiring to obtain ten times the fruit produced by bathing at Kurukṣetra today, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā confluence at the Vindhya mountains.*
Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a hundredfold the fruit arising from bathing in the Gaṅgā at its confluence with the Vindhya, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā at Kāśī.
This same fruit applies even when she flows westward.
Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a thousandfold the fruit arising from bathing in the west-flowing Gaṅgā, I shall perform a bath in the north-flowing Gaṅgā.
Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by seven *rājasūya* sacrifices and two *aśvamedha* sacrifices, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā at Gaṅgādvāra.
The same applies to Kuśāvarta.
Oṃ, desiring imperishable merit today, having bathed at Kaṇakhala, I shall perform the worship of Govinda and Rudra, the best of gods, residing there.

Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by a thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices—which is itself equal in merit to the two Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices performed by Agnicit—I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā at Śaukara-tīrtha.
And here, for the bath at Brahma-tīrtha:
Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by ten thousand Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifices and three Aśvamedha sacrifices, I shall perform a bath in Brahma-tīrtha.
Oṃ! Desiring the destruction of all diseases and the sins arising from all births, I shall perform my bath at the sacred ford named Kubjā.
Oṃ! Desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by the gift of eight times ten thousand Kapila cows, I shall perform my bath at the Kapila Tīrtha.
Oṃ. Today, desiring to go to my own celestial world with my sins shaken off, I shall perform a bath at Gaṅgādvāra.
This alone is equal to the fruit of bathing at Kuśāvarta, Vilvaka, Nīraparvata, and Kaṇakhala.
Oṃ. Today, desiring to attain merit equal to the merit produced by two Viśvajit sacrifices, I shall perform a bath at the sacred ford named Pavitra.

Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by fifty horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) and wishing for the destruction of my sins, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā conjoined with the Sarayū.
Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by the gift of a thousand cows, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā conjoined with the Gaṇḍakī.
Oṃ. Today, desiring the destruction of great sins (*mahāpātaka*), I shall perform a bath in the north-flowing Gaṅgā at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) named Campaka.
Oṃ, today, desiring the state of being a beloved guest esteemed by the enemy of Vṛtra, I shall perform a bath in the Gaṅgā conjoined with the Kauśikī.
Oṃ, today, desiring the salvation of twenty-one generations of my lineage, I shall perform a bath in the lake of Jahnu.
Oṃ, today, desiring great prosperity, I shall perform a bath at the Tīrtha of Aditi.
Oṃ, desiring to obtain imperishable merit today, I shall perform a bath at Dakṣiṇaprayāga.
Oṃ, desiring to go to the city of Śiva today, I shall perform a bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Oṃ, desiring to obtain ten times the fruit produced by an Aśvamedha sacrifice today, I shall perform a bath at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
Or thus;
[222] now, immersion.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "The auspicious Gaṅgā, the carrier of merit, by those who have bathed in her even once with devotion,
delivers a hundred thousand of their lineages from worldly existence."
Oṃ. Today, desiring to cross over the hundred thousand [births] of my own lineage by casting off worldly existence, I shall perform an immersion in the Gaṅgā.
Now, the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā). Having commenced the twilight ritual at the Gaṅgā, Paulastya [spoke].
"In the Gaṅgā, [the merit is] a hundred thousandfold. Now, regarding the libation (tarpaṇa), there is the following in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
O Maitreya, the waters offered there by sons endowed with faith to their ancestors provide an inexhaustible satisfaction that is otherwise difficult to attain.
In the future: "As many sesame seeds as are taken by mortals for the ancestral rite,
for that many thousands of years shall the ancestors dwell in heaven."
The *pitaraḥ* (ancestors) are those who dwell in the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*).
In the *Bhārata*: "Whosoever among living beings exist in the three worlds, they are all indeed [the ancestors]."
Being satiated with the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā, they attain supreme contentment.
He who desires his birth to be fruitful, as well as a truly auspicious life,
should approach the Gaṅgā and satisfy both the ancestors and the gods.
Having mentioned those fallen and others who will exist in the future:
"All those men who are suffering, if they are once properly satiated by a person with the ritual procedure using *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, and the waters of the Ganges..."
They go indeed to the heavenly world; there is no need for deliberation on this point. And as for those ancestors established in heaven who possess merit, [they too are benefited].
Even those who have been satiated but once by men with the waters of the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite attain liberation; for such indeed was the word spoken by Brahmā.
Likewise: "By merely offering libations for a month and by casting funeral cakes (piṇḍas) into the Gaṅgā, all the ancestors [ascend] into celestial chariots (vimānas) with the brilliance of the sun."
Accompanied by throngs of Apsarases, adorned with gold and jewels,
covered with nets of pearls, and resounding with the music of flutes and lutes.
Resounding with the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, and the like; adorned with garlands; beautiful with the songs of Gandharvas; and endowed with divine enjoyments.
Satisfied by the libations offered in the Gaṅgā and well-satiated by the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) of the śrāddha rite,
they ascend and go swiftly to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*):

*Oṃ*. Desiring that my ancestors, who have been worthy of libations for many thousands of years measured by the number of sesame seeds used in this libation, may dwell in heaven, I shall perform the libation for the ancestors with water from the Gaṅgā mixed with sesame seeds.
*Oṃ*. Desiring inexhaustible satisfaction for my ancestors, I shall perform the libation for the ancestors with water from the Gaṅgā.
Oṃ. Today, desiring the fulfillment of my birth and the attainment of auspiciousness in life, I shall perform the libation for the ancestors with the water of the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ. Today, desiring the attainment of heaven for ancestors residing in hell and the attainment of liberation for ancestors residing in heaven, I shall perform the libation for the ancestors with the water of the Gaṅgā mixed with sesame seeds.

Oṃ! Desiring to go to the world of Brahmā, preceded by ascending many celestial chariots (*vimāna*) endowed with divine enjoyments, beautiful with the songs of *gandharvas* adorned with garlands, resounding with the sounds of flutes, lutes, kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, and the like, decorated with nets of pearls and ornaments of gold and jewels, and joined by hosts of *apsarases* possessing the splendor of the sun—I shall today, for this month, perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors with the water of the Gaṅgā.
The same applies to the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*) for the month. However, if this is performed near water, it should be done according to the ritual of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*.
Now, the worship of Śiva. Regarding this, there is a Smṛti text:
"A man who, having bathed in the Gaṅgā, should worship the Liṅga daily..."
In a single birth, he certainly attains supreme liberation.
Likewise: "The Agnihotra sacrifices, the Vedas,
and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees are not equal even to a ten-millionth part of the worship of a Linga at the Ganges."
Likewise: "But one who bathes in the Gaṅgā, especially on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
attains joy, liberation, composure, health, and a beautiful form."
One attains [the merit] of the sun's [eclipses] through the ritual bathing in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
One should bathe those deities, intending them for one's ancestors, with the water of the Gaṅgā;
at that very moment, one's ancestors dwelling in hell shall become satisfied.
In this way they go indeed to those respective worlds and rejoice within them for a long time.
Those [offerings] beginning with the sun;
bathing with copper jars is said to be ten times more meritorious than with earthen jars;
with silver ones, the merit is a hundredfold; and with golden ones, the fruit is ten millionfold.
In this manner, regarding the offerings of water for the feet, food oblations, sacrificial gifts, worship, and so forth, performed in sequence,
the fruit increases progressively according to the specific excellence of the vessels used.
If, when the means exist, one fails to perform the ritual in detail out of delusion, one does not obtain that fruit; such a person is said to be an offender against the gods.
Beholding the gods is meritorious; touching them is better than beholding them;
worshipping them is superior to touching them; and bathing them with ghee is even more excellent than that.
The wise declare that bathing with fragrant flowers while reciting a mantra eight times, along with water from the Gaṅgā, is equal to a bath of clarified butter.
Whoever, even once, offers water for honor (arghya) with a specific substance— the water of the Gaṅgā—
measuring a māgadha-prastha and placed within a copper vessel;
One should offer the arghya to the Sun together with one's own ancestors;
joined by sons and grandsons, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, ghee, curd, as well as honey,
red karavīra flowers, and red sandalwood—
this is indeed proclaimed as the eightfold *arghya* offering for the Sun.
Likewise: "That best of men who performs the installation of Śiva, Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Durgā, or Brahmā on the bank of the Gaṅgā..."

*Pratiṣṭhā* is the consecration. Likewise, those who cause shrines for these [deities] to be built with great effort shall obtain merit ten million times ten millionfold compared to building them in other religious traditions.
Having fashioned lingas according to one's ability from clay produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
and having endowed them with the proper characteristics, one should install them day after day.
Having worshipped with mantras and offerings such as flowers and leaves according to one's ability,
if one should constantly cast [these] into the Gaṅgā, the merit thereof is even greater than that.

Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*): *Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit superior to the fruits arising from the Agnihotra, the many Vedas, large sacrificial fees, and numerous sacrifices, I shall perform the worship of the Śiva-liṅga in the Gaṅgā.* *Oṃ. Today, desiring joy, liberation, well-being, health, and a beautiful form, I shall perform the ablution of the Sun with jars of water from the Gaṅgā.*

Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit ten million times greater than the fruit arising from the installation of Śiva at other holy sites (*tīrtha*), I shall perform the installation of Śiva in the Gaṅgā.
The formula for the installation of Viṣṇu, Sūrya, Durgā, and Brahmā is likewise [to be recited].

Oṃ. Today, desiring the immediate satisfaction of my father, his departure to the world of Śiva, and the enjoyment of moving at will within that world, I shall perform the ritual bathing of Śiva with the water of the Gaṅgā from the *kalaśa* on behalf of my father.

The same applies when bathing [the image] with water from the sun and other sources dedicated to the father; likewise, it applies when bathing [the image] with water from Śiva and others dedicated to the grandfather and so forth.
Now, regarding the recitation (*japa*): on this point, the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa* states:
For that best of men who recites the eight-syllabled mantra with devotion at the Gaṅgā, which bestows all bliss, liberation rests within his hand.
If one bathes in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite and recites the eight-syllable mantra,
he obtains the fruit of all sacrifices as well as the fruit of all gifts.
The fruit of all vows and the fruit of all austerities shall belong to him;
indeed, within six months, the supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā* arise here.
"Namo Nārāyaṇāya" is the eight-syllable mantra preceded by the *praṇava*.
Likewise: "The mantra 'Namaḥ Śivāya', joined with the Praṇava at the beginning,
immediately bestows all dharmas when practiced according to the rules with devotion to Śiva."
Likewise: "When recited twenty-four hundred thousand times, one will certainly attain success;
having fully mastered even a single mantra, one becomes happy and equal to Śiva."
The five-syllabled perfected mantra is Śiva himself, there is no doubt;
whether one is impure or pure, even when situated in any state whatsoever.
"Even one who is burdened with great sins shall become qualified for all [rites] through the recitation of this mantra; thus spoke the Lord Śiva."

Through the recitation (*japa*) of the eight-syllable mantra, one attains liberation; or else, the fruit of all-knowledge, all-giving, all-vows, and all-austerities. By reciting this for six months, the fruit is the attainment of the supernatural powers (*siddhi*) such as *aṇimā*. Through the recitation of the five-syllable mantra, the fruit is the attainment of all dharmas and devotion to Śiva. By reciting the five-syllable mantra twenty-four hundred thousand times, the fruit is equality with Śiva. Furthermore, in the case of recitation for specific desires (*kāmyajapa*), it should be stated that the diet consists of barley-meal (*yāvaka*) and so forth.
[229] Now follows the worship of the Gaṅgā.
In this regard, the Smṛti states:
"When the Gaṅgā is worshipped, all the deities are worshipped;
therefore, one should worship the river of the immortals with every effort."
In the future, she will have four arms and beautiful eyes, adorned with all her limbs;
she will hold a jewel-filled pitcher and white [lotuses], and grant boons, food, and fearlessness.
Then one should meditate upon her of beautiful form, clothed in white garments, adorned with pearls and gems,
and possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons.
She was being fanned with yak-tail whisks and adorned with white garments;
she was exceedingly serene, possessed of a beautiful countenance, and her inner heart was moistened with compassion.
The Ganges, whose surface bathes the earth in nectar, who is anointed with the fragrance of moisture, who is bowed to by the three worlds, and who is praised by the gods and others;

Having meditated upon her as described— possessing divine form and ornaments, and adorned with divine garlands and unguents— one should worship her in the image just as she was described in the water.
Likewise, one obtains all desired objects even by propitiating the deities of desire;
this applies to anyone who worships in this manner continuously for even half a month.
That person alone is the best of men who practices continuity, for such continuity is difficult to achieve;
and thus, he who should worship continuously for a long period of time.
Even the Lord of Speech himself is not capable of describing the fruit of his merit,
acquired through great sacrifices, great gifts, and austerities performed according to the rules.

That fruit is not obtained even by hundreds of thousands; and "plurality" here is relative to the immediate preceding category, whereby three fortnights and so forth are understood. As stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
In ancient times, on the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha,
Jahnu drank up the Gaṅgā out of anger and then released her again from his right ear-canal.
There, one should worship that goddess Gaṅgā, the girdle of the sky.
Regarding the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa states:
"Having performed a night vigil, one should worship Viṣṇu, Gaṅgā, and Śambhu with devotion using barley, bilva fruits, and sesame seeds."
Likewise, with fragrant flowers, saffron, agallochum, and sandalwood;
with *tulasī* and *bilva* leaves and the like, and with fruits such as the *mātuluṅga*.
With incense, lamps, and food offerings, according to the extent of one's wealth,
for thousands of millions of kalpas and hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Having ascended a divine celestial chariot, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu;
then, returning to the surface of the earth, he is born as a lord in Khāṇḍava.
Having become a king, however, he shall be righteous-souled, endowed with various pleasures,
possessed of beauty and good character, and joined with the favor of the twice-born.
At the end of the body, having become possessed of knowledge, one shall attain union with Śiva.
[231] Now, the ritual application (*prayoga*):
*Oṃ, today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by the worship of all deities, or desiring to obtain my own desired fruit such-and-such, I shall perform the worship of Gaṅgā.*

Having thus formed the resolve and performed the meditation as described, one should worship her with the five offerings (pañcopacāra) using her name preceded by the dative case and ending in *namaḥ*.
"Oṃ, desiring the state of being the most excellent person (*puruṣaśreṣṭhatva*), from today for half a month, I shall perform the worship of Gaṅgā.

"Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by duly performed hundreds of thousands of great sacrifices, great gifts, and austerities, from today for a long time, I shall perform the worship of Gaṅgā."

Having thus formed the resolve and meditated as prescribed, one should worship with the five offerings using the name ending in the dative case followed by *namaḥ*. Having praised with the hymn recited for the Daśaharā vow and prostrated, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*visarjana*). Now, regarding the gift (*dāna*): in that regard, it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, recitation, ancestral rites, and the worship of the gods— all these,
when performed at the Gaṅgā, become multiplied millions upon millions of times.
In the future,
listen to the meritorious fruit for him who indeed gives a cow of ghee according to the prescribed rite on the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
For thousands of millions of eons and hundreds of millions of eons,
he shall possess all desires and resemble a thousand suns,
dwelling in a variegated celestial palace made of gold and jewels and adorned with swans.
[232] He is glorified in the world of Rudra together with his own ancestors;
thereafter, he is born as a Brahmin endowed with wealth on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
But having first become a knower of Brahman, one attains liberation without a doubt;
likewise, he who performs the gift of a cow according to the prescribed rule [attains the same].
For as many kalpas as there are hairs on the body, and for as many as there are pores,
he dwells in Goloka or Śivaloka, accompanied by Kāmadhenu and her offspring.
Having remained together with his kinsmen, he enjoyed all kinds of manifold and abundant desires, even those unattainable by the gods.
Adorned with all kinds of jewels by his ancestors and friends,
he is later born into a noble family abounding in wealth and grain.
In a realm filled with jewels and gold, endowed with virtue, knowledge, and fame,
he shall enjoy vast pleasures together with his sons and grandsons.
Freed from all suffering and endowed with all desires,
having become beloved by all living beings, one shall thereafter attain liberation.
If a tawny cow is given according to the prescribed rite by one who has mastered the Vedas,
she then leads all the ancestors dwelling in hell to heaven.
Two nivartanas of land on the bank of the Gaṅgā, especially so.
To a brahmin learned in the Vedas, especially on that lunar day,
if a man gives with devotion, this indeed is the fruit of his merit.
By the number of atoms in those respective realms— ten thousandfold in the worlds of Soma, Indra, and Viṣṇu, and likewise in the world of Brahmā— [one attains residence].
Likewise, in the world of Śiva, the illustrious one enjoys pleasures according to the prescribed rites.
He is born endowed with beauty, entirely free from sorrow;
possessing every prosperity and abundance, he becomes the lord of the seven continents.
He is awakened from sleep by the resounding blasts of kettledrums and conchs, by the sounds of songs and musical instruments, and by the praises of the bards.
Having attained all happiness here in this world, being devoted to all dharmas,
and having caused all his ancestors dwelling in hell to reach heaven,
that one of great splendor likewise liberated all his ancestors residing in heaven.
Having severed the fivefold ignorance with the sword of knowledge,
one who has attained supreme dispassion reaches the highest Brahman.
In the phrase "by the number of ten thousand," the previously mentioned term "for so many kalpas" is to be supplied. The definition of a *nivartana* is stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"A staff shall be seven cubits long; thirty such staves constitute a *nivartana*.
Prajāpati declares that a *gocarma* is three-quarters of a *nivartana*."
And so it is said in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*: "He who bestows a village on the banks of the Gaṅgā upon the Brahmins,
and upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Durgā, and the Sun..."
Whatever merit is found in all forms of giving, whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices,
whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, and in all vows and ascetic practices;
There, the fruit resulting from the gift of land shall be multiplied a thousandfold;
one shall dwell amidst ten million celestial women who resemble ten million suns in brilliance.
Endowed with all prosperity, he sports in the city of Viṣṇu and likewise in the city of Śaṅkara, in various celestial palaces made of divine jewels.
He sports together with his own ancestors for eternal time.
However, according to the number of atoms in the land of the village,
having enjoyed enjoyments in that manner in the world, he is born into a family of yogins.
Endowed with the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, he himself becomes an enjoyer;
yet at the end of the body, he is absorbed into the supreme Brahman, which is stainless and eternal.
Likewise, on that third day, he who gives even sixteen māṣas or a piece of gold to a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas—
In a beautiful, all-pervading celestial chariot inlaid with gold and jewels,
he is liberated from all sins and adorned with every ornament.
And he shall always possess the fullness of all sovereignty in all worlds,
as well as various kinds of jewel-like enjoyments situated within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
Having experienced this together with his ancestors until the dissolution of the universe as called for, he thereafter attains union with Rudra; of this there is no doubt.
Likewise: By the gift of *kuśa* grass at the Gaṅgā, one attains the world of Brahmā;
and by the gift of barley to Viṣṇu, one likewise attains the world of Rudra.
By the gift of sesame seeds one attains [merit], and through fire-offerings (homa) one shall obtain sovereignty;
by the gift of jewels, one shall directly attain the state of Sadāśiva; and by the gift of cows, land, and gold, performed with devotion even once on the banks of the Gaṅgā, one attains the same.
A person is not born again in this cycle of existence fraught with suffering;
through the gift of clothing one gains long life, and through the gift of food, prosperity.
Through the gift of knowledge one gains wisdom; through the gift of a daughter, fame;
and all other gifts, as well as observances, vows, and ascetic penances [are likewise rewarded].
Sacrifice, charity, as well as silent recitation, ancestral rites, and the worship of the Lord— all these,
when performed at the Gaṅgā, become multiplied millions upon millions of times.
Likewise:
clothing, gold, jewels, leaves, flowers, and fruits,
as well as gifts of food and whatever else is most dear to oneself.
Whatever a person gives here to Gaṅgā with devotion to each respective deity,
that very thing is obtained in this very birth at the end of one's stay in heaven.
And after passing away, that man who dwells on the bank of the Gaṅgā, which is covered with Jambu, mango, and Bakula trees, will certainly attain the stainless Nirvāṇa.
With plantains and coconuts, wood-apples, aśoka and campaka trees, breadfruit trees and bilva trees, as well as kadamba, aśvattha, and pāṭala trees.
Having thus caused a garden to be constructed, adorned with flowers and densely filled with orange trees, citron trees, and other varieties, as well as jasmine, vijaya, punnāga, and karavīra trees;
Whether to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, or Bhāskara,
one who offers [this] with devotion, having resolved upon every goal, likewise [attains it].
[236] I shall describe the fruit of his merit in brief, but not in detail: as many flowers, roots, and fruits as there are of those trees, so great shall be his reward.
And for as many thousands of kalpas as there are various seeds and likewise their roots, for that long they are honored in the world.
Now, the ritual procedure (*prayoga*).

First, the rules for the sugar-cane cow (*guḍadhenu*). Regarding this, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states: "Whatever is the form and whatever is the fruit of the ritual for the sugar-cane cow in this world..."
I shall now proclaim that which destroys all sins.
One should place a black antelope skin, four cubits in size with the neck pointing eastward,
upon the ground that has been smeared with cow dung after carefully spreading darbha grass over it.
In the same way, one should provide a young deer-skin for the calf;
one should place the cow facing east with her feet toward the north, together with her calf.
The best molasses-cow (guḍadhenu) should always consist of four bhāras;
one should make the calf from one bhāra, while the middling cow is recorded as being two bhāras.
A calf should be one half-load for the youngest [wife], but one full load for the eldest;
a calf should also be one-fourth [of a load] according to the wealth of the household.

Thus, when there is a deficiency in one's capacity, there is a corresponding deficiency in the substance [of the rite]; therefore, one who is capable of the primary alternative (mukhyakalpa) should not resort to another alternative. "He who, though capable of the primary alternative, proceeds by means of a secondary alternative—no fruit pertaining to the hereafter exists for that person of dull intellect."

This is because of the prohibition by Kātyāyana. "Sāmparāyika" means pertaining to the next world. Here, the substance of the calf is distinct from the substance of the cow, as the two substances are mentioned separately.
However, this is not the case in the *Kāmadhenu-mahādāna*, because there the substance of the calf is not mentioned separately. [The verse continues:
"The cow and the calf have mouths of ghee and are covered with fine white garments."
His ears were like oyster shells, his feet like sugarcane, and his eyes like pure pearls.
Bound with white thread-like veins, they were covered with white woolen blankets;
their backs were like copper-colored water-jars, and their hair was as white as yak-tail whisks.
They possess eyebrows made of coral, are endowed with breasts of fresh butter,
have tails of fine linen, udders of bell-metal, and pupils of sapphire.
Adorned with golden horns and ornaments, equipped with silver hooves,
filled with various fruits, and provided with baskets for fragrant scents.
A "perfume-casket" (*gandhakaraṇḍaka*) consists of substances rich in fragrant scents, such as camphor and the like.
Having prepared [the offerings] in this manner, one should then worship with incense and lamps.
That prosperity which belongs to all beings and that which resides among the gods—
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, grant me peace—
she who dwells within the body as Rudrāṇī, the eternal beloved of Śaṅkara.
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin—
she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu and Svāhā of the Fire-god.
That power of the Moon, the Sun, and Indra which takes the form of a cow leads to prosperity;
for she is indeed the Lakṣmī of the Four-faced One and the Lakṣmī of the Giver of Wealth.
May that Lakṣmī who belongs to the world-protectors be a boon-granting cow for me;
may she who is Svadhā for the foremost of the ancestors, and she who is Svāhā for the partakers of the sacrifice, [be so].
"The cow is the remover of all sins; therefore, may she grant peace. Having thus addressed the cow, one should present her to a Brāhmaṇa.
This procedure for all cows is recited here;
those ten cows which are recited as the destroyers of sin [are now described].
O lord of men, I shall describe their essential nature and their names:
the first is the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu), and the next is the ghee-cow (ghṛtadhenu).
The third is the sesame-cow, while the fourth is known as the water-cow;
the milk-cow is well-known, and the honey-cow is another.
The seventh is the sugar-cow, the eighth likewise the curd-cow,
the ninth the juice-cow, and the tenth is [the cow] in its own natural form.
For liquid cows, there should be jars; for others, however, there are heaps.
Some men also desire a golden cow in this case.
With fresh butter and oil, as well as other [substances], other great seers likewise maintain that this very same procedure should be followed;
the necessary implements for that rite are thus prescribed.
[239] Always, on every festival day, she should be offered according to the śrāddha rite, accompanied by the invocation of mantras; she bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Bestowing the fruits of immeasurable sacrifices, removing all sins, and auspicious—
whether during the solstices, the equinoxes, or on the occasion of the Vyatīpāta yoga.
Gifts such as the "molasses-cow" (guḍadhenu) and others should be given on festival days such as lunar eclipses;
here, even the measurement of the materials for the "clarified-butter-cow" (ghṛtadhenu) and so forth is exactly as stated for the molasses-cow,
for this same procedure is prescribed for all such cows.

This is because of the general extension [of the rule] (*atideśa*): "There should be jars for the liquid-cows, but for the others, there should be heaps. This is a statement regarding the arrangement of substances measured by four *bhāras* and so forth. Likewise, in the case of cows made of ghee and other substances, there is the wearing of a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*), because that is not contradicted by the mention of jars, and because of the statement: "This very same procedure should apply."
Some, however, do not desire a deer-skin here;
rather, the weight consists of two thousand *palas*.
Regarding this, they say:
"One hundred palas should be known as a tulā; twenty tulās would be a bhāra.
This is the application here.

On ground smeared with cow dung, having spread *kuśa* grass and laid down a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) four cubits long with its neck facing east for the sake of the cow, and having placed a small black antelope skin nearby with its neck likewise facing east for the sake of the calf, one should prepare the two animals as follows: Upon that [skin], according to one's capacity—with four *bhāras*, two *bhāras*, or one *bhāra* of cow’s clarified butter (*gavyaghṛta*) kept in jars—one prepares the cow; and with one *bhāra*, half a *bhāra*, or a quarter of a *bhāra* of cow’s clarified butter kept in jars, one prepares the calf. Both should face east with their feet toward the north, their mouths filled with clarified butter, wrapped in white, smooth cloth, their ears made of mother-of-pearl, their four legs made of sugarcane, their eyes made of white pearls with two sapphire pupils set within them, their veins bound with white thread, their dewlaps made of white woolen cloth, their backs made of copper bowls, their hair made of white yak-tail fans, their pair of eyebrows made of coral, their udders made of fresh butter, their tails made of linen, their milking vessels made of bell-metal, their horns made of gold, their hooves made of silver, adorned with various fruits, and their nostrils fashioned from fragrant substances such as *agaru*. Having thus fashioned the cow and the calf, one should recite: "Oṃ, salutation to the cow of clarified butter together with her equipment and her calf."

Having thus offered incense, a lamp, and food offerings, and having worshipped three times with "Oṃ, obeisance to Brāhmaṇa," one should pour water into the hand of the twice-born while saying, "Oṃ, I give this ghee-cow together with its accessories and her calf. Then, having sprinkled the cow and recited the five verses beginning with "Oṃ, she who is Lakṣmī," one should take kuśa grass, sesame seeds, and water.

Oṃ. Today, on the Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day, on the banks of the Gaṅgā, desiring—along with my own assembly of ancestors—to attain liberation after reaching the state of a knower of Brahman at the end of my existence as a wealthy Brāhmaṇa on the further bank of the Gaṅgā, which is honored in the world of Rudra, endowed with all desires, resembling a thousand suns, and situated within a celestial chariot adorned with various golden and jeweled swans that has endured for many hundreds of millions of kalpas; and [desiring this] for my ancestors... [The sentence continues with the specific recipients of the merit].

[I offer] this cow made of ghee, whose calf is likewise made of ghee and measures one-fourth of her size; who stands upon a ground smeared with cow-dung and strewn with *kuśa* grass, situated on a four-cubit altar facing east, covered with a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) whose neck-point faces east; whose mouth is anointed with ghee; who is clothed in fine white garments; whose ears are adorned with mother-of-pearl; whose four legs are made of sugarcane; whose eyes are pure pearls; whose veins are bound with white thread; who is draped in white woolen blankets (*kambala*); whose back is fashioned from a copper vessel (*tāmra-ḍaḍḍuka*); whose hair is white chowries (*cāmara*); who is endowed with a pair of eyebrows made of coral; whose udders are filled with fresh butter (*navanīta*); whose tail is made of silk (*kṣauma*); whose milking vessel is of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*); whose pupils are sapphire (*indranīla*); whose horns are decorated with gold ornaments; whose hooves are silver; who is provided with various fruits; whose nose is made of fragrant substances; and who has Viṣṇu as her presiding deity (devatā). I give her to you, O Brāhmaṇa of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*) and such-and-such name (*śarman*). Om, may it be auspicious!

"Oṃ! Today, for the sake of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of this gift of a ghee-cow together with its appurtenances and calf, this gold, whose deity is Agni," and so forth. Then, having touched the cow at her tail, the twice-born should recite the *kāmasūkti*.
Now follows the gift of a cow on the third day of the month of Akṣaya.
The procedure for this is as follows: having worshipped the cow and the Brāhmaṇa, and having poured water into the hand of the twice-born, one should touch the cow—

Oṃ! On this Akṣaya Tṛtīyā day, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, desiring—through this cow dedicated to Rudra as the deity—the attainment of liberation after the enjoyment of vast and manifold pleasures performed by myself; a state of existence endowed with all desires unattainable even to various divine beings, accompanied by wish-fulfilling cows, progeny, and joined by kinsmen, fathers, mothers, and friends; a residence for billions of kalpas equal in number to the hairs on a cow’s tail on either Goloka or Śivaloka; a birth in a noble family characterized by virtue, learning, fame, and wealth, filled with gold, jewels, and grain, and accompanied by sons and grandsons; and being liberated from all suffering and beloved by all living beings—[I offer] this cow... and so forth.

Regarding the gift of a tawny cow (*kapilā*): having consecrated the tawny cow with "Oṃ, obeisance to the tawny cow; Oṃ, obeisance to the Brāhmaṇa," one should say: "On this Akṣaya Tṛtīyā day, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, desiring to lead all my ancestors residing in hell to heaven—Oṃ, I give this tawny cow, whose deity is Rudra, to you, the Brāhmaṇa named [Name], of the [Name] lineage, who has mastered the Vedas. Then: "Oṃ, it is yours," and so forth. One should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as before.
Now follows the gift of land (*bhūmidāna*).

Oṃ! On this day, the third of the waxing moon (Akṣayatṛtīyā), on the bank of the Gaṅgā, I, [Name], desiring the severance of ignorance, the arising of supreme dispassion, and the attainment of the Supreme Brahman—[desiring] for myself, as the donor, the state of being a sovereign of the seven continents, awakening from sleep through the sounds of drums, conchs, songs, musical instruments, and the praises of bards; possessing all forms of excellence following many enjoyments and pleasures upon a ground equal in measure to the atoms of the earth to be given, lasting for ten thousand kalpas, with a residence in the worlds of Soma, Indra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; endowed with all prosperity, free from all diseases, and awakened by the resonance of drums, conchs, and the like, along with songs and instrumental music and the hymns of Māgadha bards; intent upon all dharmas; the attainment of all happiness for myself as the agent; the leading of all ancestors residing in hell to heaven, and the granting of liberation to all ancestors residing in heaven; and possessing great splendor—give this land, measuring two nivartanas, beloved by the donor, with Viṣṇu as its deity, and so forth.
[243] Now follows the gift of a village.

Having honored the village and the Brahmins, [he should say]: "Oṃ! On this Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, desiring the dissolution into the pure, eternal Supreme Brahman at the end of the body, possessing a birth in a family of yogins, preceded by the enjoyment of many pleasures based upon worlds as numerous as the atoms of the earth granted as a village, accompanied by my own ancestors, for an inexhaustible period of time by means of many celestial chariots made of various divine jewels and joined by millions of celestial women resembling ten million suns—the fruit of which is a thousandfold the merit arising from all gifts, all sacrifices, all sacred fords, and all austerities—this village, whose presiding deity is Viṣṇu," and so forth.
Now, the gift of gold:

*Oṃ*. Today, on this Akṣaya-tṛtīyā day, on the bank of the Gaṅgā, desiring for myself—along with my ancestors—the attainment of union with Rudra after the enjoyment of various manifold pleasures throughout the dissolution of the world (saṃplava), accompanied by all sovereignty and prosperity, and being entirely liberated from all sins, through the basis of a beautiful celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that moves everywhere and is inlaid with gold and jewels; [I give] this gold, weighing sixteen māṣas, whose presiding deity is Agni, and so forth.

Now, whenever a gift of *kuśa* grass is given, there is attainment of the world of Brahmā; by a gift of barley, attainment of the world of Viṣṇu; by a gift of sesame seeds, attainment of the world of Rudra; by an oblation of sesame seeds, sovereignty; by a gift of jewels, attainment of the state of Śiva; by a gift of any one of cows, land, or gold, there is no further rebirth; by a gift of clothing, long life; by a gift of food, prosperity; by a gift of knowledge, wisdom; by a gift of a daughter in marriage, fame.

By giving any one of clothing, gold, jewels, leaves, flowers, fruits, or one's own beloved things to the Gaṅgā, the fruit is the attainment of heaven, the attainment of those specific objects therein, and thereafter, the attainment of *nirvāṇa*.

[244] Whatever prescribed rite is performed on the banks of the Gaṅgā, its fruit is ten millionfold. Having caused a grove (*ārāma*) to be established on the banks of the Gaṅgā—adorned with *jambu*, mango, *vakula*, plantain, coconut, wood-apple, *aśoka*, *campaka*, breadfruit, *bilva*, *kadamba*, *aśvattha*, *pāṭala*, orange, citron, myrobalan, pomegranate, *sahakāra* (mango), and other such trees; beautified by *jāti*, *vijaya*, *puṃnāga*, *karavīra*, *vicikīla*, and other flowers—and having offered it to Śiva, Viṣṇu, Durgā, and Bhāskara, the fruit is the attainment of being honored in the worlds of Śiva and the other deities for a thousand *kalpas*, equal in number to the trees, flowers, roots, fruits, and seeds in that grove.

Likewise, in this regard: having caused a grove to be made on the bank of the Gaṅgā as prescribed, and having worshipped Śiva on the fourteenth day and other such occasions and sprinkled the grove—[one should recite]:

"Oṃ, today, on the [specified] lunar day of the [specified] month, desiring to attain honor in the world of Śiva for a thousand kalpas equal in number to the flowers, roots, fruits, seeds, and their very foundations belonging to the trees of this grove, I give this grove, situated on the bank of the Gaṅgā and dedicated to the deity Vanaspati, to the Blessed Śiva. The same formula applies to the gift to Viṣṇu and others; the only difference is that one substitutes "in the world of Viṣṇu" for "in the world of Śiva.
Now, the fruit of the vow at the Gaṅgā:
In that regard, [I ask] Bhaviṣya:
"Tell me that vow, the means by which mortals may quickly behold Gaṅgā herself in her divine form, bearing her eightfold manifestation."
Having cooked milk-rice with one prastha of śāli rice and two prasthas of milk,
along with honey, sugar-candy, and ghee;
Having respectfully placed one *pala* each of that milk-rice (*pāyasa*),
cakes (*apūpa*), sweetmeats (*modaka*), and circular offerings (*maṇḍala*) therein, [one should proceed].
Likewise, one should offer half a guñjā of gold and silver,
as well as sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, and guggulu resin.
Bilva leaves, the aforementioned [substances], yellow pigment (rocanā),
white mustard seeds, and blue lotus flowers— or even petals in the absence of flowers.
Whoever, according to their ability and with great devotion, should cast [the offering] into the Gaṅgā on the full moon day and on the new moon day every month, during the two watches of the day;
With faith, by means of this mantra, for as long as a year, [one should recite]:
"Oṃ, salutations again and again to Gaṅgā, to Nārāyaṇī, and to Śivā."
Standing within the waters of the Gaṅgā, with mind fixed on that [deity] and free from doubt, one should constantly recite this mantra one hundred and eight times.
Eating sacrificial food and restricting his diet during those days,
at the end of the year, Ganga appeared before him, assuming a celestial form.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with celestial jewels,
she stands visibly before one, bestowing boons.
Thus, having seen with his own eyes the Gaṅgā in person before him in her divine form in the mortal world, intent upon bestowing a boon;
Whatever desires a mortal may long for, he shall attain those very desires;
but one who is free from desire shall obtain liberation in that very same birth.
*Mandala* refers to a specific type of fried cake (*śaṣkulī*) shaped like a circle, such as *pūrikā* and the like. Here, there is an alternative reading:
*yāvakāni*. "Listen with devotion, O best of sages; I shall speak of the supreme vow of Dharma, the king of all vows."
This was told of old by Śiva, whose emblem is the bull, out of compassion when he was affectionately questioned by the Goddess while dwelling on the banks of the Gaṅgā.
The gods eat in the forenoon, likewise the sages at midday,
the ancestors in the afternoon, and the Guhyakas and others during the night.
Transcending all other times, eating at night is the supreme practice.
Alms-seeking is superior to fasting; not asking for anything is superior to alms-seeking; eating at night is superior to not asking; likewise, one should subsist by eating only at night.
One who eats at night should practice these six: eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), bathing, truthfulness, moderation in food, performing fire-rites, and sleeping on the ground.

Regarding "lightness": first, food should fill only half the stomach, according to the injunction, "One should fill half with food. The lightness of even that [half] is established by the principle, "It should be equal, as there is no scriptural statement to the contrary. The fire-rite is the *homa*; and that is performed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and the *mahāvyāhṛti* mantra, having Prajāpati as its deity.
In *juhoti* offerings where no substance is specified, clarified butter is prescribed as the material.
It is an established rule that Prajāpati is both the deity and the mantra.
According to this statement by Kātyāyana,
the number [of oblations] is one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight.
In the worship of the planets and other deities, the fire-oblation (homa) should consist of one hundred and eight.
Twenty-eight or eight [offerings] are prescribed according to one's capacity.
Thus, from the statement in the Devīpurāṇa;
likewise, in that very same [text]:
"He who should observe the practice of eating only at night on the banks of the Gaṅgā during the month of Māgha..."
But near the temple of Śiva, one should offer kṛsara mixed with ghee.
Having offered the food oblation of kṛsarānna to Śiva,
one should eat using a wooden ladle and avoid greed of the tongue.
Eating from a *palāśa* leaf, recollecting Śiva, and having conquered his senses,
he should separately offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to Dharmarāja and the gods.
One should observe a fast on the fourteenth day of both fortnights;
likewise, on the full moon day, one should perform worship with perfumes and the waters of the Gaṅgā.
Having established Śiva with milk and honey according to one's capacity,
one should likewise place a gold plate upon the top of the liṅga.
Then, according to one's own capacity, one should offer a "butter-blanket" (ghṛtakambala) to Śiva;
one should scatter one āḍhaka of black sesame seeds upon the Śiva-liṅga.
One should worship all the lords with blue lotuses and even with white lotuses;
if these are unavailable, one should have a lotus made of gold weighing at least a single *māṣa*.
And here, one should offer milk-rice mixed with honey and ghee, as well as guggulu incense,
a lamp of ghee, and anointment with sandalwood and other fragrant substances.
One should devoutly offer leaves and fruits according to one's capacity,
and likewise present a pair of black cows along with one's own form.
At the end of the month, he should feed eight Brahmins along with ritual fees;
during that month, he should avoid honey and meat and observe celibacy.
Having performed this vow exactly as prescribed once,
one who is endowed with self-restraint and observances, and who is devoted to faith and devotion—
In this world one obtains enjoyments, and after death, the unsurpassed state,
traveling in celestial chariots resembling sapphire and accompanied by peacocks.
Accompanied by all his own kinsmen, he goes to the beautiful city of Śiva, which consists of divine jewels and is endowed with celestial enjoyments.
Together with many friends, having enjoyed all various and desired pleasures without exception until the dissolution of all beings at the end of the kalpa.
Thereupon he becomes a righteous soul and likewise a lord of the seven islands;
there he enjoys all pleasures, free from all thorns.
Handsome, fortunate, and with his commands never disregarded,
and completely freed from all diseases— he too shall obtain this fruit.

Likewise: "On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, being composed in mind, he who performs the practice of eating only at night (naktabhojana), consisting of śāli rice mixed with milk,"
Having worshipped Śiva with flowers and other offerings, and having presented food to him,
he then eats while using a wooden ladle and indeed a *vaṭa*-wood spoon.
Having become restrained through silence, one should indeed perform the cleansing of the teeth;
then one should sleep at night near a Śiva-liṅga or on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
On the full moon day, at dawn, having bathed in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite and having made a formal vow for fasting, one should keep a vigil throughout the night.
Having bathed the Liṅga with ghee, and likewise having worshipped the auspicious Bull with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, as well as with food offerings, incense, and lamps,
one should honor it with very white garments, flowers, and the like, as well as with turmeric and sandalwood.
Having adorned golden turmeric according to the prescribed rite, one should offer it to Śiva;
and one should feed Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (pāyasa) according to one's capacity.
Thus, he who performs this even once with devotion and endowed with faith obtains [the merit of] two thousand yugas among the gods.
Whatever merit is gained through performing austerities according to the rules,
that is undoubtedly attained by means of celestial chariots resembling the moon and possessing the luster of swans and jasmine flowers.
Accompanied by his own ancestors, who are joined with celestial bulls and adorned with nets of pearls, he proceeds happily to the abode of the Lord.

Surrounded on all sides by beloved women of divine form, who possess the fragrance of blue lotuses and are beautiful in their natural appearance, he enjoys every kind of sensual pleasure without exception.
Having possessed sovereignty for an infinite period of time, he is thereafter born on earth as a protector of the world, endowed with fame and beauty.
Under a single umbrella, he rules the earth together with his command;
in the end, endowed with dispassion, he attains the Gaṅgā once again.
Endowed with that faith, he may meet death in the Gaṅgā;
having regained his mindfulness there, he certainly attains liberation.
Now, the Daśarātra-vrata. In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "In the month of Jyeṣṭha, during the bright fortnight, on the tenth day conjoined with the asterism Hasta..."
On the banks of the Gaṅgā, whether it be a man or a woman, with a spirit of devotion—
Having kept a vigil at night, one should likewise worship the Gaṅgā with ten kinds of flowers,
perfumes, food offerings, and fruits, each numbering ten.
