In the same manner, one endowed with faith should worship with lamps and betel leaves;
having bathed with devotion in the Ganges ten times according to the prescribed rite.
One should offer ten handfuls of black sesame seeds and clarified butter into the water,
as well as ten balls of flour and ten balls of molasses;
thereafter, on the beautiful bank of the Gaṅgā, [one should perform the rite] with gold or silver.
Having fashioned an image of the Gaṅgā with the form to be described hereafter,
one should place it upon a lotus marked with a svastika that is properly situated there.
Having placed [the image] upon a full water-pot whose neck is adorned with a bound garland of flowers, one should worship the Goddess; or, in the absence of that, even with clay.
Furthermore, if one is unable even to do that, one should indeed draw [the form] on the ground using a mound of earth.
Four-armed and with beautiful eyes, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons,
she holds a jewel-filled pitcher and makes the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness with her hands.
Clad in white garments, adorned with networks of pearls,
with a smiling face and beautiful hair, she was radiant in all her limbs.
She was being fanned with yak-tail whisks and adorned with a white parasol;
she was exceedingly gracious, bestowing boons, and her inner heart was moistened with compassion.
The Ganges, whose surface washes the earth with nectar, who is anointed with the fragrance of moisture,
who is bowed to by the three worlds, and who is praised by the gods and others.
Having meditated upon her as described— surrounded by divine jewels and adorned with celestial garlands and unguents— one should worship her both in the water and in the image.
One should perform the worship in its entirety with the mantra that is about to be taught;
furthermore, one should especially perform the bathing of the image with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
In front of the image, on an altar smeared with cow dung,
[one should worship] Nārāyaṇa, Maheśa, Brahmā, and likewise Bhāskara.
And one should worship King Bhagīratha and Himavat, the lord of mountains,
with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to one's ability.
One should give ten *prasthas* of sesame seeds for the benefit of ten cows;
according to the *Kalpataru*, a *prastha* consists of sixteen *palas*.
One should also give aquatic creatures such as fish, tortoises, frogs, crocodiles, and the like.
Having had it fashioned according to one's ability, either with gold or silver.
If those are unavailable, having worshipped images made of flour with flowers and other offerings,
one should cast clarified butter and lamps into the Ganges at a place where the current flows swiftly.
On that day, if one possesses the means,
one should perform a chariot procession for the image of Gaṅgā mounted upon the chariot, facing northward.
Those of evil deeds wander about in the world without being seen, for they are difficult to find;
one should act in this matter just as one would during the procession of a difficult-to-manage chariot.
Having performed it in this manner according to the prescribed rite, free from stinginess regarding wealth,
one is instantly liberated from the ten sins that will be described hereafter.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules, and consorting with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
Harsh speech, falsehood, slander in every form,
and idle chatter— this constitutes the fourfold nature of vocal misconduct.
Coveting the wealth of others, thinking of what is undesirable with the mind,
and adherence to falsehood— these are recorded as the threefold mental [unwholesome actions].
By these ten kinds of sins arising from ten million births, one is liberated; there is no doubt here, for it is the word of Brahmā.
[One should remember] ten ancestors, thirty, and a hundred, as well as those who follow; Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇī, to Gaṅgā, the remover of sins, salutations again and again.
Any mortal who recites this mantra five thousand times day and night on that day shall obtain the fruit of the ten dharmas.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one who recites this hymn about to be described shall rescue ten preceding generations of his family from the ocean of worldly existence.
On that day at the head of the Gaṅgā, one should perform the recitation twice and carry out her worship with the mantra:
"Oṃ, salutation to Śiva; salutation be to you, Gaṅgā, the bestower of auspiciousness."
Salutations be to you, Gaṅgā, who possess the form of Viṣṇu; salutations, salutations to you!
O best of physicians, salutations be to you, the healer of all diseases for everyone.
O destroyer of poison produced from both stationary and moving sources, homage be to you!

Salutations again and again to you, the destroyer of the poison of saṃsāra and the giver of life; salutations again and again to you, the mistress of the vital breaths and the remover of the threefold suffering.
Homage to you, who bring about the lineage of peace; homage to you of pure form;
homage to you, who effect the complete purification of all; homage to you, whose form is the enemy of sin.
Salutations again and again to you, Bhadrā, the bestower of worldly enjoyment and liberation; salutations again and again to you, Bhogavatī, the giver of enjoyments and pleasures.

Salutations to you, O Mandākinī; salutations again and again to you, the giver of heaven. Salutations to you who are the being of the three worlds; salutations again and again to you, the goddess of the thirty [deities].
Salutations to you who abide in the three pure [states]; salutations again and again to you, the possessor of security.
Salutations again and again to Tejovatī, who abides in the three paths of the gods;
salutations again and again to Nārāyaṇī, who is slow-moving and bears the marks of divinity.
Homage to you, O Viśvāmitrā; homage again and again to you, O Revatī.
Homage be to you, O Bṛhatī; homage again and again to you, O Lokadhātrī.
Salutations to you, the foremost of all; salutations again and again to you, Nandinī.
Salutations again and again to Pṛthvī, to Śivāmṛtā, and to Virajā.
Homage again and again to you, Tārā, who are enriched by the attainment of the higher and the lower; homage again and again to the indivisible one, who cuts through the net of evil.
Salutations again and again to you, the peaceful one, the foundation, the bestower of boons;
salutations again and again to the fierce one, the speaker of pleasant words, the life-restorer.
Salutations again and again to the one who goes to Brahman, who bestows Brahman, and who destroys misfortune; salutations again and again to Maṅgalā, the adversary of all calamities.
Salutations again and again to the Mother of the World, who shatters the suffering of those who bow before her;
salutations again and again to you, the one free from impurity, the destroyer of difficulties, and the skillful one.

Salutations to you, who are higher than the highest; salutations to you, the eternal bestower of liberation. May the Gaṅgā be before me, may the Gaṅgā be at my sides, and may the Gaṅgā be everywhere for me; O Gaṅgā, may my abiding place be in you.
In the beginning, at the end, and in the middle, you are everything, O auspicious Gaṅgā;
you alone are the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), for you are indeed the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
you, O Gaṅgā, are the Supreme Self and Śiva—salutations to you, O auspicious one!
Thus, whoever is devoted to this recited hymn daily,
and whoever listens with faith through the actions of body, speech, and mind;
One is liberated from all ten types of established faults;
one who is afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one is freed from calamities.
One is liberated from enemies, from bonds, and from all fears;
one attains all desires and, after death, merges into Brahman.
Whoever, having written this hymn, should even place it within their home,
for them there is no fear of fire or thieves, nor indeed any fear from evil deeds.
Standing in the waters of the Gaṅgā, one should recite this hymn ten times;
even a poor man or one who is weak may do so ten times.
He too obtains that fruit which is proclaimed as the result of worshipping the Gaṅgā with effort according to the previously mentioned procedure.
As is Gaurī, so is Gaṅgā; therefore, whatever ritual procedure is intended for the proper worship of Gaurī, that same one applies to the worship of Gaṅgā.
As is Śiva, so is Viṣṇu; as is Viṣṇu, so is Umā;
as is Umā, so is Gaṅgā—no fourfold distinction exists.
He who speaks of a difference between Viṣṇu and Rudra, or between Gaṅgā and Gaurī,
or between Lakṣmī and Gaurī, is indeed a fool of mind.
Now, the procedure for the vow (*vrataprayoga*).

On any full moon day free from defects such as *viṣṭi* and the like, having performed his daily obligatory rites (*kṛtanityakriya*), [he should resolve]: "Oṃ, O Blessed Sun, O Blessed Deities! From today onwards, for one year, I shall perform the vow consisting of the offering of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other substances into the Ganges during the two watches (*prahara*) of time on every fifteenth day."

Taking *kuśa* grass, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as follows: "Desiring the direct realization of Gaṅgā, beginning from today, on every full moon and new moon, for two watches of the day, I shall perform the casting of milk-rice mixed with pieces of honey and ghee, many cakes, sweetmeats, and *maṇḍala* offerings, along with gold, silver, sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, pieces of *guggulu*, many *nimba* leaves, much *dūrvā* grass, *gorocanā*, white sandalwood, blue lotuses, and various *tatpatra* leaves, each measuring half a *guñjā* in weight, into the Gaṅgā.
Thus one should resolve.

Then, having prepared a milk-pudding (*pāyasa*) made from two *prastha* measures of cow’s milk and unhusked *śāli* rice, one should add one *pala* each of honey, sugar-candy, and cow’s clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Placing that *pāyasa*, along with three cakes (*apūpa*), three sweetmeats (*modaka*), three mandalas, half a *vartikā* of gold, half a *vartikā* of silver, sandalwood, agallochum (*aguru*), camphor, saffron, *candana*, *guggulu*, *bilva* leaves, *dūrvā* grass, yellow orpiment (*gorocanā*), white sandalwood, and blue lotuses or their petals—all these together in a single vessel—and taking it with his right hand, one who has performed his daily rites, seated facing east in the middle of the day, holding a purifier (*pavitra*) and a water-vessel (*upagraha*) in his hands, having sipped water (*ācānta*), and being single-minded, should cast it all at once into the current of the Gaṅgā with faith and devotion, reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, salutations again and again to Gaṅgā, Nārāyaṇī, and Śivā."

There, having entered the waters of the Gaṅgā and meditating upon the Gaṅgā, one should recite this very mantra one hundred and eight times. Then, on that day, one should remain with the senses restrained and eat only a limited amount of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*). In this manner, one should continue from the first day of the lunar fortnight until the completion of the year. On the day of completion, which is the new moon (*amāvāsya*), one should feed three Brahmins.
[257] Now follows the practice for the month of Māgha.

On the morning of the first day, having made the declaration: "Oṃ, according to the procedure prescribed in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, I shall observe the *nakta* vow of Māgha starting from today," one should take *kuśa* grass and other required items.

Oṃ! Desiring the attainment of manifold enjoyments and pleasures in this life, followed immediately by the attainment of the unsurpassed state, accompanied by a divine palace made of celestial jewels, adorned with a crest resembling sapphire, endowed with divine luxuries, and beautiful; desiring to go to the City of Śiva along with all my kinsmen and many friends for as long as the world lasts at the dissolution of the elements, and desiring various desired manifold enjoyments and pleasures therein—from today until the month of Māgha, according to the method described in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa, I shall perform the *nakta* vow on the bank of the Gaṅgā beside a temple of Śiva.

Having thus resolved, one should perform the worship of Śiva every day in the forenoon, accompanied by the offering of *kṛsara* (rice and pulse mixture) prepared with white *dāna* rice and sesame-mung beans, and one should also perform the prescribed fire-sacrifice (*homa*).
Regarding this *homa*, some maintain that its deity is Śiva, because the status of having Śiva as the deity is extended to it by implication through a consideration of the nature of the vow.

Then, after the evening twilight rites, having placed *kṛśara* rice alone upon a *palāśa* leaf and having recollected Śiva, one should offer two oblations with the words "Salutation to Dharmarāja" and "Salutation to Durgā," and then eat while reciting the *hūṃkāra* and so forth in reverse order.

Then, at night, one should sleep on a bed placed upon the ground. On the fourteenth day, a fast must indeed be observed. On the full moon day, however, having bathed Śiva with perfumes, Ganges water, milk, and honey—measuring one hundred and eight *palas* or even less according to one's ability—and having placed a golden band upon the head of Śiva, having offered a ghee-lamp lotus according to one's means, having placed black sesame seeds amounting to one *āḍhaka* upon the Śiva-liṅga, and having worshipped Śiva with blue lotuses—or in their absence, with lotuses fashioned from gold weighing one *māṣa*—one should then offer an oblation (*naivedya*) of milk-porridge mixed with honey, as well as incense of *guggulu* resin with ghee, a ghee lamp, anointing with sandalwood paste and the like, fruits, roots, and so forth, and a handsome pair of black cows. Thereafter, one should feed eight Brahmins and give them some small sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
And for this month, he should be one who abstains from honey, meat, and sexual intercourse, endowed with self-restraint and observances, and possessed of faith and devotion. Now, another vow follows.

On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, being composed in mind, one should worship Śiva in the forenoon with the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), present food to Śiva, and at night, having eaten rice with cow’s milk while observing great silence (*mahāmauna*), one should clean the teeth with a *vaṭa* twig while observing great silence and sleep at night on the bank of the Gaṅgā near a Śiva-liṅga. Then, in the morning, having bathed in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rite, one should announce: “Oṃ! O Bhava, Sūrya, and the divine goddesses! Today, I shall perform the vow consisting of a fast according to the procedure declared in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa,” and then take hold of *kuśa* grass and other materials.

Oṃ. Desiring the attainment of liberation preceded by the recollection of past births, through death in the Gaṅgā accompanied by faith in obtaining my own Gaṅgā, and endowed with detachment at the time of the end of my existence as a protector of the earth—possessing the command of a single umbrella, endowed with fame, form, and the enjoyment of manifold pleasures for an infinite duration of time following that, together with a multitude of beautiful women, fragrant blue lotuses, and sovereignty; desiring to go to the abode of Īśvara accompanied by my own group of ancestors in many celestial chariots adorned with nets of pearls, yoked to a bull resembling the moon and possessing the luster of swans and jasmine, and having attained merit equal to the merit produced by performing austerities for two thousand years less a quarter—I shall perform a fast according to the procedure prescribed in the *Bhaviṣya Purāṇa*.

Having thus resolved, one should observe a fast on that day and keep a vigil at night. Then, in the morning, having bathed the Śiva-liṅga with cow’s ghee weighing one hundred and eight *palas* and worshipped it with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*), one should worship a bull adorned with white cloth, flowers, sandalwood paste, and gold ornaments, as well as the two bulls of Śiva (*śivavṛṣau*). One should then give [the bull] with the mantra: "Oṃ, today I give this bull, adorned with white cloth, flowers, turmeric, and sandalwood, whose deity is Rudra, to Śiva.
Thereafter, one should feed Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice (*pāyasa*) according to one's capacity.
Now follows the ritual procedure for Daśaharā:
Having performed the night vigil on the ninth day (navamī), and having performed the ritual bath and other preliminary rites on the tenth day (daśamī), one should say:

"Om! Today, on the tenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyaiṣṭha, conjoined with the asterism Hasta, desiring the destruction of the ten kinds of sins accumulated over ten million births, I shall perform the worship of Daśaharā according to the method prescribed in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa."

Having thus resolved, and having bathed duly in the Gaṅgā and performed the worship of the deities and other rites, one should worship the Gaṅgā with ten kinds of perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, fruits, and betel leaves.

Then, having bathed ten times in the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rules, one should cast ten handfuls of black sesame seeds, ten balls of flour, and ten balls of molasses into the Gaṅgā while reciting the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā."

Then, having drawn an eight-petaled lotus on the bank of the Gaṅgā and having placed there a water-filled jar whose neck is wrapped with cloth and garlands, one should fashion upon it an image of Gaṅgā made of gold or silver—four-armed, holding a jewel-jar, a white lotus, and making the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she should have beautiful eyes, be adorned in all her limbs, dressed in white garments, decorated with nets of pearls, exceedingly serene, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand moons, being fanned by chowries by gods and others, praised by the divine beings, and arrayed in celestial jewels, garlands, and unguents. Having thus meditated upon Gaṅgā both in the current and in the image—

Having prepared the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) using twenty-one *palas* each of cow’s milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar—each weighing two *tolakas* and thirty-two *raktikās* more than that—and having bathed the image with them, one should recite: “Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇī, to Gaṅgā who removes the ten sins; salutations, salutations! and then offer to her individually the water for the feet (*pādya*), this water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), this water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), this water for bathing (*snānīya*), and so forth.

Then, having offered incense and worshipped three times with the recited mantra, and having presented incense and other offerings, one should smear a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of the image with cow dung and worship Nārāyaṇa, Maheśa, Brahmā, Bhāskara, Bhagīratha, and Himavat with the five-fold service (pañcopacāra). One should then give ten *prasthas* of sesame seeds to ten Brahmins.

[261] Likewise, having given ten *prastha* measures of barley to ten cows, and having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings ten aquatic creatures—a fish, a tortoise, a frog, a crocodile, a porpoise, a *duṇḍubha*, a *bhadraka*, a leech, a snail, and a conch—either made of silver or of flour, one should cast them into the Gaṅgā.

Then, one should offer ten ghee lamps in the current. If one has the means, one should place an image of Gaṅgā upon a chariot and have it circumambulated. Then, for the sake of greater fruit, one should mutter the mantra "Oṃ nārāyaṇyai daśaharāyai gaṅgāyai namo namaḥ" five thousand times. In this regard, the fruit is the deliverance of ten generations of one's family, preceded by the rescue from the ocean of worldly existence.
Now, the fruit of performing a *śrāddha* at the Gaṅgā.
On that point, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states:
By him the Gayā-śrāddha was performed, and likewise the bull was released;
by him the śrāddha was also offered on that bank drenched by its waves.
For him, there is no need for visiting sacred fords or purifying the body,
by whom a bath has been taken in the waters of the Gaṅgā and a śrāddha performed with faith.
Likewise: "He who, out of devotion, casts into the waters of the Gaṅgā milk-rice mixed with honey, combined with jaggery and clarified butter, for the sake of his ancestors,"
His ancestors remain satisfied for three hundred years.
On the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, at Payoṣṇī and Amarakaṇṭaka,
and at the Narmadā and the sacred site of Gayā, one enjoys everything in its infinite fullness.
A śrāddha performed at these sacred fords is held to yield ten millionfold merit;
that which is performed at the Gaṅgā with faith, moreover, bestows liberation.

Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from the *vṛṣotsarga* (the ritual release of a bull) at Gayā-śrāddha, I shall perform the śrāddha on the bank conjoined with the waves of the Gaṅgā.

Oṃ. Today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit arising from visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and purifying the body, I shall perform the śrāddha near the Gaṅgā. Oṃ. Today, desiring the satisfaction of infinite ancestors, I shall perform the śrāddha on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
"Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit ten million times greater than that produced by an ordinary *śrāddha*, I shall perform a *śrāddha* on the bank of the Gaṅgā.
"Oṃ, desiring the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*), I shall perform a *śrāddha* with faith.

"Oṃ, desiring the satisfaction of my ancestors for a period of three hundred years, I shall cast this milk-rice (*pāyasa*) mixed with honey, jaggery, and clarified butter into the waters of the Gaṅgā. Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), sitting facing the east with his sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), he should cast it in.
Now, the fruit of dying within the waters of the Gaṅgā. Regarding this, the Smṛti states:
"During the bright fortnight, by day, on land, in the Gaṅgā, and during the northern course of the sun..."
Blessed are those who cast off their bodies while Janārdana dwells within their hearts.
In the *Āgneya Purāṇa*, Viṣṇu’s words addressed to Gaṅgā:
"Those men who cast off their life-breaths while staying in your presence shall go to my world, being honored by the inhabitants of heaven."
In that very place:
"He who dies by fasting in the water of the Ganges at its confluence [with the ocean] goes to no further rebirth and attains union with Brahman."
Half-immersed water reaches up to the feet; water reaching up to the navel is [the next stage].
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Whatever is the destination of the wise man who is established in goodness (*sattva*) and joined in yoga..."
That is the destination for an embodied being who gives up their life-breaths in the Gaṅgā.
The man who, having undertaken a fast unto death, dies on the bank of the Gaṅgā,
immediately attains supreme liberation along with his ancestors.
What wise person would wish to abandon their life-breaths by dying in the Gaṅgā?
Many births have passed, and deaths occurred here and there;
a vast amount of time has elapsed as we wandered from place to place.
In this regard, two yojanas—whether far or near—are equal;
by dying here in the Gaṅgā, there is no need for further deliberation.
From the Brāhma Purāṇa:
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, whether intentionally or unintentionally,
a mortal who dies in the Gaṅgā attains both heaven and liberation.

[264] In the future, when his life-breaths are being released, that man who remembers the Gaṅgā— even if he is of sinful character— whether he merely remembers her or touches her, shall go to the supreme goal.
In Bhārata,
those wise ones who, having gone to the Gaṅgā, have cast off their bodies, have attained equality with the gods.
Beginning with the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean:
"Whether one dies in the atmosphere, on the earth, or in the water— even if that person is most sinful—
they attain the imperishable state worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva."
Likewise:
"He who, being composed at the time of death when the vital breaths are departing, and being esteemed by the learned,
should contemplate the Gaṅgā with his mind, shall attain the supreme goal."
In the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*: "Wherever he may die, or when death has arrived,
the man who remembers Saṅgā with devotion shall go to the city of Śiva upon his passing."
Now, regarding the fruit of [casting] bones in the Gaṅgā:
in that regard, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa states:
"The bone-fragments that issued forth from the mass of Śambhu’s matted hair..."
Having flooded [the earth], he led those sinful sons of Sagara to heaven.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*: "As many bones as belong to a person remain in the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world."
He who, having taken [the image], is carried by men into the waters of the Gaṅgā and placed therein,
shall have a residence in heaven for thousands of years.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"From the very moment that a man's bone is cast into the Gaṅgā by men, his residence shall be in the heavenly world for that duration of time."
Yama: For that person of auspicious deeds whose bones float upon the waters of the Gaṅgā,
there is no return whatsoever from the world of Brahmā.
The Gaudas say:
"If one's bone sinks into the waters of the Gaṅgā within ten days [of death],
one obtains a fruit equal to that of dying in the Gaṅgā itself."
Now, the method for casting the bones:
regarding this, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"Having bathed, one should then sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*)."
It should be mixed with gold, clarified butter, and sesame seeds;
then, having placed it within a vessel of clay,
one should look toward the direction inhabited by the hosts of pretas.
Saying, "Homage be to the Dharma," he should enter the water and cast [the flower] while saying, "May he be pleased with me."
[266] Having bathed and likewise emerged from the water, and having beheld the sun, one should then bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
When this has been done, for one who resides in the city of the departed spirits (pretapura),...
But his destination shall be heaven, equal to that of the great Indra.
*Pañcagavam* means the five products of the cow. Now follows the determination of the banks and other locations; regarding this, it is stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Having established the boundary of the flow for a distance of four cubits, Nārāyaṇa alone is the master here; no other is ever the master.
One should not accept [an offering] there, even if one's life-breaths have reached the throat.
Regarding the duty of giving:
as long as the water covers [the ground] on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
Up to that point one should understand it as the "womb" (garbha); beyond that, it is called the "shore" (tīra).
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"The distance from the center of the riverbed to the bank is said to be one hundred and fifty cubits.
In the *Skandapurāṇa*:
An area extending for one *gavyūti* all around the riverbank is called a sacred field (*kṣetra*).
Whatever gift, austerity, or fire-oblation is performed here is equivalent to that done on the Ganges; of this there is no doubt.
On both banks, the sacred field extends for two *krośas* each. As it will be said in the *Bhaviṣya-purāṇa*:
"All sins without exception do not cross the boundary of the Gaṅgā."
"They flee in the ten directions like deer upon seeing a lion; the boundary of the field extends for one *yojana* from both banks. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
O Great King, where the Gaṅgā flows, there lies the penance grove of Śambhu;
that field of spiritual attainment (siddhikṣetra) should be known to extend for two yojanas in every direction.

In this regard, the prohibition against accepting gifts applies everywhere within a distance of four cubits; however, the prohibition applies within a distance of one hundred and fifty cubits on the banks of well-known rivers such as the Gaṇḍakī—this is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).

As for the prohibition against accepting gifts specifically within a sacred field (*kṣetra*), the settled rule is that it applies only at the Gaṅgā, because it is there alone that the term "field" is used. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
A man should not accept gifts at sacred fords, nor in holy shrines, nor at any of the [auspicious] occasions; he should remain vigilant in all such matters.
For one who accepts [gifts] at sacred fords (tīrtha), at holy shrines, at all auspicious occasions, and likewise in sacred fields—
his visit to that sacred ford is fruitless as long as he consumes those riches.
Also in that very same place, it says regarding the Gaṅgā:
"If one accepts [offerings] on her bank, the Jahnavī becomes as if sold.
O King, from the selling of the Gaṅgā, there occurs the selling of Viṣṇu."
When Janārdana is sold, the three worlds are sold.
[268] Now, the fruit of riverbank soil.
In the *Bhārata*:
He who bears upon his head the clay produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā bears the very form of the sun,
solely for the destruction of darkness.
Thus ends the third section, the "Manifestation of the Gaṅgā," in the *Tīrthacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Vācaspati Miśra.
Having seen the Vāyavya, Garuḍa, Kalpa, and Vṛkṣa [images], and having also deliberated according to the principles of the scriptures;
Having bowed to the venerable Gadādhara, Vācaspati composes this work established by his illustrious father, Tīrtha.
Now, the ritual procedure for Gayā.
Regarding this, the Matsya Purāṇa in the Kalpataru states:
"The sacred ford named Gayā, the best of all sacred fords, is remembered as the Pitṛtīrtha."
Wherein the Grandfather himself, the Lord of the gods of gods, resides.
Regarding this, a verse was sung by the ancestors who desired worldly enjoyment:
"One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or sets free a dark-colored bull."
In the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*, these are the words of Brahmā:
"O Vyāsa, I shall briefly proclaim the supreme majesty of Gayā, which is the most essential of essences and bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation."
In former times, there was a most powerful and supreme Asura named Gaya;
he performed a most terrible penance that caused distress to all living beings.
[269] The gods, scorched by his asceticism, went to Hari for refuge in order to slay him. Hari said to them, "Those who seek the welfare of Śiva must accept what is destined to be.
When he said, "Once his body has been struck down by me," the gods said to Hari, "So be it."
Once, having brought lotuses from the Ocean of Milk for the sake of worshipping Śiva, he lay down to sleep in a forest in the land of Kīkaṭa.
Deluded by the Māyā of Viṣṇu, he was slain by Viṣṇu with a mace;
therefore, Viṣṇu, the wielder of the mace (Gadādhara), remains at Gayā as the bestower of liberation.
Viṣṇu, who abides in his pure body in the form of a *liṅga*, then said to Pitāmaha: "This shall become a meritorious field established by me."
Whatever man performs sacrifices, ancestral rites, the offering of funeral cakes, bathing, and so forth, he shall go to heaven and the world of Brahmā; he shall not go to hell.
Having recognized Gayātīrtha as supreme, the Grandfather (Brahmā) performed a sacrifice there.
He honored the Brāhmaṇas and the officiating priests who had assembled;
he created the river Rasavatī, which stood pervading the quarters of the sky.
The Lord likewise created the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu) for edible foods and fruits,
and he bestowed the Gayā-tīrtha, extending five krośas, upon the Brāhmaṇas.
But at the sacrifice of Dharma, having accepted wealth and other gifts out of greed,
the Brahmins then remained there and were consequently cursed by Brahmā at Gayā.
[270] May there be no knowledge transmitted through three generations; may there be no wealth inherited through three generations. May you have a river flowing with water from a mountain of stone!
Entreated by those who had uttered curses, the Lord Brahmā granted them this favor:
"Those meritorious people at Gayā who perform ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall go to the world of Brahmā;
and those who worship you, by them I am always worshipped."
Knowledge of Brahman, the performance of śrāddha at Gayā, death in the house of a cowherd,
and residence for men in Kurukṣetra— this is the fourfold liberation.
O Vyāsa, all the oceans, rivers, ponds, wells, and lakes go to the sacred site of Gayā with the desire to bathe; of this there is no doubt.
Those who have committed the murder of a Brahmin, those who died at the hands of cattle-thieves,
and those bitten by snakes— all go to heaven, liberated through the Śrāddha performed at Gayā.
The fruit that a man obtains by offering funeral cakes at Gayā cannot be described by me even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.

Regarding "brahmahatyāyāi" (for the sake of the killing of a Brahmin): the meaning is that even the great sin (*mahāpātaka*) of one for whom a *gayāśrāddha* has been performed is destroyed. Regarding "asaṃskṛtāḥ" and so forth: the meaning is that these indeed, being in miserable states, become happy states through the *gayāśrāddha*. The phrase beginning with "gayāyām" refers to this fruit as pertaining to the agent.
Likewise, in the *Kalpataru*, in the *Varāhapurāṇa*, Sanatkumāra said:
Listen to these words: there was a king named Viśāla who dwelt in the blessed city of Viśālā;
he was steadfast, yet remained childless.
The lord of Viśālā himself [honored] the foremost of the twice-born.
The slayer of enemies asked for the sake of a son; those brahmins of undaunted spirit said to him:
"O King, satisfy the ancestors for the sake of a son."
"O hero among men, by performing the ancestral rites with funeral cakes (piṇḍas) according to the rules at Gayā,
your son will certainly become a lord of the entire earth and a giver of thousands."
When this was said by the brahmins,
O lord of the twice-born, the king, the ruler of Viśālā, being greatly delighted, arrived at that excellent sacred ford with great effort.
One should recite this Gayā-mantra with one's mind fixed upon it.
Then that eminent man, seeking a son and devoted to the sacrifice at Gayāśiras for the sake of his ancestors, arrived and began to offer the funeral cakes according to the prescribed rites.
Meanwhile, [he saw] those endowed with supreme forms in the sky.
Seeing men who were white, red, and black, the king said: "What is this that you are gathering? Tell me everything."
Curiosity has arisen in my mind.
Sita said: "O King, I am Sita, your father, both by name, by complexion, and by my deeds."
And this father of mine is red-colored, a doer of cruelty, a slayer of a Brahmin, and a perpetrator of evil.
O Āndheśvara, listen: his supreme father was named Kṛṣṇa by name, deed, and caste;
indeed, he was formerly slain by this very Kṛṣṇa.
The ancient seers have [attained] many births.
Both of these, father and son, having died, have entered the Avīci hell;
this lord of Āndhra was my father, and I was the priest.
That [state] belongs even to Kṛṣṇa and Rakta for a long time;
and I, having attained the throne of Śakra through my own pure karma, which is very difficult to obtain, [shall remain there] from that point on.
Furthermore, by you, a knower of mantras, these two have been liberated through the offering of funeral cakes at Gayā, by the power of the grace of that most excellent sacred ford.
They both went to the hell known as Avīci.
"O subduer of enemies, the water which you have offered with the thought, 'I gratify my fathers, grandfathers, and likewise great-grandfathers'— "
"O best of men, by that speech, our simultaneous enjoyment has arisen;
through the power of the sacred ford, we shall go to the world of the ancestors, without a doubt."
There, by the offering of this funeral ball of rice, these two grandfathers of yours,
though perfected even from an evil state, have been freed from their deformed forms due to their sins.
For this reason, my son, having taken these two with me, I have come to you; indeed, I shall now go to the place I desire.
Likewise:
"O best of men, by the power of a sacred ford, even for the slayer of a Brahmin,
a son may effect his father's deliverance through the diligent offering of funeral cakes."

Thus, even for those who have committed great sins (*mahāpātakin*), by being designated as recipients of the *śrāddha*, the performer attains a good rebirth through the *gayā-śrāddha*; furthermore, if there is a desire for a son, a son is also born—this is the purport of the section. Regarding the passage beginning with "the ancestors" (*pitṝn*): one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the formula, "May the father of such-and-such lineage, named Amukadevaśarman, be satisfied; may this water with sesame seeds be *svadhā* for him; I gratify the father. This same formula should be applied to all the handfuls of water, from the grandfather onwards, up to the king. According to tradition, the plural number used in the root text for "ancestors" (*pitṝn*) is not intended to be significant. Likewise:
To visit Gayā even once, and to offer funeral cakes there even once, is difficult to achieve; how much more so, then, to reside permanently in this very place!

In that very same Brahmapurāṇa: "In some cases, for those who have become outcasts, [the rite] is performed by their kinsmen at the sacred pools of Gayā after a year has passed, because the local custom is authoritative."
In that very same Vāmana Purāṇa,
the King of the Departed (Pretarāja) then spoke to a certain merchant for the sake of his complete liberation:
"Having bathed at Gayā, which is frequented by sacred fords, and being endowed with ritual purity..."
Perform the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) in my name;
by the giving of that rice-ball there, I shall find happiness from the state of a preta.
"Once liberated, I shall attain the auspicious worlds of all those who give gifts.
Having spoken thus to the merchant, the King of the Pretas, together with his younger brothers, [departed].
Having correctly and duly announced his own names in private,
he departed for the supreme Gayāśiras after having performed his religious duties.
There, Vasudāya performed the offering of funeral cakes for the deceased ancestors in due order, and immediately thereafter, he honored his own paternal forefathers.
And the one of great intelligence performed the offering of funeral cakes for himself toward Great Enlightenment without sesame seeds, as well as for his other kinsmen.
When the morsels of food had been thus given by the merchant, those hungry ghosts were liberated from their state as pretas; O twice-born one, they then departed for the world of Brahmā.

Regarding "Gayāśirasam": thus, when a *piṇḍa* is offered to a preta at Gayāśiras, his liberation from the state of a preta and his attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) occur. Regarding "to oneself" (*ātmanaḥ*), this refers to the offering of one's own *piṇḍa*. The offering of the *piṇḍa* must be performed with the left hand alone; for the *Vāyupurāṇa* states: "The offering of the *piṇḍa* for oneself and others is done with the left hand alone, even without sesame seeds, provided it is accompanied by the mantra. (274)
Likewise:
"The flesh of a rhinoceros offered at the ancestral sacrifice leads to infinity;
so too do black iron and a goat lead to infinity."
At Gayā, the Śrāddha rite is inexhaustible, as are recitations, fire-offerings, and austerities;
for that is the abode of the ancestors, O son, and therefore there it becomes imperishable.
Bṛhaspati said:
Ancestors, terrified by the fear of hell, long for sons, thinking:
"That son who goes to Gayā will deliver us."
What is given at Gayā, on Dharmapṛṣṭha, in the assembly of Brahmā,
at Gayāśīrṣa, and at Akṣayavaṭa, as well as in the assembly, becomes inexhaustible.
Having visited Brahmāraṇya, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Dhenukāraṇya,
and having honored one's ancestors, one shall uplift twenty generations of one's lineage.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The sin committed during a great kalpa (mahākalpa) perishes upon reaching Gayā. Likewise:
A śrāddha offered at Gayā, on Dharmapṛṣṭha, in the assembly of Brahmā, at Gavi, and at Gṛdhravaṭa yields great fruit.
In Bharata’s holy hermitage, which is constantly filled with those most meritorious,
the footprint of Mataṅga is seen there by all human beings.
The entire essence of the Dharma has been proclaimed by way of this illustration for the world;
it is that meritorious grove of lotuses frequented by those who perform virtuous deeds.
In that [place] where Pāṇḍu enters the sacred ford (tīrtha) which is the manifestation of all,
likewise on the third quarter, in the Niḥkṣaurā and the Maṇḍala.
A Śrāddha offered at the Mahāhrada on the Kauśikī yields great fruit;
moreover, the wise Mahādeva set foot upon Muṇḍapṛṣṭha.
Austerities difficult to perform have been practiced for many hundreds of years at sacred fords;
yet here, even in a short time, a man devoted to dharma [attains the same].
One quickly casts off evil, like a snake sheds its worn-out skin;
this divine tirtha is renowned in the world by the name Kaṇakhala.
To the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is a place frequented by hosts of Brahman-sages;
having bathed there, human beings go to heaven in their own bodies.
Furthermore, whatever śrāddha is offered there is declared to be inexhaustible;
having bathed there for three days, O best of the twice-born, at the Niḥkṣīrā [river], one attains this merit.
Having bathed in Lake Mānasa, a person should perform the Śrāddha rite; at Dakṣiṇa-mānasa,
and having gone to Uttara-mānasa, he attains unsurpassed perfection.
One should perform the śrāddha rite for him according to one's capacity and according to one's strength;
thus, one obtains divine desires and all the means to liberation in their entirety.

And thus—the meaning of the verse is that after bathing for three days at the Niḥkṣīrā river located on the northern side of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one should perform the Śrāddha rite at Dakṣiṇamānasa and then perform it at Uttaramānasa.
However, that which is stated differently in another version of the Vāyu Purāṇa refers to a different ritual cycle (kalpāntara).
In the Mahābhārata, during Pulastya’s pilgrimage to sacred sites—
Then, O Bhārata, having arrived at Gayā while remaining celibate and with senses subdued, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice simply by going there.
[276] There stands the tree named Akṣayavaṭa, renowned throughout the three worlds;
there, whatever is offered to the ancestors becomes truly inexhaustible.
Having touched the waters of a great river, one should offer libations to the ancestors and the gods;
by that, one shall uplift both the ancestors to imperishable worlds and one's own lineage.
From there, one should go to the Brahma-lake, adorned by the Brahma-forest;
having spent the night until dawn, one attains the world of Brahmā.
There, in that lake, a meritorious sacrificial post (yūpa) was established by Brahmā;
by circumambulating that post, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to Dhenuka, renowned throughout the world,
where, having stayed for one night, one should offer a cow made of sesame seeds.
One whose self is liberated from all sins will certainly go to the world of Soma;
O Great King, even today there is a great wonder as a sign of that place.
Indeed, a tawny cow with her calf roams about on that mountain; even today, the footprints of that cow with her calf are still visible there.
But in each of those places, O Indra among kings, O best of monarchs,
whatever inauspicious karma there may be, that is destroyed, O Bhārata.
Then one should go to Gṛdhravaṭa, the abode of the wise deity;
having approached the bull-bannered Lord, one should bathe there with ashes.
O Hero, for Brāhmaṇas there shall be a twelve-year vow;
however, for the other castes, all sin is utterly destroyed.
From there, O bull of the Bharatas, one should go to Mount Udyanta, which resounds with songs; there, the footprint of Sāvitrī is seen.
[277] Therein, a Brāhmaṇa of firm vows should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyā). By performing it, that twilight worship becomes equivalent to twelve years' worth.
And right there, O bull of the Bharatas, the door of the womb is located;
by approaching that place, a person is liberated from the distress of rebirth.
O King, that monarch who dwells at Gayā during both the bright and dark fortnights purifies his lineage up to the seventh generation; of this there is no doubt.
One should desire many sons, in the hope that even one of them might go to Gayā,
or perform an Aśvamedha sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull.
Thence, O King, the ruler of men who frequents sacred fords should proceed to Phalgu;
he obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and attains supreme perfection.
From there, O king of kings, one should go to Dharmapṛṣṭha, which yields great fruit;
there, O great king Yudhiṣṭhira, Dharma dwells eternally.
Having approached it there, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice;
from there, O king of kings, one should go to the supreme tirtha of Brahmā.
Having reached Brahmā there, O Indra among kings, O bull of the Bharatas,
a human being obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
The meaning of this section is that one should proceed in sequence to these seven: Mahānadī, Brahmasaras, Dhenuka, Gṛdhravaṭa, Udyanta, Dharmapṛṣṭha, and Brahma-tīrtha.
Likewise, in the account of Dhaumya’s pilgrimage:
"O King, first [go] to the eastern direction, which is frequented by hosts of royal sages."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall relate that delightful account to you according to my recollection.
In which [direction] is the holy Gayā, the best of mountains, honored by royal sages;
where lies the auspicious Brahmasaras, frequented by the gods and seers.
O tiger among men, for this purpose the ancient legal codes proclaim:
"One should desire many sons, so that even if but one among them goes to Gayā."
O King, Mahānadī, Mahādeva, and likewise Gayaśiras rescue those who are tormented, ten ancestors and ten descendants.
O Lord, where that banyan tree, known as Akṣayyakaraṇa, is praised by the Brahmins,
the food offered there to the ancestors becomes inexhaustible.
And there, O bull of the Bharatas, is the great river named Phalgu with its waters of merit,
as well as the Kauśikī, which abounds in roots and fruits.
Likewise, in the *Lomaśa-tīrthayātrā*:
"Then they went to Mahīdhara, which is protected by the righteous royal sage Gaya, a performer of meritorious deeds, and which is also frequented by him."
There is the lake Gayaśiras and the sacred Mahānadī river;
there is also the Brahma-saroruha, a most meritorious holy site frequented by sages.
Where the blessed Agastya went toward Vaivasvata,
there the eternal Dharmarāja constantly dwelt.
O lord of the people, it is there that all rivers originate;
it is there that Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, is eternally present.
There those heroic Pāṇḍavas performed the Cāturmāsya rites at that great Akṣayyavaṭa, which is [the site of] the great sacrifice of the sages.
[279] There, during the pilgrimage to Balabhadra-tīrtha, there was a great sacrifice for the elephant-like sacrificer, just like that of Gaya.
Indeed, the Sarasvatī, the best of rivers, was summoned to Gaya’s sacrifice.
But the sages of rigid vows say that Viśālā is among the Gayas.
Regarding the phrase "of Gaya": this comparison with the sacrifice of the elephant (*gajayajña*) is for the purpose of praise.
In that context, concerning the pilgrimage (*yātrā*) of Aṅgiras:
"Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, Gaya, Nairṛta, and Devaparvata."
And by the third, the *krauñcapādī*, one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*, regarding the pilgrimage of Prahlāda: "That great Asura went to Gayā to behold Gopati;
having bathed in the lake of Brahmā, he performed its circumambulation."
He indeed performed the meritorious offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for his ancestors.
As stated in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa:
"Śiva is present at the Śivanadī, and Janārdana is present at Gayā."
He who perceives the Supreme Self everywhere is liberated.
It is located near the city of Vihāranagara on the Śivanadī.
Furthermore, in the Matsya Purāṇa, in the context of describing the ritual bathing of Gaurī:
"Viśālākṣī is in Vārāṇasī, and likewise Lalitā is at Prayāga."
In Gayā, she was named Maṅgalā; having performed her purification, she became Saiṃhikā.
Yājñavalkya said: Whatever one who resides at Gayā gives as a gift, all that attains infinity;
may there arise in our lineage some such preeminent man.
Whoever, being composed in mind, should perform a śrāddha for us at the banyan tree on Gayāśīrṣa;
Yama said:
One should desire many sons who are virtuous and endowed with good qualities;
for if even one among those gathered together should go to Gayā, [the ancestors are liberated].
Or he should sacrifice with the horse-sacrifice, or he should set free a dark-colored bull.
Vasiṣṭha said: The ancestors rejoice because of that, just as farmers do at a bountiful rain;
for when one staying at Gayā gives food, the ancestors thereby become possessed of a son.
Thus ends the glorification of Gayā in the *Tīrthakāṇḍa* of the *Kalpataru*.
Regarding the ritual at Pretaśilā, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"Then, its foot was covered by the mountain Prabhāsa."
Prabhāsa was showered upon by sages, and Śilāṅguṣṭha emerged.
Even the Lord who resides on the big toe is proclaimed as Prabhāseśa;
that which is a portion of the big toe of the stone is the Pretaśilā situated there.
Because by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at that place, a man is released from the state of a preta;
likewise for a man who performs ablutions at the confluence of the Mahānadī, the Prabhāsa, and the mountain.
Rāma, having bathed together with the Queen, was thereafter known as Rāmatīrtha.
Then he was entreated by the great river: "O Rāma, if you have indeed bathed..."
[281] Here lies Rāmatīrtha, which purifies all worlds;
whatever evil deeds I have committed throughout more than a hundred lifetimes, [they are cleansed here].
May all that go to dissolution through ablution at Rāmatīrtha;
that man who, having bathed with this mantra, performs the śrāddha ceremony.
"By offering funeral cakes at Rāmatīrtha, he shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having said, "So be it," Rāma remained with Sītā in Bharata’s hermitage.
Having bathed at Rāmatīrtha, a man should offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas) accompanied by mantras;
thereby his ancestors are liberated from the state of being a ghost (preta) and attain the status of true progenitors (pitṛ).
"Rāma," and so forth, as before.
Having paid homage to Prabhāseśa, one who shines [with purity] shall go to Śiva. Likewise:
Having arrived and paid obeisance, he should then perform the southern offering (yāmyabali), [reciting]:
"O Lord of Gods, you are water, and you are indeed the lord of the luminaries."
O Lord of Gods, destroy the evil born of the actions of mind, speech, and body;
once again, the hips were stepped upon by the Mountain upon the stone.
The mountain was told by Dharmarāja, "Do not go," and thus it is remembered as Naga.
Yama and Rājabhramarja are both remembered as having been driven away with certainty.
Without having offered bali to those two, a śrāddha performed at Gayā would be fruitless.
There are two dogs, one dark and one brindled, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata;
to them I shall offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa), so that these two may be free from harm.

"Covered" means that the foot of the *pretaśilā* (the stone of the departed) is covered by the mountain named Prabhāsa. There, the thumb of the Prabhāsa-stone indeed protrudes; and the Lord who resides upon that thumb is Prabhāseśa. That portion of the stone's thumb which is together with Prabhāseśa is itself the *pretaśilā*. The rounded meaning is this: whoever offers a funeral *piṇḍa* on that [stone], for him there is liberation from the state of being a *preta*. Regarding "the great river": even one who performs an ablution at the confluence of the Mahānadī and the Prabhāsa mountain is liberated from the state of being a *preta*; such is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "janmāntareti": the meaning is that whoever, having bathed with this mantra, performs the *piṇḍa* offering or the *śrāddha* ceremony here in the presence of Rāmeśa, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Regarding "rāma rāmeti":
O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one, you who grant fearlessness to the gods!
"O Lord of Gods, by following you here, may my sin perish"—
this means that Rāma is to be saluted.

"The giver of the *piṇḍa*"— the meaning is that one who desires the liberation of his ancestors from the state of being *preta* and their subsequent attainment of the respective status of *pitṛ* (ancestors) must perform the offering of the *piṇḍa* for his father and others there.

Regarding the phrase "having paid homage" (*namaskṛtya*): the meaning is that one should perform homage to the Lord of Prabhāsa with the desire to proceed toward Śiva, whose nature is the manifesting agent. Regarding the phrase "and him" (*taṃ ca*): the word "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction; thus, the meaning is that both Rāma and the Lord of Prabhāsa are to be honored once again.
Regarding the phrase "the southern power" (*yāmyabala*): from there, on Mount Prabhāsa—
O Lord of Gods, you are the waters and indeed the lord of the luminaries;
O Lord of Gods, destroy the evil born of the actions of mind, speech, and body.
Having recited this, the meaning is that the offering (*bali*) should be given with *kuśa* grass and water, saying: "Yamāyaiṣa balir namaḥ" (This is the offering for Yama).

Regarding the phrase "upon the stone," on this *pretaśilā* (the ghost-stone), the hip-limb was pressed down by the mountain named Naga; and for the stabilization of that mountain named Naga, the kings Yama and Bhrama were established upon it.

Therefore, on the mountain named Naga, situated at the rear of the Pretaśilā in its southern portion, one should recite the two verses beginning with "Two dogs... out of a desire for the success of the *gayāśrāddha*, and offer a single oblation (*bali*) to Yamarāja and Bhramarāja, saying: "This is the offering (*bali*) for you both.
This concludes the ritual duties for the first day, as it constitutes the preliminary equipment for the *śrāddha* at the Pretaśilā which liberates one from the state of being a *preta*.

"Having bathed"—the meaning is: having bathed in the great river at Bharata’s hermitage, and having seen, and bowed to, Rāmeśa (Rāma) and Sītā, one should recite, "O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! Here, on the first day, the *pretaśilā* rite is performed according to the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) throughout all regions.

And regarding the sacred site (*tīrtha*), the *pretaśilā*, and so forth: "Having invoked the ancestors with sacrificial porridge (*caru*) mixed with ghee, one should offer them funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) with the [prescribed] mantras."

This is because there is the first mention of the *pretaśilā* (the stone for the departed) in the *Vāyupurāṇa*. Furthermore, this [rite] should be performed according to the procedure prescribed for the *pretaparvata* (mountain for the departed), because the *Vāyupurāṇa* states: "O Nārada, the offering of the *piṇḍas* should be done in this same manner at all locations," thereby extending that procedure by analogy (*atideśa*).
And likewise, regarding the rite for the *pretaparvata* (the mountain of the departed), the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"Having made himself one with the ancestors on the *pretaparvata*, being self-restrained,
he should wear the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*) and, facing south, perform the recollection."
Kavyavāḷa, Anala, Soma, Yama, and Aryaman,
as well as the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa Pitṛ-devatās.
"May my illustrious ancestors come here, protected by you— those who were born in my lineage and those who are my kinsmen."
I have come to this Gayā for the purpose of offering funeral cakes to them;
may they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha.
Having sipped water (ācamana) and recited the five-limbed prayer, and having diligently restrained the vital breaths (prāṇāyāma), one should form this resolve:
"For the sake of attaining the world of Brahmā from which there is no return.
Having thus resolved according to the rule, one should perform the śrāddha ceremony in the proper sequence.

Having invoked and worshipped the ancestors with mantras, one should become the giver of the *piṇḍas*. At a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), on the *pretaśila*, and so forth, one should first wash that place thoroughly with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) individually, and then offer the oblation of cooked rice (*caru*) mixed with clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
Likewise:
Having performed the Śrāddha for those sapindas,
one should spread kusha grass on their southern side and offer them water with sesame seeds once.
Having taken [the flour] from them with joined palms, one should diligently offer an imperishable piṇḍa using a handful of flour by means of the pitṛ-tīrtha.
One should add sesame, clarified butter, curd, honey, and so forth to the materials for the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Then, one should invoke the relatives with sesame, water, and kusha grass.
Having gathered all these mantras ending in the feminine gender,
one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) as before, having invoked the ancestors as previously described.
Whether within one's own lineage or another's, when the husband and wife offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas),
the Śrāddha rite, the rice-ball offering, and the water libation (tarpaṇa) are fruitless if performed separately.
Having placed sesame seeds in the alms-bowl and filled it with auspicious water,
one should circumambulate those rice-balls clockwise while reciting this mantra.
"One should sprinkle water three times over all [the offerings], prostrate, and ask for forgiveness.
Having dismissed the ancestors and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should announce the gods as witnesses.
O Nārada, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) should be performed in this same manner at all places."

"Having made oneself [ready]" means: having washed one's hands and feet, having sipped water (ācānta), having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (kṛtāpasavya), and facing south, one should recite the mantra beginning with "Kavyavāla" and ending with "śāśvatam," and then recite that which constitutes the invocation of the ancestors (pitṛ-āvāhana).

"Having sipped water" (ācamya) means: having sipped water with the left hand, one should perform the breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma)—consisting of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka)—just as in the Sandhyā-vandana, accompanied by the five-limbed recitation consisting of the syllable *Oṃ*, the seven *Vyāhṛtis*, the *Gāyatrī*, the *Śiras*, and the *Oṃkāra*.
"In all places" means: because this procedure is extended by implication (*atideśa*) to every instance within the scope of the instruction, it is established for all cases.
In the northwestern direction at Gayā, a wise person should offer the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) at all times, even during an intercalary month,
on one's birthday, or when Jupiter and Venus are in eclipse.
One should not abandon the *śrāddha* at Gayā even when Jupiter is situated in Leo;
yet, having gone to Gayā, a mendicant should not offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) while displaying hypocrisy.
By placing [the offering] at the foot of Viṣṇu, one is liberated along with one's ancestors.

The offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) is prescribed at Gayā with milk-rice (pāyasa), or with parched grain flour (śaktu), or with flour-cakes (piṣṭaka), or with sacrificial oblation (caru), or with rice and other grains.
Concerning the Muṇḍapṛṣṭha rock, in that very same place [it is said]:

"Having seen it and all the world, even one who is a great sinner or a perpetrator of heinous crimes becomes purified; he gains authority over the Kṛtyās, performs ancestral rites (śrāddha), and attains the world of Brahmā."
Thus, the sequence of performance is as follows:

on the first day, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), "Desiring to obtain a fruit distinct from the fruit produced by a thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), I shall perform a bath at Phalgutīrtha," one should bathe.
This is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa* in the section concerning bathing.

"He who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which one obtains at Phalgutīrtha. As for the libation (tarpaṇa): "Oṃ! May my father, of such-and-such lineage, named Amukadevaśarman, be satisfied today; may this water with sesame seeds be *svadhā* unto him; I gratify my father."
This is stated in the *Kalpataru* based on the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"O subduer of enemies, O best of beings, by that water given by you with the words 'I gratify [the ancestors],' our simultaneous union has been brought about through that speech."
Immediately after uttering *svadhā*, one should add, "I shall gratify the ancestors," because newcomers are placed at the end [of the lineage].

Then, having performed the worship of the gods and other rites, one should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), saying, "Today, for the occasion of reaching this sacred ford (*tīrtha*), I shall perform a *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. One should then perform the *pārvaṇa* rite according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *gṛhya-sūtra*, omitting the offering of the *arghya* water and the invocation (*āvāhana*). If that is impossible, the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should also be performed in that same manner;
for the offering of rice-balls is highly commended and extremely difficult for the ancestors to obtain.
One must not cause delay at all, nor should one create any obstacle.
According to this statement,
one should go on that very day to the Pretaśilā located to the north of Gayā and situated on the western bank of the Mahānadī river, and perform that rite as follows:

Having performed the five-fold purification (*pañcabhūsaṃskāra*) on the *pretaśilā*, having sipped water (*ācānta*), and sitting down with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), facing south, he recites from "Oṃ kavyavāla" up to "śāśvatīm. Then, having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), sipped water, performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) as in the *saṃdhyāvandana* rite, and remembered the lotus-eyed Lord (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*), he sprinkles the materials for the *śrāddha* with water mixed with *kuśa* grass. He then declares: "Oṃ, today, desiring the liberation from the state of a *preta* for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather named so-and-so Devaśarman of such-and-such lineage; for my mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother named so-and-so Devī of such-and-such lineage; for my maternal grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather named so-and-so Devaśarman of such-and-such lineage; and for my maternal grandmother, great-grandmother, and great-great-grandmother named so-and-so Devī of such-and-such lineage—I shall perform the *śrāddha* upon the *pretaśilā*."

Having thus resolved, one should perform the *śrāddha* for twelve deities according to the procedure of the *pārvaṇa* rite. However, according to the opinion of Hemādri, the remainder—excluding the maternal grandmothers and others—is as before. According to the opinion of Jayaśarman and others, it is indeed the standard *pārvaṇa*, but with the qualification that all six deities are accompanied by their wives.
In the traditional view (*saṃpradāya*), the status of being a deity here belongs to the six males alone and not to the women, nor even by virtue of them being accompanied by their wives.
Both views are incorrect.

On the Anvaṣṭakā, on an occasion of prosperity (vṛddhi), at Gayā, and on the anniversary of death, one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; on other occasions, it is performed together with the husband.
Thus, because of the contradiction with the *Vāyu Purāṇa*.

Having thus performed the *pārvaṇa* rite ending with the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should sit to the south of the knower of that [rite], place the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), face the south, hold three blades of *kuśa* grass, recite from "The fire is the devourer of offerings" (*kavyālo 'nala*) up to "eternal" (*śāśvatīm*), and perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) upon those *kuśa* blades by offering once a handful of water containing sesame seeds.

Then, having worshipped the ancestors and others in due order with the five services (*pañcopacāra*)—beginning with these *pādya* waters and so forth, saying "Oṃ, obeisance to the father and others"—one should proceed.
Oṃ! From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, may the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, as well as all the paternal ancestors, mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others, be satisfied.
May this water mixed with sesame seeds reach the millions of ancestors of past generations who dwelt in the seven continents, throughout all the worlds up to the realm of Brahmā.

Thus, having performed the invocation as before by joining the palms in the form of offering water and scattering leaves, one should offer the *piṇḍa*—consisting of milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and other ingredients mixed with honey and sesame—to the father alone, saying: "Oṃ, today, O father of such-and-such lineage, [named] Śarman, this is your *piṇḍa*; *svadhā*! In the same manner, one should offer to the eleven ancestors, beginning with the grandfather, according to their respective order from left to right. Then, sitting to the south and spreading *kuśa* grass with roots facing south, one should recite from "Oṃ, Kavyavāla... up to "...the eternal" as before. Having performed the invocation in the form of offering water with sesame once, and having worshipped as before, one should perform the invocation as before in the form of offering a handful of water with sesame, reciting "From Brahmā down to a blade of grass," and so forth.
Oṃ, father and grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather;
mother and grandmother, and likewise great-grandmother.
To the maternal grandfather, his father, the great-grandfather, and the others—
may this pinda offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible.

Having recited this verse from the Purāṇas, one should offer a single *piṇḍa* made of a handful of roasted barley flour mixed with sesame, ghee, curd, honey, water, and milk, to twelve gathered [ancestors].
Then follows the *ṣoḍaśī-karma*. It is as follows:
*Oṃ, those who have died in our family, and those whose destination is not known...*
I shall invoke them all upon the surface of the darbha grass with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Oṃ! Those in the family of my maternal grandfather, and those whose destination is unknown—I shall invoke them all upon the surface of the *darbha* grass with water mixed with sesame seeds.
Oṃ! To those in my circle of kinsmen and family, and to those whose destination is unknown—I shall invoke them all upon the surface of the *darbha* grass with water and sesame seeds.

Having thus invoked them upon the darbha grass spread with Purāṇic mantras and worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings—and if the *ṣoḍaśī* rite is performed at this stage, then having worshipped that [deity] also with its specific mantra—one should offer a handful of water with sesame seeds once there, as before, with the two verses beginning "Oṃ, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass," and then offer the *piṇḍas* starting from the root [mantra]. The ritual procedure (*krama*) therein is as follows:
"Oṃ! To those who have died in our family and whose destination is unknown, for the sake of their liberation, I give this *piṇḍa*."
Oṃ! For the sake of the deliverance of those in the family of my maternal grandfather and those whose destination is unknown, I offer this pinda.
Oṃ! For the sake of uplifting those in my circle of kinsmen and family, and those whose destination is unknown, I offer this rice-ball (piṇḍa).
Oṃ! For the sake of the deliverance of all those who have not yet cut their teeth and those who were tormented in the womb, I offer this ball of rice.
Oṃ! To those who have been cremated by fire, and likewise to those others who have not been cremated by fire, and to those killed by lightning or thieves—to them I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
To those who died in forest fires, and those killed by lions or tigers,
or by fanged or horned beasts— to them I offer this funeral cake.
To those who died by hanging, those killed by poison or weapons,
and those who committed suicide— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
To those beings, ghosts, and piśācas who have perished from hunger and thirst in the wilderness, on the road, or in the forest, I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
For the sake of uplifting those who have died in Raurava, Andhatāmisra, and Kālasūtra, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
And for those who have gone to the world of hungry ghosts, existing in various states of torment,
I give this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
To those who have been led by the servants of Yama to undergo manifold torments,
I give this funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the sake of their deliverance.
For the sake of uplifting those who abide in all the hells and in the various torments, I offer this funeral ball (piṇḍa).
And to those who have entered the womb of animals— whether they be birds, insects, or reptiles—
or those dwelling in the womb of trees, to them I offer this rice-ball.
To those who, wandering through thousands of different births by their own karma,
find human birth difficult to obtain— to them I offer this funeral cake.
To the ancestors and kinsmen dwelling in heaven, the intermediate space, and on earth, and to those who have died without having received the sacraments— to them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of hungry ghosts,
may they all forever attain satisfaction through this offering of funeral cakes.
Those who were not kinsmen but have become kinsmen, and those who were kinsmen in another birth—
may this funeral cake offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible.
Those who have died in the paternal lineage, those who have died in the maternal lineage,
and those other kinsmen of the teacher, father-in-law, and relatives who have passed away.
Those in my family for whom the funeral offerings have been interrupted, those deprived of sons and wives, those who have failed in their religious duties, as well as those born blind and the lame;
May the funeral offering given by me reach those of my family who were deformed or born prematurely, whether they were known or unknown; may it remain inexhaustible for them.
Those who are born in my paternal lineage up to Brahmā, as well as those born in my maternal lineage,
and those who have been my servants in both families— [may they all be liberated].
Likewise, the servants and those who have come as dependents.
Friends, companions, animals, and trees—
both those seen and those unseen— have indeed rendered me assistance; they were all associated with me in other lifetimes.
To them I offer this funeral cake (piṇḍa) with the cry of "svadhā."

Having recited thus and uttered [the names] preceded by *oṃ*, one should offer nineteen piṇḍas of the stated measure, each individually, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). Thus it is said.

However, in the *Strīṣoḍaśī* (the sixteen-fold rite for women)—beginning from the invocation mantra "Those who have died in our family" up to "Friends and companions"—one should adapt the text by changing the gender to feminine wherever possible; otherwise, everything else remains the same as in the *Puṃṣoḍaśī* (the sixteen-fold rite for men).

Then, one should perform the sprinkling of water three times clockwise around all the *piṇḍas* using a vessel filled with sesame seeds and water. The mantra for this is: Oṃ! Those who are yours and those who were ours; those females who are yours and those females who were ours—let them be summoned, let them be summoned! May you sirs be satisfied; may you ladies be satisfied! O waters, sweet as honey, satisfying the ancestors and their sons of such-and-such lineage, yielding the *svadhā* offering and nectar to the fathers, may these divine, fearless waters be satisfied! Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied!

Then, having prostrated, he should dismiss them with the words: "Oṃ, O ancestors and others, please forgive me. Then, having sipped water with his left hand and joining his palms in reverence, he should say:
"Oṃ, may the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Īśāna, be my witnesses;
having reached Gayā, I have performed the rite of expiation for my ancestors."
O Lord Gadādhara, I have come to Gayā for the sake of my ancestral rites;
you alone are the witness, O Blessed One, that I am now free from the three debts.
Thus one should recite while facing the east. If one is unable to perform this entire range of ritual acts, the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) upon the *pretaśilā* must also be performed.
It is as follows:

Oṃ! Desiring the liberation from the state of a *preta* for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage; for my mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage; for my maternal grandfather, great-grandfather, and great-great-grandfather, named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage; and for my maternal grandmother, great-grandmother, and great-great-grandmother, named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage—I shall perform the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) upon the *preta-śilā*.

Having thus formed the resolve and placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should invoke [the ancestors] with the mantra beginning "Kavyavāla is the fire" and so forth, and then perform the section written previously ending with "I am free from debt regarding the three debts"—this is the meaning.

Some, however, maintain that the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍadāna*) must be performed specifically for six persons with the desire for their liberation from the state of a preta; and in that regard, they say that for a Vājasaneyin, only those rites prescribed in his own *sūtra*—namely, the making of two altars (*vedī*), the drawing of lines, the circumambulation of the limbs, the holding of the blade with its base cut, the sprinkling (*avanejana*), the offering of the rice balls, the re-sprinkling (*pratyavanejana*), the holding of the breath, the loosening of the waist-knot (*nīvī*), the giving of the thread, and the giving of perfumes—should be performed, and likewise by anyone else, it should be done strictly according to their own *sūtra*.

Immediately after performing one of these [rites], having descended from the mountain to the earth at a great river joined by the Prabhāsa and other streams, well-known as Rāmatīrtha—in the Prabhāsa pool—one should make this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, desiring the dissolution of the evil deeds committed during more than a hundred previous births, I shall perform a bath in this sacred ford. Having performed the bath and the libations (*tarpaṇa*), and after reciting all the mantras pertaining to the bathing materials there, one should recite:
"Oṃ, whatever evil deed has been committed by me during more than a hundred previous births, may all that go to dissolution through the immersion in Rāmatīrtha."
Having recited this Puranic mantra, one should bathe.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to go to the world of Viṣṇu today, I shall perform the *śrāddha* or the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa-dāna*) at Rāmatīrtha," one should then perform either the *pārvaṇa* rite or the mere offering of the funeral cakes there.

This *pārvaṇa* and *piṇḍadāna* must be performed strictly according to the Sūtras, because there is an absence of the status of being a paternal ancestor (*pitṛ-arhatva*) that results in the fruits mentioned for Gayā.

Having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of the status of a paternal ancestor preceded by liberation from the state of a *preta*, I shall perform the offering of *piṇḍas* to the ancestors at Rāmatīrtha," one should offer the twelve *piṇḍas* for the ancestors and so forth, as well as the inexhaustible *piṇḍa* (*akṣayya-piṇḍa*) and the sixteenth *piṇḍa*, according to the procedure prescribed for the *preta-śilā*.
[295] Since one may lack the capacity to perform both of these, which have the attainment of Viṣṇuloka as their fruit, that very other [practice] must be performed.
Therefore: Oṃ Rāma Rāma Mahābāho, bestower of fearlessness upon the gods!
I bow to you today, O Lord of Gods; may my sin be destroyed.

Having recited this, one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) should pay homage to Rāma. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, desiring to go to the world of Śiva with myself as the manifest agent, I shall perform the prostration to Prabhāseśa," one should pay homage to Prabhāseśa. Thereafter, one should pay homage to both Rāma and Prabhāseśa. Oṃ! You are the waters, O Lord of Gods, and indeed the lord of lights.
Destroy my sin, O God, born of the actions of mind, speech, and body.

Having recited this Puranic mantra, one should offer the *bali*—consisting of cooked rice and other offerings—in the manner prescribed for the gods, using water from three *kuśa* blades, with the formula: "Oṃ, obeisance to Yama; this is the *bali*.
On the mountain named Naga, situated on the hip of the *preta-śilā* (the stone of the departed) in the southern direction of Mount Prabhāsa:
"Oṃ, there are two dogs, dark and brindled, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata..."
I offer this ball of rice to those two; may they both be free from harm.

Having recited this, one should offer a bali consisting of rice or any other such food to Yamarāja and Bhramarāja with the words, "This bali is for you both," once the two have joined together. This offering of the bali is obligatory (*nitya*), because it is heard in scripture that undesirable consequences follow from its non-performance.

However, all other rites are optional (*kāmya*) and independent; thus, it should be noted that among those [optional rites], only as much as one desires to perform should be done, and not necessarily everything. Thus concludes the first day's ritual at Gayā.
Now follows the ritual for the second day.
Regarding this, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"On the following day, having become pure, one should go to the Pretaparvata."
Then, having bathed in the Brahmakuṇḍa, the wise person should offer libations to the gods and other beings.
Having performed the invocation of the ancestors on the Pretaparvata mountain, being self-restrained,
wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), and facing south while remaining mindful [of them].

Having invoked the ancestors with the verses beginning with "kavyavāla" and ending with "śāśvatīm," one should perform the rites as previously described—starting from the breath-control (prāṇāyāma) up to the proclamation before the witnesses—as prescribed for the *pretaśilā*.
