Then, one should scatter barley-meal mixed with sesame seeds upon the *pretaparvata*.
O Nārada, by this, his ancestors shall be liberated from the state of being a *preta*.
Through his greatness, even the state of being a preta does not exist for him.
Therefore, the sequence of performance here is as follows:

on the day following one's arrival at Gayā, having bathed according to the rules at Phalgutīrtha or another such site and performed the rites up to the worship of the deities, one should go to Pretaparvata—located more than two *gavyūtis* to the northwest of Gayā—and bathe in the Brahmakuṇḍa situated in its northeastern corner, adjacent to its base, with the desire for heaven. Having offered libations (*tarpaṇa*) and ascended that Pretaparvata, one should perform there everything from the invocation of the ancestors up to the proclamation of witnesses, exactly as prescribed for the Pretaśilā.

However, the specific distinction is as follows: the *pārvaṇa* formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) is: "Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of the world of Brahmā from which there is no return, I shall perform the *śrāddha* on Pretaparvata. And it is the established practice that this *pārvaṇa* rite is performed upon the altar of Brahmā (*brahmavedī*). Then, after the proclamation to the witnesses, one should make the resolve: "Today, desiring the liberation of my ancestors from the state of being *preta*s and the removal of their *preta*-status, I shall perform the scattering of barley-meal mixed with sesame seeds on Pretaparvata. Having made this resolve, one should, facing south, scatter the barley-meal mixed with sesame seeds on Pretaparvata while reciting this mantra:
Oṃ! Whatever ancestors of mine exist in the form of pretas, may they all attain satisfaction through these barley-meals mixed with sesame seeds.
Oṃ! Whatever there is, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, including all that is moving and unmoving—
May they attain complete satisfaction through the water offered by me.
With this mantra, one should offer a handful of water. Then, according to one's ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as if it were already accomplished.
This is the ritual procedure for the mountain of the deceased (*pretaparvata*).
Now, the procedure for the Five Tīrthas (Pañcatīrthī).
Regarding this, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"First, the rule for the Five Tīrthas begins with the Northern Mānasa."
Having sipped water and sprinkled his head with water while holding kuśa grass in his hand.
One should go to Uttaramānasa and perform the ritual bath with the mantra:
"Oṃ, I perform the bath at Uttaramānasa for the purification of the self."
For the sake of attaining perfection in the worlds of the Sun and others, and for the liberation of one's ancestors,
one should bathe and then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) for the gods and other beings according to the prescribed rule.
From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, may the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans,
as well as all the paternal ancestors, mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others, be satisfied.
One should perform the Śrāddha rite accompanied by the Sapiṇḍana ceremony according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra,
on the Aṣṭakā days, on occasions of prosperity (vṛddhi), at Gayā, and on the anniversary of the death day.
One should perform the Śrāddha for one's mother separately, except when it is together with the husband;
however, at a Vṛddhi-śrāddha and in Gayā, the rites beginning with the recitation of mantras are performed starting with the father.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather;
the mother, the maternal grandmother, and likewise the great-grandmother.
To my maternal grandfather, his father, and the great-grandfather and others beyond him—
may this pinda offered by me reach them as an inexhaustible offering.
Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of Mānava, who takes the form of the Moon, Mars, and Mercury;
who possesses the very nature of Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu.
Having bowed to and worshipped the Sun, one leads one's ancestors to the world of the Sun;
for there is indeed a mental lake here, and therefore it is called Uttaramānasa.
Silent, one should go from the Northern Mānasa to the Southern Mānasa;
that which is called the Northern Tīrtha bestows liberation in the north.
To the north of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the holy site Kanakhala, frequented by celestial sages and ancestors,
which bestows liberation upon the ancestors.
A man who has bathed there shines like gold and attains purity;
therefore, this unsurpassed sacred site is renowned in the world as Kanakhala.
On its southern side is the sacred site Dakṣiṇamānasa;
indeed, three sacred sites are declared to be in Dakṣiṇamānasa.
Having bathed in them according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the Śrāddha rite separately for each.
I perform my bath in the southern Mānasa lake for the purification of my self,
for the attainment of perfection in the worlds of the Sun and other realms, and for the liberation of my ancestors.
Therefore, I bow to the Sun, who grants liberation through the mere act of bathing as "Golden Joy," for the sake of satisfying the ancestors and for their deliverance.
For the sake of sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty, and for the increase of long life and health.
O Sun, for the sake of liberation from the torments of the flood of sins such as the slaughter of a Brahmin,
I perform my bath here at Dakṣiṇamānasa.
With this [mantra], one should perform the ritual bathing, worship, and so forth, as well as the *śrāddha* ceremony with the *sapiṇḍana* rite;
having performed these and bowed to Maunārka, one should then recite this mantra:
Kavyavāla, Anala, Soma, Yama, and likewise Aryaman;
the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa ancestors— may these illustrious deities of the ancestors come, for you shall be protected by them here.
I have come to this Gayā as the giver of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for my fathers and those born in my lineage who are my kinsmen.
From there, one should go to Phalgutīrtha, the most excellent of all excellent holy places;
O gods, liberation is attained for the performers [of rites] and their ancestors through the performance of śrāddha.
In ancient times, Viṣṇu, being entreated by Brahmā, indeed became Phalgu;
that which was certainly offered as an oblation into the Dakṣiṇāgni fire became the Phalgutīrtha.
In this place where even a worthless cow yields fruit, where the earth yields water,
and because the Phalgutīrtha within one's sight is never fruitless.
All the sacred fords (tīrthas) that exist throughout all the worlds come together with the gods to bathe at Phalgutīrtha.
The Gaṅgā is the water for washing the feet of Viṣṇu, while the Phalgu is indeed the primordial wielder of the mace;
therefore, the Moon considers the Gaṅgā to be superior.
One who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices does not obtain that fruit which one obtains at Phalgutīrtha.
At Phalgutīrtha, in the waters of Viṣṇu, I perform my bath with devotion for the sake of the ancestors' attainment of Viṣṇu’s world, and for the accomplishment of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha, a person should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ancestral rite (śrāddha), including the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka), as prescribed by his own sūtra; he should then bow down to his grandfather.
Oṃ, homage to the auspicious God, to Īśāna and Puruṣa,
to Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, and Śambhu.
Having bowed to the divine Grandfather (Brahmā), one should worship him with this mantra.
Having bathed at Phalgutīrtha and beheld the god Gadādhara,
a man shall lead himself along with his ancestors to that Vaiṣṇava abode.
Oṃ, salutation to Vāsudeva, and salutation to Saṅkarṣaṇa,
to Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Śrīdhara, and Viṣṇu.
Having bathed at the five sacred fords (pañcatīrtha), a man leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
this bath is performed with the five nectars (amṛtas) and adorned with flowers, garments, and other ornaments.
From Nāgakūṭa, from Gṛdhrakūṭa, and from the beloved Uttaramānasa—
this is declared to be Gayāśiras, and that is called Phalgutīrtha.
Below Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is the unsurpassed Phalgutīrtha;
by performing śrāddha and other rites here, all the ancestors attain liberation.

"At the beginning" means that in the ritual of the five sacred sites (*pañcatīrthī*), the procedure for the *uttaramānasa* lake is performed first. "With the mantra" means that after reciting the mantra beginning with "In the *uttaramānasa*," one should perform the bathing and immersion following the mantra prescribed for the current rite.

Then, after the current *tarpaṇa*, one should offer a handful of water according to the divine procedure using the mantra beginning with "As far as Brahmā and the post. Thereafter, having performed the *pārvaṇa* for the paternal ancestors, maternal grandfathers, mothers, and maternal grandmothers, one should offer the inexhaustible rice-ball (*akṣayyapiṇḍa*) as in the case of the *pretaśilā*.

By the passage beginning with "at the Aṣṭakās," etc., the intended meaning is that at the Aṣṭakās, on the day of prosperity (ābhyudayika), on the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), and at Gayā—these four occasions—a separate Śrāddha for women is prescribed.

Regarding the term "vṛddhi": the meaning is that the performance of the Śrāddha is commenced with the mother on the occasion of prosperity (ābhyudayika), whereas at Gayā it is commenced with the father.
Furthermore, in this context, those who are the objects of the Śrāddha attain eternal Brahman; for Phalgu is within the Uttarāmānasa, which is itself within Gayāśiras. And therein—
One should offer a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Gayāśira, even if it is only the size of a śamī leaf;
by offering the piṇḍa under whose name, one leads that person to the eternal Brahman.
Because of this statement:

"In this way, the fruit is inexhaustible satisfaction," having begun with the words "the *śrāddha* at Puṣkara is inexhaustible," [it continues] "in the same manner at Gayāśīrṣa, Akṣayavaṭa, Phalgutīrtha, Uttaramānasa, Mataṅgavāpī, and Viṣṇupada"—so says the word of Viṣṇu.
Regarding "Sūryam": by the desire to go to the world of Sūrya, one should perform salutation to Sūrya and worship of Sūrya.

In both cases here, the meaning is that the mantra begins with "Oṃ namo bhānave. In that regard, when the Dakṣiṇamānasa is divided into three parts, the middle portion facing north is Kanakhala, and the southern portion is Dakṣiṇamānasa.

At each of these three holy sites (tīrtha), the fruit of performing a Śrāddha or a ritual bath is the liberation of one's ancestors. For the bath at Dakṣiṇamānasa, however, the mantra begins with "Oṃ dakṣiṇe mānase. The two additional verses beginning with "brahmahatyādī" and "namāmi sūryam" are for the purpose of beholding the Dakṣiṇārka [the Sun]; this is the summarized meaning.

Having recited the mantra beginning with *kavyavāla*, one should proceed from Dakṣiṇamānasa to Phalgutīrtha. Here, one should perform a bath with the desire to obtain the fruit of ten horse-sacrifices; the mantra for that Phalgutīrtha begins with [the words] "there, at Phalgutīrtha. Having bathed there, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) should be performed; in that rite, after uttering *svadhā*, one should employ the formula "I gratify my father," and so forth. Thereafter, one should perform a *śrāddha* ceremony there with the desire for the liberation of one's ancestors—this is the summarized meaning.

The word *atha* means "immediately after. The meaning is that one should bow to and worship Pitāmaha (Brahmā), who resides on the southern bank of the Madhusravā river, having recited "Obeisance to Śiva" (*namaḥ śivāya*) and so forth. Then again, to the east of Gadādhara, one should bathe at Phalgutīrtha with the desire to lead oneself and one's ancestors to the state of Viṣṇu, and there behold Gadādhara. Gadādhara refers both to the deity in the form of an image and to Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, which serves as his locus. This has been stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa.
"I bow to the primordial Gadādhara, the Lord whose form is unmanifest, who appears in the form of Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, Phalgutīrtha, and other such forms. Thus,
he has assumed manifest forms such as the stone mountain and Phalgu.
He exists in manifest and unmanifest forms as the stone-pillar and so forth;
as Ādigadādhara, he is manifest in the form of Gadādhara and others.

Immediately after the sight [of the deity]—having performed obeisance and worship with the mantra "Oṃ, obeisance to Vāsudeva" and so forth, and having made the formal declaration of intent (*saṃkalpa*) beginning with "desiring to go to the world of the Pitṛs and Brahman," and so on—the practitioner, holding the sacred grass (*pavitra*) and the water-vessel (*upagraha*) in his hands, should perform ritual sipping (*ācamana*), sprinkle his head with water, and then perform the ritual bath and libations (*tarpaṇa*) according to the prescribed rules at each of the following sites in their proper order: Uttaramānasa, Udīcī, Kanakhala, Dakṣiṇamānasa, and the Phalgutīrtha. Thereafter, he should bathe [the deity] with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consisting of milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar, measuring one hundred and eight *palas* in total, and then worship [the deity] with garments, flowers, and ornaments; this is the meaning.
[304] Now follows the sequence for its performance:

On the third day after reaching Gayā, having performed the rites from bathing at the Phalgu-tīrtha up to the worship of the deities, with the sacred thread (*pavitra*) and the water-pot (*upagraha*) in hand, one should perform *ācamana* and sprinkle oneself with water. Then, having gone to the Uttara-mānasa lake and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring the destruction of sins today, I shall perform a bath in the Uttara-mānasa," and having recited the mantras for bathing:
"Oṃ, I perform a bath in the Uttara-mānasa for the purification of the self."
For the sake of attaining perfection in the worlds of the Sun and others, and for the liberation of one's ancestors.
Having recited thus, one should perform the ritual bathing (*majjana*).

Then follows the libation (*tarpaṇa*): therein, in the *añjali* offerings for the ancestors and others, after the utterance of "svadhā," one should employ the formula, "I gratify the father. Then, at the conclusion of the libation, according to the rite for the gods:
"Oṃ! From Brahmā down to a blade of grass—gods, sages, ancestors, and humans..."
May all the ancestors—the mothers, maternal grandfathers, and others—be satisfied.

Having recited this, one *añjali* (salutation with joined palms) should be offered. Then: "Oṃ! Desiring the attainment of eternal Brahman, or desiring inexhaustible satisfaction, for my father, grandfather, and great-grandfather named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage (*gotra*); for my mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage; for my maternal grandfather, maternal great-grandfather, and maternal great-great-grandfather named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage; and for my maternal grandmother, maternal great-grandmother, and maternal great-great-grandmother named so-and-so, of such-and-such lineage—I shall perform the *śrāddha*."
Having thus resolved, one should perform the *śrāddha* for twelve deities. Hemādri states that this excludes the triad beginning with the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*).
The ancients maintain that at Gayā, the *śrāddha* for all six ancestors must be performed everywhere.
And so it is said: having performed one of these *śrāddhas* there, one should sit in the southern direction, spread out *kuśa* grass together with its roots pointing toward the south, and—
Oṃ! Kavyavāla, Anala, Soma, Yama, and likewise Aryaman;
the Agniṣvātta, Barhiṣad, and Somapa ancestors are the deities of the manes.
"Let those highly fortunate ones come; let my fathers and those born of my lineage who are my kinsmen be protected here by you."
I have come to this Gayā for the purpose of offering funeral cakes to them.
May they all attain eternal satisfaction through this śrāddha.

Having recited this and performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) by offering a single handful of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*), one should worship the ancestors and others with the fivefold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) beginning with water for the feet (*pādya*), saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the ancestors and others. Then:
"Oṃ! From Brahmā down to a blade of grass—may the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans, and all the ancestors, including mothers, maternal grandfathers, and the rest, be satisfied."
May this water mixed with sesame seeds reach those of the past, numbering in the millions of families dwelling in the seven continents, and all worlds up to the realm of Brahmā.
Having recited this and performed the invocation once more by offering a handful of water with sesame seeds (*tilodakāñjali*), [he says]:

*Oṃ pitā pitāmahaś caiva tathaiva prapitāmahaḥ | mātāmahas tatpitā ca pramātāmahakādayaḥ ||* [Oṃ! Father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather; maternal grandfather, his father, and the maternal great-grandfather and so forth.]
To my mother, my paternal grandmother, and likewise my paternal great-grandmother—
may this pinda offered by me reach them and remain inexhaustible.

Having recited this Puranic mantra, one should offer a single ball (*piṇḍa*) made from a handful of parched grain mixed with sesame, curd, honey, ghee, and water, to those who have assembled. Thus it is said. [306] Then: "Oṃ, with the desire for the vision of the world of the ancestors and the Sun, I shall perform the prostration to the Northern Sun (*uttarārka*). This is the very same ritual resolve (*saṃkalpa*) used in the worship. Then:
"Oṃ, salutations to the Sun, the sustainer, who possesses the forms of the Moon, Mars, and Mercury."
To you who possess the essential forms of Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu.

With this mantra, one should perform prostration and worship. Then, having gone to Dakṣiṇamānasa, one should form the resolve (*saṃkalpa*) there in the north, saying: "Oṃ, today, desiring the liberation of my ancestors, I shall perform a bath at the Udīcī-tīrtha. Having performed the ritual bathing and libations (*tarpaṇa*) as before, and having performed the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha for twelve or six deities as previously described, one should proceed to the middle Kanakhala-tīrtha.

There too, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring the liberation of my ancestors, I shall perform a bath at the Kanakhala-tīrtha," and having performed the ritual bathing and libations (*tarpaṇa*) with the desire for the liberation of the ancestors, as well as the ancestral offering (*śrāddha*) there; then, having made the resolve: "Oṃ, desiring the liberation of my ancestors, I shall perform a bath at Dakṣiṇamānasa," at the end of all the mantras for bathing, [one recites]:
"Oṃ, I perform a bath in Dakṣiṇamānasa for the purification of the self, for the attainment of perfection in the worlds of the Sun and others, and for the liberation of the ancestors."
O Divākara, I perform my bath here at Dakṣiṇamānasa.
Having recited this, one should bathe.

Then, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as before and having performed the *śrāddha* ceremony there with the desire for the liberation of the ancestors, one should say: "Oṃ, I bow to the Sun for the sake of the satisfaction of the ancestors and for their deliverance."
For the sake of sons, grandsons, wealth, and sovereignty, and for the increase of longevity and health.

With this mantra, the beholding and worship of the Southern Sun must be performed in silence alone, for that [sun] is named Maunārka. Then, having recited from "Oṃ Kavyavālo 'nalaḥ Somo Yamaś caivāryamā tathā" up to "I have come to Gayā" at the Dakṣiṇamānasa itself, one should proceed to the most excellent Phalgutīrtha situated to the east of Gadādhara.

And there, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring today to obtain a fruit distinct from the fruit of the merit arising from ten lakhs of horse-sacrifices, I shall perform a bath at Phalgutīrtha," one should recite at the end of the standard bathing mantra:

"Oṃ, with reverence, I perform this bath in the meritorious waters of Phalgutīrtha, for the sake of my ancestors' attainment of Viṣṇu’s world, and for the realization of worldly enjoyment and liberation."
Having recited this, one should bathe.

Then, having performed the libation (*tarpaṇa*) as before, one should perform there a *śrāddha* rite for twelve or six deities with the desire for the liberation of one's ancestors. Then, [one should worship] the grandfather situated in the southern direction from Madhuśravas:
"Oṃ, salutation to the auspicious God, to Īśāna and Puruṣa."
To Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta, and Śambhu.

Having recited this, one should bow to and worship the Grandfather (Brahmā). Then, returning again to Phalgutīrtha, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, desiring to lead myself and my ancestors to the state of Viṣṇu, I shall bathe in Phalgutīrtha and perform the vision of Gadādhara. Having thus resolved, one should perform the ritual bath there according to the rules. Gadādhara consists of both the form of the image and the form of the Muṇḍapṛṣṭha mountain which serves as its locus. Immediately after that vision: "Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva and salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa."
To Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, and to Viṣṇu, the bearer of Śrī.
Having recited this, one should bow to and worship Gadādhara.

Then, having gone to Uttaramānasa, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, desiring to lead my ancestors to the world of Brahmā, I shall perform the ritual bath at the five sacred sites (*pañcatīrthī*). Thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath and libations (*tarpaṇa*) at each site individually according to the prescribed rules, in their proper order: at Uttaramānasa, at Kanakhala to the north, at Dakṣiṇamānasa, and at Phalgu-tīrtha.

Then, having gone to the presence of Gadādhara, one should bathe Gadādhara with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*)—consisting of milk, curd, ghee, honey, and sugar—in a quantity of one hundred and eight *palas*, and worship Him with flowers, garments, and ornaments.

Among these rites, the final bath with the five nectars alone is mandatory, because there is a deprecatory explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) regarding its omission. The others, however, are optional and independent; they should be performed according to one's capacity.
Thus concludes the ritual of the Five Tīrthas.
[309] Now, with reference to the five types of heretics, he describes their duties up until the second day.
The Vāyu Purāṇa: The procedure for the first day has been declared; on the second day, one should go to Dharmāraṇya, where Dharma caused a sacrifice to be performed.
Having bathed in the Mataṅga-vāpī, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the ancestral rite (śrāddha). Having gone there and bowed to Mataṅgeśa, one should utter this mantra:
"May the deities be my authority and the world-protectors be my witnesses;
having come here, I have performed the expiation for my ancestors at this Mataṅga [tirtha].
As before, one should perform the śrāddha and other rites at the Brahma-tīrtha and the well."
By performing [this] between that well and the sacrificial post, one causes one's ancestors to cross over;
having bowed to Dharma, the Lord of Dharma, one should pay homage to the Mahābodhi tree.

This is the sequence of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-krama*). Having bathed and performed the rites ending with the worship of the deity, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) established by authoritative tradition as follows: "Oṃ, desiring to go to the world of Brahmā today, I shall perform the journey to Dharmāraṇya. Having gone there, at the Mataṅgavāpī, one should bathe after making the resolve: "Oṃ, desiring the destruction of all sins today, I shall perform a bath in the Mataṅgavāpī. This is because of the statement of Viṣṇu, which begins: "By merely bathing at Puṣkara, one becomes purified from all sins," and continues: "In the same way [it is so] at Phalgutīrtha, at Uttaramānasa, and at Mataṅgavāpī."

Then, having performed bathing and libations there, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, desiring the inexhaustible satisfaction of my ancestors today, I shall perform the *śrāddha* at the Mataṅgavāpī. Having performed the standard *pārvaṇa* rite and having bowed to Mataṅga situated to the north of the Mataṅgavāpī itself, one should say:
"Oṃ! May the deities be my authority and the guardians of the world be my witnesses;
having come here, I have performed this expiation for my ancestors at this Mataṅga."

Having recited this and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to cross over the ancestors, I shall perform the *śrāddha* between the well and the sacrificial post," one should perform the *pārvaṇa* rite. Now, there is a single well; this is situated in the middle of the area of the southeast corner of the pond (*vāpī*) in the form of a pit (*avaṭa*). On its bank, one may perform the *śrāddha* or the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), even for one who has fallen [from grace]. However, in that case, the designation must be made as follows: "the killer of an embryo" or "one who has violated the Guru’s bed. Then, one who desires heaven should pay homage in due order to Dharma, Dharmeśvara, and the Great Bodhi Tree. Thus concludes the ritual duties for the day of the Five Tīrthas and the day of Agnimat.
Now follows the ritual for the third day after the Pañcatīrthī day.
Regarding this, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"On the third day, one should perform the Śrāddha rite with the offering of piṇḍas at Brahmasaras."
I perform my ablution at this sacred ford for the sake of liberation from the three debts.

By performing the ancestral Śrāddha, the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa), the libation (tarpaṇa), and self-purification between that well and the sacrificial post, one causes one's ancestors to cross over to liberation.
Having bathed, the sacrificial post (yūpa) is raised; therefore, it is said that the sacrificial post belongs to Brahman.
Having performed the śrāddha at the Brahma-lake, one leads one's ancestors to the world of Brahman.
The mango trees situated near the cow-pasture were established by Brahmā;
by merely watering them, one's ancestors attain liberation.
I sprinkle this mango, which has arisen from the Brahmaśiras [mantra], which embodies all the gods, which is all-pervading,
and which is the form of Viṣṇu, for the liberation of the ancestors.
The mango trees are watered and the ancestors are satisfied;
this single action is renowned for accomplishing two purposes.
One who pours water at the root of the mango tree—
A human being must not be neglected by the wise.
By circumambulating the sacrificial post (yūpa), one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
and by bowing to Brahmā, one leads the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
Oṃ, salutations to Brahmā, the unborn, the cause of the birth and other states of the world;
salutations be to you, the savior of both devotees and ancestors.
Then, having offered the *yama-bali* with this mantra, the two are restrained;
indeed, King Yama and King Bhrama remain stationed there for the sake of immobility.
I offer an oblation to those two for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors;
thereafter, O Nārada, one should give an oblation to the dogs with this mantra.
To the two dogs, Śyāva and Śabala, born of the lineage of Vaivasvata, I offer this oblation; may they protect me at all times upon my path.
Then, having offered the *kākabali* (the oblation to the crows), one should perform the bath again;
[the deities] are those of Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and likewise those of Nirṛti.
"May the crows accept the ball of rice (piṇḍa) released by me upon the ground," [adding] "sapiṇḍakam," which means "together with the imperishable ball of rice."

Regarding the word *tat*: having performed his bath, one who performs that *śrāddha* between the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and the well saves his ancestors; this is the meaning. Regarding the word *kṛtvā*: having performed the *śrāddha* at the Brahma-lake (*brahmasaras*), one leads the ancestors to the world of Brahmā; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the combination of these two results follows from their connection to a single location. Regarding the phrase *gopracāra*: having recited the verse beginning with "the mango tree" (*āmram*), the watering of the mango tree should be performed; and according to the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*), this is done with the water of the Brahma-lake and with *darbha* grass. "Oṃ namo brahmaṇe" and so forth is the mantra for saluting Brahmā. "Yamarāja" and so forth is the mantra for the offering to Yama. "Vaivasvata" and so forth is the mantra for the offering to the dog. "Aindra" and so forth is the mantra for the offering to the crow.

Thus, the ritual procedure is as follows: on the third day following the Pañcatīrthī day, having performed the rites up to the worship of the deity at Phalgutīrtha, one should go to Brahmasaras and make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, desiring the destruction of my sins, I shall perform a bath in this Brahmasaras. Then, at the conclusion of the standard mantra, [one recites]: "Oṃ, I perform this bath in this sacred ford for the sake of liberation from the three debts, for the performance of the *śrāddha*, for the offering of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), for the libations (*tarpaṇa*), and for the purification of the self."

Having recited this and performed the circumambulation—[313]—having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to lead my ancestors to the world of Brahmā, I shall perform the *śrāddha* ceremony between the Brahmakūpa and the Upayū," and having performed the *śrāddha* for twelve, nine, or six deities, and having offered the inexhaustible rice-ball (*akṣayyapiṇḍa*) from the Uttaramānasa lake, one should make the resolve: "Oṃ, desiring the liberation of my ancestors, I shall perform the watering of the mango tree ordained by Brahmā.

Then: "Oṃ, I sprinkle the all-pervading mango tree, which has arisen from the lake of Brahmā, which consists of all the gods, and which is the form of Viṣṇu, for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors."

Having recited this, one should, according to custom, water with three blades of *kuśa* grass the mango trees established by Brahmā near the *gopracāra* (the pasture ground) using water from the *Brahmasaras* lake.

Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by the Vājapeya sacrifice, I shall perform the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of the Brahma-pillar," one should perform the circumambulation.
Then, having made the formal resolve thus: "Oṃ, desiring to go to the city of the Pitṛs and Brahmā, I shall perform the salutation (*namaskāra*) to Brahmā," [one should proceed].
Oṃ, salutations to Brahmā, the unborn, the cause of the birth and other states of the universe;
salutations be to you, the savior of both devotees and ancestors.
Having recited this, one should pay homage to Brahmā, who resides in the north-western corner of the Brahma-lake.
Then:
"Oṃ! Yamarāja and Bhramarāja are stationed here indeed for the sake of stability."
To those two I offer this oblation for the sake of the liberation of my ancestors.
Having recited this, one should offer the *yamabali* with *kuśa*-grass water, as for a deity, using the mantra: "Oṃ, obeisance to Yama, this is the *bali* offering.
Then:
"Oṃ, the two dogs, Śyāva and Śabala, born from the lineage of Vaivasvata..."
I offer this food-ball to you both; may you protect me always on the path.
Having recited this, one should offer the dog-oblation (*śvabali*) with water on *darbha* grass, as one would for a deity, saying: "Oṃ, this is the offering for the dogs; obeisance.
Then:
"Oṃ, those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and likewise to Nirṛti..."
May the crows accept the morsel of food cast upon the ground by me.

Having recited this, one should offer the *kākabalim* (oblation to the crows) with water on *darbha* grass, just like the oblation to the gods, saying: "This offering is for the crows; *namaḥ*. Others maintain that the offerings to Yama, the horse, and the crows should be made using the verse itself, and not even with a prose formula. Following the *kākabalim*, however, comes the bath.
Now follows the ritual for the fourth day after the day of the *pañcatīrthī*.
Now follows the ritual for the fourth day after the day of the *pañcatīrthī*.
In that regard, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"On the fourth day, one should perform the ritual bathing and other rites at Phalgutīrtha;
then, one should perform the Śrāddha ceremony together with the Sapiṇḍana rite at the Padas on Gayāśiras."
There, Gayāśiras itself has been established, taking its support from Phalgutīrtha;
from Krauñcapāda as far as Phalgutīrtha is indeed Gayāśiras itself.
Gayāśiras, Nagādya, and others are directly that Phalgutīrtha;
this is the mouth of the Asura Gaya, and having bathed there, the Śrāddha becomes inexhaustible.
The primordial Lord Gadādhara exists as both the manifest and the unmanifest,
in the form of the stations of Viṣṇu and others, for the sake of the liberation of the ancestors.
[315] Therein lies the divine Viṣṇupada, which destroys sins through the mere sight of it;
and through touching it and worshipping it, it bestows liberation upon the ancestors.

Having performed the *śrāddha* ceremony with the offering of rice-balls (*sapiṇḍaka*), a man shall uplift a thousand members of his lineage along with himself and lead them to the world of Viṣṇu, the abode of Viṣṇu.
Having performed a śrāddha, a man leads a hundred generations of his lineage, along with himself, to the abode of Rudra; likewise, in the abode of Brahmā, he leads them to the city of Śiva.
Having uplifted a hundred generations of his lineage, he leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā;
by performing a Śrāddha at the site of the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, the performer obtains the fruit of a Vājapeya sacrifice.
One who performs a śrāddha at the site of the Gārhapatya fire shall obtain the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
having performed a śrāddha at the Āhavanīya fire, one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
Having performed a śrāddha at Satyapada, one obtains the fruit of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
one who performs a śrāddha at Āvasathyapada shall attain the world of Soma.
Having performed a śrāddha at Candrapada, one leads the ancestors to the world of the Moon;
a performer of śrāddha at Sūryapada leads five sinners to the city of the Sun.
O Viṣṇu, among all of them, Kāśyapa is the most excellent; indeed, the station of Rudra and the station of Brahmā are also proclaimed there as supreme.
O Nārada, at both the commencement and the conclusion of those [rites], the recollection of any one of them is said to bring about the welfare of the performer of the Śrāddha.
[316] In ancient times, at the divine site of Kaśyapa, the sage Bharadvāja,
having performed the *śrāddha* ceremony, was prepared to offer the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) to his ancestors and others.
Then his two hands, white and black, emerged after bursting through the ground;
seeing those two hands there, he fell into doubt regarding his father.
Then Bhāradvāja asked his mother Śāntā:
"O mother, in which quarter of Kaśyapa’s foot—in the white or the black part—should the rice-ball (piṇḍa) be offered by me? You know; tell me of my father."
Śānti said: "O Bhāradvāja, O highly wise one, give this rice-ball to Kṛṣṇa.
Thereupon, Bhāradvāja prepared himself to offer the rice-ball to Kṛṣṇa.
Śveta, who was invisible, said, "Give me your own legitimate son. Kṛṣṇa replied, "You are my son born of my wife; therefore, give me the funeral cake (piṇḍa)."
Śukla said, "Since she was unchaste, you are my legitimate son";
but the unchaste woman replied, "First [the son belongs] to the owner of the field, and then to the sower of the seed."
Then Bhāradvāja offered the funeral cake at the station of Kaśyapa;
both of them went to the world of Brahmā by means of a vehicle yoked with swans.
Bhīṣma, however, having summoned his own ancestors, [offered it] at the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
Having performed the śrāddha according to the prescribed rules and being intent on offering the pindas,
Śāntanu’s two hands emerged at Gayāśiras.
Bhīṣma offered the funeral cake (piṇḍa) upon the ground because he had no authority over his hand;
Śāntanu, laughing and satisfied, said, "You are steadfast in the meaning of the scriptures."
"May you possess vision of the three times, and may Viṣṇu be your refuge at the end;
may there be death according to your own will"—having spoken thus, he attained liberation.
While Rāma was intent on offering funeral cakes at the beautiful site of Rāmapada,
his father Daśaratha arrived, extending his hand from heaven.
Then Rāma placed the morsel of food into his hand at the feet of Rudra;
Daśaratha spoke to Rāma, who was afraid of transgressing the meaning of the scriptures.
"I have been delivered by you, my son; indeed, the world of Rudra has become mine through the offering of the funeral cake at your feet, for the attainment of heaven does not depend on the hand."
And you, having ruled and protected the kingdom and its subjects for a long time,
and having performed sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, shall go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having spoken thus, Daśaratha, together with all the people of Ayodhyā and even down to the worms and insects, went to the supreme world of Rudra along with his son.
Whoever should offer a funeral cake (piṇḍa) at Gayāśiras by the name of those [ancestors],
those residing in hell go to heaven, and those residing in heaven attain liberation.
Whoever offers a funeral cake at Gayāśiras, even if it is only the size of a Śamī leaf,
or with bulbs, roots, fruits, and the like, shall lead his ancestors to heaven.
Wherever the footprints of Viṣṇu and others are seen,
a man who performs the Śrāddha rite along with the Sapiṇḍana ceremony there shall lead his ancestors to their divine realm.
[318] Everywhere, Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha is clearly marked by these footprints;
all the ancestors go to the healthy world of Brahmā.
When the head of the asura Heti was severed by the mace in that manner,
the place where it was washed in the sacred ford (tīrtha) was thereafter known as Gadālola.
"Directly" (sākṣāt) means "praiseworthy. Krauñcapāda [is so called] because he was on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha;
for the sage performed austerities on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha in the form of a crane (krauñca). Since he was marked by its foot (pāda), he is therefore remembered as Krauñcapāda.

Thus, from the *Vāyupurāṇa*. The phrase "even the five sinners" means even those who have committed the five great sins (*pañcamahāpātakin*). Regarding the other sites, such as Krauñca and so forth, they endure for a *caturyuga*; this is stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "The site of Viṣṇu, the site of Rudra, the supreme site of Brahmā, and the divine site of Kāśyapa, where two cubits protrude."
Here are the sites of the five fires; beyond them are the sites of Indra and Agastya, as well as those of Ravi, Kārtikeya, and Krauñcamātaṅgaka. Understand that all these sites are auspicious liṅgas.
Regarding the term *śreyaskaram*: "śreyaḥ" means liberation (*mokṣa*), according to the lexicon which states, "śreyaḥ is liberation; śreyaḥ is the nectar of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa-amṛta*).
Thus, the meaning is that through faith in this word, the performer also attains liberation. Therefore, the formal ritual procedure (*prayoga*) here is as follows:

having made the resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—"Oṃ, today, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to the fruit produced by ten million horse-sacrifices, I shall perform a bath at Phalgutīrtha"—at the conclusion of the prescribed rite for the bath:
Oṃ, at the Phalgutīrtha of meritorious waters, I respectfully perform this bath for the sake of my ancestors’ attainment of Viṣṇu’s world, and for the realization of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having recited this mantra, one should bathe at Phalgutīrtha. Then, regarding the libation (*tarpaṇa*) there—at the beginning of the libation for the ancestors (*pitṛtarpaṇa*) and so forth—one should employ the formula "I gratify my father" after uttering *svadhā*. Following that is the *śrāddha* rite at the sacred sites (*padas*). Although it is prescribed that one may begin and conclude either at the site of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, or Kaśyapa, nevertheless, the commencement should be at the site of Rudra.
Having bathed on the fourth day at Phalgutīrtha and performed the libations for the gods and others, one should perform the *śrāddha* here at Gayāśīrṣa, starting from the site of Rudra.
Thus it is stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*.

Accordingly, having first approached the vicinity of the Rudra-pada and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, desiring non-return [to saṃsāra], I shall perform the touching of the Rudra-pada," and having commenced the *śrāddha* and sprinkled the ritual materials with water, he should make the resolve: "Oṃ, desiring to lead my own self along with a hundred members of my lineage to the city of Śiva, I shall perform the *śrāddha* at the Rudra-pada. Then, he should perform the *śrāddha* for twelve deities, nine deities, or six deities.

Then, having gone near Viṣṇupada, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, desiring the destruction of my sins, I shall behold Viṣṇupada. Having beheld Viṣṇupada, one should make the resolve: "Oṃ, today, desiring the liberation of my ancestors, I shall touch Viṣṇupada. Having touched it, one should make the resolve: "Oṃ, today, desiring the liberation of my ancestors, I shall perform the worship of Viṣṇu at Viṣṇupada. Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu with the five-fold offerings (*pañcopacāra*) using a mantra that reveals Viṣṇu, one should sprinkle the materials for the *śrāddha* with water on *kuśa* grass while recollecting the Thousand-eyed One (Puṇḍarīkākṣa). Then, making the resolve: "Oṃ, today, desiring to lead [my ancestors] to the world of Viṣṇu by first effecting the upliftment of a thousand generations of my family including myself, I shall perform the *śrāddha* at Viṣṇupada," one should perform the *Pārvaṇa-śrāddha*—whether for twelve deities, nine deities, or six deities—along with the *Viśvedevas*. Then, sitting to the south of that [altar], beginning with the words "sitting down... and ending with "from the three debts... while facing east, one should perform the rite pertaining to the Preta-stone. However, for renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*), the touching of the staff (*daṇḍa*) at Viṣṇupada must be performed.
If a monk goes to Gayā and does not offer alms, he should touch the staff;
by laying down the staff at Viṣṇupada, he is liberated along with his ancestors.

Thus, from the *Vāyupurāṇa*. Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to lead [my ancestors] to the world of Brahmā by first rescuing my hundred lineages, including myself, from hell, I shall perform a Śrāddha for the station of Brahmā," one should perform the Śrāddha there in the same manner as the Śrāddha for the station of Rudra.

Now, a *śrāddha* performed at the site of the *dakṣiṇāgni* yields the fruit of the *vājapeya* sacrifice; a *śrāddha* at the site of the *gārhapatya* yields the fruit of the *rājasūya*; a *śrāddha* at the site of Kārttikeya yields the fruit of leading the ancestors to the world of Śiva; a *śrāddha* at the site of Krauñca yields the fruit of leading the ancestors to the world of Brahmā; and a *śrāddha* at the site of Kaśyapa yields the fruit of leading the ancestors to the world of Brahmā. Furthermore, the conclusion of the *śrāddha* must be performed at the site of Kaśyapa.

Then, at Gayāśiras—having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of heaven for [the deceased] of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, I shall perform the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) at Gayāśiras"—one should perform the rites beginning with the *avanejana* (water-offering) and ending with the lifting of the rice-balls, according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Sūtra. Then, having made the resolve thus: "Oṃ, today, desiring the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*) for [the deceased] of such-and-such gotra and such-and-such name, I shall perform the offering of the rice-ball at Gayāśiras"—one should perform the rites beginning with the *avanejana* and ending with the lifting of the rice-balls. In this same manner, the rice-ball for a woman (*strīpiṇḍa*) should also be offered.

In this context, there is no requirement for specific relationship (*saṃbandha*), as indicated by the natural sense of the general term "by name" (*nāmnā*). Furthermore, this offering of the funeral cake (*piṇḍadāna*) must be performed somewhere within the area bounded by the Madhusravā, Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, Uttaramānasa, and Dakṣiṇamānasa, starting from the Gadādhara-āvasa;

for it is said: "From Krauñcapāda to Phalgutīrtha is the manifest Gayāśiras. And Krauñcapāda is located on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, with reference to the Pretaśilā marked by footprints, according to the Vāyupurāṇa.
Upon seeing her, every person in the world— even one burdened by a flood of great sins—
is purified, becomes eligible for ritual action, and as a performer of ancestral rites (śrāddha), attains the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed in the waters situated upon the rocks and having performed the libations (tarpaṇa),
those who perform the Śrāddha ceremony along with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka) go to the world of Brahmā.

Whether they remain or die, those men— be they born from a womb or born from an egg— who cast off their bodies upon this stone shall go to the city of Brahmā and attain union with Viṣṇu along with seven hundred generations of their lineage.
Now, the ritual duties for the five days following the five holy sites (*pañcatīrthī*).
Regarding this, the *Vāyupurāṇa* states:
"On the fifth day, having performed the bathing and other rites at Gadālole as previously described,"
Then a person should perform the Śrāddha rite with the offering of rice-balls (sapiṇḍaka) at the Akṣaya-vata tree.
Having performed there the ancestral rites and other ceremonies, one should lead the ancestors to the city of Brahmā;
then, one should feed and worship the Brahmins appointed by Brahmā.
Having performed the śrāddha rite with food at Akṣayavaṭa with great effort,
and having seen, bowed to, and worshipped Vaṭeśa with a concentrated mind;

One leads one's ancestors to the eternal and imperishable city of Brahmā. What is given to the ancestors at Gayā, on the Ridge of Dharma (Dharmapṛṣṭha), at the lake of Brahmā, at Gayāśīrṣa, and at the Akṣayavaṭa tree, becomes inexhaustible.
Likewise:
"In the great holy ford Gadāloka, the excellent place for washing the mace,
I perform this bath for the sake of purification, for the imperishable, and for the attainment of heaven."
And thus, in this case, the destruction of evil and the attainment of heaven are the fruits. The mantra, however, is:
"Salutation to You, the one who lies in yogic sleep, who reclines at the tip of the banyan tree upon the single ocean, assuming any form at will."
Salutations indeed to the weapon against the tree of saṃsāra, to the remover of all sins without exception,
to the giver of imperishable Brahman, and to the one who is himself imperishable.
In the Kali age, the worlds became devotees of Maheśvara; therefore, Gadādhara assumed the form of a *liṅga*. I bow to him, the glorious great-grandfather.
Regarding "Gadālole": in the Phalgu river, there is a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) named Gadālole.
This is stated in the Vāyupurāṇa:
"And when the head of the asura Heti was split in two by the mace..."
Because it was washed there at the sacred ford (tīrtha), it is therefore remembered as Gadālola.

The meaning is that *Gadālola* is the name of the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) where the mace (*gadā*) was washed by Gadādhara after he had severed the head of the asura named Heti. The narrative concerning Heti is found in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"The Rākṣasa Heti, the son of Brahmā, performed a great and wonderful penance.
When Brahmā and the other gods were pleased by his austerity, he chose a boon from those bestowers of boons."
May I be of great strength and invincible against Daityas, Ādityas, and others, with various weapons and the like, as well as by men, and even by Kṛṣṇa, Īśāna, the Cakra, and so forth.
Having said "So be it," they vanished; then Heti conquered the gods.
Heti assumed the position of Indra, while the gods, including Brahmā, Hara, and others, were defeated.
They went to Hari for refuge and said, "Abandon the weapon!
Hari replied, "O gods, this one cannot be slain by either gods or asuras."
"Give me the Brahmāstra weapon, by which I may slay him.
Having been addressed thus, the gods then gave that mace to Viṣṇu.
"O Upendra, abandon this weapon! thus spoke Brahmā and the other gods.
Having been addressed by the gods, Gadādhara first took up that mace;
having struck down the weapon with his mace, he returned to the celestial realm for the sake of the gods.

And there, one should perform a bath at the Gadālolatīrtha. The meaning here is that after reciting all the relevant mantras, one should perform the immersion while reciting "gadālola" and so forth. Regarding the word "tatra" (there), the meaning is that the fruit of performing a *śrāddha* or offering *piṇḍas* at Gadālola is the leading of the ancestors to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). As for "Brahmā": first, by performing a *śrāddha* at the foot of the Akṣaya-vaṭa tree, the fruit is inexhaustible satisfaction for the ancestors; thereafter, by feeding Brahmins born of the lineage established by Brahmā, the fruit is the leading of the ancestors to the world of Brahmā.

Then follow the sight, salutation, and worship of Vaṭeśa; even there, the meaning is that the fruit for each [act] is specifically the leading of the ancestors to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). For the salutation to him, however, the mantra begins with "In the single ocean" (*ekārṇave*). Then, for the salutation to Akṣayavaṭa, according to the sequential order of the *pravṛtti* [kalpa], the mantra begins with "The tree of saṃsāra" (*saṃsāravṛkṣa*). Regarding the phrase "should lead," the fruit of the salutation to the great-grandfather is the leading [of the ancestors] to the station of Rudra. For his salutation, the mantra begins with "In the Kali age, the worlds of Maheśvara" (*kalau māheśvarā lokāḥ*).

Thus, the procedure here is as follows: having performed the concluding rites after the worship of the deity, one should go to Gadālole and bathe there after making this formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): "Oṃ, today, desiring the destruction of sins and the attainment of heaven, I shall perform a bath at Gadālole. There, following the recitation of the standard mantra, [one should say]: "Oṃ, at the great sacred ford (tīrtha) Gadālole, the excellent place for washing the mace, I perform this bath for the sake of purification, for imperishability, and for the attainment of heaven."
Having recited this mantra, one should immerse oneself. Then follows the libation (tarpaṇa).

Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring to lead my ancestors to the world of Brahmā, I shall perform the *śrāddha* at Gadālole," one should perform the *śrāddha*. Even if only the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is performed, the resolve should be made in exactly this same way. However, the offering of the rice-balls must be carried out according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *sūtra*. Then, having gone to Akṣayavaṭa, one should perform the *śrāddha* there after making the resolve: "Oṃ, desiring inexhaustible satisfaction for my ancestors, I shall perform the *śrāddha* at Akṣayavaṭa"—this being done on the northern side of the tree, in accordance with traditional practice (*ācāra*).

Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: “Oṃ, desiring to lead my ancestors to the world of Brahmā, I shall feed the Brāhmaṇas appointed by Brahmā,” he should feed those three. In their absence, he may feed other Brāhmaṇas as well. Having made the resolve thus: “Oṃ, desiring to obtain a fruit equal to that produced by feeding ten million Brāhmaṇas today, I shall feed one Brāhmaṇa at the Akṣaya-vaṭa,” he should feed one Brāhmaṇa there. This is stated in the *Vāyu Purāṇa*, in the section concerning the Akṣaya-vaṭa: “When one Brāhmaṇa is fed, it is as if ten million have been fed.”

Then, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) thus: "Oṃ, desiring today to lead my ancestors to the world of Brahmā, I shall perform the vision of Vaṭeśa," one should behold Vaṭeśa in the form of an image. In this very sequence, one should perform prostration and worship. Likewise, in that same place: "Then, having fasted, at the Gāyatrī-tīrtha situated on the Mahānadī, one who has bathed in front of Gāyatrī should perform the morning twilight ritual (*prātaḥ-saṃdhyā*)."

Having performed the *śrāddha* ceremony with the offering of rice-balls (*sapiṇḍaka*), a man who bathes at this sacred ford (*tīrtha*) in front of Sāvitrī shall lead his family to devotion for Brahman.
Having performed the midday twilight worship, one leads a hundred of one's lineage to heaven;
then, having bathed in the Prācīsarasvatī, one should proceed further along the Sarasvatī.
Having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), one should lead the family to omniscience;
liberation comes from performing the three daily devotions, whereas it results from the omission of the twilight devotion accumulated over many lifetimes.
At Viśālā, at Lelihāna, at the sacred ford of Bharatāśrama,
at Padāṅkita, on Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, and in the vicinity of Gadādhara.
At the sacred ford of the celestial Gaṅgā and at the openings of the mountain’s ears,
one who performs śrāddha and offers funeral cakes shall lead a hundred generations of his lineage to the world of Brahmā.
One who bathes in the Godāvarī and the Vaitaraṇī shall uplift twenty-one generations of his lineage;
one who performs a śrāddha at the Devanadī or in Gopracāra shall lead his ancestors to heaven.
At Puṣkariṇī, Ghṛtakulyā, and likewise Madhukulyā;
at the Puṣkariṇī, at the Gadālola Tīrtha, and likewise at Makara.
One who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at Koṭitīrtha in Rukmakuṇḍa shall lead his ancestors to heaven;
by bowing to Mārkaṇḍeyeśa and Koṭīśa, one becomes a savior of one's ancestors.
Referring to Pāṇḍuśilā at that very place, [it is said]:
"O Sage, Yudhiṣṭhira went there indeed to perform a Śrāddha;
the son of Vyāsa was greatly delighted by the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) upon the stone."
He granted a boon to his son: "Rule the kingdom upon the earth;
may it be entirely free of thorns. You shall be my protector, my dear son;
go to heaven in this very body, surrounded by your brothers."
"By a mere glance, lead those who are utterly perished and dwelling in hell to heaven"—
having spoken thus, Pāṇḍu departed for the eternal, imperishable state.
The Ghṛtakulyā, the Madhukulyā, and the great river Devikā.
The Madhusravā is proclaimed to be located there, meeting with the Śilā;
a man who performs a ritual bath there obtains the merit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices.
Having gratified the assembly of ancestors and performed the *śrāddha* ceremony with the offering of rice-balls (*sapiṇḍaka*),
a man shall uplift a thousand families and lead them to the abode of Viṣṇu.
Whether born from sprouts, born from sweat, born from eggs, or born from a womb—
having reached Madhusravā, even those who had died went to the city of Viṣṇu.
By performing a śrāddha at the Haṃsatīrtha in Daśāśvamedhika, one leads [one's ancestors] to heaven;
and by bowing to both Daśāśvamedha and Haṃsa, one shall go to the city of Śiva.
One who performs the ancestral rites (śrāddha) at the site of Mataṅga attains the world of Brahmā;
having churned the fires within the womb of a Śamī tree, Vidhi (Brahmā), together with Viṣṇu and the others [performed it].

He obtained a sacred ford (tīrtha) renowned throughout the three worlds for the purpose of sacrifice; indeed, that tīrtha is named Makha, and it bestows liberation upon the ancestors. By performing libations, offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas), and bathing there, one attains liberation.
By bowing to Rāmeśa and Aṅgārakeśvara, one leads one's ancestors to heaven;
by offering funeral cakes (piṇḍas) at Gadākūpa, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Therefore, by bathing with ashes at that well, a man rescues his ancestors;
likewise, a man who bathes at the confluence of the Niḥkṣīrā where the Dhautapāda river meets it [attains the same].

One who performs the *śrāddha* rite at Puṣkariṇī leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā. At Suṣumnā and Mahākauśī, one may uplift twenty-one generations of one's lineage. Having bathed and bowed to Vaśiṣṭheśa on its bank, one partakes in the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
One who offers a funeral ball (piṇḍa) at Dhenukāraṇya and at the sites of the wish-fulfilling cow (Kāmadhenu),
having bathed and bowed to Kāmadhenu, leads his ancestors to the world of Brahmā.
Having bathed at Kardamāne and Gayānābhi near Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, one who performs the śrāddha rite shall lead his ancestors to heaven after bowing to Caṇḍikā;
and having worshipped Īśa at the confluence known as Śmaśāna in Phalgutīrtha.
Gayāgaja, Gayāditya, Gāyatrī,
Gadādhara, Gayā, and Gayāsura— these six constitute the Gayā-ṣaḍga, which bestows liberation.
By performing the rite of releasing a bull at Gayā, one may deliver twenty-one generations of one's lineage;
wherever a Brahmin stands, he is uplifted and has his senses conquered.
Meditating upon the primordial Gadādhara, one should perform the śrāddha, the offering of piṇḍas, and other rites;
having delivered a hundred generations of one's lineage, one shall certainly lead them to the world of Brahmā.
Then, having offered the supreme food offering consisting of curd and rice to the divine Janārdana, he should worship him according to the prescribed rite.
One should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) after depositing them; with the very remains of that [offering], one should offer for the living.
Because the rock remained in the evening on the back of the head of the Daitya Muṇḍa.
This mountain, Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, bestows the world of Brahmā upon the ancestors;
when Rāma had gone to the forest, Bharata remained there after ascending the mountain.
Having offered the funeral cakes and other oblations to his father, and having established Rāmeśa there,
he bathed and, with a concentrated mind, bowed to Rāmeśa, Rāma, and Sītā.
Having performed the ancestral rites and the offering of funeral cakes, the righteous-souled one shall lead [the deceased] to the city of Viṣṇu,
together with his ancestors and hundreds of lineages.
And Mount Kuṇḍa has been established in the right hand of Śilā;
by performing śrāddha and other rites there, one leads all the ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
Then, having performed austerities at Kuṇḍa on the mountain to the south of Sītādri,
one who offers funeral cakes (piṇḍa) at the holy site of Mataṅga shall cause his ancestors to attain heaven.
And in his left hand, the sage held a mountain of stone;
indeed, the Udaya mountain was brought [there] by the high-souled Agastya.
The giver of funeral cakes established there shall lead the ancestors to the city of Brahmā;
having bathed there at the Udyantaka pool, one has sufficiently prepared oneself for austerity.
And there Brahmā was stationed together with Sāvitrī and Kumāra;
Hāhā, Hūhū, and others set up the sound of singing.
Having bathed there at midday and having performed the worship of Sāvitrī,
one becomes a Brahmin for ten million births, wealthy and a master of the Vedas.
Having bathed at the site of Agastya and offered funeral cakes, that righteous-souled man goes to the world of Brahmā,
honored by his ancestors and by the inhabitants of heaven.
That man who, having entered the womb of Brahman, then emerges,
goes to the Supreme Brahman here, liberated from the peril of rebirth.
By bowing to Gayākumāra, a man attains the status of a Brahmin;
and by bathing in Somakuṇḍa and other rites, he leads his ancestors to the world of Soma.
An offering made at Kākaśilā grants liberation from debt to crows;
by bowing to Svargadvāreśvara, one leads others from heaven to the city of Brahmā.
One who offers funeral cakes at the celestial Gaṅgā leads his ancestors to the stainless heaven;
on the stone slab, he held a heap of ashes in his right hand.
Dharma was the goat, and Hara performed the naming ceremony there;
consequently, that mountain of heaps of ashes became the giver of heaven through the ash-bath.
There stands the banyan tree and Vaṭeśvara, as well as the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā);
to the north is Rukmiṇīkuṇḍa, and to the west is the Kapilā river.
At the confluence of the Umā and Soma on the riverbank,
a man who bathes in the Kapilā and bows to and worships Kapileśa [attains merit].
One who performs ancestral rites (śrāddha) shall partake in heaven at Maheśīkuṇḍa;
and there Gaurī, as Maṅgalā, is worshipped as the bestower of all auspicious fortune.
Janārdana, offering the funeral ball (piṇḍa) into his hand upon a heap of ashes,
[performs the rite] for himself and others with a mantra using the left hand even without sesame seeds.
And all those who offer a ball of food mixed with curd go to the world of Viṣṇu;
such a man leads himself along with his ancestors to the world of Viṣṇu.
"O Janārdana, this funeral cake (piṇḍa) has been placed by me in your hand;
when I am dead, you must offer this cake for me at Gayāśīrṣa."
O Janārdana, O Lord, grant that auspicious merit to him for whom this rice-ball was offered by me, dedicated to you,
upon his death at Gayāśīrṣa.
O Janārdana, salutations to you; salutations to you who take the form of the ancestors.
O Lord of the ancestors, salutations to you; salutations to you, the cause of liberation.
At Gayā, Janārdana himself exists in the form of the ancestors;
by beholding that lotus-eyed one, one is liberated from the three debts.
Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one, who liberates from the three debts;
salutations be to you, O beloved of Lakṣmī; salutations to you, the giver of liberation to the ancestors.
Having worshipped Puṇḍarīkākṣa, one shall go to heaven, O Janārdana;
having prostrated himself with his left knee and bowed to Janārdana, Bhīma [attained this].
Having performed the *śrāddha* ceremony with the offering of rice-balls (*sapiṇḍaka*), one attains the world of Viṣṇu along with one's brothers;
on the rock, at the left foot, the mountain Pretakūṭa is held.
By the King of Dharma, the sinful mountain, which was the refuge of the Preta-stone and bore the burden of the Pretas upon its stone surface,
was cast far away with his foot.
Pretas in the form of archers, who collect taxes,
stand apart in great numbers and act as creators of obstacles.
Performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and other ceremonies at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) grants liberation to one's ancestors;
even Pretakūṭa attained purity through contact with Śilādri.
The Pretakuṇḍa is situated there, and the gods abide at that spot.
One who has bathed and offered the ancestral rice-balls (piṇḍa) and other offerings shall liberate his ancestors from the state of being a preta.
Gayā is meritorious among the Kīkaṭas, and the Rājagṛha forest is sacred.
The hermitage of Cyavana is meritorious, as is the meritorious river Punar-punā;
and there are Vaikuṇṭha, Lohadaṇḍa, and the beautiful Girikūṭa.
One who performs ancestral rites, such as offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), there shall lead the ancestors to the city of Brahmā;
at the right foot of Śilā, Gṛdhrakūṭa is established as the goal.
In order to quickly establish Dharmarāja in his rightful state,
the purified great sages, having perfected themselves through austerity, assumed the form of vultures.
Therefore, there is the Gṛdhrakūṭa mountain; there resides Śiva as Gṛdhreśvara.
Having seen Gṛdhreśvara and bathed there, a man goes to the abode of Śambhu.
Having bowed there at Gṛdhravaṭa, one who has reached the end of their time shall go to heaven;
having seen Śiva at Ṛṇamokṣa and Pāpamokṣa, one shall go to the auspicious state.
The interior of the rock was stepped upon by the mountain with its first foot;
there dwells Vighneśa, the destroyer of obstacles, in the form of an elephant.
Having seen it, one is liberated from obstacles; one leads the ancestors to the city of Śiva.
Having bathed and beheld Gāyatrī and Gayāditya, one shall go to heaven.
Having seen Brahmā situated at the first foot, one becomes a savior of one's ancestors;
and he who offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) at the navel shall lead his ancestors to the city of Brahmā.
On the slope of Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, there was a forest of lotuses;
by beholding the mountains of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha and Aravinda, one shall destroy all evil.
[333] For the sage performed austerities on Mount Muṇḍapṛṣṭha in the form of a curlew;
because it was marked by his footprints, it is celebrated as Krauñcapāda.
Having bathed there in that reservoir of water, one shall lead three generations of one's lineage to heaven.

"Having fasted" (*upoṣita*) means having observed a fast on the preceding day. "With the Gāyatrī" (*gāyatryā*) means that one should bathe at the Gāyatrī-tīrtha in the Mahānadī river—located in the eastern direction facing Gayā village—and perform the morning *saṃdhyā* worship there. "Accompanied by the rice-balls" (*sapiṇḍaka*) means that the *śrāddha* rite should be performed there together with the offering of the rice-balls mentioned previously; and the fruit here is the leading of one's lineage to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*).

But this is to be considered: since bathing and the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) are prescribed here as independent acts, like the Ārambhaṇīyā rite, their fruit is heaven according to the Viśvajit-nyāya; thus, there is an introductory statement based on the Vedic text.

Regarding "at a *tīrtha*": the meaning is that by bathing at midday before Sāvitrī and performing the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), one gains the fruit of leading a hundred generations of one's lineage to heaven. Regarding "the East" (*prācī*): the meaning is that by bathing in the Sarasvatī river in the east in front of Sarasvatī and performing the evening twilight worship, one gains the fruit of leading one's entire lineage to omniscience. Regarding "many" (*bahu*): the meaning is that by performing the salutation of the three twilights, one gains the fruit of liberation from the sins produced by the omission of twilight worship over many lifetimes. Regarding "in Viśālā": the meaning is that by performing a *śrāddha* or offering the funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) at any one of the seven *tīrthas* beginning with Viśālā, one gains the fruit of leading a hundred generations of one's lineage to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Regarding "having bathed" (*snāta*): the meaning is that at each of the Godāvarī and Vaitaraṇī rivers, there is the fruit of rescuing twenty-one generations of one's lineage. And the Vaitaraṇī is the divine river situated to the east of Bhasmakūṭa. And here, for crossing [it], there is a mantra obtained through traditional practice (*ācāra*).
That river known as Vaitaraṇī, renowned throughout the three worlds—
O illustrious one, she too has been crossed by you for the sake of delivering your ancestors.

And here, out of a desire to deliver their fathers and others from hell, people also perform the gift of a cow (*godāna*). Regarding the phrase "at the Devanadī": the meaning is that by offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) at each of the nine sites beginning with the Devanadī, one leads each of one's ancestors to heaven. Regarding "Mārkaṇḍeya": the meaning is that by bowing to Mārkaṇḍeyeśa and Koṭīśa, the fruit is the rescue of one's ancestors individually. Regarding "having seen": the meaning is that by beholding the Pāṇḍuśilā stone, the fruit is the purification of ancestors residing in hell and their leading to heaven.

Having said this—the meaning is that for Pāṇḍu, who had performed the *śrāddha*, there was the attainment of such a fruit as the recollection of the eternal and imperishable state during the *śrāddha* at the Pāṇḍu-stone (*pāṇḍuśilā*). And this Pāṇḍu-stone is located in the Campaka forest near Pitāmaha (Brahmā). Regarding "the streams of ghee" (*ghṛtakulyā*): these four stones situated on the southern side of Muṇḍapṛṣṭha are designated by the term Madhusravā; and the meaning is that bathing therein yields the meritorious fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*). Regarding libation (*tarpaṇa*) and the *sapiṇḍaka-śrāddha*, the meaning is that the fruit is the leading of one's family—each up to a thousand members—to the world of Viṣṇu. Regarding "those born from sprouts" (*udbhijjā*): [this refers] to the recollection of Madhusravā.
"Ten" means that at Daśāśvamedhika, Haṃsatīrtha, and Śrāddha, the fruit in each case is the leading of the ancestors to heaven.

"At the Mahānadī to the south of Pitāmaha" refers to Daśāśvamedha. Regarding "of Mataṅga," the meaning is that for one who performs a śrāddha at Mataṅgapada, there is the attainment of the world of Brahmā. Regarding "having churned"—by bathing in the Kuṇḍa, liberation occurs for the performer; likewise, by libations and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas), liberation occurs for the ancestors. This is the meaning.

"Near the Udayanta mountain, at Maghakuṇḍa, for the ancestors"—the meaning is that by bowing to Rāmeśvara and Aṅgārakeśvara, the fruit is the leading of each ancestor to heaven. "At Gayā"—this means that by giving at the Gayākūpa, the donor obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

And here, even for those such as outcasts (patita), the Śrāddha and the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) for one's ancestors should be performed with the desire for their attainment of heaven, after the first year has passed;
however, the rite for outcasts is performed only once, when a year has elapsed.
Because the local custom is authoritative, one should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony at the wells of Gayā or at the well of Mārtaṇḍapāda, while remembering Hari and Hara along with one's kinsmen.

Thus, from the *Brahmapurāṇa*. The word "smaran" (remembering) is used in the nominative case by transposition to convey the sense of the instrumental. Those who have fallen [into such states] are described in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One who dies while playing with horns, fangs, claws, serpents, poison, fire, women, or water must be avoided with great care."
Having acted against the interests of the Nāgas, he was consumed by lightning;
then, somewhere else, he was himself seized by the king on account of the crime of theft.
Delighting in the wives of others, they were slain by their husbands out of hatred; having engaged in conflict with those of unequal status, with mixed castes, and with Cāṇḍālas and the like,
they were then killed by them and subsequently took refuge among the Cāṇḍālas and others.

Those lowest of men who, being heretics of cruel intellect, out of anger resort to poison, fire, fasting, weapons, hanging, water, or leaping from mountains and trees; and those who administer poison, fire, and weapons— [these are the ones excluded].
Those who live by ignoble crafts, those who work as slaughterhouse decorators,
those with female organs on their faces, and those who are mostly impotent or neuter;

"Those who have been struck by the *brahmadaṇḍa* (the curse of a Brahmin), those who have been killed by Brahmins, and those who are great sinners (*mahāpātakinaḥ*)—these are proclaimed to be the fallen (*patitāḥ*).

[336] [Furthermore, there are: playing with horns and the like out of arrogance; playing with wild beasts or poisons out of the conceit of being a snake-charmer (*jāṅgalika*); playing with fire out of the conceit of being a master of mantras (*māntrika*); and [playing] with women out of the intoxication of youth, or with water by swimming with one's arms and so forth.

Regarding "by lightning" (*vidyutā*): one who has gone to a place where lightning strikes due to grief and other such causes, and is killed there, is "struck by lightning. *Gara* is a specific preparation made from coconut water and camphor that resembles poison. *Pāṣaṇḍas* are those outside the three Vedas. Those of "cruel intellect" are those who contemplate the misfortune of others for as long as they live. "Bad craftsmen" refers to Brāhmaṇas and others who make their living through crafts such as leatherwork. "Those who decorate slaughterhouses" refers specifically to Brāhmaṇas and others who are appointed to positions at places of execution.

"From that"—the meaning is that by bathing with the ashes from that well, the result is the deliverance of one's ancestors from hell. "Having washed his feet"—the meaning is that by bathing at the confluence of the Niḥkṣīrā at the place called Rāmapuṣkariṇī while the feet are washed, and by performing the *śrāddha* for one's ancestors and others, the specific result is the leading of one's ancestors and others to the world of Brahmā. "Of the Suṣumnā"—the meaning is that the result of a *śrāddha* performed at the Suṣumnā is the upliftment of twenty-one generations of one's lineage; the Suṣumnā is located in the middle of the village of Gayā. "Having bathed"—the meaning is that by bathing in the Vaśiṣṭhakuṇḍa at the holy site of Vaśiṣṭha and by bowing to Vaśiṣṭheśa, the result is equal to that of a horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). To the north of Gṛdhrakūṭa is the hermitage of Vaśiṣṭha; there are the Vaśiṣṭhakuṇḍa and Vaśiṣṭheśvara.

Regarding "Piṇḍada": the meaning is that the fruit of offering the *piṇḍa* at Dhenukāraṇya, likewise the offering of the *piṇḍa* at the site of Kāmadhenu, and likewise the prostration to Kāmadhenu, is individually the leading of [the ancestors] to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). Regarding "Kardamāna": the meaning is that at Kardamāna—the navel of Gayā—as well as near Muṇḍapṛṣṭha, the fruit of a *śrāddha* preceded by bathing is the leading of the ancestors to heaven; and this same fruit applies to the prostration to Caṇḍikā as well. Regarding "Phalgu": the meaning is that the fruit of prostrating to Phalgvīśa, Caṇḍīśa, and Saṃgameśa is individually the leading of the ancestors to heaven.

Regarding "Gayāgaja": these six bestow liberation at Gayā; and here, the focus on worship is understood from the context. Gayā, moreover, is the great river, the celestial river, flowing northward, situated between Kanakhala and Nandā, and containing all tīrthas without interruption. Gayāśiras, however, is located between Nagakūṭa, Gṛdhrakūṭa, and Uttaramānasa. Regarding "in Gayā": the fruit of performing the rite of releasing a bull (vṛṣotsarga) at Gayā is the deliverance of twenty-one generations of one's lineage.

The phrase *yatra yatra* means that at Gayā, or in any other region, the fruit of performing a *śrāddha* and offering the funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) is the leading of one hundred generations of one's lineage to the world of Brahmā. The phrase *snātvā* means that after bathing in the great river at Bharata’s hermitage and beholding Rāma—the Lord of Rāmā (Rāmeśa)—and Sītā, one should recite the mantra: “O Rāma, Rāma, O mighty-armed one! The phrase *śrāddham* means that in the presence of Rāmeśa, one should perform the *śrāddha* and the offering of the rice-balls with the desire to lead oneself, along with a hundred generations of one’s paternal lineage, to the station of Viṣṇu.

Regarding "Śilā": on the right hand of the rock is situated the mountain named Kuṇḍa; the meaning is that by performing ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) and offering funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) there, the result is the leading of the ancestors to Brahmapura. Regarding "Mataṅga-sveta": on the southern mountain of Sītā-dri, at the site of Mataṅga-pada, the result of offering funeral cakes is the leading of the ancestors to heaven. Regarding "Vāma-hasta": by offering funeral cakes on the Udyantaka mountain on the left hand of the rock, the result is the leading of the ancestors to Brahmapura. Regarding "Kuṇḍa-udyantaka": having bathed there in the Udyantaka-kuṇḍa at midday and performed the midday *saṃdhyā* worship known as Sāvitrī, the result is the attainment of the status of a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas and is wealthy throughout ten million lifetimes. [338]

Regarding "of Agastya": the meaning is that the fruit for the giver of the *piṇḍa* is the attainment of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), accompanied by ancestors who are honored by the hosts of celestial beings. Regarding "the womb of Brahmā" (*brahmayoni*): the meaning is that one should perform the entry into and exit from the womb of Brahmā with the desire to attain the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*) preceded by liberation from the confusion of births (*yonisaṃkara*). Regarding "not, however": the meaning is that the fruit of bowing to Gayākumāra is the attainment of Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*). Regarding "Soma": the meaning is that by bathing, offering libations (*tarpaṇa*), and giving the *piṇḍa* at the Soma-pool (*somakuṇḍa*), the ancestors are led to the world of Soma. Regarding "Bali": the meaning is that the performer of the *bali* offering to the crows at Kākaśilā attains immediate liberation (*mokṣa*). Regarding "heaven": the meaning is that by bowing to Svargadvāreśvara, one attains heaven and, beyond that, the world of Brahmā. Regarding "the giver of the *piṇḍa*": by giving the *piṇḍa* at the Ākāśagaṅgā, both personal purity and the leading of the ancestors to heaven occur. Regarding "at Pretaśilā": on the right hand of Pretaśilā is the mountain named Bhasmakūṭa; the meaning is that by bathing there with ashes, heaven is attained.

Regarding "Vaṭa": on that very mountain, at the Akṣayavaṭeśvara [shrine], in front of the great-grandfather (Brahmā), is the Rukmiṇī-kuṇḍa; to its west is the river named Kapilā; to its north is Kapileśvara. Regarding "Umā": having bathed at the confluence of Umā and Soma in that river, by bowing to or worshipping Kapileśvara, the fruit is heaven according to the principle of the Viśvajit sacrifice. Regarding "Śrāddhada": for one who performs a śrāddha at the Māheśvarī-kuṇḍa—and because of the word "and" (ca), also at the Rukmiṇī-kuṇḍa—the same result follows. Regarding "Gaurī": there at the Māheśvarī-kuṇḍa is Maṅgalā; the meaning is that from her worship, the attainment of all auspicious fortune occurs.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Gayā-prakāśa, in the Tīrthacintāmaṇi composed by the Great Mahopādhyāya Vācaspati Miśra.
[339] Now, the majesty of Vārāṇasī:
[It is the refuge for] those wandering in saṃsāra who are being burned by the fires of hell.
Beholding the moon struck down upon his crest,
Hara fashioned that city in the sky which removes all suffering; I remember it incessantly.
In the Matsya Purāṇa:
"O daughter of the King of Mountains, Vārāṇasī is the essence of the three worlds; it is my delightful city."
Even those mortals who have arrived there having committed various misdeeds appear stainless, their sins having been exhausted.
This most secret field is always Vārāṇasī for me;
it is at all times the cause of liberation for all living beings indeed.
