In the *Skanda Purāṇa*: "Those who kill a Brahmin, those who kill a cow, those who violate the bed of their guru, those who have broken their conduct, those who misappropriate deposits, those who are deceitful, and others of forbidden livelihoods [are excluded]."
May the world, its body liberated from the firm fetters of the elements of saṃsāra, come to my city, Vārāṇasī.
Having reached this field of mine, frequented by gods and siddhas, a mortal through the power of his meritorious deeds shall become renowned among all the gods and asuras.
And having died, he shall go to the supreme state.
Those virtuous men who always fall upon this field—

beholding it daily with reverence, being pure, righteous, and ever free from envy— those mortals are liberated from the bonds of the suffering of existence, their ritual actions being perfectly purified.
Having pierced through the dense web of bonds of worldly existence, they attain the state of liberation.
Now, regarding the measurement of the field:
here in the Matsya Purāṇa it is said,
"It extends for two and a half yojanas from east to west."
It extends for half a yojana from south to north.
There is the river Vārāṇasī and likewise the Śuklanadī,
beginning from Bhīṣmacaṇḍika as far as Parvateśvara nearby.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, the words of Brahmā are as follows:
"The Varaṇā and the Asi are two rivers beloved by the gods;
the sacred field (kṣetra) situated between them is especially distinguished even upon the earth."
"A field measuring five *krośas* has been given by me to you. (From the *Skanda Purāṇa*):
"This sacred field is proclaimed to extend four *krośas* in each of the four directions."
Know, O lady of beautiful limbs, that at the time of death, this *yojana* bestows immortality.

[341] Here, a difference in measurement should be understood according to the difference in the *kalpa*. However, it is an absolute rule that the region of Vārāṇasī lies between the Asī and the Varaṇā; therefore, it should be considered that Asitā is to the east and Varaṇā is to the west of Vārāṇasī. In that very place: "My Caṇḍeśvara is to be known as being in the northern course (*ayana*)."
Śaṅkukarṇa is my southern [oṃkāra], while Oṃkāra is my northern; ten crores of sacred fords (tīrthas) enter into this place on the day of the lunar festival.
In the Liṅgapurāṇa, there is a statement by Śiva:
"The channel named Piṅgalā is proclaimed to be fiery;
it should be known as the dry river where Lolārka resides."
The channel named Iḍā is proclaimed to be lunar;
it is to be known as equal to Varaṇā and Asī, where Keśava is established.
Between these two, the channel that is proclaimed as Suṣumnā is to be known as Matsyodarī; that is proclaimed as the Viṣuva.
In Vārāṇasī, at the eastern gate, there are two liṅgas named Mitra and Varuṇa;
these two, named Mitra and Varuṇa, are situated at the gateway—
thus it is stated in the Liṅga Purāṇa.

And thus, the area between Lolārka and Keśava, situated on the banks of the Varaṇā and the Śuṣkanadī, is marked by the river known as Matsyodarī; the space between the Asi and the Varaṇā is the sacred field (kṣetra) of Vārāṇasī—this is the meaning of the circular [enclosure]. [342] As stated in the Mātsya Purāṇa:
"Because it has not been abandoned by me, it shall never be forsaken."
Therefore, this great field is remembered as Avimukta.
This very place is remembered as greater even than Prayāga, the foremost of sacred sites;
for here, liberation is attained with little effort.
Likewise, in that very same place:
"There are Cāṇḍālas of various complexions and discolored, who are loathsome,
their bodies filled with impurities as well as the most heinous sins."
The wise know that for them, the unliberated state is the supreme medicine.
Whether they be wicked, wretched and miserable, sinful, or doers of evil deeds,
the Lord leads them all out of compassion to His own supreme goal.
O Brahmā, this is the word of Brahmā:
"When the Gaṅgā flows from the midst of the field toward the lord of rivers,
by that she shall become greatly meritorious in the past, O Rudra."
The Gaṅgā is meritorious when flowing northward, as is the Sarasvatī when flowing eastward;
the river Jāhnavī flows for two yojanas while facing north.
All these gods, together with me and Indra, will assemble at the highest [place]; release the skull there.

Having gone to that most excellent sacred ford (tīrtha), they shall indeed gratify their ancestors with offerings of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) during śrāddha rites; for them, there will be the highest worlds in heaven.
[343] Although it might appear at first glance from the statement "from the middle of the field" that the flow of the Gaṅgā is within Vārāṇasī itself, nevertheless:
"Both Varaṇā and Asi are rivers fashioned by the gods;
the field is specifically between them on the earth."

Thus, by reflecting upon the previously cited statements, it is established that if a place is not entered by the *asi-vāraṇā* (the warding off of the sword), it lacks the status of being the sacred field (*kṣetra*) of Vārāṇasī; consequently, the term "within the field" (*kṣetramadhya*) refers merely to contact with the field, just like the expression "gone into the middle of a village. Now, regarding the fruit of entering Vārāṇasī, [it is stated] there in the *Laiṅga Purāṇa*:
If even a slayer of a Brahmin should ever go to Avimukta,
his sin of Brahmin-slaughter is removed by the majesty of that sacred field.
Those men who have indeed gone to Avimukta, even if they were doers of great sins,
become truly imperishable, ageless, and bodiless.
Whether through ignorance or even knowingly, by a woman or by a man.
Whatever unwholesome karma has been committed by means of human intellect,
all of it shall be reduced to ashes upon entering Avimukta.
[344] Now, regarding the fruit of that residence:
on this point, the *Laiṅga-purāṇa* states:
A man who remains established in Avimukta always performs sacrifice with a ritual, always bestows gifts, and is indeed always an ascetic.
That destination which is ordained for men dwelling in Avimukta is not found at Kurukṣetra, nor at Gaṅgādvāra, nor at Puṣkara.
For all living beings, austerity and truth are the supreme essence; of this there is no doubt.
But that man who should dwell in Avimukta would become equal to me.
Those deluded men who are dominated by darkness do not resort to Avimukta;
they dwell amidst feces, urine, and menstrual blood—of this there is no doubt.
Those of evil deeds who are touched by the dust raised by the wind while they stand eternally in Avimukta shall go to the supreme goal.
The brahmin who should dwell there, self-restrained and concentrated,
should eat only at the three times of day and always subsist on air alone.
Regarding this one-month residence:
there the hero, subsisting on barley and having conquered his senses, should dwell for a month;
by him the great, divine Pāśupata vow has been perfectly performed.
Having crossed over the fear of birth and death, he attains the supreme goal;
he shall obtain the auspicious, meritorious state as well as the state of Yoga.
[345] Separation cannot be attained even in hundreds of future births;
yet, through the greatness of the sacred field and by the power of Śaṅkara, it is obtained. O fair-faced one, he who remains there for a month eating but a single meal a day—
The sin committed throughout one's entire life is destroyed in a single month.
Now, regarding the non-abandonment of residence in Vārāṇasī for as long as one lives— at least with respect to the [sacred] emblem:
"He who does not abandon the sacred field until the fall of his body."
Through the vows of celibacy and through sacrifices properly performed, it shall be rightly attained.
For one who does not leave the sacred field until the fall of the body,
not only the sin of killing a Brahmin but even ordinary worldly existence ceases.
The bondage of saṃsāra is natural. As it is said in the Mātsya Purāṇa: "He who, even when stirred up by obstacles, does not abandon Avimukta."
He abandons old age, death, and this impermanent birth.
O Brāhmaṇa,
those men who frequent this sacred field until the fall of their bodies go,
upon death, by means of a swan-vehicle to the divine realm, free from all fear.
The divine state is the station of the gods.
[346] Now, in this regard, the fruit is death.
In that very place: "Even a man whose mind is attached to sense objects, if his intellect has abandoned [all else] for devotion and dies in this field, he shall not enter saṃsāra again."
This supreme sacred site on earth is the cause of both heaven and liberation;
whoever meets their death there attains liberation, without a doubt.
That which a yogi might attain by practicing for thousands of other births,
he attains here in this very life as supreme liberation after death.
"In this life" is the meaning.
Whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those of mixed castes, as well as worms, Mlecchas, and others who are of mixed or sinful birth—
Insects, ants, and whatever other beasts and birds there may be—
listen, O beloved, they all meet their death in time within Avimukta.
O Goddess, all those men who are born there in my city of Śiva have the crescent moon as their crest-jewel, an eye on their forehead, and the bull as their emblem.
Those living beings and trees there who give up their lives attain the state of Rudra and rejoice together with me.
Whether free from desire or possessed of desire, even if one has been reborn among the animals,
by casting off one's life-breaths at Avimukta, one is glorified in my world.
Those men who are eternally devoted to me and have no devotion to others,
having cast off their lives in that place, go to the supreme goal.
[347] With his mind fixed on me, devoted to me, and having dedicated all his actions to me—
he attains liberation here in this world in a way that he cannot attain anywhere else.
Those people who, through discernment, perform the act of entering the fire at Avimukta,
enter me with ease and are no longer subject to rebirth.
But those devotees of mine who, having made a firm resolve, practice fasting unto death—
for them there is no return, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
For at the time of death, in Avimukta, the Lord himself bestows the whispered instruction into the ear upon his devotees who are impelled by their past actions.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa: "At the time of death, when the vital points of men are being severed and they are driven by the wind, memory does not arise at all."
The Rudras who abide in Avimukta, bestowing joy upon their devotees—
such as Ḍimi, Caṇḍeśvara, and others— grant the whispered instruction into the ear.
In the Rāmatāpinī, Śrī Rāma’s words to Śiva are as follows:
"O Śiva, to anyone at all—be they on the verge of death or otherwise—you yourself shall impart my mantra; he shall become liberated."

In this regard, although supreme liberation (*paramamukti*), union (*sāyujya*), residence in the same world (*sālokya*), and similarity of form (*sārūpya*) are heard of as the fruits of death, it should nevertheless be understood that supreme liberation belongs to the pure ones who are devotees of the Supreme Self and have dedicated their actions to Him; union belongs to those inferior to them who enter the fire and so forth; similarity of form belongs to animals and others who are exceedingly sinful; and residence in the same world belongs to those even lower than them. This is precisely because of the natural sense of the various scriptural statements cited previously.
Some, however, say that within the fourfold measurement of Kāśī, to the extent that there is a distance from the Yogapīṭha, to that same extent there is a reduction in the fruit of death;
yet for all [who die there], there is an absence of going to hell. Thus it is said in the Laiṅga Purāṇa: "No sinner who dies in Avimukta goes to hell."
For all those who are favored by the Lord attain the supreme goal.
The qualities of your state of non-release have been described merely by way of summary;
the full detail of this non-release is like that of jewels belonging to Susudra.
Likewise: "The destination ordained for those men who are established in knowledge and discernment and who desire supreme bliss— that same destination belongs to one who dies in Svarṇāla."
Beginning with the golden stalk: "Having abandoned his vital breaths here, a man is not born again anywhere;
infinite is his destination, that which is remembered as belonging only to yogins."
Near Hiraṇyagarbha and Vyāghreśvara is Svarṇāleśvara;

likewise, at the site of Viśvanātha, outside the three names of the great cremation ground (mahāśmaśāna) known as Avimukta and Yogapīṭha, I shall explain that for one who dies there, supreme liberation (paramamukti) is attained. Furthermore, according to the Tāpanī [Upaniṣad], for one who dies in Maṇikarṇikā, supreme liberation is attained.
Now, regarding the fruit of bathing and other rites here,
the *Mātsya Purāṇa* states: "Whatever fruit is remembered for ten horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*), [that fruit is obtained here]."
Having bathed there, O fair-faced one, that righteous-souled person attains that [fruit].
Whoever gives even a very small gift here to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas attains an auspicious state and shines like fire itself.
That man who, having observed a fast, gratifies the Brahmins,
certainly obtains the fruit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice.

The plural number in the word *viprān* (to the Brahmins) refers to three, according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya* (the maxim of the partridges). In the *Brāhma-purāṇa*, with reference to Vārāṇasī, it is said:
"There, by the offering of a lamp, one's senses shine forth like knowledge."
By the offering of incense, one attains the abode frequented by Rudra.
He who marks with a sign and then releases a young, gentle bull accompanied by four heifers, attains the supreme goal.
Accompanied by her ancestors, she goes to liberation; of this there is no doubt.
[She is marked] with the goad and the discus on the right and left sides respectively.
Because it is seen otherwise in other cases.

For this very reason, there is also a different set of procedural details (*itikartavyatā*). Nor is there a sublation of these by the specific instruction "having branded [the bull]," because—according to the principle that "a single ritual action is recognized across all Vedic branches" (*sarvaśākhāpratyayam ekaṃ karma*)—the procedural details of other [Vedic schools] regarding the *vṛṣotsarga* (release of a bull) are also connected here. Nor is there a sublation of another [procedure] in this case of the *gavotsarga* (release of a cow), which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of that [original rite], due to a specific instruction; for there is no relationship of archetype and modification (*prakṛti-vikṛtibhāva*) between the two, such that its properties would either be extended (*atideśa*) or prohibited here. Rather, this rite is enjoined as entirely independent, like the *godāna* and other such acts. As for the statement "he goes to the supreme goal," that is merely an explanatory praise (*stutyarthavāda*), similar to the injunction "one chooses one [priest]."
Likewise: What need is there for much speaking here? Whatever gift is given by men with the aim of performing a righteous deed, one shall obtain its infinite fruit.
Furthermore, O Goddess of beautiful countenance, I shall declare the merit that a human being attains by worshipping me here in Avimukta.
O beloved, hear [the fruit]: he who offers a flower made of ten pieces of gold at Avimukta gains the merit of the Agnihotra; likewise for the offering of incense and the gift of fragrance.
The fruit of giving land is remembered as equal to that of the gift of a cow;
for sweeping [the ground] the merit is five hundredfold, and for anointing it, a thousandfold.
The meaning is as follows: for offering garlands, the merit is one hundred thousandfold; for song and instrumental music, it is infinite.

For a single flower, the fruit is equal to that produced by the gift of ten gold pieces; likewise, for incense, it is equal to that produced by the *agnihotra* sacrifice; for fragrance, it is equal to the gift of land; for sweeping [the temple], it is equal to the gift of five hundred cows; for ointment, it is equal to the gift of a thousand cows; for a wreath, it is equal to the gift of a hundred thousand cows; and for song and instrumental music, the fruit is equal to the gift of infinite cows.

Regarding the word "thousand" (*sahasra*) here, since the *Kalpataru* explains it as referring specifically to a thousand cows— given that the result is subsequently stated to be "attaining liberation together with the ancestors"—
this applies there in the case of the worship of the *liṅga*.
Those who worship and praise Mahādeva in Avimukta are liberated from all sins; they abide free from old age and death.
If a person, having reached Avimukta, worships the Liṅga,
there is no rebirth for him even after hundreds of millions of kalpas.
For he indeed plays in the presence of Bhava, immortal and undecaying;
but those who, having attained meditative absorption, are self-disciplined and composed in mind—
Those best of the twice-born who, having restrained the collection of their senses, constantly reside in Avimukta and recite the Śatarudriya, have achieved their life's purpose.
Likewise:
"O illustrious lady, he who observes a fast for a single day,
being devoted to me, obtains here the fruit of a hundred years."
The meaning is "of one who has fasted for a hundred years. Regarding the *liṅga*:
beyond this, however, is the Gaṅgāvaraṇa-saṃgama, which is to be experienced.
When Wednesday occurs in conjunction with the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī lunar day, [it is known as] Śravaṇa-budha-dvādaśī.
Then, having bathed there at that place, a man shall obtain the fruit of the Saṃnihatyā;
O illustrious lady, he who performs a Śrāddha ceremony there at that time,
having delivered all his ancestors, goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
The river situated at Kurukṣetra is [known] as Saṃnihatyā;
according to the Mātsya Purāṇa, it is at the world-renowned confluence of the Vārāṇasī and the Jāhnavī.
Having given food according to the prescribed rule, he is not born again.
[352] Avimuktā, Varaṇā, and Vārāṇasī. In the Skanda-purāṇa: "This river Vārāṇasī which has joined with the Jāhnavī..."
And that man who, having bathed at the confluence of the divine river, becomes pure;
One should worship Saṅgameśāna; whence could there be fear of rebirth for him?
Saṅgama is to the east of Anantakeśava, and Keśava himself stands to the east of Vedeśvara.
And to the east of Keśava is the famous Saṅgameśvara.
Thus, from the *Liṅgapurāṇa*, in the description of the northeast corner of Vārāṇasī; and from the *Mātsya*:
"O beautiful one, in the northwest quarter of that sacred seat (*pīṭha*)."
There, Sagara installed a four-faced linga.
Pīṭha is the Yoga-pīṭha.
To the northwest of the ocean, the lake Bhadradoha is remembered;
it was produced from the milk of cows and destroys all sins.
Whatever fruit is obtained from the proper gift of a thousand tawny cows, that same fruit a mortal attains by bathing there; of this there is no doubt.
When the full moon coincides with the asterism Pūrvabhādrapadā,
that is the most meritorious time, bestowing the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
To the northwest of the temple of Viśvanātha and to the east of the Varaṇā river is Bhīṣmacaṇḍikā. Regarding that, it is stated in the Matsya Purāṇa, in the section on pilgrimage sites (tīrthayātrā):
"Where that goddess renowned as Bhīṣmacaṇḍikā is seen, she dwells forever in a terrifying, hideous, and fearsome cremation ground."

[353] To the east of Antakeśvara, to the south of Sarveśvara, and to the north of Mālatīśvara is the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga. Regarding that, the Laiṅga Purāṇa states: "Those people who reside there in Vārāṇasī are liberated."
Even worms and insects, as well as those who have committed great sins, are liberated.
Likewise: "Those seekers of auspiciousness who go to the Kṛttivāseśvara Liṅga enter the body of Rudra and are no longer subject to rebirth."
With this very body, one attains supreme nirvāṇa,
where the renown of ten thousand times ten million sacred fords is found.
Where Kṛttivāseśvara is, there all are established;
in that Liṅga indeed resides the presence of the three worlds—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise: "Liberation may or may not be attained after a thousand other births;
but there at Krittivasa, it is attained in a single birth."
Even sin committed in a previous birth is purified by austerity;
however, that sin perishes at that very moment from the sight of that linga.
Likewise:
"In the Kṛta age, he is called Tryambaka; in the Tretā, Kṛttivāsas;
and in the Dvāpara, the name Maheśvara is sung for the God."
In the Kali age, the Lord known as Hastipāleśvara is celebrated by the perfected ones (siddhas).
Likewise: "The deity Kṛttivāseśvara should be beheld again and again."
If one should desire the saving knowledge and the eternal, immortal state.
Likewise: "By the sight of the God of gods, even a slayer of a Brahmin is liberated;
by both seeing and worshipping him, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices."
Those who, with supreme faith and composed minds, worship the eternal God on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Phālguna;
With flowers, fruits, as well as incense, lamps, and food offerings,
and with milk, honey, water, and clarified butter;
They gratify the supreme Liṅga and worship the auspicious Śiva with the sounds of "ḍuḍukka" and prostrations,
as well as with dances and songs.
Having fasted for one night with supreme devotion to Hara, [one should worship] with various musical instruments and likewise with hymns and mantras.
Those who go to the supreme abode, which is eternally auspicious and free from ailment.
On the full-moon day of the month of Caitra, one should worship the Supreme Lord;
having attained the status of Viśveśvara, he sports like the king of the Yakṣas.
He who, being self-restrained, worships Śiva on the fourteenth day of the month of Vaiśākha,
shall reach the world of Viśākha and become an attendant of that very deity.
He who worships Hara with faith on the fourteenth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha attains the heavenly world for as long as the moon and stars endure.
O fair-faced one, he who worships the Lord of the Gods on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight sports in the world of the Sun for as long as he desires.
On the fourteenth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one who is endowed with the Kāmaliṅga goes to the world of Varuṇa and sports together with the Apsarases.
Having worshipped Śaṅkara at night during the month of Bhādrapada with various flowers and fruits, one becomes a partaker of the world of Indra.
Having likewise worshipped Īśvara on the fourteenth day of the fortnight of the ancestors,
he attains the world of the ancestors and sports there, honored by them.
Having worshipped Maheśvara, the Lord of Gods, in the month of Prabodha,
he reaches the world of the Moon and sports there for as long as he desires.
Having worshipped Piṇākin during the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one attains the world of Viṣṇu and sports there for an inexhaustible time.
Having thus worshipped Sthāṇu with a joyful heart under the Puṣya asterism,
one indeed attains his abode and rejoices there forever.
Having worshipped [the deity] in the month of Māgha with auspicious flowers, roots, and fruits,
one indeed attains the world of Śiva after having crossed the ocean of worldly existence.
One should worship that god Kṛttivāseśvara with great effort;
and one should dwell in Avimukta if one desires the state of [liberation] within a month.

These rites are performed on the fourteenth days in the sequence beginning with Kṛṣṇa, as they are described starting from Śivarātri at the beginning of Phālguna. Likewise, to the west of Vyāseśvara is the Ghaṇṭākarṇa lake. Having bathed there in that lake and having beheld the Liṅga of Vyāseśa, O Goddess, wherever one may die, one shall be as if dead in Vārāṇasī.
Likewise:
"O Goddess, having bathed in Daṇḍakhāta and having offered libations to one's own ancestors—
those who reside in hell and those who dwell in the world of the Pitṛs— "
For those men who have indeed become piśācas due to their sinful deeds,
the liberation of their bodies may be achieved through the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
By the sight of that pit, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done.
In that very place, beginning with the description of Lalitā:
"And those who, remaining personally in that sacred spot, shall worship you,
to them you will bestow various enjoyments, O Mānavī."
O auspicious lady, you shall lead those who keep vigil before you while holding lamps to imperishable worlds.
For those who prepare the dwelling place and sweep the ground,
there shall be the fruit of eight thousand pieces of gold.
O Goddess, O Queen of the Gods, listen to the fruit of merit for him who, with you in mind, shall feed a Brāhmaṇa and likewise a Brāhmaṇī.
In this very world of Bhārata, one shall dwell for an eon; furthermore,
whether it be a man or a woman, endowed with all enjoyments and possessed of wealth and grain, they are born into a family of great beings.
O Goddess, may they both be fortunate and handsome, proud of their beauty and youth, and possessors of every kind of good fortune.
Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and as fleeting as a flash of lightning—
he who has beheld you, O lady of beautiful hips, from where could he have any fear of rebirth?
Whatever fruit a man obtains by circumambulating the entire earth, that same fruit is obtained at Lalitā in Vārāṇasī; of this there is no doubt.
O Goddess, he who, having fasted at that time on the fourteenth day of the month of Māgha, worships and performs a vigil there—
his family, O Goddess, attains a prosperity that is difficult to find even in the three worlds.
Likewise,
O Goddess, to the south of that very place is the one named Nalakūbareśvara, who bestows all spiritual perfections; it is renowned as Maṇikarṇī.
And at its front, in that great sacred ford which destroys all sins,
stands the god Maṇikarṇīśvara in the midst of the pool.
Indeed, his vision is accomplished with this very body. Likewise:
"On its right side, there was formerly established by Gaṅgā..."
He who bears the name Gaṅgeśvara is the bestower of the world of the gods.
[358] Likewise: O Goddess of the Gods, I shall describe another sacred site in Vārāṇasī,
which is the desired and beautiful abode of the God of Gods.
O Goddess, in former times, that linga of the moon-crested Lord was being carried away through the atmosphere by Rākṣasas who were traveling swiftly.
When they arrived in this place, the Lord thought:
"How will my liberation come about through Avimukta?"
While the Lord, the master of the gods, was reflecting upon this matter,
the sound of a cock suddenly arose in that place.

O Goddess, upon hearing that sound, the Rākṣasas, their hearts filled with terror, abandoned the liṅga; terrified, they departed at the time of dawn. Once the Rākṣasas had gone, O Goddess, Śiva remained right there at that very liṅga.
In that beautiful and radiant place, the Lord himself, the God of gods, resides;
in the center of that Avimukta, it is remembered as the most unforsaken (Avimuktatara).
Then, indeed, because it was liberated by the gods, the name of Hara was remembered as "Avimukta," the most meritorious;
it is the bestower of liberation upon all things, both moving and stationary.
Those living beings who pass away into death.
O Goddess of gods, cocks also always remain in that place;
even today they are killed there while being worshipped by those seeking auspicious results.
O Goddess, for that man who would always go to Avimukta with devotion,
there is no returning again, even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
By means of the skillful and dexterous [method], beginning from the south— that is to say, in the form of entering the place of Avimukta—
there stands a beautiful pond on the right side of the Lord.
Having drunk the water of its sacred bathing-place (tīrtha), there is no returning again.
O Goddess of the Suras, by merely drinking that very water,
three lingas manifest within the heart of the person.
But those men who have drunk the water there are indeed successful;
for them, the liberating knowledge will arise, without a doubt.
Having bathed in the water of the Vāpī and beheld Daṇḍanāyaka,
and then having seen Avimukta, one attains liberation (kaivalya) in an instant.
Having performed the twilight devotions there even once,
a Brahmin becomes one who has fulfilled his twilight duties for five hundred or six hundred years.
Having beheld that city of Vārāṇasī, the cremation ground of Avimuktaka,
and indeed Avimukteśvara, one becomes a Gaṇapati.
Likewise: "Having properly beheld the Avimukteśvara Liṅga, a human being is immediately liberated from sin and released from the bonds of Paśu."
The cremation ground (*śmaśāna*) is another name for the field of Avimukta. In the *Laiṅga-purāṇa*: "In front of Avimukta, however, the Liṅga is remembered as facing west."
The one named Prītikeśvara bestows eternal joy.
To the north of Avimukta, there is a linga known as Paścānmukha;
therefore, O Goddess, it is indeed called Avimukta by name, while [the other] is Lakṣaṇeśvara.
O Goddess of the gods, by beholding that, a man becomes possessed of knowledge.
And to the north of that, O Goddess, is the Linga which indeed has four faces.
[360] In the *Skānda*, it is said: "The holy field of Vārāṇasī shall be the giver of liberation; it is named Caturtheśvara and is the deliverer from the fear of sins."
Indeed, whatever person shall behold me here as Avimukteśvara, [shall attain liberation].
Whether he remains wherever he may be, his goal is the state of the Lord of Ganas;
for by renouncing his vital breaths here, he attains supreme liberation.
To summarize this:

in the sacred field known by the dual designation of Avimukta and Śmaśāna, there is the Liṅga established by Śiva called Avimukteśvara, which is renowned in the world by the name Viśvanātha. That very place is the site of Kukkuṭamaṇḍapa; and entering there through the southern gate results in the fruit of non-return to rebirth. To the south of that is a pond, famous as the Vijñānavāpī because it generates higher knowledge (*vijñāna*); by drinking its water, the three Liṅgas arise within the heart, the knowledge of the *Tāraka*, and non-return to rebirth come to pass.

Having seen Vārāṇasī, the sacred field of Viśvanātha known as Avimukta, and Viśvanātha himself, one becomes a Gaṇapati. In the first enclosure (*prathamāvaraṇa*) of this field, there is a *liṅga* named Prītikeśvara facing west in the east; in the north, a *liṅga* named Lakṣaṇeśvara facing west; in the northwest, Magadheśvara; and in the south, Vijñānavāpī, with the Kāmeśvara *liṅga* to its south. For one who dies within this innermost field of Avimukta, supreme liberation occurs.

Likewise, in the second enclosure, Maṇikarṇikeśvara is in the east, Caturtheśvara is in the north, and Gaṅgeśvara is in the south. Furthermore, there are indeed seven Kīṭya-liṅgas situated in this place.
By the mere sight of them, one shall obtain the fruit of sacrifices.
These are the established marks of success; likewise, the wells, lakes, ponds, rivers, and pools have been proclaimed by you as such.
And whoever, with a concentrated mind, shall perform an ablution in these very places and touch the lingas, shall not enter into saṃsāra again.
Whatever sacred fords exist on earth and whatever exist in the intermediate space—
among those, I have proclaimed to you the auspicious ones that are the most excellent.
O lady of beautiful hips, this pilgrimage to sacred sites has been described as the destroyer of sins;
whoever performs it or even witnesses it shall indeed become a partaker of liberation.
And, O lady of beautiful hips, the auspicious Avimuktaka is situated in my middle;
therein is that which is named Kaṇṭaka, which bestows immortality at the time of death.
Henceforth, O All-pervading One, I shall proclaim the times for pilgrimage;
this auspicious pilgrimage was ordained by the gods in the month of Caitra.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, this pilgrimage was performed in ancient times by the Siddhas, who were intent upon bathing and worship at that very Kāmakuṇḍa.
At the pool of Rudrāvāsa, where this [rite] was formerly performed by the Gandharvas, those intent upon bathing and worship may do so even in the month of Āṣāḍha.
This procession was undertaken by the Vidyādharas, who were intent on the bathing and worship of the goddess Śrī while stationed at her sacred pool,
and who were devoted to these rites during the month of Śrāvaṇa.
This [river] was reached by the ancestors who were intent on bathing and worship at Lakṣmīkuṇḍa,
and who were likewise devoted to it during the month of Āśvina.
This auspicious festival was established by the Yakṣas residing at Lake Mārkaṇḍeya, who are devoted to ritual bathing and worship, to be held every month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
O fair-faced one, this procession takes place in the month of Pauṣa, attended by Guhyakas who remain at Kapālamocana, intent upon bathing and worship.
This pilgrimage takes place in the month of Māgha, undertaken by those intent on bathing and worship at the pool of Kāleśvara, as well as by the serpents who are likewise devoted to it.
When the fourteenth day of the month of Phālguna arrived, the Piśācas, stationed at Koṭitīrtha and intent upon bathing and worship, [gathered there].
Therefore, that goddess is proclaimed by the well-known name Piśācī.
Hereafter, I shall describe the supreme expiation for the pilgrimage.
Water-pots filled with sweet food should be given;
by that, O Goddess, he then obtained the very fruit previously described.
Henceforth, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the processions which yield great fruit; that which takes place on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight is the beloved of Bhava.
There, O fair-faced one, Gaurī is to be seen; listen to [the account] of her, O illustrious lady. Having performed your ablutions, you should go to Goprekṣā.
On that day, that goddess should be worshipped with great effort;
from that place, one should proceed to the north of Avimukta.
There, the goddess Gaurī should always be worshipped with diligence; another supreme goddess is also proclaimed, the auspicious Saṃvartānamitā.
That goddess, who bestows the fruits of all desires, must indeed be beheld;
if a human being meditates upon her, he attains all his desires.
Then, however, he fed the Brahmins who were my devotees and observed auspicious vows,
with abundant dwellings and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) according to their merit.
O Goddess, he who, being composed and full of devotion, having fashioned an image of Pañcagaurī,
offers all juices and fragrances to Brahmā while dedicating them to Gaurī;
Endowed with good fortune, he attains the highest welfare.
The "All-Flavor" (*sarvarasa*) is that which is taught in the *Gandharva-śāstra*; the ellipsis is that one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, in that very same [text]:
"I shall describe the Vināyakas who cause obstacles for this field."
Having first seen Ḍhoṇḍī as well as Vināyaka.
[He saw] Divya Vināyaka, Goprekṣa, Hastidantin,
and another Vināyaka well-known by the name Sindūrya.
O Goddess, they should be viewed on the fourth day; thus are the five Vināyakas.
And sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) should be offered, dedicating them to these Brāhmaṇas.
By this very dharma, a man becomes successful;
hereafter I shall proclaim the Caṇḍikās who protect the sacred field.
Durgā protects in the south, and Uttareśvarī in the southwest.
Aṅgāreśī is in the west, while Bhadrakālikā is in the northwest;
Bhīmacaṇḍā is in the north, and likewise Mahāmatteśā is in the northeast.
Śaṅkarī, endowed with upward-pointing hair, is remembered in the east;
likewise, Adhaḥkeśī is in the southeast, while Citraghaṇṭā is in the center.
Whatever man shall behold these goddesses Caṇḍikās,
they will all be pleased with him and, being devoted to it, protect that sacred field.
O Goddess, they constantly create obstacles for the wicked at all times;
therefore, O Goddess, Caṇḍikā and Vināyaka should always be worshipped.
[364] Furthermore, O Goddess of the Gods, I shall tell you another thing regarding that field:
three rivers situated there flow with auspicious waters.
By the mere sight of them, the murder of a Brahmin is averted;
among them, one is the triple-streamed Mandākinī, and likewise another.
The third is Matsyodarī; these three are indeed bestowers of merit. Likewise, the holy Mandākinī is situated at Madhyameśvara.
Pitāmahasrotikā bestows merit in Avimukta,
while Matsyodarī always indeed bestows merit at Oṃkāra.
O lady, when the Gaṅgā arrives at that place,
it will then be a most meritorious time, difficult even for the gods to attain.
Having bathed there at the holy Nādeśvara, where the waters of the Varaṇā flow and are mingled with the waters of the Jāhnavī, why should one grieve?
And at that time, O Goddess, I performed my ablutions right there;
by that means, O Goddess, the skull fell from the palm of my hand in an instant.
Right there is a very great lake named Kamālamocana,
which purifies all beings and bestows merit upon those who possess bodies of merit.
The Gaṅgā is within the waters of Matsyodarī in the vicinity of Oṃkāreśvara;
having bathed in those waters at that time and beheld the Lord Oṃkāra.
A man is not touched by sorrow, old age, or the jaws of death;
for within him resides Śiva himself, known by the name Oṃkāreśvara.
This secret has been handed down out of affection for you, O fair-faced one;
it is proclaimed as the syllable A, the syllable U, and the syllable M.
In that regard, the letter *a* should be known as bestowing the attainment of the world of Viṣṇu;
on its right side, however, the letter *u* is proclaimed.
There, Bṛhaspati, the teacher of the gods, attained supreme perfection;
therein the syllable *U* is to be known as the imperishable state of Brahman.
Likewise, on the northern part of those two is the letter *ma*, known as the *bindu*;
it was upon that *liṅga* that the great sage, the seer Kapila, attained perfection.
Therefore, O son of Gaṅgā, if you also desire steadfastness of mind,
exert yourself in the worship of the Liṅga with disciplined vows.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, one attains the eternal state.
Likewise: having approached Vārāṇasī, the supreme place of the five sense-bases.
Always remaining in that place, he propitiated the Lord of Gods.
Gāṅgeya refers to Skanda by way of context. In the *Skandapurāṇa*:
"Then, O Goddess, I myself indeed took my stand in this very place."
He was renowned as Goprekṣaka, praised by all the gods.
Having come to Goprekṣeśvara, having seen it, and having worshipped it,
a person does not meet with misfortune and is liberated from sins.
Then, while being scorched by those fragrant blossoms, they approached this lake and fell into it; once cooled, they then drank the water.
From that time forth, it has been called Kapilāhrada;
and here too, I myself am known as Vṛṣadhvaja.
O Goddess, may your presence always remain visible within my abode;
having bathed in this Kapilāhrada tīrtha with a restrained mind, [one attains this].
Having seen this bull-bannered [Lord], one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
and having worshipped me here, even after death, one attains the heavenly world.
Upon the dissolution of the body, he attains the state of being a Gaṇa, which is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
for in this region of the gods, cows were indeed created by Brahmā himself.
For the sake of the peace of all worlds,
that lake, which yields auspiciousness at will, is meritorious, removes evil, and is auspicious, even for those in every state of distress.
Becoming the head, I shall be fearless; heaven shall come to pass from the sight of me.
"Having brought me here, I was established by Parameṣṭhin; and having taken me from Brahmā as well, I was established again by Viṣṇu."
Furthermore, Brahmā then installed my linga named Svarṇāleśvara in the world known as Svarlokeśvara.
Having seen even this Lord of Gods, one is glorified in my world;
having cast off his life-breaths here, a man is not born again anywhere.
Infinite is his destination; he is remembered as one among yogins alone.
In this very great region, there was a Daitya who was a thorn in the side of the gods.
Having assumed the form of a tiger, I slew that proud and powerful one;
thus I became renowned as Vyāghreśvara and have resided here eternally.
Furthermore, having seen this Lord of the Immortals—
the Linga established on the Himavat mountain known as Śaileśvara—
O Goddess, sages do not fall into an evil rebirth after seeing it.
The two Daityas Utpala and Vidala, who became arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, were both slain by you upon seeing that very Liṅga. O auspicious one!
Here, this mark was placed by Kaṇṭhaka as a sign of his contempt.
Upon merely seeing my Liṅga situated at the Jyeṣṭha-sthāna,
a mortal no longer grieves, becoming perfected in birth after birth.
And all around here, lingas have been installed by the gods for my sake;
having seen them, a mortal will certainly become a member of the Gaṇa upon the dissolution of the body.
The holy river Vārāṇasī, which destroys sins,
has adorned this sacred field by uniting with the Jāhnavī.
O Goddess, behold that supreme Liṅga established by Brahmā at that confluence, renowned as Saṃgameśvara.
For that man on earth who, having bathed at the confluence of the celestial river,
worships Saṅgameśāna— whence can there be any fear of rebirth for him?
And this Liṅga was installed by your son Śukra;
the Liṅga is named Śukreśvara, worshipped by all the Siddhas and immortals.
Upon merely seeing it, a person is instantly liberated from all sins;
and having died, that man shall not undergo rebirth in saṃsāra.
The Daitya Jambūka was slain here by me; therefore, it is called Jambūkeśvara. Having seen this very [liṅga] there, one shall obtain all desires.
These meritorious liṅgas, which grant all desires, were established here by the gods, with Śakra at their head.
Thus, O Pārvatī, these meritorious places of my residence within your sacred field have been described to you; now hear this most secret word.
By beholding me, who reside in Mahālaya and am established in Kedāra,
one attains the status of a Gaṇa in this field beloved by Hara.
Therefore, the state of being a leader of the Gaṇas (Gāṇapatya) results from that; hence, that liberation is supreme.
Having beheld my Liṅga, Avimukteśvara, a human being [attains it].
Instantly liberated from sin, one is released from the bonds of *paśu*;
[one should worship] Śaileśa, Saṅgameśa, and Svarṇāla in the city of Madhyama.
Hiraṇyagarbha, Īśāna, Goprekṣa, Vṛṣadhvaja,
and Upaśāntaśiva, who dwells in the Jyeṣṭha station.
Having beheld the renowned Śukreśvara, Vyāghreśa, and Jambūkeśvara,
a mortal is not born again into this ocean of suffering that is saṃsāra.
Thus ends the *Māhātmya* of Vārāṇasī in the *Kalpataru*. Now follows the *Māhātmya* in the *Kāśīkhaṇḍa*:
even that which is merely the sight of Avimukteśa shall attain imperishability.
Having gone to Avimukta, no sinner whatsoever goes to hell.
Whatever sin is committed at Avimukta becomes as firm as a diamond.
In the future,
whatever holy fords and sacred fields exist throughout the three worlds—
They constantly resort to the Gaṅgā as it flows northward in Kāśī.
Having bathed at Daśāśvamedha and beheld Śiva, the Lord of the Universe,
one is immediately liberated from sins and is released from the bondage of worldly existence.
For the Gaṅgā is meritorious in every respect and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin;
she is especially so at Vārāṇasī, where she flows northward.
At the confluence of the Varaṇā and this Jāhnavī,
a man is liberated from all sins merely by bathing.
Having bathed in Kāśī at the northern-flowing Gaṅgā, or likewise at Kāritaka during the month of Māgha, one is liberated from great sins and heinous crimes.
Whatever holy places are renowned throughout all the worlds—
all of them without exception are present in Vārāṇasī within the Jāhnavī.
Day after day, they come toward the north— the auspicious direction—
constantly on all festival days, together with their meritorious abodes.

People, for the sake of removing their own sins, have dispelled the sin arising from the touch of those defiled by the faults of the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) and so forth, in order to ward off evil.
Even for one devoted to virtuous deeds throughout a hundred lifetimes,
liberation may or may not be attained elsewhere, even by the sages.
O Sage, by dying here in the Gaṅgā in a single lifetime,
even a man of undisciplined mind attains liberation in Kāśī;
from that time on, the lake in Kāśī became renowned as Dharmanada.
[370] Then, regarding the Pañcanada;
therein, in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa:
Dharma, in the form of Hara, is the destroyer of great sins;
and that auspicious river Dhūtapāpā embodies all sacred fords.
Hari [uprooted] the herds of great bulls like trees from the riverbanks;
and the Sarasvatī, with its holy waters, shook away all sins with its rays.
The Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, as well as the five rivers, are celebrated here;
therefore, this sacred site is renowned throughout the three worlds by the name Pañcanada.
There, one who has not yet crossed over should not assume a physical body composed of the five elements;
for at this confluence of the five rivers, which shatters the flood of sins,
by merely bathing, one indeed departs, having pierced through the pavilion of the cosmic egg.
Whatever fruit is obtained by one who has properly bathed at Prayāga during the month of Māgha,
that same fruit shall certainly be attained here at Pañcanada in Kāśī by means of a single [bath].
Having bathed at the Pañcanada tīrtha and performed the libations for the ancestors,
and having worshipped Vindumādhava, one shall not undergo birth again.
For as many sesame seeds as are offered to the ancestors in the water libation at the meritorious Pañcanada Tīrtha, for that many years shall their satisfaction endure.
Those by whom the śrāddha rite was performed with faith at the auspicious Pañcanada tīrtha—
their ancestors were liberated, even those who had entered various wombs.
In the world of Yama, this verse is sung by the hosts of ancestors upon beholding the greatness of the land of the Five Rivers resulting from the performance of śrāddha rites.
"Perhaps someone in our lineage will perform a *śrāddha* here at Pañcanada in Kāśī, by which we may be liberated."
Whatever is given there at the Pañcanada Tīrtha,
even at the end of a kalpa, there shall be no exhaustion of that merit.
Even a barren woman, having bathed for a year in the Pañcanada lake and having worshipped the goddess Maṅgalā, will certainly give birth to a son.
By bathing one's chosen deity with the holy waters of the Pañcanada, purified by a cloth, one obtains great fruit.
A single drop of the water from the Five Rivers outweighed and surpassed even a hundred and eight jars filled with the five nectars.
Purification of the body is declared to result from drinking the five-fold *kūrca*;
that purification is attained by drinking with faith even this drop of the Pañcanada water.
Whatever fruit may be obtained from the final purificatory bath of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices,
a hundred times that fruit is obtained then by bathing in the Pāñcanada.
The Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices may serve as means for attaining heaven;
however, for the sake of liberation, bathing in the Pañcanada [Sarasvatī] is peaceful and effective from the very moment of death (brahmaghaṭikā).
Even the consecration to the kingdom of heaven is not as esteemed by the virtuous as the consecration at the Pañcanada, which bestows no small measure of happiness.
The fruit that is obtained by performing austerities for a hundred years in the Kṛta age is attained by bathing but once at Pañcanada during the month of Kārttika.

Whatever fruit may result from meritorious deeds performed throughout one's entire life— whether through sacrifices, works of public utility, or other religious duties— that shall be obtained by bathing in the Dharmanada River during the month of Kārttika.
There is no sacred ford on the surface of the earth equal to Dhūtapāpa,
by a single bath in which the sin accumulated over three lifetimes may be destroyed.
In the Kṛta age it is named Dharmanada; in Tretā, Dhūtapāpaka; in Dvāpara, Vindutīrtha; and in the Kali age, it is remembered as Pañcanada.
Having given gold even in the measure of a single *kṛṣṇala* at Vindutīrtha,
a man shall never become poor, nor shall he ever be deprived of gold.
Having given cows, land, sesame, gold, horses, garments, as well as garlands and ornaments,
or whatever food one may give at Bindu-tīrtha, one shall obtain inexhaustible merit.
By offering even a single oblation into a well-consecrated fire according to the prescribed rite at the sacred ford of Dharmatīrtha on the Dharmanadī, one obtains the fruit of ten million homas.
Who indeed is capable of describing the infinite majesty of that Pañcanada-tīrtha, which is the auspicious abode of the four goals of human life?
Thus ends the *Kāśīmāhātmya*.
Thus concludes the fifth chapter, the *Kāśīprakāśa*, in the *Tīrthacintāmaṇi* composed by the venerable Mahāmahopādhyāya Vācaspatimiśra.
It reached completion.
